docs.title: Introduction
docs.text:
This repository contains the official user documentation for suanPan. For an optimized reading experience, users browsing this GitHub repository are encouraged to visit the web-based documentation.

As an alternative, a continuously updated version is hosted on gitbook. Note, however, that certain dynamically generated components may be absent in the GitBook version due to platform limitations regarding Jupyter Notebook conversions.

This documentation remains under active development. Users are invited to submit issues via GitHub to report gaps in information or seek clarification.

A comprehensive overview of the manual is available via the table of contents. For insights into the software's underlying software engineering paradigms and system architecture, please refer to the technical slides.

docs.title: Motivation and Core Advantages
docs.text:
The development of suanPan is driven by two critical architectural requirements: flexibility and high performance.

While commercial finite element analysis (FEA) software packages offer robust capabilities, they are often constrained by prohibitive licensing costs, limiting access for individual researchers and smaller institutions. Furthermore, implementing novel constitutive models or element formulations in traditional commercial environments (e.g., via C/Fortran user subroutines) is frequently hindered by legacy programming constraints and laborious tensor algebra implementations. Conversely, many open-source alternatives are tailored to narrow domains or lack comprehensive multi-dimensional modelling capabilities. For instance, packages like OpenSEES primarily optimize for uniaxial frame structures, offering limited support for complex 2D and 3D continuum mechanics.

suanPan addresses these challenges by integrating cutting-edge research into a unified, high-performance platform. The framework provides an extensive, multi-domain library comprising:

  1. Advanced Element Formulations: A comprehensive suite of 1D, 2D, and 3D elements incorporating modern finite element techniques;
  2. Constitutive Models: High-fidelity uniaxial and multiaxial nonlinear material models for metals, concrete, timber, geomaterials, etc.;
  3. Advanced Numerical Solvers: State-of-the-art solution routines and modern time-integration schemes;
  4. Extended Domain Capabilities: Additional specialized modelling features.

To maximize computational efficiency, suanPan natively exploits modern multi-core processor architectures with hybrid parallelization. Key pipeline operations, including element/material state determination, global matrix assembly, and constraint enforcement, are fully parallelized. Consequently, the framework systematically outperforms conventional single-threaded or distributed-memory MPI-based packages on modern workstation hardware.

Built on modern C++ and powered by the Armadillo linear algebra library, suanPan offers an expressive API where core structural code closely mirrors the underlying mathematical expressions. This significantly lowers the barrier to entry for researchers implementing and validating novel computational mechanics theories.

suanPan delivers distinct architectural and operational advantages over alternative finite element packages:

docs.title: Operational Efficiency & Functional Scope (User Perspective)
docs.text:
• Declarative Workflow: Eliminates the overhead of complex scripting, streamlining model preparation and execution.
  • Native Parallelization: Fully parallelized execution pathways significantly accelerate computational throughput and shorten engineering design cycles.
  • Extensive Library Ecosystem: Provides a comprehensive suite of advanced element formulations and constitutive material models absent in conventional packages.

docs.title: Research Agility & Extendability (Developer Perspective)
docs.text:
• Modular Architecture: Minimizes data coupling via a highly decoupled, modular design to facilitate rapid prototyping and algorithmic experimentation.
  • Mathematical Expressiveness: Leverages high-level abstractions that closely mirror underlying tensor and matrix algebra, simplifying the implementation of complex multiaxial models.
  • Reduced Cognitive Load: Employs built-in structural scaffolding to manage low-level internal routines, allowing researchers to focus exclusively on core mechanics.

docs.title: Getting Started
docs.text:
The input file logic in suanPan shares syntax paradigms with ABAQUS, enabling users familiar with commercial software to transition efficiently.

To establish a baseline understanding, users should start from the Basic overview, review the initial demonstration in Your First Analysis, and then read the foundational overviews in Model Syntax and Model Structure.

For practical applications, the Example section offers a tiered learning path ranging from introductory benchmarks to complex simulations. Recommended entry points include:

  • >Linear Analysis of A Truss Roof<
  • >Dynamic Analysis of A Portal Frame<

Detailed command syntaxes and programmatic entities are catalogued across the Collection and Library sections. To streamline workflow productivity, a dedicated VS Code extension is available, providing syntax highlighting and auto-completion capabilities.

Additionally, the comprehensive test suite in the repository's Example directory provides an exhaustive reference of validated input configurations.

docs.title: Collaborative Contribution
docs.text:
Contributions to the suanPan ecosystem are highly encouraged. Feature requests or inquiries regarding the implementation of specific elements or material models can be directed to the core development team.

Documentation improvements, including errata and clarifications, should be submitted as pull requests or tracking issues. Documentation contributions for third-party libraries must consist of a self-contained markdown file outlining usage guidelines and relevant theoretical foundations. Detailed instructions for local compilation of this manual are provided in Build the Manual.

docs.title: Citation
docs.text: If suanPan facilitates or supports your research publications, please cite the framework via its registered DOI at 10.5281/zenodo.1285221, selecting the version appropriate to your work.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: This section introduces the fundamentals of using suanPan. It follows a guided path from obtaining the application to running an analysis and, when necessary, compiling it from source.

docs.title: Features
docs.text:
suanPan is an open-source finite element simulation platform for solid mechanics and civil, structural and seismic engineering. It is written in modern C++ and aims to provide an efficient, concise, flexible and reliable simulation environment.

Its main capabilities are summarised below.

Area Highlights Analysis static, dynamic, arc-length, frequency, buckling and optimization steps Elements beams, trusses, membranes, plates, shells, 3D solids, contact, joints, mass and springs Materials elasticity, metal plasticity, concrete damage, orthotropic, hysteresis and user-defined models Sections structural, fibre, NM and code-based design sections Constraints MPC, rigid and restitution walls, embedding, node-line/facet and gap constraints Integrators implicit (Newmark, generalized-α, Bathe, GSSSS) and explicit (Bathe, Tchamwa, GSSE, WAT2) schemes Parallelism shared-memory (TBB), distributed-memory (MPI) and GPU acceleration (CUDA / MAGMA)

A complete catalogue of commands and models is available in the model library and the command collection.

docs.title: Learning Path
docs.text:
1. Obtain the Application explains how to install or download a ready-to-run copy.
  2. Your First Analysis walks through a complete model and shows the expected output.
  3. Model Syntax describes the rules for writing commands.
  4. Model Structure explains how a model file is organised into setup, analysis and post-processing.
  5. Command-Line Configuration lists the available command-line options.
  6. Editor Setup shows how to configure common editors for model files.
  7. Performance Tweaks gives practical advice for faster analyses.
  8. Automation and System Integration covers file associations and helper scripts.
  9. Compile the Application explains how to build suanPan from source.
  10. Build Options documents the main CMake options.
  11. Build the Manual explains how to build this documentation locally.

docs.title: Advanced Topics
docs.text:
The following pages describe the internal design and parallel execution model. They are not required for everyday use.

  • Architecture Design
  • Parallelism Mechanisms
  • Run on Clusters

docs.title: Architecture Design
docs.text: The MPI-based distributed design could take various forms in the context of OOP.

docs.title: A Straightforward Method
docs.text:
One approach is to serialize and send all associated data to another process, the receiving process deserializes the byte stream and creates all necessary objects and performs the computation. This involves intensive data exchange, and packing/unpacking associated data every iteration is not a light task. This approach does not scale well as the analysis would quickly be bottlenecked by encoding/decoding messages and latency.

This is unfortunately the approach used by OpenSees. OpenSees is outdated in terms of both shared-memory parallelism (which does not exist at all) and distributed-memory parallelism (which is too fine aggregated and lacks both performance and flexibility). OpenSees effectively requires every class that needs to be distributed to provide a schema, in order to serialize/deserialize objects, manually, as there is a lack of reflection mechanism. Imagine that for general nonlinear problems, in order to update the status of an element, it needs to send element history variable sets and that of associated material objects over the network. However, if it is an elastic step, the trial status can be simply computed by a matrix multiplication; the cost of message passing is disproportional and thus kills performance. It does not scale well by the nature of its design.

docs.title: Remote Objects with P2P Communication
docs.text:
An alternative is to create the same object on every process; the actual computation is done on one of the processes, and only the results are sent back to the root process. With this approach, there is no need for object 'proxies', as all objects on all processes are complete, fully functional, homogeneous objects. They manage all necessary data internally, locally. There is also no need to pack/unpack complex data structures, making the implementation extremely simple and maintainable. The only message to communicate is the elemental matrices (stiffness, mass, etc.) and the corresponding resistance vector. The size is significantly smaller than the previous approach.

To illustrate, consider the following class definition. Based on different obj_tag, the assign_process method labels each object with a process rank. For each process, it can be queried whether a specific object is_local or not. The computation logic can be triggered based on this flag, and calling the gather method will collect the designated quantity on the root process.

C++
class Distributed {
    static constexpr int root_rank{0};

    static auto assign_process(const int obj_tag) { return obj_tag % comm_size; }

    const int tag, process_rank;

public:
    const bool is_local;

    explicit Distributed(const int obj_tag)
        : tag(obj_tag)
        , process_rank(assign_process(tag))
        , is_local(comm_rank == process_rank) {}

    template<mpl_data_t DT> std::optional<mpl::irequest> gather(const Mat<DT>& object) {
        if(root_rank == comm_rank) {
            if(!is_local) return comm_world.irecv(const_cast<DT*>(object.memptr()), mpl::contiguous_layout<DT>{object.n_elem}, process_rank, mpl::tag_t{tag});
        }
        else if(is_local) return comm_world.isend(object.memptr(), mpl::contiguous_layout<DT>{object.n_elem}, root_rank, mpl::tag_t{tag});

        return std::nullopt;
    }
};

With such an approach, in the context of FEM, elements can be distributed on the process grid, and only elemental resistances and matrices need to be communicated. This minimises the data to be circulated as all other associated data (e.g., element and material internal states) can be kept on local processes.

This approach only requires three MPI primitives: MPI_Send, MPI_Recv and MPI_Bcast, excluding the part of solving the global system. This approach initiates MPI communication per element per iteration. The number of messages is related to the number of elements in the problem.

However, the number of messages does not change and latency is still a problem.

docs.title: Collective Communication
docs.text:
At the cost of communicating larger messages, it is possible to drastically reduce the number of calls to MPI functions. Given that elements are distributed on the process grid, each process handles a subset of elements. The corresponding resistances and matrices (of those elements that are is_local to the specific process) can be assembled locally into the local copy of the global vectors/matrices.

Then all local copies can be reduced to formulate the complete global quantities via MPI_Reduce or MPI_Allreduce. In most cases, reducing to the root process is enough so that there is no need to further broadcast to other processes.

For example, the following code assembles local elemental stiffness into local global stiffness, which is then reduced.

C++
void Domain::assemble_trial_stiffness() const {
    factory->clear_stiffness();

    for(const auto& I : element_pond.get()) {
        if(I->is_local) factory->assemble_stiffness(I->get_trial_stiffness(), I->get_dof_encoding(), I->get_dof_mapping());
    }

    factory->get_stiffness()->allreduce();
}

The allreduce() method calls the MPI_Allreduce under the hood.

C++
void DenseMat::allreduce() override {
    comm_world.allreduce(mpl::plus<T>(), memory.get(), mpl::contiguous_layout<T>{this->n_elem});
}

This approach only requires two MPI primitives: MPI_Reduce/MPI_Allreduce and MPI_Bcast, excluding the part of solving the global system. This approach initiates MPI communication per iteration. The number of messages is related to the number of processes in the process grid.

Given that it is preferable to communicate fewer but larger messages, this collective approach is preferable.

docs.title: Run on Clusters
docs.text:
The element state determination, as well as solving the global system, can be distributed over a process grid. By enabling MPI, the application can be executed on clusters. The architecture design is explained in this page. The detailed parallelism mechanisms, covering both shared-memory (oneTBB) threading and distributed-memory (MPI) execution, are analysed in the Parallelism Mechanisms page.

There are a few caveats. The distributed solvers for linear systems rely on external libraries, typically an implementation of ScaLAPACK. There are not many choices; one can use the reference implementation, which may not have superb performance. One can also use AMD's implementation or Intel's implementation.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
Considering that the procedure of manually compiling dependencies is cumbersome, we only support Intel's ecosystem for the moment. That means, MKL must be enabled via the option -DSP_ENABLE_MKL=ON. MKL can be installed a priori.

For example, according to the official documentation, with APT, it can be installed via the following commands.

Bash
sudo apt update
sudo apt install -y gpg-agent wget
wget -O- https://apt.repos.intel.com/intel-gpg-keys/GPG-PUB-KEY-INTEL-SW-PRODUCTS.PUB | gpg --dearmor | sudo tee /usr/share/keyrings/oneapi-archive-keyring.gpg > /dev/null
echo "deb [signed-by=/usr/share/keyrings/oneapi-archive-keyring.gpg] https://apt.repos.intel.com/oneapi all main" | sudo tee /etc/apt/sources.list.d/oneAPI.list
sudo apt update
sudo apt install intel-oneapi-mkl-devel

It is likely that Intel's MPI library is also required; otherwise a working implementation shall be pre-installed. Note, the MPI bundled by your distro may not work.

Bash
sudo apt install intel-oneapi-mpi-devel

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
The minimum configuration requires two flags: -DSP_ENABLE_MKL=ON and -DSP_ENABLE_MPI=ON. CMake will try to locate the installation of MKL and automatically configure the project. To ensure everything works as intended, it may be necessary to activate the oneAPI environment.

Bash
source /opt/intel/oneapi/setvars.sh

This can be done via, for example, environment file in the toolchain configuration in CLion, and environmentSetupScript in cmake-kits.json in VS Code.

By default, it will use Intel's MPI. If another implementation, for example, MPICH and/or OpenMPI, is used, use MPI_HOME to override the path, for example, -DMPI_HOME=~/Documents/OpenMPI.

The project tries to automatically detect the vendor of MPI via its path, but it may fail. You may need to set MKL_MPI to a proper value. The available values can be found in /opt/intel/oneapi/mkl/latest/lib/cmake/mkl/MKLConfig.cmake. For example, on my machine, there are

Text Only
# MKL_MPI
#    Values:  intelmpi, mpich, openmpi, msmpi, mshpc
#    Default: intelmpi

Note

If two different implementations of MPI are used, the compilation may succeed, the application can still crash on execution.

Typically, for problems that need to be run on clusters, the default 32-bit indexing is not sufficient. The limit of a 32-bit integer is slightly above 2 billion, meaning that, if the global matrix is stored in dense full format, the maximum size is 46340. If each node has 2 DoFs (2D node with translational DoFs only), this corresponds to 23170 nodes. If each node has 6 DoFs (3D node with both translational and rotational DoFs), this corresponds to 7723 nodes. But in the context of FEM, the full storage is rarely used, so this is the lower bound. Considering the banded storage, where the bandwidth is typically a small fraction of the global size, say, 1%, the lower bound should be at least 800000 3D shell nodes.

If the problem is sizeable, it is possible to enable 64-bit indexing via -DSP_ENABLE_64BIT_INDEXING=ON. This will link ilp64 version of MKL, and compile all dependencies with the proper settings.

docs.title: Parallelism Mechanisms
docs.text: An analysis of shared-memory (thread-based) and distributed-memory (cluster/MPI) parallelism in the suanPan finite element framework.

docs.title: 1. Overview
docs.text:
suanPan is an open-source finite element framework whose performance-critical compute path (element stiffness computation, global system assembly, and linear solving) is parallelised at two distinct levels:

Parallelism Layer / Abstraction Backend Build switch Compile definition Shared memory (node-level threads) Element & assembly loops oneTBB (Threading Building Blocks) SP_BUILD_PARALLEL SUANPAN_MT Shared memory (BLAS) Linear algebra kernels Intel MKL / OpenMP SP_ENABLE_MKL SUANPAN_MKL Distributed memory (cluster) Cross-rank assembly & solving MPI via the MPL library SP_ENABLE_MPI SUANPAN_DISTRIBUTED Heterogeneous (offload) GPU solvers CUDA / MAGMA SP_ENABLE_CUDA SUANPAN_CUDA

Both shared and distributed parallelism funnel through the Domain object, which owns the element/node/constraint ponds and the global stiffness container. This report focuses on the shared-memory (SUANPAN_MT) and distributed-memory (SUANPAN_DISTRIBUTED) mechanisms and the data flows through them.

The two mechanisms are orthogonal: the same problem can be run single-node multithreaded, or across a cluster of MPI ranks, or both simultaneously (MPI ranks that are themselves multithreaded).

docs.title: 2. Compile-time selection & configuration
docs.text:
The parallelism backend is selected entirely at build time via CMake options (CMakeLists.txt), which map onto compile-time macros in suanPan.h.

Text Only
CMake option                       Compile definition            Activates
─────────────────────────────────  ──────────────────────────   ──────────────────────────────
SP_BUILD_PARALLEL    (line 63)  →  SUANPAN_MT            (275)   oneTBB loops & concurrent containers
SP_ENABLE_MKL        (line 71)  →  SUANPAN_MKL           (202)   MKL PARDISO / FGMRES / ScaLAPACK
SP_ENABLE_MPI        (line 86)  →  SUANPAN_DISTRIBUTED   (182)   MPI collectives + distributed solvers
SP_ENABLE_CUDA       (line 121) →  SUANPAN_CUDA          (224)   GPU solvers
SP_ENABLE_SYSLIB     (line 81)  →  (none)                        use system TBB/HDF5 instead of bundled

docs.title: 2.1 The SUANPAN_MT switch (suanPan.h:184-192)
docs.text:
The single most important macro for shared-memory parallelism. When defined, the generic suanpan_sort / suanpan_for_each primitives map to their oneTBB equivalents; otherwise they degrade to the standard library serial versions:

C++
// suanPan.h
#ifdef SUANPAN_MT
#include <oneapi/tbb/parallel_for_each.h>
#include <oneapi/tbb/parallel_sort.h>
#define suanpan_sort      tbb::parallel_sort
#define suanpan_for_each  tbb::parallel_for_each
#else
#define suanpan_sort      std::sort
#define suanpan_for_each  std::for_each
#endif

Because every parallel call site goes through these two abstractions, the entire program compiles to either a parallel or a serial build by toggling one flag.

docs.title: 2.2 The SUANPAN_DISTRIBUTED switch (suanPan.h:209-253)
docs.text:
When defined, the MPI MPL library is pulled in and three global objects/concepts are made available:

C++
// suanPan.h
#ifdef SUANPAN_DISTRIBUTED
#include <mpl/mpl.hpp>
inline auto& comm_world{mpl::environment::comm_world()};   // the world communicator
inline const auto comm_rank{comm_world.rank()};
inline const auto comm_size{comm_world.size()};
// ... mpl_data_t concept ...
#else
inline constexpr auto comm_rank{0};
inline constexpr auto comm_size{1};
#endif

Crucially, three reduction/broadcast helpers are defined with an identical name signature in both branches:

Helper Distributed behaviour Serial fallback bcast_from_root(x) comm_world.bcast(0, x) — rank 0 → all identity (std::forward) allreduce(x) comm_world.allreduce(mpl::plus, x) — sum over all ranks identity reduce(x) sum to rank 0 only identity

This lets ordinary analysis code call allreduce(...) / bcast_from_root(...) unconditionally — on a serial build these are no-ops. MPI init is owned by mpl::environment (invoked in suanPan.cpp:48), and the ezp/BLACS layer is told not to manage its own MPI (ezp::blacs_env<>::do_not_manage_mpi()), so a single world communicator is shared everywhere.

The rank is surfaced in logging via the [P{n}] prefix (suanPan.h:267) and in recorder filenames (Recorder/Recorder.cpp:99) whenever comm_size > 1.

docs.title: 3.1 The analytic model: element colouring
docs.text:
The principal challenge in parallel global assembly is avoiding concurrent writes to the same global matrix/vector entry. suanPan solves this without locks or atomics on the hot path by partitioning elements into "colours" such that:

Two elements in the same colour never share a node, and therefore never share a global degree-of-freedom (DOF) index.

Within a colour, element DOF encodings are pairwise disjoint, so their += contributions to the global stiffness/resistance cannot collide. Colours are processed sequentially; elements within a colour are processed concurrently via oneTBB.

This is formalised in Toolbox/sort_color.hpp (sort_color_wp weighted-priority and sort_color_mis maximal-independent-set variants) and driven by Domain::assign_color() (Domain/Domain.cpp:919-945):

C++
int Domain::assign_color() {
    if(ColorMethod::OFF != color_model) {
        const auto color_algorithm = ColorMethod::WP == color_model ? sort_color_wp<unsigned> : sort_color_mis<unsigned>;
        const auto [element_map, element_register] = get_element_connectivity(false);
        color_map = color_algorithm(element_register);
        suanpan::for_all(color_map, [&](std::vector<unsigned>& color) { /* map back to tags */ });
    }
    // ...sparse preallocation via std::transform_reduce(par_unseq)...
}

get_element_connectivity (Domain.cpp:822-848) builds the element↔node incidence graph using the concurrent containers defined in Toolbox/container.h, which swap in oneTBB types when SUANPAN_MT is set:

C++
// Toolbox/container.h  (SUANPAN_MT branch)
template<typename T> using vector       = tbb::concurrent_vector<T>;
template<typename T> using set          = tbb::concurrent_set<T>;
template<typename T> using unordered_set= tbb::concurrent_unordered_set<T, std::hash<T>>;
template<typename T, typename D> using map         = tbb::concurrent_map<T, D, std::hash<T>>;
template<typename T, typename D> using unordered_map = tbb::concurrent_unordered_map<T, D, std::hash<T>>;

docs.title: 3.2 Visualising the shared-memory data flow
docs.text:
The following diagram shows the end-to-end pipeline for a single Newton-Raphson iteration. Parallel (oneTBB) sections are highlighted.

flowchart TD
    subgraph Setup
        A[Model input: nodes, elements, materials]
        B[reorder_dof → RCM renumbering<br/>parallel via suanpan::for_all]
        C[assign_color → element colouring<br/>concurrent containers + parallel sort/for_each]
        D[sparse preallocation<br/>std::transform_reduce par_unseq]
        A --> B --> C --> D
    end

    subgraph NewtonIteration["Solver::Newton::analyze()  (per iteration / substep)"]
        E[update_trial_status<br/>suanpan::for_all over ALL elements]
        F[each element: update_status ↔ material<br/>compute private trial_stiffness / trial_resistance]
        E --> F
        F -->|aggregate failure codes| F1[std::atomic_int code<br/>+ allreduce]
    end

    subgraph Assembly["Domain::assemble_*  (DomainState.cpp)"]
        G["for each COLOR (sequential):<br/>suanpan::for_all(color) over elements in that colour"]
        H["Factory::assemble_matrix_helper<br/>lock-free unsafe_at(...) += contribution"]
        G --> H
    end

    subgraph Solve["Linear solve  (MetaMat backend)"]
        I["sparse: PARDISO / SuperLU / LIS / MUMPS<br/>dense: LAPACK via Armadillo"]
        H --> I
    end

    F1 --> G
    I --> J[update nodal displacement / commit trial state]
    J -->|next iteration| E

Step-by-step narrative:

  1. update_trial_status (DomainState.cpp:497-511) fans out the entire element pool via suanpan::for_all. This step only reads the shared nodal trial-displacement vector and writes private per-element state, so no colouring is needed. Each element's update_status() runs at its integration points serially (e.g. C3D8::update_status, Element/Cube/C3D8.cpp:112) but in parallel across elements. Per-element failure codes are summed into a shared std::atomic_int code, then reduced across MPI ranks with allreduce.

  2. assemble_resistance / assemble_matrix (DomainState.cpp) zero the target global vector/matrix, then iterate colours sequentially; within each colour suanpan::for_all runs the elements concurrently. Each element scatters its private stiffness/resistance using Factory::assemble_matrix_helper (Factory.hpp:1466), which does a lock-free GM->unsafe_at(g_row, g_col) += EM(...). unsafe_at is deliberately named — its safety is guaranteed by the colouring invariant, not by synchronization.

  3. The resulting sparse matrix undergoes csc_condense() (merging duplicate (row,col) triplets) upon solve, and the linear system is handed to a solver backend.

docs.title: 3.3 Thread-safety summary
docs.text: Concern Mechanism Element ↔ element race during assembly Colour invariant (disjoint DOFs per colour) Element status update race Per-element private state; only reads shared inputs Failure-code aggregation std::atomic_int (DomainState.cpp:501, 509) Element connectivity building oneTBB concurrent containers (Toolbox/container.h) Out-of-band cross-thread edits (constraints, loads, recorders) std::vector<std::mutex> global_mutex{20} (Factory.hpp:171) — separate from the colour-safe hot path Logging suanpan::print_mutex (suanPan.h:259)

docs.title: 4.1 The analytic model: divide the element pond over ranks
docs.text:
SuanPan's distributed model is a classic element-by-row (data) decomposition:

Each element is tagged is_local on exactly one rank. Each rank assembles its local element contributions into its own local global matrix/vector. The partial systems are then sum-reduced across all ranks with allreduce so every rank ends up with the identical global system, which is solved by a distributed solver (or by a rank-0 solver whose result is broadcast back via bcast_from_root).

Free functions in suanPan.h provide rank-agnostic collective operations (see §2.2) that serial builds turn into no-ops.

docs.title: 4.2 The distributed data flow
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    subgraph R0["Rank 0"]
        E0["local elements<br/>(is_local subset)"]
        A0["assemble local matrix/vector<br/>coloured, multithreaded"]
    end
    subgraph R1["Rank 1"]
        E1["local elements"]
        A1["assemble local matrix/vector"]
    end
    subgraph RN["Rank N-1"]
        EN["local elements"]
        AN["assemble local matrix/vector"]
    end

    E0 --> A0
    E1 --> A1
    EN --> AN

    A0 --> AllReduce["allreduce (mpl::plus) over comm_world<br/>residual RHS vectors + MetaMat::allreduce of matrices<br/>align every rank's global system"]
    A1 --> AllReduce
    AN --> AllReduce

    AllReduce --> Solve["Distributed linear solve"]
    Solve --> BCast["bcast_from_root(X) rank 0 → all ranks<br/>shared identical solution vector"]
    BCast --> R0
    BCast --> R1
    BCast --> RN

Where the collectives are applied (all in Domain/DomainState.cpp):

  • Residual / RHS vectors — each element adds only its local DOFs, then the partial vectors are summed:
  • allreduce(trial_resistance) — assemble_resistance (line 142), update_current_resistance (line 41)
  • allreduce(trial_damping_force) (62) · allreduce(trial_nonviscous_force) (83) · allreduce(trial_inertial_force) (104)

  • generic assemble_vector returns allreduce(result) (125)

  • Stiffness/mass/damping/geometry matrices — each rank calls <matrix>->allreduce() after its local colour-scatter. The virtual MetaMat::allreduce() (declared MetaMat.hpp:220) is where the matrix is assembled across ranks:

  • Dense: element-wise in-place sum of the whole buffer via comm_world.allreduce(mpl::plus<T>, ...) (DenseMat.hpp:125-129)

  • Sparse: collect COO entry counts with allgather, then non-blocking ibcast each rank's row/col/val triplets into the concatenated pool, then csc_condense() to merge duplicates (SparseMat.hpp:92-118)

  • Status agreement — allreduce(code) at DomainState.cpp:510, 526, 565 so every rank agrees on element success/failure.

  • Post-solve distribution — the distributed solver's result (valid on a distributed set or only on root) is synchronized with bcast_from_root(X) (see §4.3).
sequenceDiagram
    participant R0
    participant R1
    participant RN
    Note over R0,RN: Each rank assembles its is_local elements (coloured + multithreaded)
    R0->>R0: local system (K, f)
    R1->>R1: local system (K, f)
    RN->>RN: local system (K, f)
    rect rgb(220,240,255)
    Note over R0,RN: MPI allreduce (sum) — global K and f identical on every rank
    R0->>RN: allreduce
    R1->>RN: allreduce
    RN->>RN: allreduce
    end
    rect rgb(235,255,230)
    Note over R0,RN: Distributed solve
    R0->>R0: ScaLAPACK pgesv / MUMPS / LIS / PARDISO
    end
    rect rgb(255,240,240)
    Note over R0,RN: bcast_from_root(X): rank 0 result broadcast to all
    R0->>R1: bcast X
    R0->>RN: bcast X
    end

docs.title: 4.3 Distributed linear solver backends
docs.text:
Solver backends are selected in Domain/Factory.hpp::get_basic_container() (Factory.hpp:1495-1517). Under SUANPAN_DISTRIBUTED it constructs the *Cluster (distributed) variants:

Storage scheme Distributed backend Underlying parallel routine Dense FULL FullMatCluster (FullMatCluster.hpp:123) ScaLAPACK pgesv → pdgetrf/pdgetrs (ezp/pgesv.hpp:111,150) Dense SYMMPACK FullSymmMatCluster (:124) ScaLAPACK pposv Dense BAND BandMatCluster ScaLAPACK pgbsv Dense BANDSYMM BandSymmMatCluster ScaLAPACK ppbsv Sparse SPARSE/SPARSESYMM SparseMatClusterPARDISO (MKL) / SparseMatClusterLIS / SparseMatClusterMUMPS (Factory.hpp:1507-1517) MKL PARDISO / LIS / MUMPS parallel sparse direct

Each distributed solver wrapper follows the same three-phase contract (e.g. SparseMatClusterMUMPS.hpp:65-77, FullMatCluster.hpp:105-117):

C++
const auto INFO = bcast_from_root(solver.solve({n_rows, n_cols, memptr()}, {B..., X...}));  // distributed solve
if(0 == INFO) bcast_from_root(X = std::move(B));                                            // broadcast result

The MUMPS wrapper (Include/ezp/ezp/mumps.hpp:98-113) attaches the shared MPL world to the Fortran MUMPS instance and reduces error codes across ranks:

C++
const mpl::communicator& comm_world{mpl::environment::comm_world()};
...
id.comm_fortran = MPI_Comm_c2f(comm_world.native_handle());   // share the world communicator
comm_world.allreduce(mpl::min<IT>(), error);                  // cross-rank error agreement

For eigenproblems under SUANPAN_DISTRIBUTED, Solver/Arnoldi.cpp dispatches to the parallel ARPACK wrapper eig_solve in Toolbox/eigen_parpack.cpp. The wrapper uses pdsaupd_/pdseupd_ over MPI_COMM_WORLD.

Not every feature is distributed: ArcLength.cpp:30-33 explicitly rejects distributed execution, while Buckle.cpp:31-33 and Frequency.cpp:31-33 warn that some backends may run independently per rank.

docs.title: 4.4 MPI init & coordination
docs.text:
• suanPan.cpp:48-52 — ezp::blacs_env<>::do_not_manage_mpi(); warns if comm_size == 1.
  • Rank-gated I/O — only rank 0 handles interactive input / help / history (Toolbox/command.cpp:1246, Toolbox/argument.cpp:107).
  • Per-rank recorder output files get a P{rank}- prefix when comm_size > 1.

docs.title: 5. Combined (hybrid) view
docs.text:
Shared-memory and distributed parallelism compose: each MPI rank runs its local element/assembly work with oneTBB threads, and the cross-rank system is reconciled with MPI collectives.

flowchart TB
    subgraph Rank["MPI Rank (comm_world, comm_rank, comm_size)"]
        subgraph Threads["oneTBB threads (SUANPAN_MT)"]
            T1["coloured element loop"]
            T2["concurrent containers"]
            T3["parallel sort / for_each"]
        end
        subgraph Local["Local assembly"]
            L1["is_local elements → local K, f"]
        end
    end
    subgraph Cluster["cross-rank coordination (SUANPAN_DISTRIBUTED)"]
        C1["allreduce: sum partial K, f across ranks"]
        C2["distributed solve: ScaLAPACK / MUMPS / LIS / PARDISO"]
        C3["bcast_from_root: broadcast solution"]
    end
    Threads --> Local --> Cluster

docs.text: File Behaviour Step/ArcLength.cpp:30-33 rejects distributed execution Step/Buckle.cpp:31-33, Step/Frequency.cpp:31-33 warns; may run per-rank

docs.title: 7. Summary
docs.text:
1. Shared-memory parallelism (SUANPAN_MT, oneTBB) parallelises the element computation and global assembly coarse-grained over elements, with correctness guaranteed by a graph-colouring invariant that makes cross-element writes to shared global storage collision-free by construction — no locks or atomics on the hot path. Concurrent containers, parallel_for/parallel_for_each/parallel_sort, and a static affinity_partitioner provide the threading substrate; parallel STL (par/par_unseq) backs a few reduction/preallocation helpers.

  2. Distributed-memory parallelism (SUANPAN_DISTRIBUTED, MPI via MPL) partitions elements over ranks and reconciles the partial systems with allreduce (exact-sum of local vectors/matrices) so every rank holds the identical global system. The system is solved by distributed backends — ScaLAPACK/ezp (pgesv/pposv/pgbsv/ppbsv) for dense, MKL PARDISO / MUMPS / LIS for sparse, P-ARPACK for eigenproblems — and the result is broadcast back via bcast_from_root. Cross-rank communication reuses one shared MPL world communicator.

  3. The two layers compose: within each MPI rank, oneTBB threads accelerate local element/assembly work, while MPI coordinates across ranks — giving a natural hybrid (MPI + threads) execution model.

docs.title: Docker
docs.text:
To avoid all the hassles, this manual can be viewed locally via docker.

Simply run the following command, and the manual will be available at http://localhost:8000.

Bash
docker run --rm -d -p 8000:8000/tcp ghcr.io/tlcfem/suanpan-manual:latest
# or via docker hub
# docker run --rm -d -p 8000:8000/tcp tlcfem/suanpan-manual:latest

docs.title: Python
docs.text: For development purposes, this manual can be built locally using mkdocs. To do so, a python environment must be created.

docs.title: Tools
docs.text:
git shall be available to clone the repository. Otherwise, you may want to manually download the archive.

python shall be available to build the documentation.

If doxygen generated documentation is required, doxygen shall be available. It also uses graphviz to generate the graph, install it according to the instructions.

docs.title: Steps
docs.text: Please follow the instructions below to create a local editing environment.

docs.title: Clone the Repository
docs.text:
Clone the repository using the following command:

Bash
git clone https://github.com/TLCFEM/suanPan-manual.git
cd suanPan-manual

docs.title: Create a Python Environment
docs.text:
Within the suanPan-manual directory, create a new virtual environment using whatever tools you have available. Here the plain python virtual environment is used.

Bash
python3 -m venv venv
source venv/bin/activate

docs.title: Install Requirements
docs.text:
Now that the virtual environment is created, install the requirements using the following command:

Bash
python -m pip install -r requirements.txt

Alternatively, if the doxygen documentation is required, the following command can be used:

Bash
python -m pip install -e .

Note that doxygen and git are required to be available. This also installs a custom mkdocs plugin to overwrite inline math expressions to properly render them.

docs.title: Build and Run
docs.text:
The following command builds and runs the server on localhost:8000.

Bash
mkdocs serve

docs.title: Make Changes
docs.text:
The server monitors changes in real time. Now you can make changes to the manual and check the changes in the browser.

Return to the Basic overview.

docs.title: Compile the Application
docs.text: suanPan can be compiled with Docker or natively on the host system. Docker provides a reproducible environment and is the recommended approach for development. Native compilation gives full control over the build and is required for some platform-specific features. If you only need a ready-to-run binary, see Obtain the Application.

docs.title: Dev Environment Images
docs.text:
Two images are provided for development purposes.

Bash
# vtk+mkl+cuda
docker pull tlcfem/suanpan-env:cuda
# vtk+mkl
docker pull tlcfem/suanpan-env

They can be used as development containers. VS Code and CLion can be configured to use these containers for development. There is no need to install any dependencies on the host machine.

The tlcfem/suanpan-env image also supports arm64, in which OpenBLAS is used as the linear algebra driver.

On AMD platforms, it is known that MKL may throttle and thus yield poor performance; it may be necessary to use a specific version of OpenBLAS or AMD Optimizing CPU Libraries (AOCL) instead.

docs.title: Docker Images
docs.text:
It is possible to compile the project with Docker. Check the provided Dockerfiles for more information. One can build the image using the example Dockerfile as it is. For example,

Text Only
# the current folder contains the file Rocky.Dockerfile
docker build -t suanpan -f ./Rocky.Dockerfile .

Once the image is built, run the container and use sp, suanpan or suanPan to invoke the program in the container. It may be necessary to map some folders to the container.

Bash
docker run -it --rm suanpan
# now in the container
suanpan -v

Docker files provide a standard reproducible environment and a reference configuration. One can always introduce adaptations to cater to various needs.

docs.title: Without Docker
docs.text: The following is a general guide that covers three main operating systems. It mainly targets the amd64 architecture.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
1. To configure the source code, CMake shall be available. Please install it before configuring the source code package.
  2. The linear algebra driver used is OpenBLAS. You may want to compile it with the optimal configuration based on the specific machine. Otherwise, precompiled binaries (dynamic platform) are available in this repository.
  3. It is strongly recommended to install Intel MKL for potentially better performance.
  4. Please be aware that MKL is throttled on AMD platforms. Performance comparisons can be seen for example here. If you have AMD CPUs please collect more knowledge to determine which linear algebra library is more suitable.

docs.title: Toolsets
docs.text:
A number of new features from new standards are utilized. To compile the binary, a compiler that supports C++20 is required.

GCC 13, Clang 18, VS 2026, Intel compilers and later versions of those compilers are tested with the source code.

On Windows, Visual Studio with Intel oneAPI toolkit is recommended. Alternatively, WinLibs can be used if GCC compilers are preferred.

On other platforms (Linux and macOS), simply use GCC which comes with a valid Fortran compiler. Clang can also be used for C/CPP code, but since Clang and GCC have different support for new C++ standards, successful compilation is not guaranteed with Clang.

docs.title: Obtain Source Code
docs.text:
Download the source code archive from GitHub Releases or the latest stable code. The archive is complete for non-MPI compilations.

To compile with MPI support, it is necessary to clone the dependencies as well. This can be done via git clone such as

Bash
git clone --recurse-submodules https://github.com/TLCFEM/suanPan.git

docs.title: Configure and Compile
docs.text:
The manual compilation is not difficult in general. The CI/CD configuration files can be referred to if you wish. Please check this page.

Choose the guide for your platform.

  • Windows
  • Linux
  • macOS

After the project is configured, see Build Options for the available CMake options and customisation details.

Continue with Build Options.

docs.title: Build Options and Customisation
docs.text: This page documents the main CMake options and customisation details. For the general compilation guide, see Compile the Application.

docs.title: Linear Algebra Driver
docs.text:
Any standard BLAS and LAPACK implementation can be used as the linear algebra driver which the application itself and Armadillo rely on. Currently, the following are supported and tested.

  1. OpenBLAS
  2. Intel oneAPI MKL
  3. AMD Optimizing CPU Libraries (AOCL)

As a general guideline, when it comes to choosing a proper implementation, the following points shall be considered.

  1. From my very personal experience, OpenBLAS is okay for small matrices on a few cores, but could be slow when the size hits some threshold. This is also seen in this benchmark.
  2. Intel oneAPI MKL is exclusively optimised for Intel CPUs, and may throttle on other platforms. This benchmark shows clear differences on AMD platforms.
  3. AMD Optimizing CPU Libraries (AOCL) is optimised for AMD CPUs based on BLIS and FLAME libraries; its performance on both platforms (and others) is superb.

Thus, use Intel oneAPI MKL if it is preferred or an Intel platform is targeted. The downside is that Intel oneAPI MKL is proprietary and the final binary may have a large size. For other cases, use AMD Optimizing CPU Libraries (AOCL) when possible. The downside is that it may need manual compilation of the libraries for the target OS. OpenBLAS shall be deemed as the last resort and the usage is discouraged as of writing.

docs.title: Build Options
docs.text:
If CMake GUI is used to configure the project, the following options are available.

  1. BUILD_SHARED_LIBS: If enabled, all libraries will be built as shared libraries.
  2. SP_BUILD_DLL_EXAMPLE: If enabled, example element/material/section implemented as external libraries will be built. This is not required for the successful build of the main application.
  3. SP_BUILD_PARALLEL: If enabled, TBB will be used for multithreading so that element update, global matrix assembly, etc., can be parallelized. OpenMP is not controlled by this option given that OpenMP support is available in major platforms. It will be used for low level parallelization such as linear algebra operations (which is controlled by Armadillo), matrix solving (which is controlled by various solvers). Thus, this flag only controls the suanPan application itself.
  4. SP_ENABLE_HDF5: If enabled, HDF5 will be used to provide support for hdf5recorder.
  5. SP_ENABLE_VTK: If enabled, VTK will be used to provide support for visualization. It will be useful to generate files that can be used in Paraview for post-processing. If enabled, VTK_PATH needs to be set to the path of VTK installation. For example, VTK_PATH=/usr/local/opt/vtk/lib/cmake/vtk-9.1.
  6. SP_ENABLE_CUDA: CUDA needs to be installed manually by the user. If enabled, CUDA based solvers will be available. With CUDA, full and asymmetric banded dense storage are available. Full storage uses cuSOLVER LU and banded storage uses GPU SPIKE. Note full matrix storage scheme is not favourable for FEM. It can, however, be used for sparse matrix solving and mixed precision solving.
  7. SP_ENABLE_MAGMA: MAGMA needs to be installed manually by the user. If enabled, MAGMA based solvers will be available. The variable MAGMA_PATH needs to be set to find necessary files.
  8. SP_ENABLE_ASAN: If enabled, address sanitizer will be enabled. This is useful for debugging purposes.
  9. SP_ENABLE_CODECOV: If enabled, compile options will be enabled to support code coverage report.
  10. SP_ENABLE_AVX: If enabled, compiler flags -mavx or /arch:AVX will be used. (~2011)
  11. SP_ENABLE_AVX2: If enabled, compiler flags -mavx2 or /arch:AVX2 will be used. (~2013)
  12. SP_ENABLE_AVX512: If enabled, compiler flags -mavx512f or /arch:AVX512 will be used. (~2016)
  13. SP_ENABLE_TBB_ALLOC: If enabled, the TBB's memory allocator will be used.
  14. SP_OPENBLAS_PATH: If assigned, link the designated OpenBLAS library, otherwise the bundled version will be used.
  15. SP_ENABLE_AOCL: If enabled, one can use the AOCL implementation via assigning library path SP_AOCL_PATH.
  16. SP_ENABLE_MKL: MKL needs to be installed manually by the user. If enabled, MKL will be used for linear algebra operations. If SP_ENABLE_MKL is enabled, set MKL_PATH to the root directory of MKL installation. For example, C:/Program Files (x86)/Intel/oneAPI/mkl/latest or /opt/intel/oneapi/mkl/latest, also the following additional options are available.
  17. SP_ENABLE_SHARED_MKL: If enabled, dynamically linked MKL libraries will be used. Otherwise, statically linked MKL libraries will be used, leading to larger binary size but faster execution and fewer dependencies.
  18. SP_ENABLE_IOMP: If enabled, Intel's OpenMP implementation will be used. Otherwise, Default ones (such as GNU OpenMP library) will be used.
  19. SP_ENABLE_MPI: Enables cluster support via MPI.
  20. SP_ENABLE_64BIT_INDEXING: Enables 64-bit integer for matrix indexing.

multiple runtimes

The SP_ENABLE_IOMP should be switched on/off based on the compilers used. In principle, there should be only one implementation of OpenMP. Thus, if the compilers used are gcc/g++/gfortran, SP_ENABLE_IOMP=OFF. If the compilers are icx/icpx/ifx, SP_ENABLE_IOMP=ON. The Spike solver also does not support mixing OpenMP implementations. Use with caution if two OpenMP implementations exist.

docs.title: Example Configuration
docs.text:
The following command is used to compile the program to be distributed via snap. See this file.

Bash
# assume current folder is suanPan/build
# the parent folder contains source code
cmake -DCMAKE_INSTALL_PREFIX= \
      -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release \
      -DMKL_PATH=/opt/intel/oneapi/mkl/latest \
      -DSP_BUILD_PARALLEL=ON \
      -DSP_ENABLE_HDF5=ON \
      -DSP_ENABLE_IOMP=OFF \
      -DSP_ENABLE_MKL=ON \
      -DSP_ENABLE_SHARED_MKL=OFF \
      -DSP_ENABLE_VTK=ON \
      -DVTK_PATH=$CRAFT_PART_BUILD/lib/cmake/vtk-9.7/

docs.title: aarch64 Architecture
docs.text:
The aarch64 architecture is supported by the source code. But one shall prepare the dependencies manually. As MKL is not available for aarch64, one shall use OpenBLAS or AOCL only.

OpenBLAS is the only necessary dependency. All other dependencies are optional.

To use AOCL, one shall manually compile the blis and flame libraries in advance.

docs.title: 64-bit Indexing
docs.text:
The FEM framework part itself uses unsigned 32-bit integer for indexing; this means it supports up to 4 billion objects, for example, nodes and elements. This is sufficient at least for the coming years. But the linear algebra driver may quickly hit the size limit. For lp64 builds, the indexing capability of a default Fortran integer is around 2 billion. If the problem is large enough, the global matrix may have more than 2 billion entries (either dense or sparse storage). In this case, it is necessary to use 64-bit indexing; see the ilp64 model.

To do so, compile the application with the flag -DSP_ENABLE_64BIT_INDEXING=ON.

Note

The bundled OpenBLAS binaries are built for lp64 only. If one decides to use OpenBLAS, an ilp64 version must be provided via SP_OPENBLAS_PATH.

Note

If SP_ENABLE_MPI=ON is also enabled, one shall make sure the linked MPI is also compiled with 64-bit integer support. MPICH is known to work well with either 32-bit or 64-bit integer size.

MKL provides both versions for lp64 and ilp64; CMake will handle the linkage automatically.

Continue with Build the Manual.

docs.title: Compiling on Linux
docs.text: This page describes native compilation on Linux. For the general prerequisites and source code instructions, see Compile the Application.

docs.title: Ubuntu
docs.text:
The following instructions are based on Ubuntu 22.04. CMake is used to manage builds. It is recommended to use CMake GUI if appropriate.

  1. Install necessary tools.

    Bash
    sudo apt-get install gcc g++ gfortran git cmake libomp5 libglvnd-dev -y

  2. Clone the project.

    Bash
    git clone -b master --depth 1 https://github.com/TLCFEM/suanPan.git

  3. Create build folder and configure via CMake. The default configuration disables parallelism -DSP_BUILD_PARALLEL=OFF and enables HDF5 via bundled library -DSP_ENABLE_HDF5=ON. Please check CMakeLists.txt file or use GUI for available options.

    Bash
    cd suanPan && mkdir build && cd build
cmake ../

  4. Invoke make.

    Bash
    make -j"$(nproc)"

Check the following recording.

docs.title: Install VTK
docs.text:
The Ubuntu official repository does not (Fedora does!) contain the latest VTK library. It's better to compile it manually.

  1. Install OpenGL first, as well as compilers if necessary.

    Bash
    sudo apt install gcc-10 g++-10 gfortran-10 libglvnd-dev

  2. Obtain VTK source code and unpack.

    Bash
    wget https://www.vtk.org/files/release/9.1/VTK-9.1.0.tar.gz
tar -xf VTK-9.1.0.tar.gz

  3. Create folder for building VTK.

    Bash
    mkdir VTK-build && cd VTK-build

  4. Configure and compile VTK library. If necessary, installation destination can be modified. Here static libraries are built.

    Bash
    cmake -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release -DBUILD_SHARED_LIBS=OFF -DCMAKE_INSTALL_PREFIX=../VTK-out ../VTK-9.1.0
make install -j4

  5. Now obtain suanPan source code and unpack it. To configure it with VTK support, users may use the following flag -DSP_ENABLE_VTK=ON. If FindVTK is present and VTK is installed to default location, there is no need to provide the variable VTK_PATH, otherwise point it to the lib/cmake/vtk-9.1 folder.

docs.title: Install MKL
docs.text:
The provided CMake configuration covers both oneMKL and Intel MKL 2020. Please note MKL is included in oneAPI toolkit starting from 2021, which has a different folder structure compared to Intel Parallel Studio.

The following guide is a manual installation based on the Ubuntu terminal using the official repository. See this page for details.

  1. Add repository. To summarise,

    Bash
    wget https://apt.repos.intel.com/intel-gpg-keys/GPG-PUB-KEY-INTEL-SW-PRODUCTS.PUB
sudo apt-key add GPG-PUB-KEY-INTEL-SW-PRODUCTS.PUB
echo "deb https://apt.repos.intel.com/oneapi all main" | sudo tee /etc/apt/sources.list.d/oneAPI.list

  2. Install the package.

    Bash
    sudo apt update && sudo apt install intel-oneapi-mkl-devel -y

  3. Now compile suanPan by enabling MKL via option -DSP_ENABLE_MKL=ON. The corresponding MKL_PATH shall be assigned, for example -DMKL_PATH=/opt/intel/oneapi/mkl/latest/, depending on the installation location. The configuration used for snap is the following one.

    Bash
    -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release
-DCMAKE_INSTALL_PREFIX=
-DMKL_PATH=/opt/intel/oneapi/mkl/latest
-DSP_BUILD_PARALLEL=ON
-DSP_ENABLE_HDF5=ON
-DSP_ENABLE_IOMP=OFF
-DSP_ENABLE_MKL=ON
-DSP_ENABLE_SHARED_MKL=OFF
-DSP_ENABLE_VTK=ON
-DVTK_PATH=$CRAFT_PART_BUILD/lib/cmake/vtk-9.7/

docs.title: VTK
docs.text:
Fedora offers the latest VTK library, simply install it.

Bash
sudo dnf install vtk-devel

docs.title: MKL
docs.text:
Intel also provides a repository to install MKL via dnf. See this page for details.

First, create the repo file.

Bash
tee > /tmp/oneAPI.repo << EOF
[oneAPI]
name=Intel® oneAPI repository
baseurl=https://yum.repos.intel.com/oneapi
enabled=1
gpgcheck=1
repo_gpgcheck=1
gpgkey=https://yum.repos.intel.com/intel-gpg-keys/GPG-PUB-KEY-INTEL-SW-PRODUCTS.PUB
EOF

Move it to the proper location.

Bash
sudo mv /tmp/oneAPI.repo /etc/yum.repos.d

Install MKL. You may perform a search sudo dnf search intel-oneapi-mkl-devel to find which package name is available and install the specific version if necessary.

Bash
sudo dnf install intel-oneapi-mkl-devel

The source can be compiled with VTK and MKL enabled.

docs.title: Compiling on macOS
docs.text:
This page describes native compilation on macOS. For the general prerequisites and source code instructions, see Compile the Application.

The following guide is based on macOS Big Sur (11).

Install tools. gfortran, llvm and libomp are used for compiling the main program, glfw and glew are required for compiling VTK. VTK does not compile with GCC. Here, we use Clang.

Bash
# install brew if not installed
/bin/bash -c "$(curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Homebrew/install/HEAD/install.sh)"
# install necessary packages
brew install gcc@10 llvm@13 libomp glfw glew git cmake

Similar to Ubuntu, compile VTK if wanted.

Bash
wget https://www.vtk.org/files/release/9.1/VTK-9.1.0.tar.gz
tar xf VTK-9.1.0.tar.gz && rm VTK-9.1.0.tar.gz
mkdir VTK-build && cd VTK-build
cmake -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release -DBUILD_SHARED_LIBS=OFF -DCMAKE_INSTALL_PREFIX=../VTK-out ../VTK-9.1.0
make install -j4

MKL can be installed if necessary. See this page.

Obtain the source code and configure.

Bash
# clone source code
git clone -b master https://github.com/TLCFEM/suanPan.git
# create build directory
mkdir suanpan-build && cd suanpan-build
# use clang, clang++ and gfortran
export CC=/usr/local/opt/llvm/bin/clang && export CXX=/usr/local/opt/llvm/bin/clang++ && export FC=gfortran-10
# configure project
cmake -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release -DSP_BUILD_PARALLEL=ON -DSP_ENABLE_HDF5=ON -DSP_ENABLE_VTK=ON -DVTK_PATH=../VTK-out/lib/cmake/vtk-9.1/ .
# compile
make -j4

docs.title: Compiling on Windows
docs.text: This page describes native compilation on Windows. For the general prerequisites and source code instructions, see Compile the Application.

docs.title: Visual Studio
docs.text:
This is highly tailored to my own machine. Thus, it is not recommended to use it directly. Instead, use VS Code with CMake extension to automatically configure the project.

A solution file is provided under MSVC/suanPan folder. There are two configurations:

  1. Debug: Assumes no available Fortran compiler; all Fortran related libraries are provided as precompiled DLLs. Use OpenBLAS for linear algebra. Multithreading disabled. Visualisation disabled. HDF5 support disabled.
  2. Release: Fortran libraries are configured with Intel compilers. Use MKL for linear algebra. Multithreading enabled. Visualisation enabled with VTK version 9.6. HDF5 support enabled. CUDA enabled.

This repository contains some precompiled libraries used.

If VTK, Intel oneAPI Toolkit and CUDA are not installed, only the Debug configuration can be successfully compiled. Simply open the solution and switch to Debug configuration, ignore all potential warnings and build the solution.

To compile the Release version, please follow these steps.

  1. Make sure both oneAPI Base and HPC toolkits, as well as VS integration, are installed. The MKL is enabled via integrated option <UseInteloneMKL>Parallel</UseInteloneMKL>.

  2. Make sure CUDA is installed. The environment variable $(CUDA_PATH) is used to locate headers.

  3. Make sure VTK is available. Then define a system environment variable $(VTK_DIR), which points to the root folder of VTK library. On my machine, it is

    PowerShell
    VTK_DIR=C:\Program Files\VTK\

    For versions other than 9.5, names of the linked libraries shall be manually changed as they contain version numbers. Thus, it is not a good idea to switch to a different version. Precompiled VTK library is also available in this repository.

Alternatively, CMake can be used to generate solution files if some external packages are not available.

docs.title: Visual Studio Code
docs.text: Open the source code folder with VS Code. Whether you choose GCC or MSVC, the configuration is done by CMake automatically.

docs.title: Your First Analysis
docs.text:
This page aims to show an overview of what a model looks like by establishing a simple model, which is an elastic cantilever beam subjected to an end load.

A native C++ parser is used by suanPan. The default syntax resembles that of OpenSees. Model files are written in plain text. Although there is no restriction, the suffix .supan is reserved by default.

The line that starts with the hash symbol (#) or the exclamation symbol (!) is a comment line. To write one command that spans a few lines, please use backslash (\) to concatenate multiple lines. Please refer to Syntax for details.

Text Only
# defines two nodes at (0,0) and (1.34,0)
node 1 0 0
node 2 1.34 0

# define an elastic material with the elastic modulus of 132
material Elastic1D 1 132

# define an (E)lastic (B)eam element 1 connecting node 1 and node 2 with A=7.213 and I=6.825 using material 1
element EB21 1 1 2 7.213 6.825 1

# fix all DoFs (E) of node 1
fix 1 E 1

# apply a load of magnitude 23 at DoF 2 of node 2
cload 1 0 23 2 2
# apply another load of magnitude 17 at DoF 1 of node 2
cload 2 0 17 1 2

# create a static step
step static 1

analyze

# print the state of node 2
peek node 2

exit

Since each command is commented, there is not much to explain. This model is similar to the one created by the example command; both are simple one-element models. The output is directly printed on screen by default. For this model, it is

+--------------------------------------------------------+

>> Current Analysis Time: 1.00000.

Node 2:
Coordinate:
  1.3400e+00  0.0000e+00
Displacement:
  2.3926e-02  2.0476e-02  2.2921e-02
Resistance:
  1.7000e+01  2.3000e+01 -2.4633e-07

The analytical solution of the horizontal tip displacement is

\[ u=\dfrac{PL}{EA}=\dfrac{17\times1.34}{132\times7.213}=0.023926. \]

The analytical solution of the vertical tip displacement is

\[ v=\dfrac{PL^3}{3EI}=\dfrac{23\times1.34^3}{3\times132\times6.835}=0.020476. \]

Continue with Model Syntax.

docs.title: Docker Image
docs.text:
A docker image is available at Docker Hub. Both amd64 and arm64 architectures are available. To use it, docker needs to be installed first. See this page for details.

Once docker is installed, it is possible to pull the image via:

Bash
docker pull tlcfem/suanpan

Then it is possible to run the container in an interactive manner via:

Bash
docker run -it --rm tlcfem/suanpan

Within the container, one can use one of the following commands to invoke the application.

Bash
suanPan
suanpan
sp

One can also attach a volume to the container to access files in the host machine. This may be the main use case. Assume there is a model file under the path /path/to/host/folder/example.model.sp; to run the analysis under this folder, one can use the following command.

Bash
docker run --rm -v /path/to/host/folder:/dirty -w /dirty tlcfem/suanpan sp -f example.model.sp

The Docker image is convenient on machines with older kernels or limited by other factors that do not allow execution of precompiled binaries.

This is now supported by the VS Code extension.

The following shall be noted.

  1. For maximum compatibility, the image is compiled without AVX support.
  2. On amd64, Intel MKL is used. On arm64, OpenBLAS is used.

If necessary, one can build images with different configurations to enable AVX and AVX2 support and/or AOCL support on AMD platforms.

docs.title: Precompiled Binaries
docs.text:
The binaries are published on GitHub. https://github.com/TLCFEM/suanPan/releases

Binaries on Windows, Ubuntu and macOS are compiled and deployed automatically on the master branch. The precompiled binaries are compiled on the following OS versions.

Platform Version Windows Windows Server 2025 Linux Ubuntu 24.04 macOS Sequoia 15

For older versions or other flavours of Linux, successful execution is not guaranteed. Please consider compiling the binaries manually.

In order to enable CUDA backed solvers, the program shall be compiled locally with preinstalled external libraries. See this page.

Currently, the following package managers can be used to install the program.

Platform Package Manager Command Windows Chocolatey choco install suanpan Windows scoop scoop install suanpan Linux snap snap install suanpan Linux flatpak flatpak install flathub io.github.tlcfem.suanPan

The binaries are tested in standard environments: fresh new Win10/11 images, docker images Ubuntu and Fedora, and macOS GitHub image.

docs.title: flatpak
docs.text:
To run the application, one shall use the following command in terminal.

Bash
flatpak run io.github.tlcfem.suanPan

Since no shim is created, it would be convenient to create an alias such that

Bash
echo "alias suanpan=\"flatpak run io.github.tlcfem.suanPan\"" >> ~/.bashrc

Then it is possible to use suanpan to invoke the application.

docs.title: Execute Program
docs.text:
By default, the AVX2 support is turned on to utilize CPU capability. For CPUs that do not support AVX2, the application cannot be successfully executed. Users can either compile the program by themselves or request a specific version by filing an issue.

The name of the executable is suanPan; however, snap/chocolatey/scoop will create a shim executable named as suanpan. Depending on how the application is installed, one may use suanpan or suanPan to invoke the application.

The parallelization is enabled mostly by the TBB library and <execution> header (C++17). If the program is compiled with SUANPAN_MT macro, parallelization is used by default. The OpenMP is enabled in several parts of the program; users can set the environment variable OMP_NUM_THREADS to customize some OpenMP based parallelization. To do so, users can, for example, in Windows, use the following command.

PowerShell
set OMP_NUM_THREADS=6

On Linux, the dynamic loading path needs to be set so that dynamic libraries such as libtbb.so can be successfully found. If the application is installed via snap/apt/dnf, it is automatically done.

Bash
# current path contains suanPan
export LD_LIBRARY_PATH=$LD_LIBRARY_PATH:$(pwd)/../lib
./suanPan

Alternatively, users can execute the program via the provided suanPan.sh script.

Bash
# create links to the executables
# the script assumes ~/.local/bin is in the path and creates a symbolic link to the executable
./suanPan.sh --create-link
# cd to other folders and execute the program
cd ~
suanpan

docs.title: Batch Mode
docs.text:
To analyze the model written in a model file named, for example, example.supan, the -f or --file parameter can be used. First, we create the file example.supan with the exit command.

Bash
echo exit > example.supan

Then we can run it by the following command.

Bash
suanpan -f ./example.supan

Or on Windows,

PowerShell
./suanPan.exe -f example.supan

If the model has been prechecked, it is possible to run the analysis without output. It is known that printing strings to terminals slows down the analysis. Users can use the -np or --noprint option to suppress output.

PowerShell
./suanPan.exe -np -f example.supan
