docs.title: Model Structure
docs.text:
The default parser accepts a three-part structure. They are:

  1. Model Properties Setup
  2. Analysis Properties Setup
  3. Post-processing

The previous cantilever beam example is used here to explain the structure. The model is shown as follows.

Text Only
node 1 0 0
node 2 1.34 0
material Elastic1D 1 132
element EB21 1 1 2 7.213 6.825 1
step static 1
fix 1 E 1
cload 1 0 23 2 2
cload 2 0 17 1 2
analyze
peek node 2
exit

docs.title: Model Properties Setup
docs.text:
Anything before the first step command is treated as the setup of model properties. This part may include the definitions of nodes, elements, material models, loads, recorders, boundary conditions, etc. In this part, the order of commands does not affect the establishment of the model. So the following reshuffled command flow creates the same model as the original one does, although the EB21 element is created before the creation of its connected nodes.

Text Only
element EB21 1 1 2 7.213 6.825 1
node 2 1.34 0
material Elastic1D 1 132
node 1 0 0

When the program parses those commands, the corresponding objects are only created and stored, but not initialized (viz., no other information is required during the creation of a particular object). So the order does not affect anything in this part.

docs.title: Analysis Properties Setup
docs.text:
The command block between the first step command and the analyze command (or the precheck command) is the setup of analysis properties. A similar analysis flow which resembles that of ABAQUS is used, that is, multiple steps can be defined in sequence in this part.

In this example, within step 1, a fixed boundary condition is applied to node 1, two concentrated loads are applied to node 2 along two directions. For the purpose of illustration, those two loads can be defined in two different steps as follows.

Text Only
fix 1 E 1
step static 1
cload 1 0 23 2 2
step static 2
cload 2 0 17 1 2
analyze

Now the horizontal load is created in step 2 that follows step 1. It shall be noted that the BC is created before the first step. By default, there is a step 0 with no step time, so the BC can be defined in either step 0 or step 1. Similar to ABAQUS, the sequence of multiple steps will affect analysis results.

docs.title: Post-processing
docs.text:
The code block between the analyze command and the exit command belongs to post-processing. This part is less concerning and most commands have instant response.

Continue with Command-Line Configuration.

docs.title: Command
docs.text:
All commands are case insensitive. Each command by default shall be written in one line.

It is not allowed to write two commands in one line.

To split one command into several lines, use the backslash (\) to concatenate. Only one backslash can serve as a concatenation symbol in one line. Other backslashes (if any) will be kept and combined with other lines and may lead to wrongly interpreted command.

The leading and trailing whitespaces would be omitted by default.

docs.title: Separator/Delimiter
docs.text: Either whitespace (_), including tab (\t), or comma (,) can be used as a separator/delimiter.

docs.title: Comment
docs.text:
Comment lines start with the hash symbol (#) or the exclamation symbol (!).

Inline comments shall be denoted with the exclamation symbol (!) only. All contents after the first ! will be treated as comments.

Comments can be mixed with concatenation. There can only be white spaces between \ and !.

Text Only
# this is a comment
! this is another comment
node 1 2 3 4 5 6 ! this is an inline comment
# split one command into multiple lines
node 2 9 7 5 1 3 \
3 4 5 \ ! comments can be put after backslash \
9 8 2

docs.title: Input
docs.text:
Inputs are mostly integers, doubles and strings. The model input file is a plain text file; scripting of any sort is not supported. Math expressions are not available.

When the required input argument is an integer, it is not allowed to have a double in place. The decimal point cannot be read by the integer parser so may cause failure of command parsing.

However, a double input can be replaced by an integer (if the desired value matches); type conversion is automatically done.

Some commands take Boolean values in the form of a string. For a true value, the following inputs are equivalent: true, yes, 1, on, t, y. For a false value, the following inputs are equivalent: false, no, 0, off, f, n. Again, commands, including inputs, are case-insensitive.

For all commands, compulsory arguments are denoted by rounded brackets (n); optional arguments are denoted by square brackets [n]. Input arguments shall be defined in sequence. To change the default value of any optional arguments, all leading optional arguments (if any) shall be explicitly defined. For group arguments, (n n+1...) means arguments n and n+1 appear as a group and must be defined due to rounded brackets, while ( ...) means this group can be repeated to define a set of arguments. For the square case, [ ...] means this group is optional.

Continue with Model Structure.

docs.title: Windows
docs.text:
A batch file named as AddAssociation.bat is provided in the archive. It associates *.sp and *.supan files with the program and copies configuration files to the default folder if Sublime Text is installed. If the package is installed via package managers, please manually search for and execute this file.

Admin privileges are required.

docs.title: Linux
docs.text:
A bash script named as suanPan.sh is provided in the archive to set up the above configurations automatically. The script can be used to both execute the program and create symbolic links.

For first-time use, the following commands create a soft link under $HOME/.local/bin so that users can execute the program anywhere by invoking the command suanpan in any folder. The Sublime Text configuration files are copied to the default folder if Sublime Text is installed.

Bash
# current path contains suanPan
chmod +x suanPan.sh
./suanPan.sh --create-link
# cd to other places such as folders that contain models
# now invoke the program
suanpan

Check the following recording.

docs.title: Changes Made to the System
docs.text:
The application itself does not write any files to folders other than the current working directory.

There are some exceptions though.

  1. If the terminal command is used, one can change files in the file system.
  2. If one decides to download new versions via the bundled updater, the archive is downloaded to the current working directory. The updater is not always bundled.

The script suanPan.sh writes the following files to the system.

  1. $HOME/.local/share/applications/suanPan.desktop
  2. $HOME/.local/bin/suanpan
  3. $HOME/.config/sublime-text/Packages/User/suanPan.sublime-build
  4. $HOME/.config/sublime-text/Packages/User/suanPan.sublime-completions
  5. $HOME/.config/sublime-text/Packages/User/suanPan.sublime-syntax

The script AddAssociation.bat changes the following settings.

  1. Associate *.sp and *.supan files with the program.
  2. Copy configuration files to default folder if Sublime Text is installed.

Continue with Compile the Application.

docs.title: Command-Line Configuration
docs.text:
All available options can be printed via the --help flag.

Text Only
Usage: suanPan [--help] [--version] [--no-color] [--no-print] [--no-update] [--verbose] [--input-file INPUT_FILE_PATH] [--output-file OUTPUT_FILE_PATH]

Optional arguments:
  -h, --help                                    show this help message and exit 
  -v, --version                                 show version information and exit 
  -nc, --no-color                               suppress colors in terminal output 
  -np, --no-print                               suppress (most) terminal output 
  -nu, --no-update                              skip new version check on startup 
  -vb, --verbose                                enable (very) verbose terminal output 
  -f, --input, --input-file INPUT_FILE_PATH     specify path to the file containing input analysis 
  -o, --output, --output-file OUTPUT_FILE_PATH  specify path to the file for terminal output redirection

docs.title: Disable New Version Check
docs.text:
Some distributions are bundled with an updater that checks for new versions of the application on startup and allows you to download new archives if necessary. In some fully automated environments, one can disable the check via the -nu option.

Bash
suanpan -nu -f <your_input_model.sp>

docs.title: Disable Color Output
docs.text:
By default, the console output is coloured to make it more readable. If the console output is redirected to a file, the ANSI color codes will be included in the file. To disable coloured output, use the -nc option.

Bash
suanpan -nc -f <your_input_model.sp>

The ANSI color codes can be properly rendered using, for example, bat.

docs.title: Redirect Console Output
docs.text:
By default, the console output is printed to the standard output. To redirect the output to a file, use the -o option.

Bash
suanpan -f <your_input_model.sp> -o <your_output_file>

docs.title: Verbose Output
docs.text:
With the release build, only info/warning/error/fatal messages will be printed. To print debug messages, use the -vb option.

Bash
suanpan -vb -f <your_input_model.sp>

docs.title: Disable Output
docs.text:
If the model has been checked, output can be disabled to speed up the analysis. To disable the output, use the -np option.

Bash
suanpan -np -f <your_input_model.sp>

Continue with Editor Setup.

docs.title: VS Code
docs.text:
The VS Code extension is available here. It provides syntax highlighting and code completion.

The plugin also provides functionalities to invoke the analysis in docker containers.

docs.title: Sublime Text Workspace
docs.text: I personally use Sublime Text as my model editor. Other tools like VS Code can also be used.

docs.title: Syntax Highlighting
docs.text:
Create a new syntax file via Tools -> Developer -> New Syntax..., copy and paste the following sample content into the new file and save as suanPan.sublime-syntax under the default path. It provides syntax highlighting for comments only. Other components can be added accordingly.

YAML
%YAML 1.2
---
file_extensions:
  - supan
  - sp
scope: source.supan
contexts:
  main:
    - match: '^[#!].*'
      scope: comment.line
    - match: '!.*'
      scope: comment.line

A syntax file with (almost) all commands is provided as suanPan.sublime-syntax in the archive. Please feel free to use/modify it. It may be necessary to manually search for the file if the application is installed via some package manager.

docs.title: Autocomplete
docs.text: All keywords used are stored in the JSON file suanPan.sublime-completions. Place the file in the folder ~/.config/sublime-text-3/Packages/User/ (Linux) or %appdata%\Sublime Text 3\Packages\User (Windows) and you are good to go with the previous syntax file. The new path has been changed to ~/.config/sublime-text/Packages/User/ (Linux) and %appdata%\Sublime Text\Packages\User (Windows) in Sublime Text 4.

docs.title: Build System
docs.text:
In order to render ANSI color codes correctly in Linux-like systems, you may wish to install the ANSIescape package. Now define a new build system via Tools -> Build System -> New Build System..., copy and paste the following contents in the file and save it as suanPan.sublime-build. You may need to replace command suanpan with the full path of the executable.

JSON
{
  "cmd": [
    "suanpan",
    "-f",
    "$file"
  ],
  "selector": "source.supan",
  "file_patterns": [
    "*.supan",
    "*.sp"
  ],
  "target": "ansi_color_build",
  "syntax": "Packages/ANSIescape/ANSI.sublime-syntax"
}

Now models can be run in Sublime Text via the shortcut Ctrl+B.

To disable coloured output, use -nc (no colour) option such as

Bash
suanpan -nc -f model_file.supan

Continue with Performance Tweaks.

docs.title: Performance Tweaks
docs.text:
suanPan prioritizes performance and designs the analysis logic in a parallel context accordingly.

Although the majority of analyses of common types can be parallelized, there are still certain parts that have strong data dependencies that cannot be parallelized. The speed-up factor is mostly determined by the serial code. According to Amdahl's law, there would be an upper bound of the theoretical speed-up.

docs.title: Benchmark
docs.text:
Benchmarking is hard. Here we try to present a baseline of performance on recent PCs.

There is a benchmark command that is designed to benchmark the platform by solving a large matrix repeatedly. The following is the main implementation. The matrix occupies 200 MB of memory. It is large enough to account for potential memory bandwidth bottleneck. It effectively reports the performance of dgesv subroutine in LAPACK.

C++
int benchmark() {
    constexpr auto N = 50;
    constexpr auto M = 5120;

    const mat A = mat(M, M, fill::randu) + eye(M, M);
    const vec b(M, fill::randu);

    for(auto I = 1; I <= N; ++I) {
        vec x = solve(A, b);
        x(randi<uvec>(1, distr_param(0, M - 1))).fill(I);
    }

    return SUANPAN_SUCCESS;
}

As FEM is essentially solving large matrices, such a benchmark is practical and close to actual performance. Profiling it on an average laptop yields the following result. This particular platform is able to achieve a CPI (cycles per instruction) of 0.686. This serves as the baseline and upper bound of practical performance.

docs.title: Large-sized Elastic Analysis
docs.text:
This example is a linear elastic analysis. There are 20124 nodes and 39990 shell elements in total, and since each node has six DoFs, there are in total 120744 DoFs.

Because an elastic material model is used, element state updating is trivial, requiring only matrix multiplication. The main computation is assembling the global stiffness matrix and solving it. Profiling this example on the same platform yields the following result. It is able to achieve a CPI close to the baseline.

docs.title: Medium-sized Plastic Analysis
docs.text:
This example contains 2990 nodes, and uses a plastic material model. Element state updating now involves local plasticity integration. It is able to achieve a CPI of 0.979 in this case.

Assuming all (or at least the majority of) instructions are useful instructions, one can conclude that decent performance can be practically achieved, even when the problem size is not significantly large.

docs.title: Analysis Configurations
docs.text:
Here are some tips that may improve the performance.

  1. If the analysis is known to be linear elastic, use set linear_system true to skip the convergence test and iteration. Note the analysis should be both material and geometric linear.
  2. If the global system is known to be symmetric, use set symm_mat true to use a symmetric storage. Analyses involving 1D materials are mostly (not always) symmetric. Analyses involving 2D and 3D materials are mostly (not always) not symmetric.
  3. Consider a proper stepping strategy. A fixed stepping size may be unnecessarily expensive. A proper adaptive stepping strategy can significantly improve the performance.
  4. Prefer a dense solver over a sparse solver if the system is small. A dense solver is generally faster than a sparse solver for small systems.
  5. Prefer a mixed-precision algorithm set precision mixed over a full-precision algorithm if the system is large. A mixed-precision algorithm is generally faster than a full-precision algorithm for large systems. See the following for details.
  6. The performance of various sparse solvers can vary significantly. It is recommended to try different solvers to find the best one.

docs.title: Mixed-Precision Algorithm
docs.text:
On some platforms, the performance of the mixed-precision algorithm can be significantly better than the full-precision algorithm. The mixed-precision algorithm converts the full-precision matrix to a lower precision matrix, and then solves the system using the lower precision matrix. Typically, only two to three iterations are required as each iteration reduces the relative error by a factor around machine epsilon of the lower precision.

The built-in tests consist of benchmarks for mixed-precision algorithms. One can execute the following command to run the tests.

Bash
suanpan -ct

One can find the following information.

Text Only
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Large Mixed Precision
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------

benchmark name                       samples       iterations    est run time
                                     mean          low mean      high mean
                                     std dev       low std dev   high std dev
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Band N=1024 NZ=3234 NE=10240 Full              100             1    39.4709 ms
                                        423.471 us    409.755 us    449.776 us
                                        93.2939 us     56.394 us    148.874 us

Band N=1024 NZ=3234 NE=10240 Mixed             100             1    11.4429 ms
                                        156.697 us    147.096 us    166.771 us
                                        50.2275 us    47.5325 us    54.2532 us

The mixed-precision algorithm is around three times faster than the full-precision algorithm. Note the results are obtained with MKL on a platform with a 13-th generation Intel CPU. For platforms that have a low memory bandwidth, the performance gain may not be as significant.

One could always benchmark the platform to find the best algorithm.

docs.title: Tweaks
docs.text: It is possible to tweak the performance in the following ways, which may or may not improve the performance.

docs.title: OpenMP Threads
docs.text:
OpenMP is used by MKL and OpenBLAS to parallelize the matrix operations, alongside SIMD instructions. It is possible to manually set OMP_NUM_THREADS to control the number of threads used. Pay attention to over-subscription.

OMP_DYNAMIC may affect cache locality and thus the performance. For computation-intensive tasks, it is recommended to set it to false.

docs.title: Affinity
docs.text: CPU affinity can also affect the performance. Tweaking affinity, for example, with KMP_AFFINITY, can improve performance.

docs.title: Memory Allocation
docs.text:
Memory fragmentation may downgrade analysis performance, especially for finite element analysis, in which there are a large number of small matrices and vectors. It is recommended to use a performant memory allocator, for example, a general purpose allocator like mimalloc.

On Linux, it is fairly easy to replace the default memory allocator. For example,

Bash
LD_PRELOAD=/path/to/libmimalloc.so suanpan -f input.sp

easy integration

With portable archives in POSIX systems, it is possible to place libmimalloc.so file under the lib folder and invoke suanPan.sh directly. The script suanPan.sh automatically checks the presence of the libmimalloc.so file and loads it if found.

docs.title: Smaller Memory Footprint
docs.text:
By default, Armadillo uses 64-bit indexing and embeds small fixed-size local arrays within matrix objects to avoid frequent small heap allocations. As a consequence, these objects become relatively large, on the order of roughly 100 bytes each.

Enabling the CMake option SP_ENABLE_ARMA_SMALL_MEMORY=ON removes these embedded local buffers and switches indexing to 32-bit. This optimization is considered safe because arma::vec and arma::mat are primarily used for nodal and elemental data, where large-index support is unnecessary. In practice, element objects are already large enough that cache inefficiencies dominate, so avoiding heap overhead does not materially degrade performance.

With SP_ENABLE_ARMA_SMALL_MEMORY=ON, the size of arma::mat can be reduced to around 50 bytes.

As a result, running the same DKTS3 example with this flag enabled reduces memory consumption by about $\(25\%\)$, from 3.7 GB down to 2.7 GB compared to the default configuration.

This is particularly useful if the target platform has memory constraints.

docs.title: SP_ENABLE_ARMA_SMALL_MEMORY=OFF
docs.text:
Bash
/usr/bin/time ../RelWithDebInfo/bin/suanPan-nm -np -f DKTS3.supan
Text Only
31.79user 4.44system 0:05.48elapsed 660%CPU (0avgtext+0avgdata 3880996maxresident)k
0inputs+8outputs (0major+758234minor)pagefaults 0swaps

docs.title: SP_ENABLE_ARMA_SMALL_MEMORY=ON
docs.text:
Bash
/usr/bin/time ../RelWithDebInfo/bin/suanPan-sm -np -f DKTS3.supan
Text Only
32.53user 2.52system 0:05.27elapsed 665%CPU (0avgtext+0avgdata 2887796maxresident)k
0inputs+16outputs (0major+468057minor)pagefaults 0swaps

Continue with Automation and System Integration.

docs.title: Two Forms of Storytelling
docs.text:
If you have studied a sufficient number of finite element method textbooks, you have likely noticed that content organization follows at least two distinct patterns. Viewing textbooks as narratives that convey the principles of FEM, I refer to these as two narrative approaches.

The first approach emphasizes engineering applications, beginning with truss system analysis, developing element stiffness matrices followed by the global assembly, and outlining a general solution strategy --- similar to the matrix stiffness method taught in structural analysis courses. This provides readers with an initial understanding of FEM's practical applications. After gaining this foundation, two-dimensional elements are presented, followed by increasingly advanced topics.

The second approach adopts a more mathematical perspective, beginning with partial differential equations and self-adjoint operators, then proceeding to the strong and weak forms of differential equations. Building upon the weak form, the Galerkin method is introduced, which naturally leads to shape functions, isoparametric mapping, and related concepts. This approach establishes the rigorous mathematical foundations underlying FEM.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: This section provides references to all control commands.

docs.title: At a Glance
docs.text:
Commands are grouped by the stage of an analysis in which they are used.

Stage Purpose Example commands Define build the model: nodes, elements, materials, sections, loads, constraints, groups and recorders node, element, group Configure set up a step: analysis type, integrator, solver, converger and criteria step, integrator, criterion Process run, inspect and save: analysis, querying, visualisation and object control analyze, peek, save

These commands follow the model structure, and the objects they create are catalogued in the model library overview.

docs.title: analyze
docs.text:
The analyze (or analyse) command triggers the analysis. The model is initialized by setting up the elements, the global matrix storage and other components.

All steps are analysed. Subsequent steps can be defined after performing the analysis.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text:
analyze
analyze
analyse

Before executing the analysis, the application checks for warnings and errors. If any are found, the analysis is not performed.

Warnings and errors can be ignored with the --ignore-warnings and --ignore-errors options. [available from v3.1]

analyze with options
analyze [--ignore-warnings] [--ignore-errors]
analyse [--ignore-warnings] [--ignore-errors]

Given that errors generally imply that the model is incorrect, ignoring them is not recommended.

docs.title: converger
docs.text: The term converger is not a standard English word. It refers to an object that checks whether the system converges according to a given rule. Please refer to the specific converger types for syntax and details.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text:
converger
converger (1) (2) ...
# (1) string, converger type
# (2) int, unique converger tag

docs.title: criterion
docs.text:
The criterion command constructs criteria that may be used to modify the model according to specific rules. Please refer to the specific criterion types for syntax and details.

The summary page can be found here.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text:
criterion
criterion (1) (2) ...
# (1) string, criterion type
# (2) int, unique criterion tag

docs.title: integrator
docs.text: The integrator command constructs a time integration algorithm. Please refer to the specific integrator types for syntax and details.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text:
integrator
integrator (1) (2) ...
# (1) string, integrator type
# (2) int, unique integrator tag

docs.title: precheck
docs.text: The precheck command initialises all the models created so far to check for potential errors. It does not run the analysis. To perform the analysis, use the analyze command.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text:
precheck
precheck

docs.title: solver
docs.text: The solver command creates the nonlinear equation solver used in a step. If a current step exists, the solver is assigned to it, and it also becomes the current solver. Please refer to the specific solver pages for syntax and details.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text:
solver
solver (1) (2) ...
# (1) string, solver type
# (2) int, unique solver tag

docs.title: Remarks
docs.text:
1. Available types are Newton, modifiedNewton (alias mNewton), AICN, BFGS, LBFGS, FEAST, DisplacementControl (alias MPDC), and Ramm.
  2. AICN accepts an optional length (default 1.0), and LBFGS an optional maximum history (default 20).
  3. FEAST requires a number of frequencies and a centre, with an optional radius that defaults to the centre.
  4. See Newton, AICN, BFGS, MPDC, and Ramm.

docs.title: step
docs.text: The step command defines an analysis step. Please refer to the specific step types for syntax and details.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text:
step
step (1) (2) ...
# (1) string, step type
# (2) int, unique step tag

For all available steps, a default asymmetric banded dense storage is used. This storage scheme fits most problems. The LAPACK driver used is _gbsv(). The main reason behind this choice stems from two aspects.

  1. For 2D and 3D problems, most material models have asymmetric stiffness moduli. The global stiffness matrix is then asymmetric.
  2. If the problem shows softening behaviour, the stiffness matrix is not always positive definite. The symmetric solver then fails to solve such a matrix.

docs.title: amplitude
docs.text: The amplitude command defines a function of time that provides the magnitude of a load or constraint. Please refer to the specific amplitude types for the available syntax.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text:
amplitude
amplitude (1) (2) ...
# (1) string, amplitude type
# (2) int, unique amplitude tag

docs.title: bc
docs.text: Although this is called a boundary condition, only trivial Dirichlet boundary conditions are handled here.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text:
Several commands are available to define boundary conditions.

bc
fix (1) (2) (3...)
fix2 (1) (2) (3...)
multiplierbc (1) (2) (3...)
penaltybc (1) (2) (3...)
# (1) int, unique tag
# (2) string, dof identifier
# (3...) int, tags of nodes that shall be constrained

To apply boundary conditions to node groups, use the following commands.

Text Only
groupmultiplierbc (1) (2) (3...)
grouppenaltybc (1) (2) (3...)
# (1) int, unique tag
# (2) string, dof identifier
# (3...) int, tags of groups that shall be constrained

docs.title: Remarks
docs.text:
1. Both fix and fix2 serve the same purpose but use different approaches. The fix command modifies the corresponding main diagonal term by multiplying it by a large number, for example $\(10^8\)$. The fix2 command erases the column and row of the target DoF and sets the main diagonal to unity. In both cases, the corresponding right-hand-side entry is erased.
  2. The fix and penaltybc commands are computationally efficient but lead to an ill-conditioned matrix. This may not be a problem for direct solvers but can greatly affect the performance of iterative solvers. The penalty number can be controlled with the constraint_multiplier option of the set command.
  3. The fix2 and multiplierbc commands require more operations, but the final matrix is well conditioned.
  4. The performance difference is almost negligible. Either one can be used with direct solvers. The error does not accumulate because a special mechanism prevents it.
  5. A nontrivial Dirichlet boundary condition is treated as a displacement load.

The DoF identifier (2) can take the following values. Accepted inputs vary with the selected element type(s) and the problem type.

identifier implies of type PINNED, P DOF::U1, DOF::U2, DOF::U3 displacement ENCASTRE, E DOF::U1, DOF::U2, DOF::U3, DOF::UR1, DOF::UR2, DOF::UR3 XSYMM, X DOF::U1, DOF::UR2, DOF::UR3 YSYMM, Y DOF::UR1, DOF::U2, DOF::UR3 ZSYMM, Z DOF::UR1, DOF::UR2, DOF::U3 1, U1 DOF::U1 2, U2 DOF::U2 3, U3 DOF::U3 4, U4, UR1 DOF::UR1 5, U5, UR2 DOF::UR2 6, U6, UR3 DOF::UR3 FU1 DOF::FU1 fluid FU2 DOF::FU2 FU3 DOF::FU3 FUR1 DOF::FUR1 FUR2 DOF::FUR2 FUR3 DOF::FUR3 RADIAL DOF::RADIAL axisymmetric AXIAL DOF::AXIAL axisymmetric, rod/beam like RS DOF::RS beam RW DOF::RW 3D beam DAMAGE DOF::DAMAGE special damage DoF PRESSURE DOF::PRESSURE special pressure DoF TEMPERATURE DOF::TEMPERATURE thermal DOF WARP DOF::WARP special warp DoF (in some beams)

docs.title: constraint
docs.text:
The constraint command defines a constraint between nodes or between a node and a geometric entity. Please refer to the specific constraint types for the available syntax.

All constraints are processed in parallel.

Most constraints are implemented using both the penalty function and the Lagrange multiplier methods. A brief discussion of the differences can be found on the Constraint page.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text:
constraint
constraint (1) (2) ...
# (1) string, constraint type
# (2) int, unique constraint tag

docs.title: Short Forms
docs.text:
The leading constraint keyword can be replaced by a dedicated first-level command with the same arguments.

Shortcut Equivalent constraint type mpc MPC fixedlength2d, fixedlength3d FixedLength2D, FixedLength3D maxforce2d, maxforce3d MaxForce2D, MaxForce3D maxgap2d, maxgap3d MaxGap2D, MaxGap3D mingap2d, mingap3d MinGap2D, MinGap3D nodefacet, nodeline NodeFacet, NodeLine finiterigidwall, finiterigidwallpenalty, finiterigidwallmultiplier the corresponding FiniteRigidWall* types finiterestitutionwall, finiterestitutionwallpenalty the corresponding FiniteRestitutionWall* types rigidwallpenalty, rigidwallmultiplier RigidWallPenalty, RigidWallMultiplier particlecollision2d, particlecollision3d ParticleCollision2D, ParticleCollision3D moleculardynamics2d, moleculardynamics3d MolecularDynamics2D, MolecularDynamics3D sleeve2d, sleeve3d Sleeve2D, Sleeve3D

docs.title: domain
docs.text: The domain command creates a new problem domain or switches to an existing one.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text:
domain
domain (1)
# (1) int, domain tag

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
The program uses a domain concept so that it can hold multiple domains (problems) at the same time. It starts with a default domain labelled with tag 1. The following output is seen when a debug build is executed. Irrelevant information has been removed for simplicity.

Text Only
+--------------------------------------------------+
|   __        __        suanPan is an open source  |
|  /  \      |  \          FEM framework (64-bit)  |
|  \__       |__/  __   __          Acrux (0.1.0)  |
|     \ |  | |    /  | |  |                        |
|  \__/ |__| |    |__X |  |     maintained by tlc  |
|                             all rights reserved  |
+--------------------------------------------------+

debug: Storage of Domain ctor() called.
debug: Domain 1 ctor() called.
suanPan ~<>

Use the domain command to create or switch to other domains.

Text Only
suanPan ~<> domain 2
debug: Domain 2 ctor() called.
create_new_domain() successfully creates Domain 2.
suanPan ~<>

Domains can be deleted with erase, remove or delete.

Text Only
suanPan ~<> domain 2
debug: Domain 2 ctor() called.
create_new_domain() successfully creates Domain 2.
suanPan ~<> domain 3
debug: Domain 3 ctor() called.
create_new_domain() successfully creates Domain 3.
suanPan ~<> domain 4
debug: Domain 4 ctor() called.
create_new_domain() successfully creates Domain 4.
suanPan ~<> domain 5
debug: Domain 5 ctor() called.
create_new_domain() successfully creates Domain 5.
suanPan ~<> remove domain 2
debug: Domain 2 dtor() called.
suanPan ~<> erase domain 5
debug: Domain 5 dtor() called.
erase_domain() switches to Domain 1.
suanPan ~<> domain 4
create_new_domain() switches to Domain 4.
suanPan ~<> delete domain 3
debug: Domain 3 dtor() called.
suanPan ~<> remove domain 4
erase_domain() switches to Domain 1.
suanPan ~<>

Five domains are created. When remove domain 2 is invoked, the current domain is 5, so 2 is safely removed. When erase domain 5 is invoked, the current domain 5 is deleted. By default, the program then switches to the first domain in storage, which is not necessarily 1. When domain 4 is invoked, 4 already exists in storage, so the program switches to the existing domain instead of creating a new one.

Within each domain, an independent model can be defined. When the analyze command is called, all domains are analyzed.

docs.title: element
docs.text: The element command constructs finite elements. Please refer to the specific element types for syntax and details.

docs.title: General Syntax
docs.text:
In general, the syntax uses the following pattern:

Text Only
element <name> <tag> <connected_nodes> <associated_material> <other_specific_parameters>

docs.title: Output Types
docs.text:
All elements support recording the elemental stiffness and mass with the tokens K and M. Use the following commands to record them. The detailed syntax is described on the Recorder page.

Text Only
hdf5recorder (1) Element K (2...)
hdf5recorder (1) Element M (2...)
# (1) int, unique recorder tag
# (2...) int, element tags that K or M needs to be recorded

The matrices are vectorised.

Most elements do not support recording additional quantities. There are some exceptions, however, which are documented on the corresponding element pages.

The recording command is forwarded directly to the attached material models. For example, the CP4 element uses second-order Gaussian quadrature, that is, four integration points per element. Each integration point is assigned a copy of the material model. If the stress is recorded with a command similar to plainrecorder 1 Element S 1, the request is forwarded to the material models of all four integration points. Each point returns a vector of size 3, $\(\begin{bmatrix}\sigma_{11}&\sigma_{22}&\sigma_{12}\end{bmatrix}\)$. The four vectors are concatenated so that the final record in the file is a row of size 12.

time IP1 IP1 IP1 IP2 IP2 IP2 IP3 IP3 IP3 IP4 IP4 IP4 time $\(\sigma_{11}\)$ $\(\sigma_{22}\)$ $\(\sigma_{12}\)$ $\(\sigma_{11}\)$ $\(\sigma_{22}\)$ $\(\sigma_{12}\)$ $\(\sigma_{11}\)$ $\(\sigma_{22}\)$ $\(\sigma_{12}\)$ $\(\sigma_{11}\)$ $\(\sigma_{22}\)$ $\(\sigma_{12}\)$

The detailed quadrature schemes for elements are not well documented at present. The most commonly used schemes are Gauss and Lobatto with various orders.

docs.title: Creation
docs.text:
Creating an element validates nothing beyond the scope of the element itself. For example, suppose the correct syntax is the following.

Text Only
element MyEle (1) (2) (3) (4)
# (1) int, unique tag
# (2) int, tag of the first node
# (3) int, tag of the second node
# (4) int, tag of the material

Then element MyEle 7 8 9 10 creates an element with tag 7, nodes 8 and 9, and material 10. In contrast, element MyEle 7 8 9 or element MyEle 7 8 9 unexpected_str fails the creation. Whether nodes 8 and 9 and material 10 exist is not validated at this point. Instead, these validations are performed during initialisation, before the analysis stage. This means the order in which basic components are defined is not important. It is valid to define an element before defining its connected nodes.

docs.title: Initialisation
docs.text: Before performing the analysis, all defined elements are initialised. During this stage, each element checks that the connected nodes are active and able to accommodate the DoFs required by the element. Local copies of the attached material models are retrieved from the global storage. If any mismatch is found, for example, a uniaxial material model assigned to a 3D element, the element is disabled.

docs.title: Analysis
docs.text:
During the analysis stage, the global solving algorithm solves the global system and updates the nodal displacements accordingly. The new nodal displacements are dispatched to all active elements for further analysis.

From the element's perspective, it returns the elemental nodal force vector for the given nodal displacement vector.

docs.title: Interaction
docs.text:
The problem domain holds all the information that elements need to update themselves. Elements do not interact with the global data storage directly. Instead, they only communicate with the associated nodes and sections/materials.

A complete interaction graph is shown below. For elements themselves, apart from the connected nodes, they do not share information with any other objects. Some elements may not even need sections and/or materials.

graph LR
  A[Domain] -->|update_trial_status| B[Element];
  A -->|update_trial_status| J[Node];
  J -->|get_trial_displacement| B;
  B -->|update_trial_status| D[Section];
  D -->|update_trial_status| F[Material];
  F -->|get_trial_stress| D;
  F -->|get_trial_stiffness| D;
  D -->|get_trial_resistance| B;
  D -->|get_trial_stiffness| B;
  B -->|get_trial_resistance| A;
  B -->|get_trial_stiffness| A;

docs.title: expression
docs.text:
The expression command defines mathematical expressions that can later be used to customise relevant material models.

The command parses a block of plain text into mathematical expressions. The parsing and evaluation functionality is powered by exprtk.

exprtk generates an AST from the input text. The evaluation of the expression has performance on par with native C++ code.

A customisable expression, however, allows more flexibility and makes it easier to experiment with different functions.

docs.title: Simple Scalar-valued Expression
docs.text:
SimpleScalar
expression SimpleScalar (1) (2) (3)
# (1) int, unique expression tag
# (2) string, input variable list
# (3) string, expression string or name of file containing expression

This evaluates a scalar-valued function $\(f(x_1,x_2,\cdots,x_n)\)$. The input arguments can be either scalars or vectors. For example, "x_1|2|x_2" represents two variables: 1) $\(x_1\)$ is a vector of size 2 and 2) $\(x_2\)$ is a scalar. The function value is returned as a result. For example, the expression can be $\(x_1^2+x_2^2\)$.

This form supports automatic computation of derivatives. Thus, it can be used in models that require automatic computation of derivatives.

docs.title: Simple Vector-valued Expression
docs.text:
SimpleVector
expression SimpleVector (1) (2) (3) (4)
# (1) int, unique expression tag
# (2) string, input variable list
# (3) string, output variable list
# (4) string, expression string or name of file containing expression

This evaluates a vector-valued function $\(y:=f(x_1,x_2,\cdots,x_n)\)$. An assignment must be used to explicitly assign values to the output variables. The input arguments can be either scalars or vectors. The output argument should be a vector; the size shall be given such that "y|3" represents a vector of size 3.

This form does not support automatic computation of derivatives. Thus, it cannot be used in models that require automatic computation of derivatives.

docs.title: Remarks
docs.text:
1. The variables in the expression must be explicitly given as arguments. They can be unquoted or enclosed in double quotes ".
  2. Multiple variables must be separated by a vertical bar |.
  3. The expression can be given as a string or as a file name. The program tries to load the file first. If the file does not exist, the program tries to parse the string as an expression.
  4. No whitespace (including , and ) is allowed in any argument.

exprtk provides powerful functionality. Logical operations and control flow can be used in an expression.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
For example, consider a uniaxial nonlinear elastic model with the following stress-strain relationship:

\[ \sigma=\varepsilon^3+\varepsilon \]

The expression can then be defined as

Text Only
expression SimpleScalar 1 x x^3+x

Here, x is used as the free variable and the corresponding expression is x^3+x.

For the uniaxial nonlinear elastic model, the input is strain, which maps to x. The output maps to stress.

Alternatively, the expression can be stored in a file and loaded by the program.

cubic.txt
x^3+x

The expression can then be defined as

Text Only
expression SimpleScalar 1 x cubic.txt

For complex expressions, using a file is more convenient.

To use the expression, the CustomElastic1D model is used here.

Text Only
# using expression 1
material CustomElastic1D 1 1

materialTest1D 1 1E-2 200

exit

The response can be tested with the material tester.

docs.title: file
docs.text: The file command loads external suanPan model files, with or without the .supan extension, from the current working directory.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text:
file
file (1)
# (1) string, external file name

Use pwd to change the current working directory.

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
The main file:

Text Only
# main file calling external file
file pre
step static 1
cload 1 0 23 2 2 ! this is an example
step static 2
cload 2 0 17 1 2
analyze
peek node 2
exit

The pre.supan file:

Text Only
# pre.supan
node 1 0 0
node 2 1.34 0
material Elastic1D 1 132
element EB21 1 1 2 7.213 6.825 1
fix 1 E 1

docs.title: generate
docs.text:
The generate command creates node or element groups according to predefined rules.

For custom rules, refer to CustomNodeGroup.

precision

For all forms, whenever floating-point operations are involved, the criterion is evaluated within machine precision (machine epsilon). Coordinates should therefore be specified as accurately as possible, with at least 16 significant digits.

docs.title: form one: generate based on a fixed interval
docs.text:
Text Only
# to hold one node/element only
generate nodegroup (1) (2)
generate elementgroup (1) (2)
# (1) int, unique group tag
# (2) int, object tag

# generate from tag (2) to tag (3) with unit increment
generate nodegroup (1) (2) (3)
generate elementgroup (1) (2) (3)
# (1) int, unique group tag
# (2) int, starting object tag
# (3) int, ending object tag

# generate according to given increment
generate nodegroup (1) (2) (3) (4)
generate elementgroup (1) (2) (3) (4)
# (1) int, unique group tag
# (2) int, starting object tag
# (3) int, interval
# (4) int, ending object tag

Note that the starting tag does not have to be smaller than the ending tag.

docs.title: form two: generate a node group based on polynomial
docs.text:
Text Only
generatebyrule nodegroup (1) (2) [(3)...]
# (1) int, unique group tag
# (2) int, DoF tag that polynomial shall be applied on
# [(3)...] double, parameters a_n, a_{n-1}, a_{n-2},..., a_0

The polynomial constraint is defined to be

\[ \sum{}a_nx^n=0, \]

Here, $\(x\)$ is the coordinate of the target DoF of the target node.

For example, to select all nodes on the line $\(y=200\)$, use the following command.

Text Only
generatebyrule nodegroup 1 2 1. -200.

docs.title: form three: generate a node group based on the line segment
docs.text:
To select all nodes that lie on a straight line segment, use the following command.

Text Only
generatebypoint nodegroup (1) [(2)...]
# (1) int, unique group tag
# [(2)...] double, coordinates of two end points

There is no restriction on the number of coordinates of each point, but the two points must have the same number of coordinates. For example, to select all points on the line segment between $\((3,~4)\)$ and $\((8,~7)\)$, use

Text Only
generatebypoint nodegroup 1 3. 4. 8. 7.

docs.title: form four: generate a node group based on plane
docs.text:
Text Only
generatebyplane nodegroup (1) [(2)...]
# (1) int, unique group tag
# [(2)...] double, parameters that define a plane

A plane is defined by

\[ \sum{}a_ix_i+b=0, \]

Here, $\(x_i\)$ are coordinates, $\(a_i\)$ are the corresponding coefficients, and $\(b\)$ is a constant.

For example, a plane can be defined as

\[ 3x+2y-z+7=0. \]

Then

Text Only
generatebyplane nodegroup 1 3. 2. -1. 7.

This finds all nodes that lie on the plane and groups them.

There is no restriction on the number of coordinates used, so it is possible to define a hyperplane or a line. The last parameter is always the constant. For example, the following command defines the line $\(x+2y-3=0\)$ in the 2D plane.

Text Only
generatebyplane nodegroup 1 1. 2. -3.

If this is used to find nodes for a group in a 3D problem, the $\(z\)$ coordinates of all nodes are automatically skipped. Nodes such as $\((2,1,0)\)$ and $\((2,1,10)\)$ are then both added to the group.

docs.title: group
docs.text:
The group command constructs a set of nodes to which the corresponding constraints and loads can be applied. It is similar to the concept of a "set" in ABAQUS.

Please refer to generate for the available commands.

docs.title: Remarks
docs.text:
1. The type token after group selects the implementation: NodeGroup, CustomNodeGroup, ElementGroup, GroupGroup or one of the generate forms.
  2. These select nodes, custom nodes, elements and other groups respectively; see the corresponding pages in the model library.
  3. The same objects can be created by the standalone commands nodegroup, customnodegroup, elementgroup, groupgroup, generate, generatebyrule, generatebypoint and generatebyplane.
  4. Group tags are consumed by group-aware loads, constraints and recorders, and a group can be enabled or disabled by the enable/disable commands.

docs.title: import
docs.text:
The import command loads external libraries. Place the library file (.dll, .so or .dylib) in the folder containing the executable and use the following command to import it.

Text Only
import (1)
# (1) string, external library name

The file extension is optional.

If an external library exports only one function and its name matches the library name, the library does not need to be imported explicitly. It is imported automatically.

For example, the external library ElementExample.dll contains the function that creates an external ElementExample object. By default, the function is named void new_elementexample(). To define an ElementExample element, simply use

Text Only
element ElementExample !... element definition goes here

The program first looks in the built-in element library for ElementExample. If it is not found, the program looks for a function with the signature void new_elementexample() in the currently loaded external libraries. If it is still not found, the program tries to load ElementExample.dll.

If an external library exports more than one function, users must explicitly import the library to use the other functions.

In a C++ implementation, a smart pointer such as unique_ptr<Element> is passed from the DLL to the main executable. Both the DLL and the executable must be compiled with the same configuration. Otherwise, unexpected errors may occur. If possible, use a C-type interface instead.

docs.title: initial
docs.text: The initial command defines initial conditions for nodes, material models and other objects.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text:
For nodal properties:

initial
initial displacement (1) (2) [3...]
initial velocity (1) (2) [3...]
initial acceleration (1) (2) [3...]
# (1) double, magnitude
# (2) int, dof
# [3...] int, node tags

For material properties:

initial
initial material history (1) [2...]
# (1) int, material model tag
# [2...] double, initial history vector

docs.title: Short Forms
docs.text:
The keywords disp, vel and acc are short forms of displacement, velocity and acceleration respectively.

The angularvelocity (or avel) keyword initialises a rigid-body rotation about a reference node.

initial
initial angularvelocity (1) (2) [3...]
initial avel (1) (2) [3...]
# (1) double, three components of the angular velocity vector
# (2) int, reference node tag
# [3...] int, tags of nodes whose initial velocities are set

The velocity assigned to each listed node is the cross product of the angular velocity vector and the node position relative to the reference node.

docs.title: Remarks
docs.text:
Proper initial nodal conditions are important for dynamic analysis. Some time integration algorithms are sensitive to initial conditions. For example, if a standard sinusoidal wave is used as excitation, its initial displacement and acceleration are zero, so nothing needs to be changed. Its initial velocity, however, must be unity. If it is not set to unity, the results may oscillate.

Some material models support user-defined initial history variables. This can be useful when modelling, for example, rolled or annealed metal. Different material models may store history variables in different layouts. Please refer to the specific model for details.

docs.title: interaction
docs.text: The interaction command defines a pairwise interaction between particles for use by molecular dynamics constraints such as MolecularDynamics2D and MolecularDynamics3D. Two interaction types are available: Hertzian and FixedParticle. Related particle contact constraints are described on the ParticleCollision page.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text:
interaction
interaction (1) (2) ...
# (1) string, interaction type
# (2) int, unique interaction tag

docs.title: Remarks
docs.text:
1. Hertzian takes no arguments beyond the tag and applies a Hertzian contact force between particle pairs.
  2. FixedParticle takes a penalty multiplier followed by the tags of the particles to be fixed, for example, interaction FixedParticle 2 1E4 3.
  3. Interaction objects are referenced by tag in molecular dynamics constraints, for example, constraint MolecularDynamics3D 1 1 2 uses interactions 1 and 2.

docs.title: load
docs.text:
The load command creates loads applied to nodes.

Currently, concentrated node-based loads can be applied in terms of force, displacement and acceleration. All external forces are eventually converted to concentrated nodal forces. Commands for distributed load patterns may therefore not be available in the foreseeable future.

All loads are initialised and processed in parallel via global mutexes.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text:
All loads share a similar syntax:

load
load <load_type> <unique_tag> <arguments that define the specific load...>

docs.title: Nodal Load
docs.text:
To apply loads to nodes,

nodalload
# to apply nodal concentrated force
cload (1) (2) (3) (4) (5...)
load cload (1) (2) (3) (4) (5...)
# to apply nodal displacement
displacement (1) (2) (3) (4) (5...)
load displacement (1) (2) (3) (4) (5...)
# (1) int, unique tag
# (2) int, amplitude tag, 0 to use a default `Ramp` amplitude
# (3) double, nominal magnitude
# (4) string, dof identifier
# (5...) int, node tags

# to apply nodal acceleration
acceleration (1) (2) (3) (4) [5...]
load acceleration (1) (2) (3) (4) [5...]
# (1) int, unique tag
# (2) int, amplitude tag, 0 to use a default `Ramp` amplitude
# (3) double, nominal magnitude
# (4) string, dof identifier
# [5...] int, node tags

The keyword cload is the abbreviation for concentrated load.

docs.title: Body Force
docs.text:
Some elements support body force. The corresponding element pages indicate which elements support it.

bodyforce
bodyforce (1) (2) (3) (4) (5...)
load bodyforce (1) (2) (3) (4) (5...)
# (1) int, unique tag
# (2) int, amplitude tag, 0 to use a default `Ramp` amplitude
# (3) double, nominal magnitude
# (4) string, dof identifier
# (5...) int, element tags

docs.title: Load Applied to Node/Element Groups
docs.text:
To apply loads to groups,

groupload
# on node groups
groupcload (1) (2) (3) (4) (5...)
groupdisplacement (1) (2) (3) (4) (5...)
load groupcload (1) (2) (3) (4) (5...)
load groupdisplacement (1) (2) (3) (4) (5...)

# on element groups
groupbodyforce (1) (2) (3) (4) (5...)
load groupbodyforce (1) (2) (3) (4) (5...)

# (1) int, unique tag
# (2) int, amplitude tag, 0 to use a default `Ramp` amplitude
# (3) double, nominal magnitude
# (4) string, dof identifier
# (5...) int, group tags

docs.title: Support Excitation
docs.text:
For response history analysis, it is sometimes necessary to apply excitations to supports. Multi-support excitation is automatically supported when different excitations are assigned to different supports.

support
supportdisplacement (1) (2) (3) (4) (5...)
supportvelocity (1) (2) (3) (4) (5...)
supportacceleration (1) (2) (3) (4) (5...)
load supportdisplacement (1) (2) (3) (4) (5...)
load supportvelocity (1) (2) (3) (4) (5...)
load supportacceleration (1) (2) (3) (4) (5...)
# (1) int, unique tag
# (2) int, amplitude tag, 0 to use a default `Ramp` amplitude
# (3) double, nominal magnitude
# (4) string, dof identifier
# (5...) int, node tags

Essentially, supportdisplacement, supportvelocity and supportacceleration are all implemented as displacement loads. A displacement-controlled scheme is therefore enabled automatically.

Although designed for response history analysis, these commands can also apply acceleration or velocity to any nodes, not only supports.

difference in explicit and implicit dynamic analysis

Implicit time integration schemes use displacement as the primary variable. Thus, supportdisplacement, supportvelocity and supportacceleration all convert to the corresponding nodal displacement. Explicit time integration schemes use acceleration as the primary variable. Because they are explicit methods, there is no way to obtain the corresponding nodal displacement or velocity from the acceleration. Thus, in explicit dynamic analysis, supportdisplacement is identical to supportacceleration, as both apply acceleration to the nodes. supportvelocity is not available in explicit dynamic analysis.

docs.title: Validation
docs.text:
The algorithms implemented are not a naive integration. All support excitations are guaranteed to be consistent with the time integration scheme used. For all interpolating methods, the exact same input can be observed in the output. Extrapolating methods do not guarantee the exact same input in the output.

The following validation can be obtained via the script. It defines a simple column and applies a support motion at the base (fixed) end of the column. It measures both the top (free) end displacement and the base (fixed) end acceleration.

Interpolating schemes produce the same acceleration history at the base as the input. Extrapolating schemes yield some difference because they extrapolate. Such an error may cause spurious responses in the structure. This problem is discussed in this paper.

docs.title: Uniformly Distributed Load (UDL)
docs.text:
lineudl
lineudl2d (1) (2) (3) (4) (5...)
lineudl3d (1) (2) (3) (4) (5...)
load lineudl2d (1) (2) (3) (4) (5...)
load lineudl3d (1) (2) (3) (4) (5...)
# (1) int, unique tag
# (2) int, amplitude tag, 0 to use a default `Ramp` amplitude
# (3) double, nominal magnitude
# (4) string, dof identifier
# (5...) int, node tags

The magnitude can be either positive or negative, which applies the load in different directions of the assigned DoF. Only translational DoFs are supported, so use 1, 2, 3, U1, U2 or U3 only.

docs.title: Reference Load
docs.text:
For arc-length analysis, a reference load can be defined with the RefForce command.

refload
refforce (1) (2) (3) (4) (5...)
refload (1) (2) (3) (4) (5...)
load refforce (1) (2) (3) (4) (5...)
load refload (1) (2) (3) (4) (5...)
# (1) int, unique tag
# (2) int, amplitude tag, has no effect in arc-length analysis, just a placeholder, can be set to 0
# (3) double, reference magnitude
# (4) string, dof identifier
# (5...) int, node tags

docs.title: Short Forms
docs.text:
The leading load keyword can be replaced by a dedicated first-level command with the same arguments.

disp and dispload are equivalent to displacement.

groupdisp and groupdispload are equivalent to groupdisplacement.

refforce, refload and refereceload are equivalent to the ReferenceLoad type.

grouprefforce, grouprefload and grouprefereceload are equivalent to the GroupReferenceLoad type.

The misspelling refereceload is intentional in the implementation.

docs.title: Remarks
docs.text:
1. The leading load keyword can often be omitted for simplicity.
  2. By default, acceleration is applied to all active nodes in the model if [5...] is not assigned.
  3. The true load magnitude is the product of the nominal magnitude and the amplitude. This is similar to ABAQUS.
  4. The multipoint displacement control algorithm MPDC is automatically enabled if a displacement or groupdisplacement is used.
  5. Optionally, the displacement can be applied with an MPC constraint.
  6. The multipoint displacement control algorithm MPDC is automatically enabled if supportdisplacement, supportvelocity and/or supportacceleration are used.

It must be noted that nodal displacement loads are only valid for a single step. If a displacement load is defined within a step, it is activated for that step only.

All other load types stay active once activated.

The DoF identifier can take the following values. Accepted inputs vary with the selected element type(s) and the problem type.

identifier implies of type PINNED, P DOF::U1, DOF::U2, DOF::U3 displacement ENCASTRE, E DOF::U1, DOF::U2, DOF::U3, DOF::UR1, DOF::UR2, DOF::UR3 XSYMM, X DOF::U1, DOF::UR2, DOF::UR3 YSYMM, Y DOF::UR1, DOF::U2, DOF::UR3 ZSYMM, Z DOF::UR1, DOF::UR2, DOF::U3 1, U1 DOF::U1 2, U2 DOF::U2 3, U3 DOF::U3 4, U4, UR1 DOF::UR1 5, U5, UR2 DOF::UR2 6, U6, UR3 DOF::UR3 FU1 DOF::FU1 fluid FU2 DOF::FU2 FU3 DOF::FU3 FUR1 DOF::FUR1 FUR2 DOF::FUR2 FUR3 DOF::FUR3 RADIAL DOF::RADIAL axisymmetric AXIAL DOF::AXIAL axisymmetric, rod/beam like RS DOF::RS beam RW DOF::RW 3D beam DAMAGE DOF::DAMAGE special damage DoF PRESSURE DOF::PRESSURE special pressure DoF TEMPERATURE DOF::TEMPERATURE thermal DOF WARP DOF::WARP special warp DoF (in some beams)

docs.title: mass
docs.text: The mass command creates a point mass element attached to a single node for dynamic analysis. It contributes only to the mass matrix, with no stiffness, and shares the element tag pool with other elements.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text:
mass
mass (1) (2) (3) (4...)
# (1) int, unique mass tag
# (2) int, node tag
# (3) double, magnitude
# (4...) int, dof tags, at least one and at most six

docs.title: Remarks
docs.text:
1. At least one DoF tag is required, and DoF tags greater than six are rejected.
  2. For example, mass 3 2 10 1 2 3 assigns a magnitude of 10 to DoFs 1, 2, and 3 of node 2.
  3. See the Mass element page for details.

docs.title: material
docs.text:
The material command constructs a material prototype. Each prototype requires a unique tag. During the initialization procedure, all valid elements request a copy of the associated material prototype from the problem domain for local use.

Density is treated as a material property. To define a consistent mass matrix, a proper density often needs to be assigned in the material prototype definition. Most material models accept the density as the final optional argument.

Please refer to the specific material types for details.

Some material models support initial conditions. To define initial conditions for a specific material model, use the initial command. The initial conditions are defined on the material prototype. Thus, several material models must be defined if different initial conditions are required.

docs.title: modifier
docs.text:
modifier objects modify element response that is not considered in the element itself. Typical examples include the element damping matrix and the lumped mass matrix.

If several modifiers are defined, they are applied to the system sequentially in tag order. They are not executed in parallel because different orders may lead to different results.

Users should pay extra attention to the order in which modifiers are defined.

Please refer to Modifier for the available modifiers.

docs.title: node
docs.text: Nodes are basic components in FE models. The node command constructs nodes.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text:
node
node (1) [2...]
# (1) int, unique tag
# [2...] double, coordinates

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
A unique tag is required to identify different nodes. The tag must be an unsigned integer; negative values are not allowed. Although zero is a valid tag, it is recommended to number nodes starting from one. It is not recommended to use an arbitrarily large tag, although the maximum tag is about four billion (unsigned int). An unnecessarily large node tag may lead to excessive memory allocation because some functions create matrices sized by the largest node tag to ensure all nodes can be stored.

There is no limit on the dimension of a node. A trivial node (without a location) can be defined as follows. Such a node is generally not used to define elements.

Text Only
node 1

Nodes with different dimensions can coexist.

Text Only
node 1
node 2 2. 0.
node 3 0.
node 4 9. 8. 7. 1.

During initialisation, the dimension of each node is checked to ensure that the connected elements can work properly. Any excess dimensions are ignored, but not discarded, during analysis. For example, consider a 2D analysis with the following snippet.

Text Only
node 1 3.
node 2 2. 1.
# later define a 2D element connecting node 1 and node 2

The dimension of node 1 is automatically expanded to two with zero filling. Node 1 then represents $\((3.0,0.0)\)$ in the 2D space. If, on the other hand, a 1D analysis is performed, the second coordinate is ignored.

It is still recommended to define nodes with proper coordinates. Generating a node list from an ABAQUS input file is straightforward.

docs.title: Output Types
docs.text:
The following quantities can be recorded using the commands similar to plainrecorder 1 Node (output_type) (nodes...).

variable label physical meaning U all displacement components U1, U2, U3, UR1, UR2, UR3 displacement along each DoF V all velocity components V1, V2, V3, VR1, VR2, VR3 velocity along each DoF A all acceleration components A1, A2, A3, AR1, AR2, AR3 acceleration along each DoF RF all resistance components RF1, RF2, RF3, RM1, RM2, RM3 resistance along each DoF DF all damping force components DF1, DF2, DF3, DM1, DM2, DM3 damping force along each DoF IF all inertial force components IF1, IF2, IF3, IM1, IM2, IM3 inertial force along each DoF

docs.title: Remarks
docs.text:
1. For static analysis, normally only displacement U and resistance RF are activated. Recording other quantities therefore returns trivial results.
  2. If the required quantity is not active, the output is empty.
  3. The damping and inertial forces are collected from all elements in the model. It must be noted that the recorded values do not include contributions that do not stem from elements. For example, the damping force given by global damping models cannot be split among individual elements, so it is not reflected in the nodal damping force. This design is necessary because one may wish to separate contributions from various sources.
  4. To record global damping and inertial forces that account for the total force, use GDF, GDF1, GDF2, GDF3, GDF4, GDF5, GDF6, GIF, GIF1, GIF2, GIF3, GIF4, GIF5 and GIF6. These stand for global damping force and global inertial force.

docs.title: orientation
docs.text: The orientation command defines the local reference frame of a 3D beam element. The resulting object is referenced by its tag to transform between global and local coordinates.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text:
orientation
orientation (1) (2) (3) (4) (5)
# (1) string, orientation type
# (2) int, unique orientation tag
# (3) double, x component of the reference vector
# (4) double, y component of the reference vector
# (5) double, z component of the reference vector

docs.title: Remarks
docs.text:
1. The available types are B3DL, B3DC, B3DOSL, and B3DOSC.
  2. B3DL and B3DOSL use a linear transformation, while B3DC and B3DOSC use a corotational formulation.
  3. Beams such as B31/F31 require B3DL or B3DC, while the open-section beam EB31OS requires B3DOSL or B3DOSC.
  4. See Orientation for the definition of the local axes and worked examples.

docs.title: recorder
docs.text:
Model response can be recorded and output in a tabular fashion.

Two main file formats are currently supported:

  1. plain text,
  2. HDF5 file.

Please refer to Recorder.md for details.

The hdf5recorder and plainrecorder commands are shortcuts that create an HDF5 or plain text recorder directly, without the file type argument.

docs.title: section
docs.text: The section command defines a section that can be attached to beam elements. Please refer to the specific section types for the available syntax.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text:
section
section (1) (2) ...
# (1) string, section type
# (2) int, unique section tag

For code-based sections, a designation string is required between the section type and the tag, for example, section US2D W21X68 1 1.

docs.title: variable
docs.text: Although the parser is not intended to function as a scripting language interpreter, it is sometimes useful to have limited macro-like capabilities.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text:
One can use var or variable to define variables (macros).

variable
variable (1) (2)
# (1) string, name
# (2) any read as string, value

To reference a defined variable, use a dollar sign $ followed by the variable name. For example,

Text Only
variable ele_t GCMQG

element $ele_t 1 1 2 8 7 1 1

This is equivalent to the following.

Text Only
element GCMQG 1 1 2 8 7 1 1

variable must exist

The variable must exist (have been defined) when referenced. Thus, the order matters in this situation. This is because variables and macros are scanned and replaced while the command is being processed.

More advanced scripting functionality should be provided by other tools.

docs.title: benchmark
docs.text:
The benchmark command benchmarks the platform to provide a performance baseline.

The routine preallocates a square matrix of size 5120 and solves it 50 times. Unlike other approaches that normally rely on the dgemm subroutine, it uses dgesv. For FEM, the main operations are solving matrices rather than multiplying them.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text:
benchmark
benchmark

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
The basic idea of the benchmark resembles that of linpack. It is not intended to be as versatile as linpack, so it does not provide any configurable options.

The theoretical maximum GFLOPS is rarely achievable in practical applications. Modern hardware is often bounded by other factors such as memory bandwidth.

For example, use perf on this benchmark to measure the GFLOPS:

Bash
echo "benchmark" >>b
echo "exit" >>b
perf stat -e fp_arith_inst_retired.128b_packed_double,fp_arith_inst_retired.256b_packed_double,fp_arith_inst_retired.512b_packed_double,fp_arith_inst_retired.scalar_double suanpan -f b

The corresponding result is

Text Only
+--------------------------------------------------+
|   __        __         suanPan is an open source |
|  /  \      |  \           FEM framework (64-bit) |
|  \__       |__/  __   __      Betelgeuse (2.4.0) |
|     \ |  | |    |  \ |  |      by tlc @ b3918adf |
|  \__/ |__| |    |__X |  |    all rights reserved |
|                           10.5281/zenodo.1285221 |
+--------------------------------------------------+
|  🧮 https://github.com/TLCFEM/suanPan            |
|  📚 https://github.com/TLCFEM/suanPan-manual     |
+--------------------------------------------------+
|  🔋 https://gitter.im/suanPan-dev/community      |
+--------------------------------------------------+

[==================================================]
Current platform rates (higher is better): 25.58.

Time Wasted: 39.3980 Seconds.

 Performance counter stats for 'suanpan -f b':

        17,075,053      fp_arith_inst_retired.128b_packed_double                                   
         3,849,289      fp_arith_inst_retired.256b_packed_double                                   
   563,539,901,688      fp_arith_inst_retired.512b_packed_double                                   
       122,202,329      fp_arith_inst_retired.scalar_double                                   

      39.428329959 seconds time elapsed

     130.321384000 seconds user
       3.369368000 seconds sys

This roughly gives 114 GFLOPS, which is around $\(60\%\)$ of the theoretical maximum GFLOPS of an i7-1185G7 processor. Of course, the actual performance depends on many other factors. The numbers here are indicative. A rate of $\(2n\)$ means the platform is two times faster than a rate of $\(n\)$.

Practical FEM involves other processes such as updating elemental stiffness (small matrix manipulations) and assembling global stiffness (random memory accesses). As a result, the performance of an analysis is a fraction of the GFLOPS of this benchmark test.

docs.title: clear
docs.text: The clear command clears all information in the current domain.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text:
clear
clear

docs.title: command
docs.text: The command command lists all available commands.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text:
command
command

docs.title: Enable/Disable/Remove Objects
docs.text:
In suanPan, defining an object does not necessarily mean it will be considered in the analysis. Each object has an 'active' flag, and only active objects are considered. Thus, it is possible to define a set of candidate objects (for example, a number of loads) and test different cases with different objects.

Furthermore, wrongly defined objects can be removed before performing the analysis.

Text Only
enable (1) [2...]
disable (1) [2...]
remove (1) [2...]
# (1) string, object type
# [2...] int, tags

For object types, possible values are: amplitude, constraint, converger, criterion, domain, element, expression, group, integrator, load, material, modifier, node, orientation, recorder, section, solver and step.

The mute command is an alias of disable.

The erase and delete commands are aliases of remove.

The special object type all is accepted by enable only and activates every object in the current domain.

docs.title: Enable/Disable Print Output
docs.text:
Output can also be enabled or disabled. Printing to the screen buffer takes time. Once the model is confirmed to be correct, output can be disabled to improve speed. Third-party libraries are not controlled by this command and may still print.

Text Only
enable print
disable print

docs.title: example
docs.text: The example command establishes and executes a minimum example automatically. It builds a two-node elastic truss under tension, solves a static step, and reports the nodal force.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text:
example
example

docs.title: Remarks
docs.text: The command takes no arguments and builds the model in a new domain, leaving the current model untouched. Each command is echoed to the terminal and followed by a one-second pause before it is processed. The model uses two nodes, an Elastic1D material with modulus 52, and a T2D2 truss element with area 93. The reported force at node 2 is P = UEA/L = 1.4 * 52 * 93 / 2 = 3385.2.

docs.title: exit
docs.text:

The quit command is an alias of exit.

docs.title: Syntax

exit
exit
