docs.title: Iterative Solver
docs.text:
[available from v3.1]

To use iterative solvers, use the following settings:

Text Only
set sparse_mat true
set system_solver lis [1]
# [1] string, lis solver options

The Lis library is used to provide the functionality.

Lis provides a wide variety of iterative solvers and preconditioners. Not all of them yield good performance. Whether it is faster than a direct solver depends on the problem.

All possible options, which are copied directly from the Lis documentation, are listed below.

For example, to use the BiCGSTAB solver with an ILU(2) preconditioner and print statistics, use the following settings:

Text Only
set sparse_mat true
set system_solver lis -i bicgstab -p ilu -ilu_fill 2 -print out

docs.title: Solver Related Options
docs.text: Solver Option Auxiliary Options CG -i {cg\|1} BiCG -i {bicg\|2} CGS -i {cgs\|3} BiCGSTAB -i {bicgstab\|4} BiCGSTAB(l) -i {bicgstabl\|5} -ell [2] The degree $\(l\)$ GPBiCG -i {gpbicg\|6} TFQMR -i {tfqmr\|7} Orthomin(m) -i {orthomin\|8} -restart [40] The restart value $\(m\)$ GMRES(m) -i {gmres\|9} -restart [40] The restart value $\(m\)$ Jacobi -i {jacobi\|10} Gauss-Seidel -i {gs\|11} SOR -i {sor\|12} -omega [1.9] The relaxation coefficient $\(\omega\)$ ($\(0<\omega<2\)$) BiCGSafe -i {bicgsafe\|13} CR -i {cr\|14} BiCR -i {bicr\|15} CRS -i {crs\|16} BiCRSTAB -i {bicrstab\|17} GPBiCR -i {gpbicr\|18} BiCRSafe -i {bicrsafe\|19} FGMRES(m) -i {fgmres\|20} -restart [40] The restart value $\(m\)$ IDR(s) -i {idrs\|21} -irestart [2] The restart value $\(s\)$ IDR(1) -i {idr1\|22} MINRES -i {minres\|23} COCG -i {cocg\|24} COCR -i {cocr\|25}

docs.title: Preconditioner Related Options
docs.text: Preconditioner Option Auxiliary Options None -p {none\|0} Jacobi -p {jacobi\|1} ILU(k) -p {ilu\|2} -ilu_fill [0] The fill level $\(k\)$ SSOR -p {ssor\|3} -ssor_omega [1.0] The relaxation coefficient $\(\omega\)$ ($\(0<\omega<2\)$) Hybrid -p {hybrid\|4} -hybrid_i [sor] The linear solver -hybrid_maxiter [25] The maximum number of iterations -hybrid_tol [1.0e-3] The convergence tolerance -hybrid_omega [1.5] The relaxation coefficient $\(\omega\)$ of the SOR ($\(0<\omega<2\)$) -hybrid_ell [2] The degree $\(l\)$ of the BiCGSTAB(l) -hybrid_restart [40] The restart values of the GMRES and Orthomin I+S -p {is\|5} -is_alpha [1.0] The parameter $\(\alpha\)$ of $\(I+\alpha S^{(m)}\)$ -is_m [3] The parameter $\(m\)$ of $\(I+\alpha S^{(m)}\)$ SAINV -p {sainv\|6} -sainv_drop [0.05] The drop criterion SA-AMG -p {saamg\|7} -saamg_unsym [false] Select the unsymmetric version (The matrix structure must be symmetric) -saamg_theta [0.05\|0.12] The drop criterion $\(a^2_{ij}\le\theta^2\|a_{ii}\|\|a_{jj}\|\)$ (symmetric or unsymmetric) Crout ILU -p {iluc\|8} -iluc_drop [0.05] The drop criterion -iluc_rate [5.0] The ratio of the maximum fill-in ILUT -p {ilut\|9} Additive -adds true -adds_iter [1] The number of iterations Schwarz

docs.title: Other Options
docs.text: Option -maxiter [1000] The maximum number of iterations -tol [1.0e-12] The convergence tolerance $\(tol\)$ -tol_w [1.0] The convergence tolerance $\(tol_w\)$ -print [0] The output of the residual history -print {none\|0} None -print {mem\|1} Save the residual history -print {out\|2} Output it to the standard output -print {all\|3} Save the residual history and output it to the standard output -scale [0] The scaling (The result will overwrite the original matrix and vectors) -scale {none\|0} No scaling -scale {jacobi\|1} The Jacobi scaling $\(D^{-1}Ax=D^{-1}b\)$ ($\(D\)$ represents the diagonal of $\(A=(a_{ij})\)$) -scale {symm_diag\|2} The diagonal scaling $\(D^{-1/2}AD^{-1/2}x=D^{-1/2}b\)$ ($\(D^{-1/2}\)$ represents the diagonal matrix with $\(1/\sqrt{a_{ii}}\)$ as the diagonal) -initx_zeros [1] The behavior of the initial vector $\(x_{0}\)$ -initx_zeros {false\|0} The components are given by the argument x of the function lis_solve() -initx_zeros {true\|1} All the components are set to $\(0\)$ -conv_cond [0] The convergence condition -conv_cond {nrm2_r\|0} $\(\|\|b-Ax\|\|_2 \le tol * \|\|b-Ax_0\|\|_2\)$ -conv_cond {nrm2_b\|1} $\(\|\|b-Ax\|\|_2 \le tol * \|\|b\|\|_2\)$ -conv_cond {nrm1_b\|2} $\(\|\|b-Ax\|\|_1 \le tol_w * \|\|b\|\|_1 + tol\)$ -omp_num_threads [t] The number of threads (t represents the maximum number of threads) -storage [0] The matrix storage format -storage_block [2] The block size of the BSR and BSC formats -f [0] The precision of the linear solver -f {double\|0} Double precision -f {quad\|1} Double-double (quadruple) precision

docs.title: list
docs.text: The list command prints the tags of the objects of a given type that are stored in the current domain.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text:
list
list (1)
# (1) string, object type

docs.title: Remarks
docs.text: The object type can be amplitude, constraint, converger, criterion, element, expression, group, integrator, load, material, modifier, node, orientation, recorder, section, solver or step.

docs.title: magma
docs.text: The MAGMA library provides many algorithms for solving sparse linear systems on GPUs. To enable the MAGMA solver, a valid CUDA installation must be present. The application should be compiled with the -DSP_ENABLE_CUDA=ON and -DSP_ENABLE_MAGMA=ON options.

docs.title: Compiling MAGMA
docs.text:
Refer to the MAGMA documentation for compilation instructions. On Windows, the following options are used, tailored for one specific platform:

JSON
{
  "cmake.configureSettings": {
    "LAPACK_LIBRARIES": [
      "C:/Program Files (x86)/Intel/oneAPI/mkl/2023.0.0/lib/intel64/mkl_intel_lp64.lib",
      "C:/Program Files (x86)/Intel/oneAPI/mkl/2023.0.0/lib/intel64/mkl_intel_thread.lib",
      "C:/Program Files (x86)/Intel/oneAPI/mkl/2023.0.0/lib/intel64/mkl_core.lib",
      "C:/Program Files (x86)/Intel/oneAPI/compiler/2023.0.0/windows/compiler/lib/intel64_win/libiomp5md.lib"
    ],
    "MKL_ROOT": "C:/Program Files (x86)/Intel/oneAPI/mkl/2023.0.0/",
    "GPU_TARGET": "Turing",
    "FORTRAN_CONVENTION": "-DADD_",
    "CMAKE_INSTALL_PREFIX": "magma-build"
  }
}

docs.title: Compiling suanPan
docs.text:
Once MAGMA is compiled, the application should be compiled with the -DSP_ENABLE_CUDA=ON and -DSP_ENABLE_MAGMA=ON options. An additional path must be set to the MAGMA installation directory.

JSON
{
  "cmake.configureSettings": {
    "SP_ENABLE_CUDA": "ON",
    "SP_ENABLE_MAGMA": "ON",
    "MAGMA_PATH": "magma/installation/root"
  }
}

The following files must be present: ${MAGMA_PATH}/include/magma.h, ${MAGMA_PATH}/lib/libmagma.a and ${MAGMA_PATH}/lib/libmagma_sparse.a.

docs.title: Using MAGMA Solver
docs.text:
With MAGMA enabled, use the following to select the MAGMA solver:

Text Only
set sparse_mat true
set system_solver magma [(key value)...]

The following key-value options are available to customise the solver:

key value --mscale NOSCALE, UNITDIAG, UNITROW, UNITCOL, UNITDIAGCOL, UNITROWCOL --solver CG, PCG, BICG, PBICG, BICGSTAB, PBICGSTAB, QMR, PQMR, TFQMR, PTFQMR GMRES, PGMRES, LOBPCG, LSQR, JACOBI, BA, BAO, IDR, PIDR, CGS, PCGS BOMBARDMENT, ITERREF, PARDISO --precond CG, PCG, BICGSTAB, QMR, TFQMR, PTFQMR, GMRES, PGMRES, LOBPCG JACOBI, BA, BAO, IDR, PIDR, CGS, PCGS, BOMBARDMENT, ITERREF, ILU IC, ILUT, ICT, PARILU, AIC, PARIC, PARICT, PARILUT, CUSTOMIC, CUSTOMILU ISAI, NONE --trisolver CG, BICGSTAB, QMR, TFQMR, GMRES, JACOBI, VBJACOBI BA, BAO, IDR, CGS, CUSOLVE, SYNCFREESOLVE, ISAI, NONE --basic 0 or 1 --blocksize positive integer --alignment positive integer --restart positive integer --atol positive floating-point number --rtol positive floating-point number --maxiter positive integer --verbose 0 or 1 --prestart positive integer --patol positive floating-point number --prtol positive floating-point number --piters positive integer --ppattern positive integer --psweeps positive integer --plevels positive integer

Note that not all iterative solvers are stable and applicable on every system.

docs.title: materialtest
docs.text: This command category tests most material models that depend on strain input only without establishing an FE model. Some wrappers and material models that rely on other material models cannot be tested in this way.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text:
materialtest
materialTest1D (1) (2) (3) [4...]
# (1) int, unique tag of the material model to use
# (2) double, size of per strain increment
# (3) int, number of steps along increment direction
# [4...] int, optional numbers of steps for strain history

materialTest2D (1) (2...4) (5) [6...]
# (1) int, unique tag of the material model to use
# (2...4) double, size of per strain increment
# (5) int, number of steps along increment direction
# [6...] int, optional numbers of steps for strain history

materialTest3D (1) (2...7) (8) [9...]
# (1) int, unique tag of the material model to use
# (2...7) double, size of per strain increment
# (8) int, number of steps along increment direction
# [9...] int, optional numbers of steps for strain history

docs.title: Remarks
docs.text:
1. The increment size can be either positive or negative.
  2. The loading direction reverses after the given number of steps.
  3. The strain-stress history is saved to RESULT.txt. If HDF5 support is enabled, the result is additionally saved to RESULT.h5. A gnuplot file named RESULT.plt is also generated.

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
To use the tester, define a material beforehand. Here, a Bilinear1D model is defined with elastic modulus $\(E=1000.0\)$, yield stress $\(\sigma_y=10.0\)$ and a negative hardening ratio $\(h=-0.2\)$.

Text Only
material Bilinear1D 1 1000.0 10.0 -0.2

The following command loads in the positive strain direction for 300 increments of size $\(0.0001\)$. It then loads in the negative direction for another 300 increments and finally in the positive direction for 200 increments. The ending strain is $\(\varepsilon=0.02\)$.

Text Only
materialTest1D 1 0.0001 300 300 200

The output is shown below.

docs.title: materialtestbyload
docs.text: This command category tests most material models that depend on load/stress input only without establishing an FE model. Some wrappers and material models that rely on other material models cannot be tested in this way.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text:
materialtestbyload
materialTestByLoad1D (1) (2) (3) [4...]
# (1) int, unique tag of the material model to use
# (2) double, size of per stress increment
# (3) int, number of steps along increment direction
# [4...] int, optional numbers of steps for stress history

materialTestByLoad2D (1) (2...4) (5) [6...]
# (1) int, unique tag of the material model to use
# (2...4) double, size of per stress increment
# (5) int, number of steps along increment direction
# [6...] int, optional numbers of steps for stress history

materialTestByLoad3D (1) (2...7) (8) [9...]
# (1) int, unique tag of the material model to use
# (2...7) double, size of per stress increment
# (8) int, number of steps along increment direction
# [9...] int, optional numbers of steps for stress history

docs.title: Remarks
docs.text: 1. The Newton-Raphson method is implemented to solve the corresponding strain increments. Softening models should therefore not be tested in this way.

docs.title: overview
docs.text: The overview command starts an interactive guided tour of suanPan. It introduces the basic modelling workflow, such as defining nodes, elements, steps and running commands. Type q at any prompt to quit the tour and return to normal interactive mode.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text:
overview
overview

docs.title: Remarks
docs.text: The tour operates on a separate model, so it does not modify the current domain. Each topic is printed step by step and the tour waits for the requested command. Press Enter to continue after a topic is completed.

docs.title: peek
docs.text: The peek command prints predefined information. It has no effect if global screen output is switched off.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text:
peek
peek node (1)
peek element (1)
peek material (1)
peek constraint (1)
peek recorder (1)
peek solver (1)
peek integrator (1)
peek group (1)
peek nodegroup (1)
peek amplitude (1)
peek expression (1)
# (1) int, object tag

peek eigenvalue
peek output_folder
peek num_threads
peek num_nodes
peek statistics
peek stats

peek nodegroup prints every node contained in the given group.

peek output_folder prints the current output folder.

peek num_threads and peek num_nodes print the current thread and node counts.

peek statistics (or peek stats) prints accumulated timings for the major analysis phases.

docs.title: plot
docs.text:
The plot command plots and saves visualisations as files.

Only binaries compiled with VTK libraries can use this command. Otherwise, it does nothing.

Since Paraview can perform all kinds of post-processing, the objective here is not to provide full-featured visualisation support.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text:
The plot command uses a different parsing mechanism.

plot
plot [-keyword [-parameters]...]

Available keywords and corresponding parameters are listed as follows.

  1. scale controls the scale of the deformed configuration. A single double value is required as a parameter. The default is zero (undeformed). Example: scale 2
  2. type controls which quantity is extracted and plotted. A single string is required as a parameter. The available values can be found in the output types. Example: type U1
  3. fontsize controls the font size of the legend, title, etc. This has no effect if the plot is saved. Example: fontsize 14
  4. nobar disables the legend in the plot window.
  5. size controls the size of the plot window. Two double values are required. Example: size 300 400
  6. save specifies the file name. A string value is required. The extension suffix is appended automatically. Example: save S11
  7. element groups the plotted quantity by element. It requires no parameter. Example: element
  8. material groups the plotted quantity by material. It is mutually exclusive with section. Example: material
  9. section groups the plotted quantity by section. It is mutually exclusive with material. Example: section

docs.title: Remarks
docs.text: Invoking this command with proper parameters spawns an interactive rendering window using VTK. It offers a quick view of the model. The window can be closed by pressing the q key. The window does not block the application, so multiple quantities can be plotted at the same time. However, a new analysis is not performed until all windows are closed.

docs.title: protect
docs.text: In structural optimization, for example, elements are disabled when necessary. For some analyses, certain elements must never be disabled. Use protect to prevent those elements from being modified.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text:
protect
protect node (1...)
protect element (1...)
# (1...) int, node/element tags

docs.title: pwd
docs.text:
The pwd command resembles its counterpart in Unix-like systems. It can print or set the current working directory.

To load files from another path while saving keystrokes, set the current working directory to the folder containing the model script first.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text:
To check the current working directory, use

pwd
pwd

To change the current working directory, use

Text Only
pwd (1)
# (1) string, new absolute working path

On Windows, \ must be written as \\ or /. Relative paths are resolved against the current working directory.

docs.title: qrcode
docs.text: The qrcode command prints a QR code to the terminal. The code is rendered directly with Unicode block characters.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text:
qrcode
qrcode

docs.title: Remarks
docs.text: The command takes no arguments.

docs.title: reset
docs.text: Reset Model

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text:
The reset command resets the trial state to the latest converged state.

reset
reset

docs.title: response_spectrum
docs.text:
Compute Response Spectrum of a Given Accelerogram

Minimum version: v2.6

Reference:

  1. 10.1016/S0267-7261(05)80015-6

Please note the following.

  1. Only applies to an elastic system.
  2. Only trivial initial conditions are accounted for.

docs.title: Form A
docs.text:
For an accelerogram record stored in a single-column plain text file, use the following syntax.

response_spectrum
response_spectrum (1) (2) (3) (4)
# (1) string, file path of the accelerogram file
# (2) string, file path of the period file
# (3) double, sampling interval
# (4) double, damping ratio

The accelerogram stores discrete acceleration amplitudes in the first column of the file.

The desired period points where the response spectrum is computed are stored in the first column of the period file. The period file itself can have multiple columns, but only the first column is used.

Because the accelerogram only provides the amplitudes, the sampling interval must be provided as the (3) argument.

docs.title: Form B
docs.text:
For an accelerogram record stored in a double-column plain text file, use the following syntax.

Text Only
response_spectrum (1) (2) (3)
# (1) string, file path of the accelerogram file
# (2) string, file path of the period file
# (3) double, damping ratio

The accelerogram stores the time and acceleration amplitudes in the first and second columns of the file.

The time series must be equally spaced.

The desired period points where the response spectrum is computed are stored in the first column of the period file. The period file itself can have multiple columns, but only the first column is used.

docs.title: Remarks
docs.text:
The sampling interval is provided as the (3) argument in Form A and is computed from the time series in Form B.

The same sampling interval is used in Lee's algorithm to compute the response histories. If the provided interval is large, the response spectra may be inaccurate. Use the upsampling command to process the accelerogram before using the response_spectrum command.

docs.title: Example
docs.text: See this example.

docs.title: save
docs.text: The save command saves data to disk.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text:
save
save recorder (1...)
# (1...) int, tags of recorders to be saved

The command can also save analysis data such as system matrices and the model itself.

save
save stiffness [name]
save mass [name]
save damping [name]
save model [name]
# [name] optional string, output file name

The default file names are K for the stiffness matrix, M for the mass matrix, C for the damping matrix and Model.h5 for the model.

docs.title: sdof_response
docs.text:
Compute Response of a Single Degree of Freedom Oscillator to a Given Acceleration Record

Minimum version: v2.6

Reference:

  1. 10.1016/S0267-7261(05)80015-6

Please note the following.

  1. Only applies to an elastic system.
  2. Only trivial initial conditions are accounted for.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text:
The frequency of the oscillator is used. Its unit is Hertz (Hz).

The natural frequency must not be passed to the command. The natural frequency has a unit of radians per second (rad/s).

docs.title: Form A
docs.text:
For an accelerogram record stored in a single-column plain text file, use the following syntax.

sdof_response
sdof_response (1) (2) (3) (4)
# (1) string, file path of the accelerogram file
# (2) double, sampling interval
# (3) double, frequency of the system
# (4) double, damping ratio

The accelerogram stores discrete acceleration amplitudes in the first column of the file.

Because the accelerogram only provides the amplitudes, the sampling interval must be provided as the (2) argument.

docs.title: Form B
docs.text:
For an accelerogram record stored in a double-column plain text file, use the following syntax.

sdof_response
sdof_response (1) (2) (3)
# (1) string, file path of the accelerogram file
# (2) double, frequency of the system
# (3) double, damping ratio

The accelerogram stores the time and acceleration amplitudes in the first and second columns of the file.

The time series must be equally spaced.
