The quadratic interpolation represents curved edges and a varying strain field within the element, which reduces shear locking in bending relative to Q1.

The reduced scheme uses $\(2\times2\times2\)$ Gauss points and is the default. The full scheme uses the fourteen-point Irons rule and is selected by switching the reduced-integration flag off. The nonlinear-geometry switch activates the same total-Lagrangian formulation used by C3D8.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text:
C3D20
element C3D20 (1) (2...21) (22) [23] [24]
# (1) int, unique element tag
# (2...21) int, twenty corner nodes with conventional order
# (22) int, material tag
# [23] bool string, reduced integration scheme switch, default: true
# [24] bool string, nonlinear geometry switch, default: false

docs.title: Remarks
docs.text:
1. The nonlinearity is implemented by using total Lagrangian (TL) formulation, turn on the switch to use it.
  2. The reduced integration uses 2nd order Gauss scheme.
  3. The full integration uses 3rd order Irons scheme.

The reduced-integration switch is a boolean string and defaults to true, so the eight-point Gauss rule is used when it is omitted. The nonlinear-geometry switch is a separate boolean string and defaults to false. No hourglass stabilisation is implemented for C3D20.

implementation limitation

Reduced-integration quadratic bricks can still exhibit hourglass modes under some distortion patterns, and this element provides no stabilisation, so prefer the fourteen-point rule when spurious zero-energy deformation is suspected.

The full fourteen-point rule is more expensive and is mainly useful when a stiffer response or a richer sampling of the material state is desired. Use a 3D material tag with this element, and prefer C3D8 for a coarse first-order mesh or the infinite element CIN3D8 for the far field of an unbounded domain.

docs.title: C3D4
docs.text:
Linear Tetrahedral

  • Number of Nodes: 4
  • Number of DoFs: 3 (All Translation)
  • DoF Label: U1, U2, U3
  • Supports Body Force
  • Integration Scheme: Single Point At Centre
  • Constant Consistent Mass Matrix With Same Order Integration

docs.title: Theory
docs.text:
C3D4 is the four-node linear tetrahedron, the simplest three-dimensional solid element. It uses the barycentric shape functions $\(N_1=1-\xi-\eta-\zeta\)$, $\(N_2=\xi\)$, $\(N_3=\eta\)$ and $\(N_4=\zeta\)$ in a parent tetrahedron.

The implementation forms the augmented coordinate matrix $\(\mathbf X=[\mathbf 1,\mathbf x_1,\mathbf x_2,\mathbf x_3]\)$ and computes the volume as $\(V=\det\mathbf X/6\)$. The physical shape-function gradients are the last three rows of $\(\mathbf X^{-1}\)$, which are constant over the element. Consequently the strain-displacement matrix $\(\mathbf B\)$ is constant and the single integration point at the centroid integrates the element exactly.

The stiffness is $\(\mathbf K_e=V\mathbf B^{\mathrm T}\mathbf D\mathbf B\)$, while the mass and the body force use the centroid values $\(N_I=1/4\)$. With the nonlinear-geometry switch enabled the element uses a total-Lagrangian formulation with $\(\mathbf F=\mathbf I+\sum_I\mathbf u_I\otimes\nabla N_I\)$ and the Green-Lagrange strain $\(\mathbf E=\frac12(\mathbf F^{\mathrm T}\mathbf F-\mathbf I)\)$ passed to the material, together with a geometric stiffness term.

Because the strain is constant, C3D4 is overly stiff in bending and suffers volumetric locking for nearly incompressible materials. It is best used to mesh complex geometries with a fine grid, while bending-dominated problems are better served by C3D8, C3D8I or C3D20.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text:
C3D4
element C3D4 (1) (2...5) (6) [7]
# (1) int, unique element tag
# (2...5) int, four corner nodes with conventional order
# (6) int, material tag
# [7] bool string, nonlinear geometry switch, default: false

docs.title: Remarks
docs.text:
1. The nonlinearity is implemented by using total Lagrangian (TL) formulation, turn on the switch to use it.

The single integration point is located at the element centroid, which explains the property listed above. The element volume is computed from $\(\det\mathbf X/6\)$, so a badly ordered node list gives a negative volume and an invalid element. No hourglass control is needed because the one-point rule is exact for the constant strain field. The mass matrix and body-force vector use the centroid shape-function values $\(N_I=1/4\)$.

implementation limitation

The body-force vector is assembled from the centroid shape functions without an element-volume factor, so the applied nodal force is not scaled by the tetrahedron volume as it is in the brick elements.

For the phase-field fracture version with an additional damage DoF see DC3D4.

docs.title: C3D8
docs.text:
Linear Cube/Brick

  • Number of Nodes: 8
  • Number of DoFs: 3 (All Translation)
  • DoF Label: U1, U2, U3
  • Supports Body Force
  • Constant Consistent Mass Matrix With Same Order Integration

docs.title: Theory
docs.text:
C3D8 is the eight-node first-order isoparametric hexahedron, also known as the Q1 brick. Its parent domain is the cube $\((\xi,\eta,\zeta)\in[-1,1]^3\)$ and the corner nodes follow the conventional order $\((-, -, -)\)$, $\((+, -, -)\)$, $\((+, +, -)\)$, $\((-, +, -)\)$, $\((-, -, +)\)$, $\((+, -, +)\)$, $\((+, +, +)\)$, $\((-, +, +)\)$.

The trilinear shape functions are $$ N_I(\xi,\eta,\zeta)= rac18(1+\xi_I\xi)(1+\eta_I\eta)(1+\zeta_I\zeta),\qquad I=1,\dots,8, $$ where $\((\xi_I,\eta_I,\zeta_I)\)$ are the parent-domain coordinates of node $\(I\)$.

The isoparametric maps are $\(\mathbf x=\sum_I N_I\mathbf x_I\)$ and $\(\mathbf u=\sum_I N_I\mathbf u_I\)$. The Jacobian of the mapping is $\(\mathbf J=\partial\mathbf x/\partial\mathbf\xi=\sum_I\mathbf x_I\otimes abla_{\mathbf\xi}N_I\)$, and the physical gradients follow from $\( abla_{\mathbf x}N_I=\mathbf J^{-T} abla_{\mathbf\xi}N_I\)$. A positive $\(\det\mathbf J\)$ must be maintained at every sampling point.

In the small-strain setting the engineering strain vector $\(\mathbf\varepsilon=(\varepsilon_{11},\varepsilon_{22},\varepsilon_{33},2\varepsilon_{12},2\varepsilon_{23},2\varepsilon_{13})\)$ is obtained from $\(\mathbf\varepsilon=\mathbf B\mathbf u_e\)$. The implementation assembles $\(\mathbf B\)$ column by column as $$ B_{1,\,3I-2}=B_{4,\,3I-1}=B_{6,\,3I}= rac{\partial N_I}{\partial x},\quad B_{4,\,3I-2}=B_{2,\,3I-1}=B_{5,\,3I}= rac{\partial N_I}{\partial y},\quad B_{5,\,3I-2}=B_{4,\,3I-1}=B_{3,\,3I}= rac{\partial N_I}{\partial z}. $$

The element stiffness, consistent mass and body-force vector are $$ \mathbf K_e=\sum_g w_g\det\mathbf J_g\,\mathbf B_g^{\mathrm T}\mathbf D\mathbf B_g,\quad \mathbf M_e=\sum_g w_g\det\mathbf J_g\, ho\,\mathbf N_g^{\mathrm T}\mathbf N_g,\quad \mathbf f_e^{b}=\sum_g w_g\det\mathbf J_g\,\mathbf N_g^{\mathrm T}\mathbf b, $$ where $\(\mathbf D\)$ is the tangent of the associated 3D material, $\( ho\)$ is the density and $\(\mathbf b\)$ is the body force per unit volume. The mass matrix is subsequently made constant and is replicated over the three translational DoFs of each node.

With the nonlinear-geometry switch enabled the formulation is total Lagrangian. The deformation gradient is $\(\mathbf F=\mathbf I+\sum_I\mathbf u_I\otimes abla_{\mathbf x}N_I\)$, the Green-Lagrange strain $\(\mathbf E= rac12(\mathbf F^{\mathrm T}\mathbf F-\mathbf I)\)$ is passed to the material, and the tangent is the sum of the material term $\(\mathbf B^{\mathrm T}\mathbf D\mathbf B\)$ and a geometric term built from the stress returned by the material.

Element integration is selected by IntegrationPlan(3, order, type), so I uses the six-point Irons rule, R uses one-point Gauss and G uses $\(2 imes2 imes2\)$ Gauss. The one-point rule integrates the constant part of the strain field exactly but leaves twelve zero-energy hourglass modes, four per coordinate direction. Those modes are orthogonalised against the linear displacement field to give the vectors $\(\mathbf\gamma_i\)$, and the stabilisation matrix is $\( rac18(\mu/\det\mathbf J)\sum_i\mathbf\gamma_i\mathbf\gamma_i^{\mathrm T}\)$ replicated on each translational DoF. Full integration of Q1 locks in bending and near incompressibility, and this element does not provide a separate selective reduced integration switch.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text:
C3D8
element C3D8 (1) (2...9) (10) [11] [12] [13]
# (1) int, unique element tag
# (2...9) int, eight corner nodes with conventional order
# (10) int, material tag
# [11] string, integration scheme, default: "I"
# [12] bool string, nonlinear geometry switch, default: false
# [13] double, hourglassing penalty multiplier, default: 1.0

docs.title: Remarks
docs.text:
1. Three integration schemes are available, they are:

    1. "I" uses Irons six-point scheme.
    2. "R" uses reduced integration with Gauss scheme, that is one point at the center of the element. Hourglassing control is automatically enabled.
    3. "G" uses full integration (2nd order) with Gauss scheme.

  2. The nonlinearity is implemented by using total Lagrangian (TL) formulation, turn on the switch to use it.

For the hourglassing control, see 10.1016/0045-7825(84)90067-7. The hourglassing penalty multiplier (denoted as $\(\mu\)$) is an overall multiplier that is applied to the hourglassing stiffness matrix.

\[ \mu\mathbf{\gamma}_i\mathbf{\gamma}_i^\mathrm{T}. \]

In the above, $\(\mathbf{\gamma}_i\)$ is identical to Eq. (47) in the reference paper. Thus, $\(\mu\)$ shall be set to some value proportional to the elastic modulus.

The integration-scheme argument is case-insensitive in the parser and defaults to "I" when omitted. The nonlinear-geometry switch is a boolean string and defaults to false. The penalty multiplier is stored as its absolute value, so a negative input has the same effect as a positive one. A value of zero removes the hourglass resistance, which is acceptable with full integration but permits zero-energy modes with "R". The stabilisation contributes to both the stiffness and the residual, so a nonzero penalty produces the artificial force $\(\frac18(\mu/\det\mathbf J)\sum_i\mathbf\gamma_i\mathbf\gamma_i^\mathrm{T}\mathbf u_e\)$. Material records are sampled at the integration points and are extrapolated to the eight nodes for VTK output. For bending-dominated or nearly incompressible problems consider C3D8I or the quadratic C3D20 instead of the fully integrated Q1 brick. For the phase-field fracture and nonlocal-damage extensions see DC3D8 and the NonlocalC3D8 variant described below.

docs.title: Variants
docs.text: C3D8R forces the one-point reduced-integration scheme with hourglassing control, so the integration-scheme argument is dropped: element C3D8R (1) (2...9) (10) [11] [12] reads only the nonlinear-geometry switch and the hourglassing penalty multiplier. DC3D8M is the phase-field fracture cube that solves displacement and damage monolithically; element DC3D8M (1) (2...9) (10) (11) (12) takes the material tag, characteristic length and energy release rate, and adds a DAMAGE DoF at every node. NonlocalC3D8 is the nonlocal-damage cube; element NonlocalC3D8 (1) (2...9) (10) takes only the material tag, which must define exactly one nonlocal variable, and adds an NL1 DoF at every node.

docs.title: C3D8I
docs.text:
Linear Cube/Brick With Incompatible Modes

  • Number of Nodes: 8
  • Number of DoFs: 3 (All Translation)
  • DoF Label: U1, U2, U3
  • Supports Body Force
  • Integration Scheme: Irons Six-Point
  • Constant Consistent Mass Matrix With Same Order Integration

docs.title: Theory
docs.text:
C3D8I is the eight-node hexahedron with incompatible displacement modes, intended to remove the shear locking of the fully integrated Q1 brick. The displacement field is enriched by nine element-internal modes, three per coordinate direction: $$ \mathbf u=\sum_{I=1}^8N_I\mathbf u_I+\sum_{\alpha=1}^9 M_\alpha\mathbf a_\alpha, $$ with $\(M_1=1-\xi^2\)$, $\(M_2=1-\eta^2\)$, $\(M_3=1-\zeta^2\)$ and the analogous functions for the other displacement directions.

The enrichment gradients in the parent domain are $\(-2\xi\)$, $\(-2\eta\)$ and $\(-2\zeta\)$, which the implementation maps to the physical frame through $\(\mathbf J^{-1}\)$ at each sampling point. The strain field is $\(\mathbf\varepsilon=\mathbf B_1\mathbf u_e+\mathbf B_2\mathbf a\)$, where $\(\mathbf B_1\)$ is the usual Q1 strain-displacement matrix and $\(\mathbf B_2\)$ has size $\(6\times9\)$.

The enhanced modes are not global DoFs and are eliminated by static condensation of the element equations. With $\(\mathbf K_{uu}=\sum_g w_g\det\mathbf J_g\,\mathbf B_1^{\mathrm T}\mathbf D\mathbf B_1\)$, $\(\mathbf K_{ua}=\sum_g w_g\det\mathbf J_g\,\mathbf B_1^{\mathrm T}\mathbf D\mathbf B_2\)$ and $\(\mathbf K_{aa}=\sum_g w_g\det\mathbf J_g\,\mathbf B_2^{\mathrm T}\mathbf D\mathbf B_2\)$, the condensed stiffness is $$ \mathbf K_e^{\mathrm{cond}}=\mathbf K_{uu}-\mathbf K_{ua}\mathbf K_{aa}^{-1}\mathbf K_{ua}^{\mathrm T}. $$ The residual is condensed in the same way, with the internal amplitudes recovered locally from $\(\mathbf a=-\mathbf K_{aa}^{-1}(\mathbf K_{ua}^{\mathrm T}\mathbf u_e+\mathbf r_a)\)$, where $\(\mathbf r_a=\sum_g w_g\det\mathbf J_g\,\mathbf B_2^{\mathrm T}\mathbf\sigma\)$.

developer note

The internal-mode amplitudes are not recovered by iteration: the stress is evaluated with a zero enhanced strain and condensed once with the current tangent, so for nonlinear materials the orthogonality condition $\(\mathbf r_a=0\)$ is only approximately enforced.

The formulation is the three-dimensional analogue of the Wilson incompatible-mode element and belongs to the enhanced-strain family of Taylor and Simo. The static condensation enforces orthogonality of the incompatible strains to the stress field, which recovers the patch test on regular shapes. The element is integrated with the Irons six-point rule, and no geometric nonlinearity is implemented.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text:
C3D8I
element C3D8I (1) (2...9) (10)
# (1) int, unique element tag
# (2...9) int, eight corner nodes with conventional order
# (10) int, material tag

docs.title: Remarks
docs.text:
1. C3D8I is C3D8 with incompatible modes.
  2. Nonlinearity is not implemented in C3D8I.

There are no optional arguments beyond the element tag, the eight node tags and a 3D material tag. The nine internal modes are eliminated at element level, so the global system retains only the twenty-four translational DoFs of the eight nodes. The element uses the same six-point Irons rule as the default scheme of C3D8, but it does not require hourglass control. Strongly distorted elements degrade the patch-test correction, so reasonably regular bricks are recommended. For finite-strain analysis use C3D8 with the nonlinear-geometry switch or the quadratic C3D20, because C3D8I has no total-Lagrangian formulation.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. 10.1016/B978-0-12-253250-4.50008-7
  2. A non-conforming element for stress analysis
  3. ISBN 978-0-387-97520-7

docs.title: CIN3D8
docs.text:
Linear Infinite Cube/Brick

  • Number of Nodes: 8
  • Number of DoFs: 3 (All Translation)
  • DoF Label: U1, U2, U3

docs.title: Theory
docs.text:
CIN3D8 is a mapped infinite element used to represent an unbounded medium with a single layer of elements attached to the boundary of a finite mesh. It has eight nodes, with nodes one through four on the near face and nodes five through eight on the far face in the $\(\zeta\)$ direction. The far face corresponds to $\(\zeta=1\)$, which the mapping sends to infinity.

The implementation uses a mapping $\(\mathbf x=\sum_a M_a(\xi,\eta,\zeta)\mathbf x_a\)$ whose coefficient functions behave like $\(\zeta/(\zeta-1)\)$ as $\(\zeta\to1\)$. The displacement shape functions contain the factors $\(\zeta(\zeta-1)\)$ on the near face and $\(1-\zeta^2\)$ on the far face, so they remain finite near the mesh and decay towards infinity. Strain-displacement matrices are formed from the physical gradients $\(\nabla_{\mathbf x}N_a=\mathbf J^{-T}\nabla_{\mathbf\xi}N_a\)$, where $\(\mathbf J\)$ is built from the mapped geometry.

The stiffness and body-force integrals use a $\(2\times2\times2\)$ Gauss rule in the parent domain. The element is intended for small-strain analysis and has no nonlinear-geometry switch. It is normally coupled to ordinary finite elements such as C3D8 or C3D20 along the shared near face.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text:
CIN3D8
element CIN3D8 (1) (2...9) (10)
# (1) int, unique element tag
# (2...9) int, eight corner nodes with conventional order
# (10) int, material tag

docs.title: Remarks
docs.text: The only argument beyond the tags is the material tag, which is used at each of the eight integration points. Orient the element so that each edge from a near-face node to its far-face counterpart points away from the region of interest. The far-face node coordinates define the geometric mapping, so they must be placed consistently with rays extending to infinity. The source assembles a consistent mass matrix and a body-force contribution from the decayed interpolation when the material supplies a density. No hourglass control is needed with the $\(2\times2\times2\)$ Gauss rule.

docs.title: DC3D4
docs.text:
• Number of Nodes: 4
  • Number of DoFs: 4 (Translation, Translation, Translation, Damage)
  • DoF Label: U1, U2, U3, DAMAGE

docs.title: Theory
docs.text:
DC3D4 is the phase-field fracture version of the four-node tetrahedron C3D4. Each node carries three translational DoFs and one damage DoF, so the element has sixteen DoFs in total. It follows the variational phase-field fracture model described in detail in DC3D8, with the damage field interpolated by the same linear barycentric functions as the displacement field.

The crack surface is regularised by the functional $\(\Gamma_l(d)=\int_\Omega\left[\dfrac{d^2}{2l}+\dfrac{l}{2}| abla d|^2 ight]\mathrm d\Omega\)$, where $\(d\in[0,1]\)$ is the damage field and $\(l\)$ is the characteristic length. The elastic energy is degraded by $\(g(d)=\min\{1,(1-d)^2+\epsilon\}\)$, and the driving force is the history field $\(H\)$, the running maximum of $\( rac12\mathbf\varepsilon:\mathbf\sigma\)$. The discrete damage block is $\(\mathbf K_{dd}=\int_\Omega\left[(2H+G_c/l)\mathbf N^{\mathrm T}\mathbf N+G_c l\,( abla\mathbf N)^{\mathrm T} abla\mathbf N ight]\mathrm d\Omega\)$, with $\(G_c\)$ the energy release rate.

The tetrahedral element uses one integration point at the centroid, so all fields are constant over the element. If the characteristic-length argument is negative, the implementation sets $\(l=2\sqrt[3]{V}\)$ from the element volume $\(V\)$.

deviation from theory

The automatic length is twice the cube root of the element volume, whereas the hexahedral DC3D8 uses $\(\sqrt[3]{V}\)$, so the two variants regularise the crack over different widths for the same element size.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text:
DC3D4
element DC3D4 (1) (2...5) (6) (7) (8)
# (1) int, unique element tag
# (2...5) int, four corner nodes with conventional order
# (6) int, material tag
# (7) double, characteristic length
# (8) double, energy release rate

docs.title: Remarks
docs.text:
The material tag must refer to a 3D material that supplies stress and tangent, while the damage evolution is governed by the element. The energy release rate is the argument after the characteristic length and should be positive for a meaningful crack driving force. A negative characteristic length triggers the automatic value $\(2\sqrt[3]{V}\)$, so the element size controls the regularised crack width. DC3D4 uses a staggered update in which the history field is frozen at its committed value while the damage equation is solved. No tension-compression split is applied to the energy that drives damage in this implementation.

deviation from theory

Unlike the standard Miehe formulation, the history field is driven by the full $\(\frac12\mathbf\varepsilon:\mathbf\sigma\)$ without a tensile-compressive split, so compressive straining can also grow damage.

docs.title: Variants
docs.text: DC3D4M is the monolithic counterpart and is registered as new_dc3d4<true> in the element parser. It accepts the same arguments as DC3D4: element DC3D4M (1) (2...5) (6) (7) (8) reads the element tag, four node tags, material tag, characteristic length and energy release rate. Unlike DC3D4, it updates the history field to the trial value and adds the displacement-damage coupling blocks to the tangent, so displacement and damage are solved simultaneously. For the hexahedral counterpart see DC3D8 and its monolithic alias DC3D8M.

docs.title: DC3D8
docs.text:
• Number of Nodes: 8
  • Number of DoFs: 4 (Translation, Translation, Translation, Damage)
  • DoF Label: U1, U2, U3, DAMAGE

docs.title: Theory
docs.text:
DC3D8 is the phase-field fracture version of the eight-node brick C3D8. Each node carries three translational DoFs and one DAMAGE DoF, giving 32 element DoFs. The damage field is interpolated by the same trilinear shape functions as the displacement field, and a scalar field replaces a sharp crack surface.

The total potential energy is $$ \Psi=\int_\Omega g(d)\psi(\mathbf\varepsilon)\,\mathrm d\Omega+G_c\int_\Omega\left[ rac{d^2}{2l}+ rac l2| abla d|^2 ight]\mathrm d\Omega, $$ where $\(\psi= rac12\mathbf\varepsilon:\mathbf\sigma\)$ is the elastic energy density built from the strain and stress returned by the material, $\(g(d)\)$ is the degradation function, $\(G_c\)$ is the energy release rate and $\(l\)$ is the characteristic length.

deviation from theory

The quadratic form $\( rac12\mathbf\varepsilon:\mathbf\sigma\)$ equals the strain energy density only for a linear elastic host, whereas the element uses it as the damage driver for any 3D material so a nonlinear host is not driven by the true $\(\int\mathbf\sigma:\mathrm d\mathbf\varepsilon\)$.

The implementation uses $$ g(d)=\min\left{1,(1-\mathbf N\mathbf d)^2+\epsilon ight},\qquad \epsilon=\mathrm{eps}(\mathrm{float}), $$ where $\(\mathbf d\)$ collects the nodal damage values and $\(d\)$ is thereby limited to $\([0,1]\)$.

deviation from theory

The degradation is clamped so that the residual stiffness at $\(d=1\)$ is essentially zero rather than the finite residual stiffness used to keep the tangent nonsingular in regularised formulations.

developer note

The clamp uses $\(\min\{1,\cdot\}\)$ with $\(\epsilon\)$ equal to the single-precision machine epsilon.

Irreversibility of crack growth is enforced with a history field that stores the maximum elastic energy reached at a material point. At each integration point the trial value is $\(\mathcal H^\mathrm{trial}= rac12\mathbf\varepsilon:\mathbf\sigma\)$, updated as $\(\mathcal H=\max(\mathcal H_\mathrm{old},\mathcal H^\mathrm{trial})\)$. No tension-compression split of the elastic energy is applied in this implementation, so compressive straining can also increase the driving force.

deviation from theory

Standard phase-field fracture models split the elastic energy into tensile and compressive parts so that compression does not drive cracking, but this element uses the full $\( rac12\mathbf\varepsilon:\mathbf\sigma\)$ as the history-field driver, so compressive states also grow damage.

With $\(\mathbf N\)$ and $\( abla\mathbf N\)$ the shape functions and their physical gradients, the displacement and damage blocks are $$ \mathbf K_{uu}=\int_\Omega g(d)\mathbf B^{\mathrm T}\mathbf D\mathbf B\,\mathrm d\Omega,\qquad \mathbf r_u=\int_\Omega g(d)\mathbf B^{\mathrm T}\mathbf\sigma\,\mathrm d\Omega, $$ $$ \mathbf K_{dd}=\int_\Omega\left[(2\mathcal H+G_c/l)\mathbf N^{\mathrm T}\mathbf N+G_c l\,( abla\mathbf N)^{\mathrm T} abla\mathbf N ight]\mathrm d\Omega,\qquad \mathbf r_d=\mathbf K_{dd}\mathbf d-2\mathcal H\int_\Omega\mathbf N^{\mathrm T}\,\mathrm d\Omega. $$ The monolithic variant DC3D8M adds the coupling block $\(\mathbf K_{ud}=-2\int_\Omega(1-d)\mathbf B^{\mathrm T}\mathbf\sigma\mathbf N^{\mathrm T}\,\mathrm d\Omega\)$ and its transpose, and advances $\(\mathcal H\)$ to the trial value. The staggered DC3D8 variant omits the coupling blocks and holds $\(\mathcal H\)$ at its committed value during the damage solve.

The element uses the $\(2 imes2 imes2\)$ Gauss rule. If the characteristic-length argument is negative, the implementation sets $\(l=\sqrt[3]{V}\)$ from the element volume $\(V\)$.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text:
DC3D8
element DC3D8 (1) (2...9) (10) (11) (12)
# (1) int, unique element tag
# (2...9) int, eight corner nodes with conventional order
# (10) int, material tag
# (11) double, characteristic length
# (12) double, energy release rate

docs.title: Remarks
docs.text: The material tag supplies the mechanical constitutive law, and no separate damage material is needed. The characteristic length is the first numerical argument after the material tag and the energy release rate is the second. A negative characteristic length triggers automatic sizing as $\(\sqrt[3]{V}\)$, which ties the regularised crack width directly to the element size. DC3D8 solves displacement and damage in a staggered fashion, whereas DC3D8M assembles the fully coupled tangent and solves both fields simultaneously. Use a mesh with several elements across the expected crack width, since an under-resolved damage band gives a brittle and mesh-dependent response. For the tetrahedral version and its monolithic alias see DC3D4.

docs.title: CST/CSM
docs.text:
Couple Stress Mixed Triangle/Quadrilateral

  • Number of Nodes: 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8
  • Number of DoFs: 3 (Translation, Translation, Rotation)
  • DoF Label: U1, U2, UR3

docs.title: Background
docs.text: The CS family is based on the consistent couple stress theory, in which the rotation is an independent kinematic field and the strain energy depends on both the symmetric strain and the curvature. Each node carries two translations and one drilling rotation $\(\omega\)$, so the displacement and rotation fields are interpolated independently. The conjugate stress measures are the usual Cauchy stress $\(\mathbf\sigma\)$ and a couple stress $\(\mathbf m\)$, with the equilibrium equation $$ \nabla\cdot\mathbf\sigma+\mathbf b=\mathbf 0,\qquad \nabla\cdot\mathbf m+\mathbf\epsilon:\mathbf\sigma=\mathbf 0. $$ The six-field mixed variational principle used in the implementation introduces the displacement, rotation, strain, curvature, stress and couple stress as independent fields and removes the need for a local iteration. The characteristic length $\(l\)$ couples the curvature energy to the strain energy and sets the scale at which rotational effects become significant. A negative $\(l\)$ makes the element estimate the length as the square root of the element area, while a positive value fixes it explicitly. The membrane geometries mirror the CP family, so the triangular and quadrilateral variants share the node ordering of CP3 and CP8. The formulation is objective for the rotation but does not by itself regularise softening; additional regularisation is required for fracture problems, for which DCP3 and DCP4 are available.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text:
CS
element CSMT3 (1) (2...*) (3) [4] [5]
element CSMT6 (1) (2...*) (3) [4] [5]
element CSMQ4 (1) (2...*) (3) [4] [5]
element CSMQ5 (1) (2...*) (3) [4] [5]
element CSMQ6 (1) (2...*) (3) [4] [5]
element CSMQ7 (1) (2...*) (3) [4] [5]
element CSMQ8 (1) (2...*) (3) [4] [5]
# (1) int, unique element tag
# (2...*) int, corresponding number of node tags
# (3) int, material tag
# [4] double, thickness, default: 1.0
# [5] double, characteristic length, default: -1.0

docs.title: Remarks
docs.text:
1. The geometry definitions of CS elements resemble those of CP elements (e.g., CP3, CP4, CP5, CP6, CP7, CP8).
  2. The characteristic length [5] can be left as default value (negative) to automatically determine the value based on geometry (square root of area), or set to a positive value to manually specify the fixed length.
  3. Currently, only Elastic2D is supported.

implementation limitation

The elements use only the elastic modulus and Poisson's ratio from the material, so inelastic materials are not supported even though the underlying six-field formulation is materially general.

developer note

The elements read the elastic modulus and Poisson's ratio from the material and build an IsotropicCouple tangent internally instead of using the material's own stiffness matrix. Under plane stress the modulus and Poisson's ratio are first converted to $\(E/(1- u^2)\)$ and $\( u/(1- u)\)$.

  1. The drilling rotation is a genuine kinematic DoF here, unlike the fictitious rotation used in Allman or GQ12.
  2. The characteristic length controls the couple-stress contribution; larger values stiffen the rotational response.
  3. For problems without rotational size effects the simpler CP4 or CP8 membrane elements are cheaper.

docs.title: Guide
docs.text: Only general purpose elements for plane strain/stress problems are included. For other special purpose elements, there are not many options anyway.

docs.title: Background
docs.text:
A membrane element models a two-dimensional continuum that carries in-plane normal and shear stress. The displacement field is $\(\mathbf u=[u_1,u_2]^\mathrm T\)$ and the small-strain tensor is $\(\mathbf\varepsilon=\operatorname{sym} abla\mathbf u\)$. In Voigt order the strain vector is $\(\mathbf\varepsilon=[\varepsilon_{11},\varepsilon_{22},\gamma_{12}]^\mathrm T\)$ with $\(\gamma_{12}=2\varepsilon_{12}\)$, so that $\(\mathbf\sigma^\mathrm T\mathbf\varepsilon=\sigma_{11}\varepsilon_{11}+\sigma_{22}\varepsilon_{22}+ au_{12}\gamma_{12}\)$. The governing equation is $\( abla\cdot\mathbf\sigma+\mathbf b=\mathbf 0\)$ and the constitutive law is $\(\mathbf\sigma=\mathbf D\mathbf\varepsilon\)$, with $\(\mathbf D\)$ supplied by the assigned material.

The plane assumption is selected by the material rather than by the element token. Under plane stress $\(\sigma_{33}=0\)$ and $\(\varepsilon_{33}=- u(\varepsilon_{11}+\varepsilon_{22})/(1- u)\)$ follows from the constitutive law. Under plane strain $\(\varepsilon_{33}=0\)$ and a reaction stress $\(\sigma_{33}= u(\sigma_{11}+\sigma_{22})\)$ develops, so the thickness argument is overridden to unity in the implementation. The axisymmetric family uses a four-component strain vector $\([\varepsilon_{rr},\varepsilon_{zz},\varepsilon_{ heta heta},\gamma_{rz}]\)$ and replaces $\(\varepsilon_{33}\)$ by the hoop strain $\(\varepsilon_{ heta heta}=u_r/r\)$.

deviation from theory

Most membrane elements have a single element token per geometry; plane stress and plane strain are distinguished by the material plane type.

developer note

ABAQUS-style names such as CPS4, CPE3 and CPS8R are only descriptive in the source class comments. The element parser registers a single token per geometry for most membrane elements, with plane stress and plane strain distinguished by the material plane type.

All elements on this page are isoparametric, meaning geometry and displacement use the same nodal shape functions $\(N_a(\xi,\eta)\)$. $$ \mathbf x=\sum_{a=1}^{n}N_a(\xi,\eta)\,\mathbf x_a,\qquad \mathbf u=\sum_{a=1}^{n}N_a(\xi,\eta)\,\mathbf u_a,\qquad \mathbf\varepsilon=\mathbf B\mathbf a. $$ Here $\(\mathbf a\)$ collects the nodal displacements and $\(B_{ia}=\partial N_a/\partial x_i\)$ is assembled in Voigt form, with physical derivatives obtained from $\(\mathbf J^{-1}\partial N_a/\partial\mathbf\xi\)$ and $\(\mathbf J=\partial\mathbf x/\partial\mathbf\xi\)$. The element stiffness is evaluated by numerical quadrature, $$ \mathbf Ke=\int_{\Omegae}\mathbf B^\mathrm T\mathbf D\mathbf B\,t\,\mathrm d\Omega=\sum_{q=1}^{n_q}\mathbf B_q^\mathrm T\mathbf D_q\mathbf B_q\,t\,J_q\,w_q, $$ where $\(J_q\)$ is the Jacobian determinant, $\(w_q\)$ the quadrature weight, $\(t\)$ the thickness and $\(n_q\)$ the number of integration points.

The node-ordering convention is counter-clockwise around the element. For quadrilaterals node 1 is at $\((\xi,\eta)=(-1,-1)\)$ and nodes 2, 3, 4 follow counter-clockwise. The 5-, 6- and 7-node quadrilaterals add midside nodes on the bottom, right and top edges in that order, while the 8-node quadrilateral adds the left-edge midside node as well. For triangles nodes 1 to 3 occupy the vertices and nodes 4 to 6 the corresponding edge midpoints.

Low-order fully integrated elements lock in bending and in nearly incompressible plasticity because their discrete strain space is too rich in volumetric and shear modes. Reduced integration removes the locking but creates zero-energy hourglass modes that must be stabilised, as implemented in CP4 through an orthogonal hourglass stiffness. Mixed and assumed-strain formulations avoid both difficulties, either by assuming the stress field as in PS and QE2, or by adding internally condensed incompatible modes as in CP4I. The quadratic elements CP6 and CP8 improve accuracy on curved boundaries and in bending dominated problems. The phase-field fracture elements DCP3 and DCP4 add a nodal damage DoF to a standard displacement interpolation. The mapped infinite element CINP4 extends one parent direction to infinity for unbounded domains, and the couple-stress family CS adds a drilling rotation together with a characteristic length.

docs.title: Element selection
docs.text:
Try the following decision tree to find the best membrane element to use.

  1. Is the geometry regular or irregular?
  2. regular --- use quadrilateral elements that are often more flexible than triangular elements and thus provide better results with the same amount of DoFs
  3. irregular --- use triangular elements unless a good mesh can be generated to avoid distorted geometry

docs.title: Triangular Elements
docs.text:
1. Is drilling DoF required?
  2. yes --- Allman
  3. no --- go to Q2
  4. Prefer speed or accuracy?
  5. speed --- CP3
  6. accuracy --- CP6

Noting that the CP3 element is very rigid and often requires a very dense mesh to get relatively accurate results, it is not recommended for most applications.

docs.title: Quadrilateral Elements
docs.text:
1. Is drilling DoF required?
  2. yes --- go to Q2
  3. no --- go to Q3
  4. Is consistent material stiffness available?
  5. yes --- go to Q6
  6. no --- GQ12, it does not require local inversion so it works even when the material tangent stiffness is not exact (but global convergence may still be an issue)
  7. Used in elastoplastic applications?
  8. yes --- normally mixed formulation is better, go to Q4, alternatively displacement based formulation, go to Q5
  9. no --- go to Q5
  10. Prefer speed or accuracy?
  11. speed --- PS, very cheap to compute, only with a different strain matrix
  12. accuracy --- QE2, has enhanced strain field, requires more local computation
  13. Prefer speed or accuracy?
  14. speed --- CP4I or second option CP4
  15. accuracy --- CP8R or second option CP8
  16. Need faster analysis?
  17. yes --- SGCMQ, GCMQ with no enhanced strain, very cheap to compute, only with a different strain matrix
  18. no --- GCMQ, best coarse mesh accuracy, requires local inversion

docs.title: CAX3
docs.text:
Axisymmetric Linear Triangle

  • Number of Nodes: 3
  • Number of DoFs: 2
  • DoF Label: RADIAL, AXIAL

docs.title: Background
docs.text:
CAX3 is the three-node constant-strain triangle of the axisymmetric family. Its nodal DoFs are the radial and axial displacements, and the strain vector is $\(\mathbf\varepsilon=[\varepsilon_{rr},\varepsilon_{zz},\varepsilon_{\theta\theta},\gamma_{rz}]^\mathrm T\)$, with $\(\varepsilon_{\theta\theta}=u_r/r\)$ and $\(\gamma_{rz}=\partial u_r/\partial z+\partial u_z/\partial r\)$. The triangle uses area coordinates so the in-plane derivatives $\(\partial N_a/\partial r\)$ and $\(\partial N_a/\partial z\)$ are constant, derived from the inverse of the $\(3\times3\)$ coordinate matrix. The hoop strain is evaluated at the element centroid radius $\(r_c=(r_1+r_2+r_3)/3\)$, so this element is one-point integrated. The integration weight is $\(2\pi r_c A\)$, with $\(A\)$ the area of the meridian triangle.

implementation limitation

The hoop strain uses one centroid radius for the whole triangle, so elements that span a large radial extent approximate the variation of $\(u_r/r\)$ by a single value. A centroid at or near zero radius makes the strain row singular.

The stiffness is $$ \mathbf K^e=2\pi r_c A\,\mathbf B^\mathrm T\mathbf D\mathbf B. $$ The material must supply an axisymmetric tangent matrix, and the parent page CAX4 derives the full four-component formulation.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text:
CAX3
element CAX3 (1) (2...4) (5) [6]
# (1) int, unique element tag
# (2...4) int, node tags
# (5) int, material tag
# [6] bool string, nonlinear geometry switch, default: false

docs.title: Remarks
docs.text:
• The assigned material must declare an axisymmetric plane type or initialisation fails.
  • Boundary conditions use the RADIAL and AXIAL DoF labels.
  • The element is very stiff in bending, like its plane counterpart CP3, and dense meshes are needed for accurate stresses.
  • The optional nonlinear-geometry switch is parsed, but the current implementation evaluates only the small-strain strain measure.

deviation from theory

Supplying a true nonlinear-geometry switch does not activate a Total Lagrangian axisymmetric formulation.

developer note

The CAX3 constructor forwards the nonlinear-geometry flag to the base class, yet update_status never branches on it.

  • A Gauss point at zero radius is singular, so keep the centroid away from the axis of revolution.

docs.title: CAX4
docs.text:
Axisymmetric Linear Quadrilateral

  • Number of Nodes: 4
  • Number of DoFs: 2
  • DoF Label: RADIAL, AXIAL

docs.title: Background
docs.text:
CAX4 models a body of revolution by discretising its meridional $\((r,z)\)$ section with four-node quadrilaterals. The only nodal DoFs are the radial displacement $\(u_r\)$ and the axial displacement $\(u_z\)$; the circumferential displacement vanishes by symmetry. A material point is described by the triple $\((r,\theta,z)\)$ and the nonzero small-strain components are $$ \varepsilon_{rr}=\frac{\partial u_r}{\partial r},\qquad \varepsilon_{zz}=\frac{\partial u_z}{\partial z},\qquad \varepsilon_{\theta\theta}=\frac{u_r}{r},\qquad \gamma_{rz}=\frac{\partial u_r}{\partial z}+\frac{\partial u_z}{\partial r}. $$ The hoop strain $\(\varepsilon_{\theta\theta}\)$ is the essential difference from plane strain: a radial displacement changes the radius of the material circle and therefore its circumference. The strain vector is ordered as $\(\mathbf\varepsilon=[\varepsilon_{rr},\varepsilon_{zz},\varepsilon_{\theta\theta},\gamma_{rz}]^\mathrm T\)$, and the material must return a $\(4\times4\)$ tangent matrix for the axisymmetric plane type.

With the isoparametric interpolation $\(\mathbf x=\sum_aN_a\mathbf x_a\)$ and $\(\mathbf u=\sum_aN_a\mathbf u_a\)$, the strain-displacement matrix contains one extra row, $$ \mathbf B_a=\begin{bmatrix} N_{a,r}&0\ 0&N_{a,z}\ N_a/r&0\ N_{a,z}&N_{a,r} \end{bmatrix}. $$ The volume element of the revolve is $\(\mathrm dV=2\pi r\,\mathrm dA=2\pi r\,J\,\mathrm d\xi\,\mathrm d\eta\)$, so the quadrature weight at each Gauss point is $\(2\pi r_q J_q w_q\)$. The implementation evaluates $\(r_q\)$ by interpolating the four nodal radii with the quadratic monomial vector $\([1,\xi,\eta,\xi\eta]\)$, which reproduces the exact bilinear geometry. The stiffness and resistance are $$ \mathbf Ke=\sum_{q=1}{4}2\pi r_qJ_qw_q\,\mathbf B_q^\mathrm T\mathbf D_q\mathbf B_q,\qquad \mathbf fe=\sum_{q=1}{4}2\pi r_qJ_qw_q\,\mathbf B_q^\mathrm T\mathbf\sigma_q. $$ The default quadrature is the full $\(2\times2\)$ Gauss rule, and no reduced-integration token is registered for CAX4 in the element parser.

Because the hoop strain contains $\(1/r\)$, the formulation is singular on the symmetry axis and the Gauss points should stay at positive radius.

implementation limitation

The implementation does not special-case an element that crosses the axis of revolution. A Gauss point at or very near zero radius produces an unbounded hoop-strain row in $\(\mathbf B\)$ and an ill-conditioned stiffness.

The linear triangle CAX3 evaluates all quantities at the element centroid radius, whereas CAX8 uses an 8-node quadratic interpolation and a higher-order rule. The plane-stress and plane-strain counterparts of the same interpolation are CP4 and CP8.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text:
CAX4
element CAX4 (1) (2...5) (6)
# (1) int, unique element tag
# (2...5) int, node i, j, k, l
# (6) int, material tag

docs.title: Remarks
docs.text:
• The assigned material must declare an axisymmetric plane type; CAX4 rejects a plane-stress or plane-strain material at initialisation.
  • The nodal DoF labels are RADIAL and AXIAL, so boundary conditions must be applied to those labels rather than to U1 and U2.
  • The element has no thickness argument because the physical volume is obtained by revolving the section through $\(2\pi\)$.
  • Full $\(2\times2\)$ Gauss integration is used, which makes the element locking-prone in bending and in nearly incompressible plasticity; use CAX8 for higher accuracy.
  • The parser hardcodes the nonlinear-geometry switch to false, so the current command path evaluates only the small-strain axisymmetric formulation.

deviation from theory

No parser token exposes a Total Lagrangian option for CAX4, so nonlinear geometry cannot be selected from an element CAX4 command.

developer note

The element print routine reports a Total Lagrangian option, but no parser token exposes that switch for CAX4. The nonlinear branch exists in the class but is unreachable from an element CAX4 command.

  • Avoid placing Gauss points on the axis of revolution because the hoop strain $\(u_r/r\)$ is singular there.

docs.title: CAX8
docs.text:
Axisymmetric Quadratic Quadrilateral

  • Number of Nodes: 8
  • Number of DoFs: 2
  • DoF Label: RADIAL, AXIAL

docs.title: Background
docs.text:
CAX8 is the eight-node quadratic quadrilateral of the axisymmetric family. The four corner nodes are ordered counter-clockwise from $\((\xi,\eta)=(-1,-1)\)$, and nodes 5 to 8 are the midside nodes on the bottom, right, top and left edges. The isoparametric interpolation uses the serendipity shape functions also used by CP8, so curved meridian boundaries can be represented. The strain vector is $\(\mathbf\varepsilon=[\varepsilon_{rr},\varepsilon_{zz},\varepsilon_{\theta\theta},\gamma_{rz}]^\mathrm T\)$, with the hoop strain $\(\varepsilon_{\theta\theta}=u_r/r\)$ evaluated at each integration point. The radius is interpolated with the eight-term quadratic monomial vector $\([1,\xi,\eta,\xi^2,\xi\eta,\eta^2,\xi^2\eta,\xi\eta^2]\)$, and the quadrature weight is $\(2\pi r_qJ_qw_q\)$. The default rule is $\(3\times3\)$ Gauss; the parser currently constructs the element with reduced integration disabled.

implementation limitation

Reduced integration and nonlinear geometry cannot be selected from an element CAX8 command.

developer note

No parser token exposes reduced integration for CAX8, and the nonlinear-geometry argument is left at its default false. The class contains branches for both options, but they cannot be selected from an element CAX8 command.

The parent page CAX4 derives the axisymmetric strain-displacement matrix and discusses the singularity at $\(r=0\)$.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text:
CAX8
element CAX8 (1) (2...9) (10)
# (1) int, unique element tag
# (2...9) int, node tags
# (10) int, material tag

docs.title: Remarks
docs.text:
• The assigned material must declare an axisymmetric plane type or initialisation fails.
  • Boundary conditions use the RADIAL and AXIAL DoF labels.
  • Mid-edge nodes must be placed at the true geometric midpoint of a straight edge, or at the appropriate point on a curved edge, to avoid a distorted Jacobian.
  • The quadratic interpolation gives accurate hoop stresses with far fewer elements than CAX4 or CAX3, at the cost of a $\(3\times3\)$ quadrature loop.
  • The nonlinear-geometry path is not reachable from the current element parser.

docs.title: Allman
docs.text:
Allman's Triangle With Drilling DoFs

  • Number of Nodes: 3
  • Number of DoFs: 3 (Translation, Translation, Rotation)
  • DoF Label: U1, U2, UR3
  • Integration Scheme: 3-Point Mid-edge

docs.title: Theory
docs.text:
A standard three-node membrane interpolates only translations and therefore cannot contribute stiffness to the out-of-plane rotation about the element normal, called the drilling DoF.

Flat shell elements combine a membrane with a plate that provides the two bending rotations, so the third rotation must be supplied by the membrane to avoid a zero-energy mode in a general three-dimensional assembly.

Allman's device is to start from a complete quadratic displacement field and to express the midside displacement of each edge in terms of the translations and rotations at the two adjacent vertices.

Let node $\(i\)$ have translation $\((u_i,v_i)\)$ and drilling rotation $\(\theta_i\)$, and let the edge from $\(i\)$ to $\(j\)$ have length $\(\ell_{ij}\)$ and unit normal $\(\mathbf n_{ij}=(-(y_j-y_i),\,x_j-x_i)/\ell_{ij}\)$.

The midside displacement used in the implementation is

\[ \bar{\mathbf u}_{ij}=\dfrac12(\mathbf u_i+\mathbf u_j)+\dfrac18(\theta_j-\theta_i)\,\ell_{ij}\,\mathbf n_{ij}. \]

The first term is the average of the vertex translations, and the second term is the Allman correction that couples the drilling rotation to the edge-normal displacement.

The complete quadratic basis $\(\{1,x,y,xy,x^2,y^2\}\)$ is fitted through the three corner points and the three mid-edge points, giving the displacement field $\(\mathbf u=[u,v]^{\mathsf T}=\mathbf N\mathbf d\)$ with $\(\mathbf d=(u_1,v_1,\theta_1,u_2,v_2,\theta_2,u_3,v_3,\theta_3)^{\mathsf T}\)$.

Differentiating this field gives the three in-plane strains

\[ \mathbf\varepsilon=\begin{bmatrix}u_{,x}\\ v_{,y}\\ u_{,y}+v_{,x}\end{bmatrix}=\mathbf B\mathbf d , \]

and the element stiffness is the usual $\(\mathbf K=\int_A\mathbf B^{\mathsf T}\mathbf D\mathbf B\,t\,dA\)$, where $\(\mathbf D\)$ is the two-dimensional material stiffness and $\(t\)$ the thickness.

The integration is performed at the three midside points with equal weight $\(At/3\)$, where $\(A\)$ is the triangle area; this is the origin of the 3-Point Mid-edge label.

The same mid-edge idea underlies the quadrilateral drilling elements GQ12 and GCMQ, while the plate-side discrete Kirchhoff interpolation used in shells is described on DKT3.

deviation from theory

The drilling correction depends only on differences of nodal rotations, so a uniform rotation field produces no mid-edge offset and no membrane strain. The element therefore has no stiffness against a uniform drilling mode and is not a penalty-stabilized drilling element in the sense of Hughes and Brezzi.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text:
Allman
element Allman (1) (2...4) (5) [6]
# (1) int, unique element tag
# (2...4) int, node i, j, k
# (5) int, material tag
# [6] double, element thickness, default: 1.0

docs.title: Remarks
docs.text:
• Three middle points on edges are used as integration points.
  • For a plane-strain material the thickness argument is overridden to 1.0 during initialization, so it only has an effect for plane-stress materials.

implementation limitation

The thickness argument is silently overwritten for plane strain. The element does not assemble a drilling stabilization term, so the UR3 DoF must be restrained where it is not constrained by adjacent elements.

developer note

The three integration points are fixed at the edge midpoints.

  • The midside correction depends on rotation differences only, so a uniform drilling rotation produces no membrane strain and no drilling stiffness from a single element.
  • Restrain the UR3 DoF where necessary, since the Allman interpolation gives no stiffness to a uniform drilling rotation.
  • The element supports a consistent mass matrix when the material supplies a nonzero density and records the material response at the three integration points.
  • Use GQ12 instead when a four-node membrane with the same DoF layout is required.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. 10.1016/0045-7949(84)90197-4
  2. 10.1016/0045-7825(89)90124-2
  3. A robust quadrilateral membrane finite element with drilling degrees of freedom

docs.title: (S)GCMQ
docs.text:
Generalised Conforming Mixed Quadrilateral With Drilling DoFs

  • Number of Nodes: 4
  • Number of DoFs: 3 (Translation, Translation, Rotation)
  • DoF Label: U1, U2, UR3
  • Supports Body Force
  • Constant Consistent Mass Matrix With Same Order Integration

docs.title: Background
docs.text:
The GCMQ family is a four-node drilling membrane derived from a modified Hu--Washizu principle, in which displacement, strain and stress fields are treated as independent variables.

The same drilling interpolation idea as Allman and GQ12 is used, but the discrete equations are built in a 12-parameter local stress space with the linear stress modes $\(\{1,x,y,xy\}\)$.

Write the local stress as $\(\mathbf\sigma=\mathbf P\mathbf\alpha\)$, with $\(\mathbf\alpha\)$ the 12 stress parameters, and the local strain as $\(\mathbf\varepsilon=\mathbf P_\varepsilon\mathbf\beta\)$.

The compatibility and equilibrium equations reduce to solving small systems with matrices $\(\mathbf H\)$, $\(\mathbf N\)$ and $\(\mathbf M\)$ assembled from the integration points, after which the element stiffness is condensed to the nodal DoFs.

The full GCMQ adds three enhanced strain modes to avoid excessive stiffness on coarse or distorted meshes: a quadratic dilatational mode $\((3x^2-1,\,3y^2-1)\)$, a quadratic shear mode $\(x^2-y^2\)$ and a complementary mode $\(x^2+y^2-2/3\)$.

deviation from theory

The enhanced strain basis is a fixed set of three quadratic polynomials rather than a general assumed-strain expansion. The complementary mode $\(x^2+y^2-2/3\)$ is included specifically to keep the two shear modes frame invariant, so the basis is tailored to this element rather than being the standard EAS choice.

The simplified SGCMQ omits these modes and the associated internal variables, giving a cheaper displacement-like element that is the membrane part of the shell SGCMS.

The three available integration rules are a five-point Irons rule, a third-order Lobatto rule and a third-order Gauss rule, selected by the letters I, L and G.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text:
GCMQ
element GCMQI (1) (2...5) (6) [7] [8]
element GCMQL (1) (2...5) (6) [7] [8]
element GCMQG (1) (2...5) (6) [7] [8]
# (1) int, unique element tag
# (2...5) int, node i, j, k, l
# (6) int, material tag
# [7] double, element thickness, default: 1.0
# [8] double, objective length, default: -1.0 (disabled)

element SGCMQI (1) (2...5) (6) [7] [8]
element SGCMQL (1) (2...5) (6) [7] [8]
element SGCMQG (1) (2...5) (6) [7] [8]
# (1) int, unique element tag
# (2...5) int, node i, j, k, l
# (6) int, material tag
# [7] double, element thickness, default: 1.0
# [8] double, objective length, default: -1.0 (disabled)

docs.title: Remarks
docs.text:
• Three integration schemes are available: "I", "L" and "G".
  • "I": Five-Point Irons Scheme
  • "L": 3rd Order Lobatto Scheme
  • "G": 3rd Order Gauss Scheme
  • GCMQ is the full version described in 10.1002/nme.6066 with enhanced strain. SGCMQ is a PS like element with no enhanced strain, the direct result of which is that less computation is required (less than CP8R).

The default approach interpolates translations from drilling rotations using edge length, potentially causing severe mesh dependency for drilling DoFs. This is only an issue if the simulation actually uses drilling DoFs, as it can skew the accuracy of connected components. To prevent this, providing a positive objective length [8] triggers an alternative formulation that relies on this specific length for interpolation.

implementation limitation

The objective length defaults to -1, so the mesh-dependent edge-length interpolation is active unless a positive value is supplied. Initialization fails and the element is disabled if the local projection matrices are singular. The thickness argument is silently overwritten to 1.0 for a plane-strain material.

  • The parser also accepts GCMQ without a suffix, followed by an optional thickness and an optional scheme character that defaults to I.
  • A non-singular local projection matrix is required, so an element whose initialization solve fails is disabled with an error message.
  • The thickness argument is overridden to 1.0 for a plane-strain material, as in GQ12.
  • The simplified variant is used as the membrane part of SGCMS, which combines it with the DKT4 plate.

docs.title: GQ12
docs.text:
Quadrilateral With Drilling DoFs

  • Number of Nodes: 4
  • Number of DoFs: 3 (Translation, Translation, Rotation)
  • DoF Label: U1, U2, UR3
  • Supports Body Force
  • Integration Scheme: 2nd Order Gauss
  • Constant Consistent Mass Matrix With Same Order Integration

docs.title: Background
docs.text:
GQ12 is the four-node generalized conforming membrane with vertex drilling rotations introduced by Long and Xu.

The generalized conforming method replaces pointwise inter-element compatibility with an integral compatibility condition along each edge, which allows a low-order polynomial field to include the nodal rotation.

The in-plane displacement is written as a bilinear translation part plus a drilling part that depends on the four edge vectors $\(\Delta\mathbf x_i\)$ and on the differences of adjacent nodal rotations, the same physical idea as the mid-edge correction derived on Allman.

The implementation builds the strain--displacement matrix as $\(\mathbf B=\mathbf B_u+\mathbf B_\theta\)$, where $\(\mathbf B_u\)$ comes from the bilinear shape functions and $\(\mathbf B_\theta\)$ from the drilling interpolation scaled by $\(1/16\)$.

The strain is $\(\mathbf\varepsilon=(u_{,x},\,v_{,y},\,u_{,y}+v_{,x})^{\mathsf T}\)$ and the standard stiffness $\(\int\mathbf B^{\mathsf T}\mathbf D\mathbf B\,t\,dA\)$ is evaluated with 2-by-2 Gauss points.

The drilling interpolation uses the actual edge lengths, so the drilling stiffness is geometry dependent, a limitation that the enhanced mixed element GCMQ can avoid through its objective-length option.

deviation from theory

The drilling part is built from the actual edge vectors without a material-dependent penalty parameter of the Hughes--Brezzi type. The drilling stiffness therefore scales with element size, and a uniform drilling rotation still produces no membrane strain.

This element supplies the membrane part of the flat shell S4.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. 10.1016/0045-7949(94)90356-5
  2. Generalized conforming quadrilateral membrane element with vertex rigid rotational freedom
  3. 10.1016/0045-7825(89)90124-2

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text:
GQ12
element GQ12 (1) (2...5) (6) [7]
# (1) int, unique element tag
# (2...5) int, node i, j, k, l
# (6) int, material tag
# [7] double, element thickness, default: 1.0

docs.title: Remarks
docs.text:
• The thickness argument is overridden to 1.0 for a plane-strain material, so it only matters for plane stress.

implementation limitation

There is no objective-length argument to reduce mesh-size dependence. The thickness is silently overwritten for plane strain.

developer note

The 2-by-2 Gauss rule and the drilling interpolation are fixed in the code.

  • A consistent mass matrix and a body-force vector are assembled when the material provides a nonzero density.
  • A uniform drilling rotation produces no membrane strain, so the UR3 DoF still needs to be restrained or stabilized in an isolated membrane patch.
  • For an improved coarse-mesh response consider GCMQ, which adds enhanced strain modes through a modified Hu--Washizu formulation.
  • In a shell analysis this element is combined with the Mindlin plate to form S4.

docs.title: PS
docs.text:
Pian-Sumihara Quadrilateral Element

  • Number of Nodes: 4
  • Number of DoFs: 2 (Translation, Translation)
  • DoF Label: U1, U2
  • Supports Body Force
  • Integration Scheme: 2nd Order Gauss
  • Constant Consistent Mass Matrix With Same Order Integration

docs.title: Background
docs.text:
PS is the four-node assumed-stress quadrilateral of Pian and Sumihara. It is based on a Hellinger-Reissner or complementary-energy functional in which the stress field and the displacement field are interpolated independently. The stress interpolation uses the five-parameter pattern $$ \mathbf P=\begin{bmatrix} 1&0&0&T_{11}\eta&T_{12}\xi\ 0&1&0&T_{21}\eta&T_{22}\xi\ 0&0&1&T_{31}\eta&T_{32}\xi \end{bmatrix}, $$ where the first column of $\(\mathbf T\)$ is $\([(\partial x/\partial\xi)^2,(\partial y/\partial\xi)^2,(\partial x/\partial\xi)(\partial y/\partial\xi)]^\mathrm T\)$ and the second column is the same expression with $\(\xi\)$ replaced by $\(\eta\)$. The last two columns are therefore the natural-coordinate linear terms $\(\eta\)$ and $\(\xi\)$ mapped to physical strain components, which makes the element insensitive to distortion. With the strain interpolation $\(\mathbf\varepsilon=\mathbf B\mathbf a\)$ and the elastic compliance $\(\mathbf D^{-1}\)$, the compatibility and equilibrium matrices are $$ \mathbf H=\sum_q\mathbf P_q^\mathrm T\mathbf D^{-1}\mathbf P_q\,w_q,\qquad \mathbf N=\sum_q\mathbf P_q^\mathrm T\mathbf B_q\,w_q. $$ The stress parameters follow from stationarity as $\(\mathbf\beta=\mathbf H^{-1}\mathbf N\mathbf a\)$, and the stiffness reduces to $$ \mathbf K^e=\mathbf N^\mathrm T\mathbf H^{-1}\mathbf N. $$ Because the strain is recovered directly from the assumed stress through $\(\mathbf\varepsilon=\mathbf D^{-1}\mathbf P\mathbf\beta\)$, no local nonlinear solve is needed when the material is nonlinear. The element therefore keeps the low cost of CP4 while avoiding shear locking.

deviation from theory

Unlike a fully nonlinear assumed-stress formulation, the stress modes do not adapt to a changing material tangent.

developer note

A fully nonlinear assumed-stress formulation would rebuild the compatibility matrix $\(\mathbf H\)$ from the current tangent at every iteration. Here the strain interpolation is calibrated once against the initial elastic stiffness.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text:
PS
element PS (1) (2...5) (6) [7]
# (1) int, unique element tag
# (2...5) int, node i, j, k, l
# (6) int, material tag
# [7] double, element thickness, default: 1.0

docs.title: Remarks
docs.text:
1. The original five-parameter stress field is used for stress interpolation.
  2. The mixed framework is used to extend the original formulation to accommodate elastoplastic applications.
  3. As there is no enhanced strain, no local iteration is required. Hence PS is faster than elements such as QE2.
  4. The thickness argument is ignored when the material declares plane strain.
  5. Four Gauss points are used, and the characteristic length is $\(\sqrt{A}\)$ with $\(A\)$ the element area.
  6. The assumed stress is recovered from the material strain, so stress recording follows the same path as in CP4.
  7. QE2 adds two enhanced strain modes for better distortion sensitivity at a higher cost, while CP4I uses incompatible displacements.

docs.title: QE2
docs.text:
Mixed Four-Node Quadrilateral Element

  • Number of Nodes: 4
  • Number of DoFs: 2
  • DoF Label: U1, U2
  • Supports Body Force
  • Integration Scheme: 2nd Order Gauss
  • Constant Consistent Mass Matrix With Same Order Integration

docs.title: Background
docs.text:
QE2 is Piltner's four-node mixed quadrilateral with two enhanced strain modes. It is derived from a Hu-Washizu functional in which displacement, strain and stress are interpolated independently. The stress field uses seven modes assembled from the mapped polynomial vector $\([0,\xi,\eta,\xi\eta]\)$ and the seven-term stress interpolation $\(\mathbf P\)$. The compatible strain is $\(\mathbf\varepsilon_c=\mathbf B\mathbf a\)$, and two enhanced strain modes $\(\mathbf\varepsilon_e=\mathbf B_I\mathbf\lambda\)$ are added, so $\(\mathbf\varepsilon=\mathbf B\mathbf a+\mathbf B_I\mathbf\lambda\)$. The independent strain parameters $\(\mathbf\alpha\)$ and stress parameters $\(\mathbf\beta\)$ are related through the compliance matrix $\(\mathbf A=\mathbf D^{-1}\mathbf P\)$. The discrete equations contain the arrays $$ \mathbf H=\sum_q\mathbf P_q^\mathrm T\mathbf A_qw_q,\quad \mathbf L=\sum_q\mathbf P_q^\mathrm T\mathbf B_qw_q,\quad \mathbf L_I=\sum_q\mathbf P_q^\mathrm T\mathbf B_{Iq}w_q. $$ The local unknowns are eliminated by static condensation. Since $\(\mathbf H\)$ is symmetric, the condensed stiffness assembled in the code is $$ \mathbf K^e=\mathbf L^\mathrm T\mathbf H^{-1}\mathbf L-\left(\mathbf L_I^\mathrm T\mathbf H^{-1}\mathbf L\right)^\mathrm T\left(\mathbf L_I^\mathrm T\mathbf H^{-1}\mathbf L_I\right)^{-1}\left(\mathbf L_I^\mathrm T\mathbf H^{-1}\mathbf L\right). $$ The condensation matrices $\(\mathbf L\)$, $\(\mathbf L_I\)$, $\(\mathbf H\)$ and their inverses are formed once at initialisation from the initial material tangent. The local stiffness is refreshed from the current trial tangent at every iteration and the reduced matrices are recomputed from it, so the element remains usable with nonlinear materials. The enhanced modes relieve shear locking and reduce sensitivity to element distortion compared with the bilinear CP4.

deviation from theory

Unlike a fully nonlinear Hu-Washizu element, the enhancement basis does not follow the evolving material stiffness.

developer note

A fully nonlinear Hu-Washizu element would recompute the compatibility matrix from the current tangent at every iteration. Here the condensation matrices are frozen at the initial elastic tangent.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text:
QE2
element QE2 (1) (2...5) (6) [7]
# (1) int, unique element tag
# (2...5) int, node i, j, k, l
# (6) int, material tag
# [7] double, element thickness, default: 1.0

docs.title: Remarks
docs.text:
• The element stores the seven stress parameters, the seven strain parameters and the two enhanced-strain multipliers as history variables.
  • The thickness argument is ignored when the material declares plane strain.
  • Four Gauss points are used, and the characteristic length is $\(\sqrt{A}\)$ with $\(A\)$ the element area.
  • Initialization fails if the $\(7\times7\)$ compatibility matrix is singular, which can happen for severely distorted elements.
  • Stress and strain recording returns the mixed fields rather than the raw material response, with the seven components remapped to the Voigt layout.
  • PS is cheaper because it has no enhanced strain, while CP4I uses incompatible modes instead of an assumed stress.

docs.title: DCP3
docs.text:
Constant Strain Triangle With Crack Phase

  • Number of Nodes: 3
  • Number of DoFs: 3 (Translation, Translation, Damage)
  • DoF Label: U1, U2, DAMAGE
  • Integration Scheme: Single Point Centre
  • Zero Mass Entries On Damage DoFs

docs.title: Background
docs.text:
DCP3 implements a phase-field model of brittle fracture on the constant-strain triangle. The total potential energy contains a degraded bulk term and a crack-surface term, $$ \Psi=\int_\Omega g(d)\,\psi(\mathbf\varepsilon)\,\mathrm d\Omega+G_c\int_\Omega\left[ rac{d^2}{2l}+ rac{l}{2}| abla d|^2 ight]\mathrm d\Omega. $$ Here $\(d\in[0,1]\)$ is the damage field, $\(g(d)=(1-d)^2\)$ is the degradation function, $\(\psi= frac12\mathbf\varepsilon^\mathrm T\mathbf\sigma\)$ is the strain energy density, $\(G_c\)$ is the fracture energy release rate and $\(l\)$ is the characteristic length. The second integral is the regularised crack length, and the two terms give the damage stiffness blocks $\(G_c\,l^{-1}\mathbf N^\mathrm T\mathbf N\)$ and $\(G_c\,l\,\mathbf B^\mathrm T\mathbf B\)$. Stationarity with respect to the displacement gives $\( abla\cdot[g(d)\mathbf\sigma]+\mathbf b=\mathbf 0\)$, and stationarity with respect to $\(d\)$ gives the Allen-Cahn-type equation $\( rac{G_c}{l}d-G_c l abla^2d=2(1-d)\mathcal H\)$. The history field $\(\mathcal H=\max_t\psi(t)\)$ enforces irreversibility of crack growth by keeping the maximum strain energy reached so far.

deviation from theory

The implementation sets $\(\mathcal H\)$ from the total strain energy $\( frac12\mathbf\varepsilon^\mathrm T\mathbf\sigma\)$. It does not perform the tensile and compressive spectral split used in many phase-field fracture models, so compression can also drive damage.

The displacement and damage fields use the same nodal interpolation, so each node carries U1, U2 and DAMAGE. In the staggered scheme the coupling blocks are omitted and the two fields are solved in sequence; the DCP3M variant keeps the coupling blocks and solves monolithically. The element uses one centroid integration point, so the strain is constant over the triangle and $\(l\)$ defaults to $\(2\sqrt{A}\)$ when a negative value is supplied.

implementation limitation

A single integration point makes the history field constant over each triangle, so the crack band cannot vary inside an element. The resulting crack path is strongly tied to the mesh alignment and needs a sufficiently fine, well-oriented discretisation.

The quadrilateral counterpart with $\(2 imes2\)$ Gauss integration is DCP4.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
There are a lot of papers on the phase-field model. A staggered scheme with maximum strain energy is adopted as an illustration of implementation.

  • 10.1016/j.commatsci.2016.04.009
  • 10.1016/j.cma.2010.04.016

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text:
DCP3
element DCP3 (1) (2...4) (5) (6) (7) [8]
# (1) int, unique element tag
# (2...4) int, node i, j, k
# (5) int, material tag
# (6) double, characteristic length
# (7) double, energy release rate
# [8] double, element thickness, default: 1.0

docs.title: Remarks
docs.text:
• The third DoF is the damage variable. Boundary conditions can be assigned.
  • The characteristic length (6) can be set to a negative value to automatically determine it based on the element geometry.
  • The energy release rate (7) is the material parameter $\(G_c\)$ and must be positive to give a meaningful crack-driving force.
  • The damage DoF has zero mass entries, so it is intended for quasi-static analysis; dynamic crack problems need special treatment.
  • The history variable is stored at the integration point and is updated only when the current strain energy exceeds the previous maximum.
  • A mesh size comparable to $\(l\)$ is needed to resolve the diffuse crack profile.
  • DCP3M solves the coupled problem monolithically, whereas the default DCP3 uses a staggered update without coupling blocks.

docs.title: Recording
docs.text:
This model supports the following additional history variables to be recorded.

variable label physical meaning DAMAGE damage variable

docs.title: Variants
docs.text: DCP3M uses the same command element DCP3M (1) (2...4) (5) (6) (7) [8] as DCP3, but solves displacement and damage monolithically by adding their coupling blocks to the stiffness matrix instead of using a staggered update.

docs.title: DCP4
docs.text:
Bilinear Quadrilateral With Crack Phase

  • Number of Nodes: 4
  • Number of DoFs: 3 (Translation, Translation, Damage)
  • DoF Label: U1, U2, DAMAGE
  • Integration Scheme: 2nd Order Gauss
  • Zero Mass Entries On Damage DoFs

docs.title: Background
docs.text:
DCP4 implements the phase-field brittle-fracture formulation of DCP3 on the bilinear quadrilateral. The energy functional is $$ \Psi=\int_\Omega (1-d)^2\,\psi(\mathbf\varepsilon)\,\mathrm d\Omega+G_c\int_\Omega\left[\frac{d^2}{2l}+\frac{l}{2}|\nabla d|^2\right]\mathrm d\Omega, $$ with $\(d\)$ the damage field, $\(G_c\)$ the energy release rate and $\(l\)$ the characteristic length. The displacement and damage fields share the bilinear shape functions, so each node carries U1, U2 and DAMAGE. At each of the four Gauss points the strain is $\(\mathbf\varepsilon=\mathbf B\mathbf a\)$ and the local damage is $\(d=\sum_aN_ad_a\)$, which gives the degradation $\(g=(1-d)^2\)$. The stiffness contributions are $\(g\,\mathbf B^\mathrm T\mathbf D\mathbf B\)$ for the displacement block and $\(G_c\big(l^{-1}\mathbf N^\mathrm T\mathbf N+l\,\mathbf B^\mathrm T\mathbf B\big)\)$ for the damage block. The history field $\(\mathcal H=\max\psi\)$ drives damage evolution and prevents healing.

deviation from theory

The implementation uses the total strain energy $\(\tfrac12\mathbf\varepsilon^\mathrm T\mathbf\sigma\)$ as the history field. No tensile-compressive spectral split is applied, so a compressive stress state can also increase the damage-driving variable.

The staggered version omits the displacement-damage coupling blocks, while DCP4M includes the term $\(-2(1-d)\mathbf B^\mathrm T\mathbf\sigma\mathbf N^\mathrm T\)$ in the off-diagonal blocks for a monolithic solve. A $\(2\times2\)$ Gauss rule is used, and a negative characteristic length is replaced by $\(2\sqrt{A}\)$ from the element area. See DCP3 for the derivation of the coupled equations and the role of the history variable.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text:
DCP4
element DCP4 (1) (2...5) (6) (7) (8) [9]
# (1) int, unique element tag
# (2...5) int, node i, j, k, l
# (6) int, material tag
# (7) double, characteristic length
# (8) double, energy release rate
# [9] double, element thickness, default: 1.0

docs.title: Remarks
docs.text:
• The third DoF is the damage variable. Boundary conditions can be assigned.
  • The characteristic length (7) can be set to a negative value to automatically determine it based on the element geometry.
  • The energy release rate (8) is the fracture toughness $\(G_c\)$ used in the crack-surface energy.
  • The damage DoF has zero mass entries, so the formulation is intended for quasi-static crack growth.
  • One history variable is stored per Gauss point and is updated to the maximum strain energy seen so far.
  • Use at least four to eight elements across the expected crack width $\(l\)$ for a smooth damage field.
  • DCP4M adds the coupling blocks for a monolithic solution, while the default DCP4 uses a staggered scheme.

docs.title: Recording
docs.text:
This model supports the following additional history variables to be recorded.

variable label physical meaning DAMAGE damage variable

docs.title: Variants
docs.text: DCP4M uses the same command element DCP4M (1) (2...5) (6) (7) (8) [9] as DCP4, but solves displacement and damage monolithically by adding their coupling blocks to the stiffness matrix instead of using a staggered update.

docs.title: CINP4
docs.text:
Bilinear Infinite Quadrilateral

  • Number of Nodes: 4
  • Number of DoFs: 2 (Translation, Translation)
  • DoF Label: U1, U2

docs.title: Background
docs.text:
CINP4 is a mapped infinite quadrilateral for two-dimensional unbounded domains. It attaches to the boundary of a finite-element mesh through the two nodes at $\(\eta=-1\)$, while the two nodes at $\(\eta\to+1\)$ are placed at infinity. The mapping functions are $$ M_1=\frac{(1-\xi)\eta}{\eta-1},\quad M_2=\frac{(1+\xi)\eta}{\eta-1},\quad M_3=\frac{(1+\xi)(1+\eta)}{2(1-\eta)},\quad M_4=\frac{(1-\xi)(1+\eta)}{2(1-\eta)}. $$ At $\(\eta=-1\)$ the functions reduce to the linear shape functions of the two finite nodes and $\(M_3=M_4=0\)$. As $\(\eta\)$ tends to $\(1\)$ the mapping sends the parent point to infinity, so the far field is represented without truncating the mesh. The strain-displacement matrix is formed from the derivatives of $\(M_a\)$ mapped by the inverse Jacobian, $\(\nabla N_a=\mathbf J^{-\mathrm T}\nabla_{\!\xi}M_a\)$. The stiffness integral over the semi-infinite domain is evaluated on the finite parent square, with the stretching toward infinity carried by the Jacobian determinant. A $\(2\times2\)$ Gauss rule in the parent domain is used, and the thickness is applied as in CP4.

implementation limitation

The element assembles only a static stiffness and has no mass or damping matrix. It is therefore restricted to static and quasi-static unbounded-domain problems, as in the reference paper, and cannot absorb outgoing waves in a dynamic analysis.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text:
CINP4
element CINP4 (1) (2...5) (6) [7]
# (1) int, unique element tag
# (2...5) int, node i, j, k, l
# (6) int, material tag
# [7] double, element thickness, default: 1.0

docs.title: Remarks
docs.text:
1. The first two nodes are finite nodes while the latter two are infinite nodes.
  2. The finite nodes lie on $\(\eta=-1\)$ and the infinite direction is $\(\eta\to+1\)$; the element must be attached to a mesh of ordinary CP4 elements.
  3. The thickness argument is forced to unity when the material declares plane strain.
  4. A $\(2\times2\)$ Gauss rule is used in the parent domain; no nonlinear-geometry path is available.
  5. The infinite nodes should be placed so that their connecting edge points away from the region of interest.

docs.title: CP3
docs.text:
Constant Strain Triangle

  • Number of Nodes: 3
  • Number of DoFs: 2 (Translation, Translation)
  • DoF Label: U1, U2
  • Integration Scheme: Single Point Centre
  • Supports Body Force
  • Constant Consistent Mass Matrix With Same Order Integration

docs.title: Background
docs.text: CP3 is the three-node constant-strain triangle, abbreviated CST. The displacement is linear over the triangle, $\(\mathbf u=\sum_{a=1}^3N_a\mathbf u_a\)$, with area coordinates $\(N_a=A_a/A\)$. The coordinate matrix $\(\mathbf X\)$ has columns $\([1,x_a,y_a]^\mathrm T\)$, so the area is $\(A=\tfrac12\det\mathbf X\)$ and the constant gradients are $\(\partial N_a/\partial x\)$ and $\(\partial N_a/\partial y\)$, the last two rows of $\(\mathbf X^{-1}\)$. The strain vector $\(\mathbf\varepsilon=\mathbf B\mathbf a\)$ is constant over the element, with $$ \mathbf B=\begin{bmatrix} N_{1,x}&0&N_{2,x}&0&N_{3,x}&0\ 0&N_{1,y}&0&N_{2,y}&0&N_{3,y}\ N_{1,y}&N_{1,x}&N_{2,y}&N_{2,x}&N_{3,y}&N_{3,x} \end{bmatrix}. $$ Because $\(\mathbf B\)$ and $\(\mathbf D\)$ are constant, the single-centre-point rule is exact for homogeneous material and $\(\mathbf K^e=A\,t\,\mathbf B^\mathrm T\mathbf D\mathbf B\)$. The same centroid rule is used for the consistent mass matrix and the body-force vector. The quadratic triangle CP6 removes the constant-strain restriction by adding edge midnodes and a three-point rule. For axisymmetric problems the analogous constant-strain triangle is CAX3.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text:
CP3
element CP3 (1) (2...4) (5) [6] [7]
# (1) int, unique element tag
# (2...4) int, node i, j, k
# (5) int, material tag
# [6] double, element thickness, default: 1.0
# [7] bool string, nonlinear geometry switch, default: false

docs.title: Remarks
docs.text:
• The CP3 element resembles CPS3 and CPE3 elements in ABAQUS. It is a constant strain element.

deviation from theory

Only CP3 is accepted as an element token for both plane stress and plane strain; the names CPS3 and CPE3 are descriptive only and are not registered as commands. The material plane type decides whether thickness is applied.

developer note

The ABAQUS-style names CPS3 and CPE3 are descriptive only; the element parser registers a single token CP3 for both plane stress and plane strain.

  • A single integration point at the center of the element is used for integration.
  • The characteristic length used by material regularisation is $\(\sqrt{A}\)$, with $\(A\)$ the area of the triangle.
  • The thickness argument is forced to unity when the material declares plane strain.
  • The nonlinear geometry switch activates a Total Lagrangian update based on the Green-Lagrange strain.
  • The constant strain field makes the element too stiff in bending, so CP6 or CP8 should be preferred when stress gradients matter.
  • Elements with a drilling rotation are available as Allman and GQ12.

docs.title: CP4
docs.text:
Bilinear Quadrilateral

  • Number of Nodes: 4
  • Number of DoFs: 2 (Translation, Translation)
  • DoF Label: U1, U2
  • Integration Scheme: 2nd Order Gaussian (Full) or 1st Order Gaussian (Reduced)
  • Supports Body Force
  • Constant Consistent Mass Matrix With Same Order Integration

docs.title: Background
docs.text:
CP4 is the four-node isoparametric quadrilateral, also known as the bilinear quad or Q4. Its shape functions in parent coordinates $\((\xi,\eta)\in[-1,1]^2\)$ are $$ N_1= frac14(1-\xi)(1-\eta),\quad N_2= frac14(1+\xi)(1-\eta),\quad N_3= frac14(1+\xi)(1+\eta),\quad N_4= frac14(1-\xi)(1+\eta). $$ The nodes are ordered counter-clockwise starting at $\((\xi,\eta)=(-1,-1)\)$, so node 5 of a quadratic edge is inserted between nodes 1 and 2 in CP5. The isoparametric map $\(\mathbf x=\sum_aN_a\mathbf x_a\)$ gives the Jacobian $\(\mathbf J=\partial\mathbf x/\partial\mathbf\xi\)$, and the physical shape-function gradients are $\( abla N_a=\mathbf J^{-\mathrm T} abla_{\!\xi}N_a\)$. The small-strain vector is $\(\mathbf\varepsilon=\mathbf B\mathbf a\)$, with $$ \mathbf B= egin{bmatrix} N_{1,x}&0&N_{2,x}&0&N_{3,x}&0&N_{4,x}&0\ 0&N_{1,y}&0&N_{2,y}&0&N_{3,y}&0&N_{4,y}\ N_{1,y}&N_{1,x}&N_{2,y}&N_{2,x}&N_{3,y}&N_{3,x}&N_{4,y}&N_{4,x} \end{bmatrix}. $$ The stiffness and internal force are assembled as $\(\mathbf K^e=\sum_q t\,J_qw_q\,\mathbf B_q^\mathrm T\mathbf D_q\mathbf B_q\)$ and $\(\mathbf f^e=\sum_q t\,J_qw_q\,\mathbf B_q^\mathrm T\mathbf\sigma_q\)$.

Full integration uses a $\(2 imes2\)$ Gauss rule, which is exact for the bilinear stiffness of a parallelogram. Reduced integration uses one point at the element centre, where the strain sampled is the mean strain of the element. One-point integration admits the two hourglass displacement patterns $\(\mathbf h=[1,-1,1,-1]\)$ in the $\(x\)$ and $\(y\)$ directions, which produce no strain at the centre and would otherwise make the stiffness matrix rank deficient.

The stabilisation follows the orthogonal hourglass projection of Flanagan, Belytschko and co-workers. The physical hourglass vector is obtained by projecting the algebraic mode $\(\mathbf h\)$ orthogonal to the rigid-body and constant-strain modes, $$ \mathbf\gamma=\mathbf h-(\mathbf h\cdot\mathbf x)\,\mathbf b_1-(\mathbf h\cdot\mathbf y)\,\mathbf b_2. $$ Here $\(\mathbf b_1\)$ and $\(\mathbf b_2\)$ are the centre-point shape-function gradients divided by $\( exttt{double\_area}\)$, the quantity computed from the nodal coordinates that equals twice the element area $\(A\)$. The stabilisation matrix is added to the stiffness as $\(\mu\,(2t/A)\,\mathbf\gamma\mathbf\gamma^\mathrm T\)$, and the corresponding hourglass force is $\(\mu\,(2t/A)(\mathbf\gamma^\mathrm T\mathbf a)\mathbf\gamma\)$.

When the nonlinear geometry switch is set, the element uses a Total Lagrangian formulation. The trial deformation gradient is $\(\mathbf F=\mathbf I+\sum_a\mathbf u_a\otimes abla N_a\)$, and the Green-Lagrange strain $\(\mathbf E=(\mathbf F^\mathrm T\mathbf F-\mathbf I)/2\)$ is passed to the material. The second Piola-Kirchhoff stress returned by the material is contracted with the nonlinear strain-displacement matrix $\(\mathbf B_{NL}\)$, and an initial-stress geometric stiffness is assembled from that stress and the shape-function gradients.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text:
CP4
element CP4 (1) (2...5) (6) [7] [8] [9] [10]
# (1) int, unique element tag
# (2...5) int, node i, j, k, l
# (6) int, material tag
# [7] double, element thickness, default: 1.0
# [8] bool string, reduced integration switch, default: false
# [9] bool string, nonlinear geometry switch, default: false
# [10] double, hourglassing penalty multiplier, default: 1.0

docs.title: Remarks
docs.text:
• The CP4 element resembles CPS4 and CPE4 elements in ABAQUS.

deviation from theory

Only CP4 and CP4R are accepted element tokens; the names CPS4, CPE4, CPS4R and CPE4R are not registered and cannot be used in an element command. Plane stress or plane strain is selected by the material plane type, not by a separate element name.

developer note

The class documentation mentions CPS4, CPE4, CPS4R and CPE4R, but the element parser registers only the tokens CP4 and CP4R.
