  • The full integration scheme uses 2-by-2 Gaussian scheme and the reduced integration uses a single integration point at the center of the element.
  • The reduced integration scheme also imports anti-hourglassing technique.
  • The thickness (7) is ignored and forced to unity when the material uses plane strain.
  • The characteristic length used by nonlocal or damage materials is $\(\sqrt{A}\)$, with $\(A\)$ the element area computed by the shoelace formula.
  • The nonlinear geometry switch (9) activates the Total Lagrangian formulation with Green-Lagrange strain and a geometric stiffness.
  • Full integration is prone to shear and volumetric locking in bending and nearly incompressible plasticity; reduced integration with hourglass control is the cheaper alternative.
  • For assumed-stress and enhanced-strain alternatives that do not need hourglass control, see PS, QE2 and CP4I.

For the hourglassing control, see 10.1016/0045-7825(84)90067-7. The hourglassing penalty multiplier (denoted as $\(\mu\)$) is an overall multiplier that is applied to the hourglassing stiffness matrix.

\[ \mu\mathbf{\gamma}\mathbf{\gamma}^\mathrm{T}. \]

In the above, $\(\mathbf{\gamma}\)$ is identical to Eq. (19) in the reference paper. Thus, $\(\mu\)$ shall be set to some value proportional to the elastic modulus. The code forms the hourglass vectors with the centre gradients divided by $\(\texttt{double\_area}=2A\)$, then multiplies $\(\mathbf\gamma\mathbf\gamma^\mathrm T\)$ by $\(2t\mu/A\)$. The penalty argument is converted to its absolute value, so a negative entry has the same effect as a positive one.

implementation limitation

The default hourglass multiplier is unity and it is not scaled by the elastic modulus. For a material with a modulus of order GPa the default stabilisation is negligible, so reduced integration requires a multiplier scaled with the material stiffness and a reference area.

docs.title: Variants
docs.text: CP4R forces reduced integration with hourglassing control, so the reduced-integration switch is dropped: element CP4R (1) (2...5) (6) [7] [8] [9] reads thickness, nonlinear-geometry switch and hourglassing penalty multiplier. NonlocalCP4 is the nonlocal-damage variant; element NonlocalCP4 (1) (2...5) (6) [7] takes the material tag and optional thickness (default 1.0), requires a material with exactly one nonlocal variable, and adds an NL1 DoF at every node.

docs.title: CP4I
docs.text:
Bilinear Incompatible Quadrilateral

  • Number of Nodes: 4
  • Number of DoFs: 2 (Translation, Translation)
  • DoF Label: U1, U2
  • Integration Scheme: 2nd Order Gauss
  • Constant Consistent Mass Matrix With Same Order Integration

docs.title: Background
docs.text:
CP4I is the four-node quadrilateral with incompatible modes, the plane counterpart of the Wilson element and the Q6 family. The compatible displacement is the bilinear interpolation of CP4, giving the strain-displacement matrix $\(\mathbf B_1\)$. Four additional strain modes are added through internal degrees of freedom $\(\mathbf\alpha\)$ that have no nodal counterpart, giving $\(\mathbf\varepsilon=\mathbf B_1\mathbf a+\mathbf B_2\mathbf\alpha\)$. The four columns of $\(\mathbf B_2\)$ are built from the global derivatives of the parent-domain function $\(f=-(\xi^2+\eta^2)\)$, obtained as $\(\nabla f=\mathbf J^{-1}[-2\xi,-2\eta]^\mathrm T\)$. The first column enhances $\(\varepsilon_{xx}\)$ with $\(\partial f/\partial x\)$, the second enhances $\(\gamma_{xy}\)$ with $\(\partial f/\partial x\)$, the third enhances $\(\gamma_{xy}\)$ with $\(\partial f/\partial y\)$, and the fourth enhances $\(\varepsilon_{yy}\)$ with $\(\partial f/\partial y\)$.

deviation from theory

The classical Wilson or Q6 element adds two incompatible displacement modes $\((1-\xi^2)\)$ and $\((1-\eta^2)\)$, whereas this implementation adds four assumed strain modes derived from one quadratic function.

developer note

The element name and the documentation retain the incompatible-mode terminology even though the enhancement enters through the strain interpolation.

The mixed equilibrium equations are $$ \begin{bmatrix}\mathbf K_{aa}&\mathbf K_{a\alpha}\ \mathbf K_{\alpha a}&\mathbf K_{\alpha\alpha}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}\mathbf a\ \mathbf\alpha\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}\mathbf f\ \mathbf 0\end{bmatrix}. $$ Because $\(\mathbf\alpha\)$ has no external load, it can be condensed out at element level, $$ \mathbf K^\mathrm{eff}=\mathbf K_{aa}-\mathbf K_{a\alpha}\mathbf K_{\alpha\alpha}^{-1}\mathbf K_{\alpha a},\qquad \mathbf f^\mathrm{eff}=\mathbf f-\mathbf K_{a\alpha}\mathbf K_{\alpha\alpha}^{-1}\mathbf 0. $$ The same condensation is repeated with the current tangent at every iteration, so the formulation works with nonlinear materials. A $\(2\times2\)$ Gauss rule is used, and the extra modes relieve the shear locking of the fully integrated bilinear quad. The assumed-stress alternatives PS and QE2 achieve a similar improvement without incompatible displacements.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text:
CP4I
element CP4I (1) (2...5) (6) [7]
# (1) int, unique element tag
# (2...5) int, node i, j, k, l
# (6) int, material tag
# [7] double, element thickness, default: 1.0

docs.title: Remarks
docs.text:
• The element has no reduced-integration or nonlinear-geometry switch in the current parser.
  • The thickness argument is ignored when the material declares plane strain.
  • Static condensation is performed both for the initial stiffness and at every trial state, so the internal parameters follow the material tangent.
  • The incompatible modes are internal to the element and do not add global DoFs or mass.
  • Distorted quadrilaterals can make $\(\mathbf K_{\alpha\alpha}\)$ ill conditioned; keep elements reasonably rectangular.
  • Compare with CP4 for the plain bilinear quad and with QE2 for a mixed formulation with two enhanced strains.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Incompatible displacement models
  2. 10.1002/nme.1620100602
  3. ISBN 978-0-486-41181-1

docs.title: CP5
docs.text:
Five-Point Quadrilateral

  • Number of Nodes: 5
  • Number of DoFs: 2 (Translation, Translation)
  • DoF Label: U1, U2
  • Integration Scheme: 2nd Order Irons
  • Supports Body Force
  • Constant Consistent Mass Matrix With Same Order Integration

docs.title: Background
docs.text: CP5 is a five-node quadrilateral obtained from the bilinear quad CP4 by adding one midside node on the bottom edge. The shape functions are $\(N_5=\tfrac14(1-\xi^2)(1-\eta)\)$ and $\(N_a=\tfrac14(1\pm\xi)(1\pm\eta)-\tfrac12N_5\)$ for the two corner nodes of that edge, while the other two corner functions remain bilinear. The added function is a quadratic bubble that vanishes on three edges and is symmetric about $\(\xi=0\)$, so the interpolated displacement is quadratic along the bottom edge and linear elsewhere. This makes CP5 a transition element: it can share the midside node with a quadratic CP8 on one edge and a plain CP4 on the others. The nodes are ordered counter-clockwise from $\((\xi,\eta)=(-1,-1)\)$ and node 5 lies at $\((0,-1)\)$. A five-point Irons rule is used, with one point at the centre and four points at $\((\pm1,0)\)$ and $\((0,\pm1)\)$, which is exact to polynomial degree five. The stiffness is assembled as $\(\mathbf K^e=\sum_q t\,J_qw_q\,\mathbf B_q^\mathrm T\mathbf D_q\mathbf B_q\)$, exactly as in CP4. Adding the further midside nodes gives CP6 and CP7.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text:
CP5
element CP5 (1) (2...6) (7) [8] [9]
# (1) int, unique element tag
# (2...6) int, node tags that define the element
# (7) int, material tag
# [8] double, element thickness, default: 1.0
# [9] bool string, nonlinear geometry switch, default: false

docs.title: Remarks
docs.text:
• The node order is the four corners counter-clockwise from the bottom left, followed by the midside node of the bottom edge.
  • The characteristic length is computed from the first four nodes only, using the shoelace formula.

deviation from theory

The midside node does not contribute to the characteristic length or to the area used for it. A highly curved bottom edge therefore gives the same length as the corresponding bilinear CP4.

  • The thickness argument is ignored when the material declares plane strain.
  • The nonlinear geometry switch activates a Total Lagrangian update.
  • Use this element to connect a quadratic mesh to a linear mesh without hanging nodes; CP7 and CP8 add further midside nodes.

docs.title: CP6
docs.text:
Quadratic Triangle

  • Number of Nodes: 6
  • Number of DoFs: 2 (Translation, Translation)
  • DoF Label: U1, U2
  • Integration Scheme: 3-Point Mid-edge
  • Supports Body Force
  • Constant Consistent Mass Matrix With Same Order Integration

docs.title: Background
docs.text:
CP6 is the six-node quadratic triangle. Nodes 1 to 3 are the vertices and nodes 4 to 6 are the midpoints of edges 1-2, 2-3 and 3-1. The interpolation uses the complete quadratic monomial vector $\([1,x,y,xy,x^2,y^2]\)$, so the displacement is quadratic and the strain varies linearly over the triangle. The implementation inverts the $\(6\times6\)$ matrix built from the six nodal coordinate vectors to obtain the shape functions and their derivatives directly in the global frame. Three integration points are placed at the three midside nodes with weights $\(A\,t/3\)$ each, which integrates the quadratic strain energy exactly. The stiffness is $\(\mathbf K^e=\sum_{q=1}^{3}\tfrac{1}{3}A\,t\,\mathbf B_q^\mathrm T\mathbf D_q\mathbf B_q\)$.

deviation from theory

The same three-point rule is reused for the mass matrix. Since the product of two quadratic shape functions is quartic, that mass matrix is under-integrated and is only approximately the consistent mass.

Compared with the constant-strain triangle CP3, the linear strain field captures bending with far fewer elements, at the cost of three material evaluations per element.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text:
CP6
element CP6 (1) (2...7) (8) [9] [10]
# (1) int, unique element tag
# (2...7) int, node tags that define the element
# (8) int, material tag
# [9] double, element thickness, default: 1.0
# [10] bool string, nonlinear geometry switch, default: false

docs.title: Remarks
docs.text:
• The first three nodes are the triangle vertices and the last three are the corresponding edge midpoints.
  • The characteristic length used by regularisation models is $\(\sqrt{A}\)$, with $\(A\)$ the triangle area.
  • The thickness argument is ignored when the material declares plane strain.
  • The nonlinear geometry switch activates a Total Lagrangian update.
  • Midside nodes must be placed at the actual edge midpoints to keep the quadratic mapping well behaved.
  • For quadrilateral meshes the corresponding quadratic option is CP8.

docs.title: CP7
docs.text:
Seven-Point Quadrilateral

  • Number of Nodes: 7
  • Number of DoFs: 2 (Translation, Translation)
  • DoF Label: U1, U2
  • Integration Scheme: 2nd Order Irons
  • Supports Body Force
  • Constant Consistent Mass Matrix With Same Order Integration

docs.title: Background
docs.text: CP7 is a seven-node quadrilateral obtained from CP5 by adding midside nodes on the right and top edges. The three bubble functions are $\(N_5=\tfrac14(1-\xi^2)(1-\eta)\)$, $\(N_6=\tfrac14(1+\xi)(1-\eta^2)\)$ and $\(N_7=\tfrac14(1-\xi^2)(1+\eta)\)$, with the corner-node functions reduced by one half of the bubble function on the corresponding edge. The left edge remains linear, so the element is a transition between the quadratic CP8 and the bilinear CP4. The nodes are ordered counter-clockwise from $\((\xi,\eta)=(-1,-1)\)$, followed by the bottom, right and top midside nodes. A five-point Irons rule is used, giving polynomial degree five accuracy for the stiffness integral. The interpolation and quadrature are the same as in CP5, with one additional midside mode.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text:
CP7
element CP7 (1) (2...8) (9) [10] [11]
# (1) int, unique element tag
# (2...8) int, node tags that define the element
# (9) int, material tag
# [10] double, element thickness, default: 1.0
# [11] bool string, nonlinear geometry switch, default: false

docs.title: Remarks
docs.text:
• The node order is the four corners counter-clockwise from the bottom left, then the bottom, right and top midside nodes.
  • The characteristic length is computed from the first four nodes only, using the shoelace formula.

deviation from theory

The three midside nodes are ignored when the characteristic length is evaluated. The value equals the shoelace area of the four corner nodes, so curvature of the edges does not affect it.

  • The thickness argument is ignored when the material declares plane strain.
  • The nonlinear geometry switch activates a Total Lagrangian update.
  • Use this element as an intermediate step when refining from CP4 to CP8 without hanging nodes.

docs.title: CP8
docs.text:
Second Order Quadrilateral

  • Number of Nodes: 8
  • Number of DoFs: 2 (Translation, Translation)
  • DoF Label: U1, U2
  • Integration Scheme: 2nd Order Irons (Full) or 2nd Order Gauss (Reduced)
  • Supports Body Force
  • Constant Consistent Mass Matrix With Same Order Integration

docs.title: Background
docs.text: CP8 is the eight-node quadratic serendipity quadrilateral. The four corner shape functions are the bilinear functions minus one half of the adjacent midside functions, and the four midside functions are $$ N_5=\tfrac12(1-\xi^2)(1-\eta),\quad N_6=\tfrac12(1+\xi)(1-\eta^2),\quad N_7=\tfrac12(1-\xi^2)(1+\eta),\quad N_8=\tfrac12(1-\xi)(1-\eta^2). $$ The nodes are ordered counter-clockwise from $\((\xi,\eta)=(-1,-1)\)$, with midside nodes on the bottom, right, top and left edges. The quadratic interpolation allows curved edges and a strain field that varies linearly within each element. The strain is assembled as $\(\mathbf\varepsilon=\mathbf B\mathbf a\)$ with the same Voigt pattern as CP4, and the stiffness is $\(\mathbf K^e=\sum_q t\,J_qw_q\,\mathbf B_q^\mathrm T\mathbf D_q\mathbf B_q\)$. In the source the full scheme is the five-point Irons rule, which is exact to polynomial degree five and therefore comparable in accuracy to the $\(3\times3\)$ Gauss rule mentioned in the remarks. Reduced integration uses $\(2\times2\)$ Gauss points.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text:
CP8
element CP8 (1) (2...9) (10) [11] [12] [13]
# (1) int, unique element tag
# (2...9) int, node 1 to node 8
# (10) int, material tag
# [11] double, element thickness, default: 1.0
# [12] bool string, reduced integration switch, default: false
# [13] bool string, nonlinear geometry switch, default: false

docs.title: Remarks
docs.text:
• The CP8 element resembles CPS8, CPE8, CPS8R and CPE8R elements in ABAQUS.
  • The full integration scheme uses 3-by-3 Gauss scheme and the reduced integration uses a 2-by-2 scheme.
  • In the current source the full rule is the five-point Irons pattern, exact to degree five, while the reduced rule is $\(2\times2\)$ Gauss.

developer note

The original remark above states that full integration uses a 3-by-3 Gauss scheme. The source instead constructs a five-point Irons rule, which has the same polynomial degree of precision but only five sampling points.

  • The reduced-integration variant does not add an hourglass stiffness, so check for zero-energy modes in coarse meshes.

implementation limitation

Unlike CP4, the reduced-integration option of CP8 has no hourglass stabilisation and no hourglass multiplier argument. Coarse meshes with reduced integration can therefore develop zero-energy modes that are not controlled by the element itself.

  • The characteristic length used by regularisation models is the square root of the area of the four corner nodes.
  • The thickness argument is ignored when the material declares plane strain.
  • The nonlinear geometry switch activates a Total Lagrangian update.

docs.title: Variants
docs.text: The plane stress or plane strain behaviour is set by the material's plane type, not by the element token; a plane-strain material forces unit thickness. CPS8 is the plane-stress name for the same CP8 implementation and accepts the identical element CPS8 (1) (2...9) (10) [11] [12] [13] arguments. CPE8 is the plane-strain counterpart; element CPE8 (1) (2...9) (10) [11] [12] omits the thickness argument and takes the optional reduced-integration and nonlinear-geometry switches. CPE8R is the plane-strain variant with reduced integration forced; element CPE8R (1) (2...9) (10) [11] accepts only the nonlinear-geometry switch.

docs.title: PCPE4DC
docs.text:
Bilinear Quadrilateral With Pore Pressure (Drained)

  • Number of Nodes: 4
  • Number of DoFs: 4 (Solid Translation, Solid Translation, Fluid Translation, Fluid Translation)
  • DoF Label: U1, U2, FU1, FU2
  • Supports Body Force
  • Constant Consistent Mass Matrix With Same Order Integration

docs.title: Theory
docs.text:
This is the four-node member of the drained consolidation family, whose siblings are PCPE8DC, PCPE4UC and PCPE8UC.

It implements the $\(u\)\(--\)\(U\)$ formulation of saturated porous media, in which the solid displacement $\(\mathbf u_s\)$ and the fluid displacement $\(\mathbf u_f\)$ have independent nodal degrees of freedom.

The formulation follows the drained and undrained assumptions of Biot consolidation theory as classified by Zienkiewicz, Chang and Bettess.

deviation from theory

This is a $\(u\)\(--\)\(U\)$ mixture element rather than the more common $\(u\)\(--\)\(p\)$ consolidation element. Pore pressure is not a nodal unknown, and the coupling blocks use $\((\alpha-n)\)$ and $\(n\)$ rather than a single Biot coefficient $\(\alpha\)$ multiplying a pressure shape function.

Let $\(K_s\)$ be the bulk modulus reported by the solid material, $\(K_f\)$ the bulk modulus of the fluid material, $\(n\)$ the porosity and $\(\alpha\)$ the Biot coefficient.

The code first forms the pressure coefficient

\[ q=\dfrac{K_sK_f}{nK_s+(\alpha-n)K_f}=\left(\dfrac{n}{K_f}+\dfrac{\alpha-n}{K_s}\right)^{-1}. \]

This is the inverse of the storage compliance of the two compressible phases.

Define the volumetric strains $\(\varepsilon_s=\nabla\cdot\mathbf u_s\)$ and $\(\varepsilon_f=\nabla\cdot\mathbf u_f\)$.

The strain energy stored by the pore fluid is

\[ \Psi_f=\dfrac{q}{2}\big[(\alpha-n)\varepsilon_s+n\varepsilon_f\big]^2, \]

and the pore pressure reported by the element is

\[ p=-q\big[(\alpha-n)\varepsilon_s+n\varepsilon_f\big]. \]

With $\(\mathbf B_s\)$ the solid strain--displacement matrix, $\(\mathbf B_f\)$ the fluid one and $\(\mathbf m=(1,1,0)^{\mathsf T}\)$ mapping volumetric strain into the three-plane-strain components, the discrete fluid stiffness is

\[ \mathbf K_f=\int_V q \begin{bmatrix} (\alpha-n)^2\mathbf m\mathbf m^{\mathsf T} & n(\alpha-n)\mathbf m\mathbf m^{\mathsf T}\\ n(\alpha-n)\mathbf m\mathbf m^{\mathsf T} & n^2\mathbf m\mathbf m^{\mathsf T} \end{bmatrix}\,dV . \]

This reproduces exactly the four blocks meta_k(s_dof,s_dof), meta_k(s_dof,f_dof), meta_k(f_dof,s_dof) and meta_k(f_dof,f_dof) of the implementation.

The effective stress is carried by the solid material, so the remaining stiffness is the usual $\(\int\mathbf B_s^{\mathsf T}\mathbf D\mathbf B_s\,dV\)$ evaluated by 2-by-2 Gauss integration at four points.

Darcy seepage is represented by a drag force proportional to the relative velocity $\(\mathbf v_s-\mathbf v_f\)$, with coefficient $\(n^2/k\)$ per unit volume.

This produces the constant viscous matrix

\[ \mathbf C=\dfrac{n^2}{k}\int_V \begin{bmatrix} \mathbf N^{\mathsf T}\mathbf N & -\mathbf N^{\mathsf T}\mathbf N\\ -\mathbf N^{\mathsf T}\mathbf N & \mathbf N^{\mathsf T}\mathbf N \end{bmatrix}\,dV , \]

so that only relative motion of the two phases dissipates energy.

The consistent mass matrix uses $\((1-n)\rho_s\)$ on the solid DoFs and $\(n\rho_f\)$ on the fluid DoFs, and the body force is split in the same proportions.

Both damping and mass are installed once during initialization through ConstantDamping and ConstantMass.

implementation limitation

Seepage is stored as a constant velocity-proportional damping matrix rather than as a time-integrated flux. Drainage is therefore a rate effect, and a purely static analysis has no mechanism to dissipate pore pressure.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text:
PCPE4DC
element PCPE4DC (1) (2...5) (6) (7) (8) (9) (10)
# (1) int, unique element tag
# (2...5) int, node i, j, k, l
# (6) int, solid material tag
# (7) int, fluid material tag
# (8) double, alpha
# (9) double, porosity n
# (10) double, permeability k

docs.title: Remarks
docs.text:
Only plane strain is supported. Plane stress does not make sense in geotechnical engineering.

For the fluid phase, an isotropic fluid material can be provided, which mainly provides the bulk modulus of the fluid phase. For example,

Text Only
# material Fluid (tag) (bulk modulus) (density)
material Fluid 1 1000. 1E-2

The $\(\alpha\)$ parameter (8) is often close to unity for soils. The porosity $\(n\)$ ranges from zero to unity. The isotropic permeability is assumed.

Interactions with other elements (with different arrangements of DoFs) can only be fulfilled via constraints.

  • DC denotes the drained variant, where the fluid phase has its own displacement DoFs and can flow relative to the solid through the permeability argument.
  • The letter C is not expanded in the source, but the bulk modulus and Darcy drag terms are those of a Biot consolidation model, so DC is read as drained consolidation.
  • PCPE4UC is the undrained counterpart, which eliminates the fluid DoFs by assuming $\(\mathbf u_f=\mathbf u_s\)$ and therefore takes no permeability argument.
  • The solid material must be plane strain (PlaneType::E), the fluid material must be isotropic (MaterialType::DS), and both must report a nonzero bulk modulus, otherwise initialization fails.

implementation limitation

The permeability is a single isotropic scalar, so anisotropy and tensor permeability cannot be represented. A zero permeability is not a valid input because it appears in the denominator of the drag matrix.

  • The permeability $\(k\)$ appears in the denominator of the viscous matrix, so it must be strictly positive and expressed in units consistent with the drag term $\(n^2/k\)$.
  • Because seepage is a velocity-proportional damping term, pore pressure dissipation requires a transient or dynamic analysis step, while a purely static step has no time scale for consolidation.
  • Fluid DoFs are labelled FU1 and FU2 and can be restrained with commands such as fix 3 fu1 1 2 3 4.
  • The recorded pore pressure PP is sampled at the four Gauss points, and other recorded quantities are forwarded to the solid material.
  • Use PCPE8DC for a quadratic approximation with five-point Irons integration when higher accuracy per element is needed.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
Text Only
node 1 0 0
node 2 2 0
node 3 2 2
node 4 0 2
material Elastic2D 1 1500. 0.25 1E-4 1
material Fluid 2 1000. 1E-4
element PCPE4DC 1 1 2 3 4 1 2 1. 0.8 10.

docs.title: Recording
docs.text:
This model supports the following additional history variables to be recorded.

variable label physical meaning PP pore pressure

docs.title: PCPE4UC
docs.text:
Bilinear Quadrilateral With Pore Pressure (Undrained)

  • Number of Nodes: 4
  • Number of DoFs: 2 (Solid Translation, Solid Translation)
  • DoF Label: U1, U2
  • Supports Body Force
  • Constant Consistent Mass Matrix With Same Order Integration

docs.title: Background
docs.text:
This is the four-node undrained member of the porous family described in full on PCPE4DC.

It eliminates the fluid displacement field by imposing $\(\mathbf u_f=\mathbf u_s\)$, so that the fluid moves with the skeleton and no relative seepage is possible.

deviation from theory

The undrained condition is imposed algebraically by tying the fluid displacement to the solid one. Pore pressure is recovered from the volumetric strain rather than solved as an independent field, so no pressure DoF or flow equation is present.

With $\(K_s\)$, $\(K_f\)$, $\(n\)$ and $\(\alpha\)$ as defined on the canonical page, the same pressure coefficient is used.

\[ q=\dfrac{K_sK_f}{nK_s+(\alpha-n)K_f}. \]

Substituting $\(\varepsilon_f=\varepsilon_s\)$ into the pore energy of PCPE4DC gives the undrained constraint energy $\(\Psi_u=\tfrac12 q\alpha^2(\nabla\cdot\mathbf u_s)^2\)$ and the pore pressure $\(p=-\alpha q\,\nabla\cdot\mathbf u_s\)$.

The added stiffness is therefore

\[ \mathbf K_u=\int_V q\alpha^2\,\mathbf B^{\mathsf T}\mathbf m\mathbf m^{\mathsf T}\mathbf B\,dV , \]

which is exactly the meta_k matrix of the implementation, with $\(\mathbf m=(1,1,0)^{\mathsf T}\)$.

The element has no permeability argument and no viscous Darcy matrix, and its mass uses the mixture density $\((1-n)\rho_s+n\rho_f\)$.

The recorded pore pressure PP is $\(-\alpha q\)$ times the volumetric strain at each of the four Gauss points.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text:
PCPE4UC
element PCPE4UC (1) (2...5) (6) (7) (8) (9)
# (1) int, unique element tag
# (2...5) int, node i, j, k, l
# (6) int, solid material tag
# (7) int, fluid material tag
# (8) double, alpha
# (9) double, porosity n

docs.title: Remarks
docs.text:
Only plane strain is supported. Plane stress does not make sense in geotechnical engineering.

For the fluid phase, an isotropic fluid material can be provided, which mainly provides the bulk modulus of the fluid phase. For example,

Text Only
# material Fluid (tag) (bulk modulus) (density)
material Fluid 1 1000. 1E-2

The $\(\alpha\)$ parameter (8) is often close to unity for soils. The porosity $\(n\)$ ranges from zero to unity. The isotropic permeability is assumed.

Interactions with other elements (with different arrangements of DoFs) can only be fulfilled via constraints.

  • UC denotes the undrained variant, in which the fluid DoFs are suppressed and no permeability is supplied.
  • The letter C is not expanded in the source, but the added stiffness is the undrained limit of the Biot consolidation model, so UC is read as undrained consolidation.
  • The solid material must be plane strain (PlaneType::E), the fluid material must be isotropic (MaterialType::DS), and both must report a nonzero bulk modulus, otherwise initialization fails.

implementation limitation

Only plane strain and an isotropic fluid are accepted, and no permeability argument exists. The undrained constraint is exact for the chosen interpolation, but it cannot represent partial drainage or transient pore pressure dissipation.

  • The fluid bulk modulus still affects the response through $\(q\)$ even though no fluid flow is modelled.
  • Use PCPE4DC when drainage or time-dependent consolidation must be captured, and PCPE8UC for a quadratic undrained element.

variable label physical meaning PP pore pressure

docs.title: PCPE8DC
docs.text:
Quadratic Quadrilateral With Pore Pressure (Drained)

  • Number of Nodes: 8
  • Number of DoFs: 4 (Solid Translation, Solid Translation, Fluid Translation, Fluid Translation)
  • DoF Label: U1, U2, FU1, FU2
  • Supports Body Force
  • Constant Consistent Mass Matrix With Same Order Integration

docs.title: Background
docs.text:
This is the eight-node quadratic companion of PCPE4DC in the drained consolidation family.

It uses the same $\(u\)\(--\)\(U\)$ formulation, the same pressure coefficient $\(q=K_sK_f/[nK_s+(\alpha-n)K_f]\)$, the same four-block fluid stiffness and the same relative-velocity Darcy damping matrix, so refer to the PCPE4DC theory page for the derivation.

deviation from theory

As in the bilinear variant, pore pressure is not a nodal unknown and drainage is represented by a velocity-proportional Darcy damping matrix. A static analysis therefore cannot dissipate pore pressure.

The differences are the quadratic eight-node interpolation and the five-point Irons integration rule instead of the four-point Gauss rule.

The characteristic length is taken from the area of the quadrilateral formed by the first four corner nodes.

implementation limitation

The quadratic element accepts only a plane-strain solid and an isotropic fluid with nonzero bulk moduli. The permeability is a single scalar, so anisotropy and tensor permeability cannot be represented.

developer note

The quadratic element uses a fixed five-point Irons integration rule. The characteristic length is computed from the four corner nodes and ignores the four midside nodes.

# (1) int, unique element tag
# (2...9) int, node i, j, k, l
# (10) int, solid material tag
# (11) int, fluid material tag
# (12) double, alpha
# (13) double, porosity n
# (14) double, permeability k

docs.title: Remarks
docs.text:
Only plane strain is supported. Plane stress does not make sense in geotechnical engineering.

For the fluid phase, an isotropic fluid material can be provided, which mainly provides the bulk modulus of the fluid phase. For example,

Text Only
# material Fluid (tag) (bulk modulus) (density)
material Fluid 1 1000. 1E-2

The $\(\alpha\)$ parameter (12) is often close to unity for soils. The porosity $\(n\)$ ranges from zero to unity. The isotropic permeability is assumed.

Interactions with other elements (with different arrangements of DoFs) can only be fulfilled via constraints.

  • The eight nodes are ordered with four corners first and four midside nodes afterwards, as indicated by the element encoding figure.
  • The quadratic interpolation gives a better approximation of curved boundaries and stress gradients than PCPE4DC.
  • The pressure coefficient, damping and mass are assembled with five Irons points, and PP is recorded at those points.
  • As for the bilinear variant, a transient or dynamic step is required for the permeability-driven damping to dissipate pore pressure.
  • The undrained quadratic counterpart is PCPE8UC.

docs.title: PCPE8UC
docs.text:
Quadratic Quadrilateral With Pore Pressure (Undrained)

  • Number of Nodes: 8
  • Number of DoFs: 2 (Solid Translation, Solid Translation)
  • DoF Label: U1, U2
  • Supports Body Force
  • Constant Consistent Mass Matrix With Same Order Integration

docs.title: Background
docs.text:
This is the eight-node quadratic companion of PCPE4UC in the undrained porous family.

It imposes the same undrained constraint $\(\mathbf u_f=\mathbf u_s\)$, giving the added stiffness $\(\mathbf K_u=\int q\alpha^2\mathbf B^{\mathsf T}\mathbf m\mathbf m^{\mathsf T}\mathbf B\,dV\)$ with $\(q=K_sK_f/[nK_s+(\alpha-n)K_f]\)$ and $\(\mathbf m=(1,1,0)^{\mathsf T}\)$, and it records $\(p=-\alpha q\,\nabla\cdot\mathbf u_s\)$.

deviation from theory

The undrained response is obtained by tying the fluid displacement to the solid one, so pore pressure is recovered from volumetric strain rather than solved as a nodal field. No permeability or flow equation is present.

The derivation is given on PCPE4DC and the undrained reduction on PCPE4UC.

The only differences are the quadratic eight-node shape functions and the five-point Irons integration rule used in place of four-point Gauss integration.

The characteristic length is computed from the first four corner nodes.

implementation limitation

Only plane strain and an isotropic fluid with nonzero bulk moduli are accepted. Partial drainage and transient pore pressure dissipation are outside the scope of this undrained element.

developer note

The five-point Irons integration rule is fixed.

Only plane strain is supported. Plane stress does not make sense in geotechnical engineering.

For the fluid phase, an isotropic fluid material can be provided, which mainly provides the bulk modulus of the fluid phase. For example,

Text Only

material Fluid 1 1000. 1E-2

The $\(\alpha\)$ parameter (12) is often close to unity for soils. The porosity $\(n\)$ ranges from zero to unity. The isotropic permeability is assumed.

Interactions with other elements (with different arrangements of DoFs) can only be fulfilled via constraints.

  • The eight nodes are ordered with four corners first and four midside nodes afterwards, as indicated by the element encoding figure.
  • No permeability argument is taken, and no Darcy damping matrix is assembled, because relative fluid motion is suppressed.
  • The mixture density $\((1-n)\rho_s+n\rho_f\)$ is used for the consistent mass matrix.
  • Use PCPE8DC if drainage and consolidation over time are required.

docs.title: ElementalLee
docs.text: Elemental Damping Using Lee's Formulation

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. 10.1016/j.compstruc.2023.107152

Note

This modifier must be used with LeeElementalNewmark integrator to work properly.

docs.title: Background
docs.text:
ElementalLee is the element-level form of the damping model described on the Modifier page. For each selected element it writes the scaled mass and stiffness matrices

\[ \zeta_e\,\mathbf M_e,\qquad \zeta_e\big(\mathbf K_e+\mathbf K_{g,e}\big), \]

where $\(\zeta_e\)$ is the element damping multiplier, $\(\mathbf M_e\)$ the current mass matrix, $\(\mathbf K_e\)$ the current tangent stiffness and $\(\mathbf K_{g,e}\)$ the geometric stiffness when nlgeom is active and a geometric matrix exists. These containers are read by the companion integrator LeeElementalNewmark as the damping contributions of the Lee formulation.

The integrator defines a reference bell-shaped damping curve from a reference ratio and a peak frequency. The damping ratio actually applied to an element is the product of that reference ratio and $\(\zeta_e\)$, so different parts of a structure can be assigned different damping levels.

developer note

The modifier does not assemble a separate damping matrix. It overwrites the element mass and stiffness containers, which the companion integrator then interprets as damping contributions.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text:
ElementalLee
modifier ElementalLee (1) [2] [(3)...]
# (1) int, unique modifier tag
# [2] double, damping ratio, default: 0.02
# [(3)...] int, element tags

docs.title: Remarks
docs.text:
1. If no element tag is provided, this modifier applies to all active elements. In this case, it is equivalent to a global damping model such as LeeNewmark or LeeNewmarkFull.
  2. Unlike the above global damping models, damping ratio is applied to each element individually. In case of an invalid number assigned, a default one $\(0.02\)$ is used.
  3. The input value is converted to its absolute value, so a negative ratio has the same effect as a positive one.
  4. Only elements that require a viscous update and permit modification of their viscous data are affected; an element such as Damper01 sets modify_viscous to false and is skipped.
  5. Because the modified matrices are interpreted as damping by the special integrator, using this modifier with a standard Newmark integrator does not produce the intended damping.

docs.title: ElementalNonviscous
docs.text: Nonviscous Elemental Damping

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. 10.1016/j.ymssp.2024.111156

The kernel function is defined as a summation of exponential functions.

\[ g(t)=\sum_{i=1}^n m_i\exp(-s_it) \]

The parameters $\(m_i\)$ and $\(s_i\)$ are complex numbers.

docs.title: Background
docs.text:
A nonviscous damping force is the convolution of the velocity history with a kernel, as described on the Modifier page. For an exponential kernel the convolution can be updated recursively instead of storing the whole velocity history. With $\(\Delta t\)$ the time increment, the implementation forms the complex coefficients

\[ p_i=\dfrac{2}{\Delta t}+s_i,\qquad s_i'=\dfrac{p_i-2s_i}{p_i},\qquad m_i'=\dfrac{m_i}{p_i}, \]

and advances the element history force by

\[ \mathbf f_{d,e}^{n+1}=\mathbf f_{d,e}^{n}\operatorname{diag}(s') +\big(\dot{\mathbf u}_e^{n}+\dot{\mathbf u}_e^{n+1}\big)\mathbf m'^{\mathrm T}. \]

A diagonal tangent $\(\operatorname{Re}\big(\sum_i m_i'\big)\mathbf I\)$ is added to the element damping matrix. Only matrix--vector products are needed, so the cost per step is low and no velocity history is stored.

implementation limitation

The added tangent is diagonal. Off-diagonal coupling between DoFs in the nonviscous kernel is not represented.

developer note

The tangent uses only the real part of the summed coefficients. The convolution history is advanced with a trapezoidal combination of the current and previous velocities.

The parser requires the coefficients to form conjugate pairs and checks that the kernel decays to zero; a kernel that does not satisfy these conditions is rejected.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text:
ElementalNonviscous
modifier ElementalNonviscous (1) (2) ((3) (4) (5) (6)...)
# (1) int, unique modifier tag
# (2) int, element tag
# (3) double, real part of `m_i`
# (4) double, imaginary part of `m_i`
# (5) double, real part of `s_i`
# (6) double, imaginary part of `s_i`

modifier ElementalNonviscousGroup (1) (2) ((3) (4) (5) (6)...)
# (1) int, unique modifier tag
# (2) int, element group tag
# (3) double, real part of `m_i`
# (4) double, imaginary part of `m_i`
# (5) double, real part of `s_i`
# (6) double, imaginary part of `s_i`

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
Text Only
modifier ElementalNonviscous 1 1 8. 0 2. 0 4. 0 1. 0

This defines a kernel function of the following form.

\[ g(t)=8\exp(-2t)+4\exp(-t) \]

docs.title: Remarks
docs.text:
1. The four coefficients are supplied in the order real and imaginary parts of $\(m_i\)$, then real and imaginary parts of $\(s_i\)$, and this group is repeated for each exponential term.
  2. The imaginary parts must form conjugate pairs, and the kernel must decay to zero, otherwise the parser rejects the modifier.
  3. ElementalNonviscousGroup takes an element group tag instead of a single element tag and applies the same kernel to all elements in that group.
  4. Repeated element tags are detected at initialisation and disable the modifier, since each element can carry only one such history.
  5. The modifier applies only in a dynamic analysis and only to elements that permit modification of their nonviscous force and tangent.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text:
LinearViscosity
modifier LinearViscosity (1) (2) [(3)...]
# (1) int, unique modifier tag
# (2) double, \mu
# [(3)...] int, element tags

This modifier applies linear viscosity to elements with the assigned $\(\mu\)$.

docs.title: Background
docs.text:
For each targeted element, the modifier builds a diagonal viscous matrix with $\(\mu\)$ on the diagonal and computes the damping force as $\(\mu\)$ times the trial velocity. It therefore provides element-level damping proportional to the strain rate. It is applied only in a dynamic analysis and only to elements that allow their viscous properties to be modified.

For an element with $\(n\)$ DoFs and trial velocity $\(\dot{\mathbf u}_e\)$, the modifier sets

\[ \mathbf C_e=\mu\,\mathbf I_n,\qquad \mathbf f_{d,e}=\mathbf C_e\dot{\mathbf u}_e=\mu\,\dot{\mathbf u}_e . \]

This is the simplest member of the element-level damping framework described on the Modifier page, where more general damping matrices are discussed.

implementation limitation

The damping matrix is diagonal with the same $\(\mu\)$ on every DoF. A full viscous tensor with cross-coupling between directions is not supported.

docs.title: Remarks
docs.text:
Because the damping is defined at element level, each element can record its own dissipated energy. This differs from RayleighNewmark, which applies Rayleigh damping after global assembly; with that global model the dissipated energy can only be recovered from global quantities, as discussed in Recorder.

  1. The same value $\(\mu\)$ is placed on every diagonal entry, so the parameter has units of force per velocity and is not scaled by element size.
  2. If no element tag is given, the modifier applies to all active elements in the domain.
  3. Elements that disable viscous modification, such as Damper01, are skipped and keep their own material damping.
  4. For frequency-dependent damping use ElementalLee or ElementalNonviscous instead.

docs.title: Brief
docs.text:
Sometimes it is necessary to modify the existing element data. A concrete example is the damping matrix used in dynamic analyses.

In a standard element, stiffness matrix could be solely computed according to its formulation. However, mass matrix could be formulated in multiple ways such as consistent, lumped, to name a few. For lumped formulation, there are also several versions. If the Rayleigh type damping is used, damping matrix shall be related to both mass matrix and stiffness matrix. Furthermore, the weights shall be computed based on global structure properties, in other words, it is not possible to determine those weights within the element. Besides, other types of damping formulation could also be used.

Such variance existing in element formulation raises a demand of the Modifier class. A Modifier object can exist independently and can access and modify some data of the target elements. This provides great convenience in defining customizable behavior for different elements.

docs.title: Background
docs.text:
The semi-discrete equations of motion of a structure are

\[ \mathbf M\ddot{\mathbf u}+\mathbf C\dot{\mathbf u}+\mathbf K\mathbf u=\mathbf f , \]

with assembled mass, damping and stiffness matrices. A modifier acts on the element matrices $\(\mathbf M_e\)$, $\(\mathbf C_e\)$ and $\(\mathbf K_e\)$ before assembly, so it can implement choices that an individual element cannot make on its own.

The mass matrix is not unique. The consistent form

\[ \mathbf M_e^c=\int_{\Omega_e}\rho\,\mathbf N^{\mathrm T}\mathbf N\,\mathrm d\Omega_e \]

uses the same shape functions $\(\mathbf N\)$ as the displacement interpolation and preserves the kinetic energy of the interpolated field, but it couples neighbouring DoFs. A lumped matrix keeps the total mass while removing the coupling,

\[ M^{l}_{ii}=\sum_j M^c_{ij}. \]

Diagonal mass is cheaper and is required by many explicit integrators, while consistent mass is usually more accurate for wave propagation. Rotational DoFs carry entries representing the rigid-body kinetic energy $\(\tfrac12\mathbf\omega\cdot\mathbf I\mathbf\omega\)$; the point-mass elements on the Mass page are already lumped.

The damping matrix is even less uniquely defined. Rayleigh damping assumes $\(\mathbf C=a\mathbf M+b\mathbf K\)$, and the general form used below is a linear combination of mass, initial, current and trial stiffness matrices. The weights depend on global modal properties and therefore cannot be chosen inside an element; a modifier computes the element damping matrices once and lets the assembly build the global matrix.

Nonviscous damping replaces $\(\mathbf C\dot{\mathbf u}\)$ by a hereditary convolution,

\[ \mathbf f_d(t)=\int_0^t\mathbf g(t-\tau)\dot{\mathbf u}(\tau)\,\mathrm d\tau . \]

With an exponential kernel $\(\mathbf g(t)=\sum_k\mathbf m_k e^{-s_k t}\)$ the integral can be advanced recursively from the current and previous velocities without storing the whole history, which is the idea behind ElementalNonviscous. A related approach forms a bell-shaped frequency-dependent damping ratio from mass and stiffness matrices at element level, as in ElementalLee, whereas LinearViscosity simply sets a diagonal element damping matrix proportional to velocity.

deviation from theory

An element-level damping matrix is assembled from the modified element matrices, whereas a global Rayleigh model forms the damping matrix after global assembly. The two approaches do not in general give the same modal damping ratios for the same coefficients.

docs.title: Remarks
docs.text:
1. For all the following modifiers presented, if no element tag is provided, the modifier would be applied to all active elements in the domain.
  2. All modifiers would be applied in the order of how they are defined. This is because the modified data would be used in another modifier, for example, it is possible to apply a lumped mass modifier and then use the modified mass matrix to form a Rayleigh damping matrix.
  3. The lumped mass modifiers operate on element mass matrices; the lumped point masses themselves are defined by Mass and MassPoint2D.
  4. The elemental damping modifiers ElementalLee, ElementalNonviscous and LinearViscosity work on element matrices, so each element can record its own dissipated energy. In a global model such as RayleighNewmark the dissipated energy can only be recovered from global quantities.
  5. Dynamic modifiers are applied only in a dynamic analysis and only to elements that allow the corresponding matrix to be modified.

docs.title: Simple Lumped Mass
docs.text:
Text Only
modifier LumpedSimple (1) (2...)
# (1) int, unique modifier tag
# (2...) int, element tags

docs.title: Scale Lumped Mass
docs.text:
Text Only
modifier LumpedScale (1) (2...)
# (1) int, unique modifier tag
# (2...) int, element tags

docs.title: Rayleigh Damping
docs.text:
The damping matrix would be defined as

\[ C=aM+bK_C+cK_I+dK_T, \]

where $\(M\)$ is the mass matrix, $\(K_C\)$ is the current tangent stiffness matrix (converged from the last step), $\(K_I\)$ is the initial stiffness and $\(K_T\)$ is the trial stiffness of current iteration. To retain quadratic convergence rate, one shall only use $\(K_I\)$ and $\(K_C\)$. But $\(K_I\)$ also leads to unwanted response.

Text Only
modifier Rayleigh (1) (2) (3) (4) (5) (6...)
# (1) int, unique modifier tag
# (2) double, a
# (3) double, b
# (4) double, c
# (5) double, d
# (6...) int, element tags

docs.title: Elemental Modal Damping
docs.text:
The rigid body modes are assumed to be undamped. The modes whose frequencies are higher than the cut-off frequency are ignored. The Wilson-Penzien approach is applied for each element. Currently, only consistent mass matrix is supported.

Text Only
modifier ElementalModal (1) (2) (3) (4...)
# (1) int, unique modifier tag
# (2) double, cut-off frequency
# (3) double, damping ratio
# (4...) int, element tags

docs.title: Patch
docs.text:
Isogeometric Patches

In isogeometric analysis, the geometry of elements is defined by NURBS based surfaces or volumes. Several elements are grouped into patches and patches behave similarly to traditional finite elements.

To define IGA patches, the knot vectors along each dimension and the control node polygon need to be assigned.

docs.title: Theory
docs.text:
Isogeometric analysis uses the same non-uniform rational B-spline (NURBS) basis to describe the geometry and the unknown field. A univariate B-spline basis of degree $\(p\)$ is built from an open knot vector $\(\Xi=\{\xi_1,\dots,\xi_{n+p+1}\}\)$ by the Cox-de Boor recursion. The number of basis functions, and therefore the number of control points along that direction, is $\(n=\mathrm{length}(\Xi)-p-1\)$.

The rational basis functions are $$ R_i(\xi)=\frac{N_{i,p}(\xi)w_i}{\sum_{j=1}^n N_{j,p}(\xi)w_j}, $$ where $\(w_i\)$ is the weight attached to control point $\(i\)$ and $\(N_{i,p}\)$ is the corresponding B-spline basis function. In this implementation the weight is stored as the last coordinate of each control node, so setting all weights to one recovers a B-spline basis.

In several dimensions the basis is the tensor product $\(R_{ijk}(\xi,\eta,\zeta)=R_i(\xi)R_j(\eta)R_k(\zeta)\)$. The isoparametric geometry and displacement fields are $\(\mathbf x=\sum_a R_a\mathbf x_a\)$ and $\(\mathbf u=\sum_a R_a\mathbf u_a\)$. The strain is $\(\mathbf\varepsilon=\mathbf B\mathbf u_e\)$ with $\(\mathbf B\)$ assembled from the physical derivatives $\(\partial R_a/\partial x_i\)$, which follow from the Jacobian $\(\mathbf J=\partial\mathbf x/\partial\mathbf\xi\)$.

Each nonzero knot span between two distinct knots is treated as one integration cell. A $\(2\times2\)$ Gauss rule is used for surface patches and a $\(2\times2\times2\)$ rule for volume patches, with the sampling points mapped from $\([-1,1]\)$ onto each span. Because a basis function has support over several spans, one patch element couples a larger stencil of control nodes than a Lagrange finite element. Refinement by knot insertion or degree elevation can change the approximation without changing the geometry, which is the central idea of the isogeometric concept.

docs.title: Remarks
docs.text: A patch is not a single Lagrange element, so the number of connected control nodes is determined by the knot vectors and can be much larger than four or eight. Control nodes must be supplied in the tensor-product order implied by the knot spans, and their last coordinate is the NURBS weight. The basis is at least $\(C^0\)$ continuous across spans and is $\(C^{p-1}\)$ continuous at simple interior knots. Use PatchQuad for a two-dimensional membrane patch and PatchCube for a three-dimensional solid patch. For conventional hexahedral elements with polynomial shape functions see C3D8 and C3D20.

docs.title: PatchCube
docs.text:
Patch of Hexahedron Elements

  • Number of DoFs: 3
  • DoF Label: U1, U2, U3
  • Number of Nodes: varies
  • Supports Mass
  • Supports Body Force

docs.title: Background
docs.text: PatchCube is the three-dimensional solid patch element of the isogeometric framework described in Patch. It builds a B-spline or NURBS volume from three knot vectors and a rectangular grid of control nodes, whose size follows from the knot vectors. Each control node supplies three translational DoFs, and its fourth coordinate is interpreted as the NURBS weight. The displacement field is $\(\mathbf u=\sum_{ijk}R_{ijk}\mathbf u_{ijk}\)$ with the tensor-product rational basis defined in Patch. Strains are integrated with a $\(2\times2\times2\)$ Gauss rule over each knot span, and the tangent, mass and body force use the same basis.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text:
A key-value style is used.

PatchCube
element PatchCube (1) -node (2...) -knotx (3...) -knoty (4...) -knotz (5...) -material (6)
# (1) int, unique element (patch) tag
# (2...) int, node tags of control node polygon
# (3...) double, knot vector along x axis
# (4...) double, knot vector along y axis
# (5...) double, knot vector along z axis
# (6) int, material tag

docs.title: Remarks
docs.text: The key-value syntax expects the node list after -node and the knot vectors after -knotx, -knoty and -knotz. The number of control nodes must equal the product of the numbers of basis functions implied by the three knot vectors, and the nodes are ordered lexicographically in the index triple. The fourth coordinate of each control node is the NURBS weight, so use one for an ordinary B-spline volume. A 3D material tag is required, and a consistent mass and body force are assembled when the material supplies a density. The element has no nonlinear-geometry switch. For the two-dimensional counterpart see PatchQuad, and for conventional polynomial bricks see C3D8.

docs.title: PatchQuad
docs.text:
Patch of Quadrilateral Elements

  • Number of DoFs: 2
  • DoF Label: U1, U2
  • Number of Nodes: varies
  • Supports Mass
  • Supports Body Force

docs.title: Background
docs.text: PatchQuad is the two-dimensional membrane patch element of the isogeometric framework described in Patch. It builds a NURBS surface from two knot vectors and a rectangular grid of control nodes, each carrying two translational DoFs. The third coordinate of each control node is interpreted as the NURBS weight. The displacement field is $\(\mathbf u=\sum_{ij}R_{ij}\mathbf u_{ij}\)$, and the in-plane strain follows from the physical derivatives of the tensor-product basis. Each knot span is integrated with a $\(2\times2\)$ Gauss rule, and the element stiffness, mass and body force are multiplied by the thickness.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text:
A key-value style is used.

PatchQuad
element PatchQuad (1) -node (2...) -knotx (3...) -knoty (4...) -material (5) [-thickness (6)]
# (1) int, unique element (patch) tag
# (2...) int, node tags of control node polygon
# (3...) double, knot vector along x axis
# (4...) double, knot vector along y axis
# (5) int, material tag
# (6) double, thickness

docs.title: Remarks
docs.text: The keys -node, -knotx, -knoty and -material are required, while -thickness is optional. The number of control nodes must equal the product of the numbers of basis functions implied by the two knot vectors, and the nodes are ordered lexicographically. The third coordinate of each control node is the NURBS weight, so use one for an ordinary B-spline surface. For a plane-strain material the implementation overrides the thickness with one, so the supplied value is ignored. A 2D material tag is required, and a consistent mass is assembled when the material supplies a density. For the three-dimensional counterpart see PatchCube.

docs.title: DKT3
docs.text:
DKT Triangle Plate

  • Number of Nodes: 3
  • Number of DoFs: 3 (Translation, Rotation, Rotation)
  • DoF Label: U3, UR1, UR2

docs.title: Theory
docs.text:
The discrete Kirchhoff triangle is a thin-plate element based on Kirchhoff--Love assumptions, namely that normals to the midsurface remain straight and normal to the deformed midsurface, so transverse shear strain vanishes.

Let $\(w\)$ be the transverse displacement and let $\( eta_x=\partial w/\partial x\)$ and $\( eta_y=\partial w/\partial y\)$ be the rotations of the normal.

In the sign convention of the implementation the nodal rotations satisfy $\( eta_x= heta_y\)$ and $\( eta_y=- heta_x\)$, which is why the first transformation matrix maps $\( heta_y\)$ to $\( eta_x\)$ with a positive sign and $\( heta_x\)$ to $\( eta_y\)$ with a negative sign.

deviation from theory

The rotation signs follow the source transformation matrices and differ from texts that define the bending rotations with the opposite sign.

developer note

The DoF labels in the manual are $\(U_3,UR_1,UR_2\)$, while the internal constructor passes generic 2D DoF tags that are later interpreted by the element.

The curvature vector is

\[ \mathbf\kappa= egin{bmatrix} eta_{x,x}\ eta_{y,y}\ eta_{x,y}+ eta_{y,x}\end{bmatrix}, \]

and the moment--curvature relation is $\(\mathbf M=\mathbf D_b\mathbf\kappa\)$, with the plane-stress bending stiffness

\[ \mathbf D_b=\dfrac{Et^3}{12(1- u^2)} egin{bmatrix} 1 & u & 0\ u & 1 & 0\ 0 & 0 & (1- u)/2 \end{bmatrix}. \]

The implementation obtains this matrix by numerical integration through the thickness rather than by forming $\(\mathbf D_b\)$ explicitly.

deviation from theory

The bending stiffness is synthesized from the two-dimensional constitutive matrix, so the element relies on a plane-stress material to reproduce the standard $\(Et^3/[12(1- u^2)]\)$ coefficient. A plane-strain material would give a different bending stiffness.

A fibre at local coordinate $\(z\)$ carries the strain $\(\mathbf\varepsilon(z)=z\mathbf\kappa\)$, so the stiffness contribution of a layer is $\(z^2\mathbf B^{\mathsf T}\mathbf D\mathbf B\,dV\)$.

The discrete Kirchhoff condition is imposed only at the three edge midpoints instead of pointwise.

Along an edge of length $\(\ell\)$ with direction cosines $\(c=\Delta y/\ell\)$ and $\(s=-\Delta x/\ell\)$, the tangential rotation varies linearly between its nodal values $\( eta_{s,i}=c\, heta_{x,i}+s\, heta_{y,i}\)$, while $\(w\)$ is taken as a cubic function of the edge coordinate.

Enforcing $\( eta_s=-\partial w/\partial s\)$ at the midpoint gives

\[ eta_s^{\,m}=\dfrac{3}{2}\dfrac{w_i-w_j}{\ell}+\dfrac14\left( eta_{s,i}+ eta_{s,j} ight), \]

which expresses the midside rotation in terms of the nodal transverse displacements and rotations.

deviation from theory

The Kirchhoff condition is satisfied only at the three midside points rather than pointwise over the element. The element is therefore a discrete Kirchhoff approximation and does not enforce zero transverse shear strain at the corners.

The rotation values at the three corners and three midpoints are then used to fit the polynomial field in $\(\{1,x,y,xy,x^2,y^2\}\)$, and differentiation yields the curvature matrix $\(\mathbf B\)$.

The element stiffness is assembled from the three midside integration points and from the selected number of Gauss points through the thickness.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text:
DKT3
element DKT3 (1) (2...4) (5) (6) [7]
# (1) int, unique element tag
# (2...4) int, node i, j, k
# (5) int, material tag
# (6) double, thickness
# [7] int, number of integration points, default: 3

docs.title: Remarks
docs.text:
• The three DoFs are the transverse displacement $\(w\)$ and the two bending rotations, so this is a plate-only element and not a shell.
  • For a flat triangular shell with six DoFs per node use DKTS3, which combines this plate interpolation with a drilling membrane.
  • The thickness is a required argument and is used both for the fibre coordinate $\(z=\xi t/2\)$ and for the layer weight.
  • The optional number of integration points is a Gauss rule through the thickness, defaulting to three.
  • Use a plane-stress two-dimensional material such as Elastic2D with its plane-type flag set to zero, since the bending stiffness is synthesized from the in-plane constitutive matrix.

implementation limitation

The thickness rule is the only configurable integration. The element has no transverse shear strain, so thick-plate behaviour cannot be represented.

developer note

The in-plane integration is fixed at the three edge midpoints.

  • The formulation has no transverse shear strain, so it does not suffer from shear locking in the thin-plate limit, but it is not intended for thick plates where shear deformation is important.
  • For a shear-deformable quadrilateral plate use Mindlin, and for the quadrilateral Kirchhoff plate use DKT4.
  • The complete algebra of the rotation transformations is documented in the DKT.tex notes distributed with the source code.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
Text Only
material Elastic2D 1 2.0E11 0.3
element DKT3 1 1 2 3 1 0.01 3

docs.title: DKT4
docs.text:
DKT Quadrilateral Plate

  • Number of Nodes: 4
  • Number of DoFs: 3 (Translation, Rotation, Rotation)
  • DoF Label: U3, UR1, UR2

docs.title: Background
docs.text:
DKT4 is the four-node quadrilateral version of the discrete Kirchhoff plate described in detail on DKT3.

The transverse displacement and the two rotations $\((w,\theta_x,\theta_y)\)$ are interpolated at the four corners, and the discrete Kirchhoff condition $\(\beta_s=-\partial w/\partial s\)$ is enforced at the four edge midpoints.

The implementation therefore works with eight sampling points, the four corners plus four midpoints, using an eight-node serendipity interpolation for the transverse displacement and linear edge interpolation for the rotations.

The curvature matrix has the same form $\(\mathbf\kappa=(\beta_{x,x},\,\beta_{y,y},\,\beta_{x,y}+\beta_{y,x})^{\mathsf T}\)$, and a fibre at thickness coordinate $\(z\)$ contributes $\(z^2\mathbf B^{\mathsf T}\mathbf D\mathbf B\)$ to the stiffness.

The in-plane integration uses 2-by-2 Gauss points, and the thickness integration uses the selected number of Gauss points with a default of three.

No transverse shear energy is included, so the element is a thin-plate element that is free of shear locking but cannot represent thick-plate shear deformation.

deviation from theory

The discrete Kirchhoff condition is satisfied only at the four edge midpoints and not pointwise. The element is a Kirchhoff approximation with no transverse shear energy, so it differs from a fully conforming thin-plate element and from any Mindlin--Reissner element.

This plate interpolation supplies the bending part of the flat shell SGCMS.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text:
DKT4
element DKT4 (1) (2...5) (6) (7) [8]
# (1) int, unique element tag
# (2...5) int, node i, j, k, l
# (6) int, material tag
# (7) double, thickness
# [8] int, number of integration points along thickness, default: 3

docs.title: Remarks
docs.text:
• The DoF layout is the plate-only triple $\((U_3,UR_1,UR_2)\)$; a six-DoF shell uses S4 or SGCMS instead.
  • Use a plane-stress two-dimensional material such as Elastic2D so that the numerically integrated bending stiffness matches the thin-plate moment--curvature law.

implementation limitation

A plane-strain material gives a different bending stiffness because the matrix is integrated rather than prescribed. Only the thickness Gauss rule is configurable.

developer note

The in-plane rule is fixed.

  • The thickness must be supplied explicitly and sets both the fibre coordinates $\(z=\xi t/2\)$ and the layer weights.
  • The optional argument controls only the through-thickness Gauss rule; the in-plane 2-by-2 rule is fixed.
  • For moderately thick plates use Mindlin, which retains transverse shear deformation with reduced integration to avoid locking.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. 10.1002/nme.1620151205
  2. Evaluation of a new quadrilateral thin plate bending element

docs.title: Mindlin
docs.text:
Mindlin Plate Element

  • Number of Nodes: 4
  • Number of DoFs: 3 (Translation, Rotation, Rotation)
  • DoF Label: U3, UR1, UR2

docs.title: Background
docs.text:
The Mindlin--Reissner plate theory relaxes the Kirchhoff condition by treating the section rotation $\(\mathbf heta\)$ as an independent field.

The transverse displacement $\(w\)$ and the two rotations have independent interpolations, and the transverse shear strain is the difference between the slope of $\(w\)$ and the section rotation, $\(\mathbf\gamma= abla w-\mathbf heta\)$ up to the sign convention used for the two rotation components.

deviation from theory

The source assembles $\(\gamma_1=\partial w/\partial y- heta_1\)$ and $\(\gamma_2=\partial w/\partial x+ heta_2\)$, so the shear components are swapped and signed differently from texts that write $\(\mathbf\gamma= abla w-\mathbf heta\)$ with the same ordering. The rotation DoFs are local plate rotations and are not the global vector components implied by that compact notation.

The curvature is $\(\mathbf\kappa= abla\mathbf heta\)$ in the symmetric part, and the strain at a fibre of coordinate $\(z\)$ is $\(\mathbf\varepsilon(z)=\mathbf\kappa^{ m sym}\,z\)$, while the shear strain is uniform through the thickness.

The internal energy therefore contains a bending part of order $\(t^3\)$ and a shear part of order $\(t\)$.

As the thickness tends to zero, the shear energy enforces $\(\mathbf\gamma\approx 0\)$ pointwise, and a displacement element that interpolates $\(w\)$ and $\(\mathbf heta\)$ with the same order becomes over-constrained and locks, giving a response that is far too stiff.

The implementation avoids this shear locking by evaluating the shear contribution with a single reduced-integration point at the element centre.

The shear stiffness is assembled as

\[ \mathbf K_s=\dfrac{10}{3}\,G\,t\,\det\mathbf J\;\mathbf B_\gamma^{\mathsf T}\mathbf B_\gamma, \]

where $\(G\)$ is the shear modulus supplied by the material, $\(\det\mathbf J\)$ is the Jacobian determinant at the centre, and $\(\mathbf B_\gamma\)$ contains the centre values of the bilinear shape functions and their derivatives.

This one-point rule is equivalent to an assumed-shear-strain or mixed formulation of the type analysed by Malkus and Hughes.

deviation from theory

The shear energy is not integrated with the 2-by-2 rule used for bending, but is replaced by a single-point penalty with a fixed factor of $\(10/3\)$ multiplying $\(Gt\det\mathbf J\)$. No separate shear correction factor is computed from the section shape, so that factor is absorbed into the penalty coefficient.

The bending part is integrated with 2-by-2 Gauss points in the plane and with the chosen number of Gauss layers through the thickness.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text:
Mindlin
element Mindlin (1) (2...5) (6) (7) [8]
# (1) int, unique element tag
# (2...5) int, node i, j, k, l
# (6) int, material tag
# (7) double, thickness
# [8] int, number of integration points, default: 5

docs.title: Remarks
docs.text:
• A zero shear modulus reported by the material causes initialization to fail, since the reduced-integration shear penalty cannot be formed.

implementation limitation

The element is restricted to four-node quadrilaterals and requires a material that reports a nonzero shear modulus. The through-thickness integration is the only adjustable rule.

developer note

The one-point shear penalty is hard-coded.

  • The thickness is required and scales both the shear penalty and the through-thickness fibre coordinates.
  • The optional argument selects the through-thickness Gauss rule and defaults to five points, while the in-plane rule for bending is a fixed 2-by-2 Gauss rule.
  • Only the shear term uses reduced integration, so the bending part is still fully integrated and the element does not introduce an in-plane hourglass mechanism from that rule.
  • Use a plane-stress two-dimensional material such as Elastic2D so that the integrated bending stiffness has the correct $\(Et^3/[12(1-\nu^2)]\)$ coefficient.
  • This is a plate-only element with three DoFs per node; for a six-DoF flat shell use S4, which combines it with the GQ12 membrane.
  • For thin plates where transverse shear is negligible, DKT4 gives a locking-free Kirchhoff alternative.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Influence of rotary inertia and shear on flexural motions of isotropic elastic plates
  2. The effect of transverse shear deformation on the bending of elastic plates
  3. 10.1016/0045-7825(78)90005-1
  4. ISBN 978-0-486-41181-1

docs.title: DKTS3
docs.text:
DKT Triangle Shell

  • Number of Nodes: 3
  • Number of DoFs: 6 (Translation, Translation, Translation, Rotation, Rotation, Rotation)
  • DoF Label: U1, U2, U3, UR1, UR2, UR3

docs.title: Background
docs.text:
DKTS3 is a flat triangular shell that superposes a three-node membrane with drilling rotations and the DKT3 thin-plate model.

The assembly follows ShellBase, with the membrane DoFs taken from $\((U_1,U_2,UR_3)\)$ and the plate DoFs from $\((U_3,UR_1,UR_2)\)$.

The membrane interpolation samples three mid-edge points and uses the Allman-type correction in which the mid-edge displacement depends on the difference of the drilling rotations at the adjacent corners, as derived on Allman.

deviation from theory

The drilling stiffness is not supplied by a penalty term, so a uniform drilling rotation remains a zero-energy mode.

developer note

The source print() routine describes the membrane as a CST formulation, but the interpolation contains the Allman drilling correction at the mid-edge points.

The plate interpolation applies the discrete Kirchhoff constraint at the same three mid-edge points, so a single set of sampling points serves both actions.

At a fibre of coordinate $\(z\)$ the strain is $\(\mathbf\varepsilon(z)=\mathbf B_m\mathbf d_m+z\,\mathbf B_p\mathbf d_p\)$, giving the membrane, bending and membrane--bending coupling blocks described on ShellBase.

Gauss integration through the thickness uses the selected number of layers, with $\(z=\xi t/2\)$ by default for three points.

The local triad is built from the element geometry and the resistance and stiffness are rotated back to global coordinates by ShellBase.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text:
DKTS3
element DKTS3 (1) (2...4) (5) (6) [7] [8]
# (1) int, unique element tag
# (2...4) int, node i, j, k
# (5) int, material tag
# (6) double, thickness
# [7] int, number of integration points, default: 3
# [8] bool, nonlinear geometry switch, default: false

docs.title: Remarks
docs.text:
1. If the nonlinear geometry is switched on, the transformation between the global and local reference frames will depend on the current displacement. The nonlinear transformation is similar to the corotational transformation, and the local response is still linear. Thus, it follows "large displacement, small deformation" assumption.

  2. The optional integration-point count is a Gauss rule through the thickness and is capped at twenty in the constructor.

implementation limitation

Only the through-thickness count is adjustable. The element is restricted to flat geometry with the local frame taken from the first three nodes.

developer note

The membrane and plate integrations are fixed at the three mid-edge points.

  • The thickness is required and sets both the fibre coordinates and the layer weights.
  • Use a plane-stress two-dimensional material such as Elastic2D so that the bending stiffness has the correct thin-plate coefficient.
  • The print() routine of the source calls the membrane part a CST formulation, but the interpolation uses mid-edge points with Allman-type drilling coupling.
  • The uniform drilling mode can be without stiffness, as on the Allman page, so restrain UR3 where necessary.
  • For a quadrilateral shell compare S4, which uses a shear-deformable plate, and SGCMS, which uses a mixed drilling membrane with the DKT4 plate.

docs.title: Sample
docs.text: The model can be downloaded. DKTS3.zip

docs.title: S4
docs.text:
Four Node Shell Element

The S4 shell element uses Mindlin plate element combined with GQ12 element.

  • Number of Nodes: 4
  • Number of DoFs: 6 (Translation, Translation, Translation, Rotation, Rotation, Rotation)
  • DoF Label: U1, U2, U3, UR1, UR2, UR3

docs.title: Background
docs.text:
S4 is the four-node flat shell assembled by ShellBase from two distinct two-dimensional elements.

The membrane action uses GQ12, which supplies in-plane stiffness and the drilling rotation $\(UR_3\)$ through its generalized conforming interpolation.

The plate action uses the Mindlin element, which retains transverse shear deformation and evaluates the shear term with one reduced-integration point to avoid shear locking.

Both actions share the same two-dimensional material matrix, and the plate curvature is integrated through the thickness at three fixed Gauss points with $\(z=\xi t/2\)$.

At a fibre the strain is $\(\mathbf\varepsilon=\mathbf B_m\mathbf d_m+z\,\mathbf B_p\mathbf d_p\)$, so the assembled local stiffness contains the membrane, bending and coupling blocks $\(\mathbf K_{mm}\)$, $\(\mathbf K_{pp}\)$ and $\(\mathbf K_{mp}\)$ described on ShellBase.

The in-plane integration is 2-by-2 Gauss for both the membrane and the bending part, while the shear penalty is formed once at the element centre.

deviation from theory

The transverse shear energy is replaced by a one-point penalty with a fixed coefficient of $\(10/3\,G\,t\,\det\mathbf J\)$ rather than by full integration of the shear strain. No separate transverse shear correction factor is computed.

developer note

The through-thickness integration is fixed at three Gauss points.

The local triad and the corotational transformation of resistance and stiffness are inherited from ShellBase.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text:
S4
element S4 (1) (2...5) (6) [7] [8]
# (1) int, unique element tag
# (2...5) int, node i, j, k, l
# (6) int, material tag
# [7] double, thickness, default: 1.0
# [8] bool string, nonlinear geometry switch, default: false

docs.title: Remarks
docs.text:
1. If the nonlinear geometry is switched on, the transformation between the global and local reference frames will depend on the current displacement. The nonlinear transformation is similar to the corotational transformation, and the local response is still linear. Thus, it follows "large displacement, small deformation" assumption.

  2. The material must provide a nonzero shear modulus, since the Mindlin plate part builds its reduced-integration shear penalty from it.

implementation limitation

The GQ12 membrane has no drilling penalty, so the drilling rotation can be a zero-energy mode in an unconstrained patch. The material must report a nonzero shear modulus or initialization fails.

  • Use a plane-stress two-dimensional material such as Elastic2D to obtain the correct $\(Et^3/[12(1-\nu^2)]\)$ bending stiffness.
  • The number of through-thickness Gauss points is fixed at three and is not a command-line argument in this element.
  • A uniform drilling rotation carries no membrane strain with the GQ12 interpolation, so restrain UR3 where it is not otherwise constrained.
  • For a thin-plate formulation without transverse shear use SGCMS, and for a triangular mesh use DKTS3.

docs.title: SGCMS
docs.text:
Simplified Generalized Conforming Mixed Shell Element

A planar shell element uses SGCMQ for membrane action and the DKT4 element for plate action.

  • Number of Nodes: 4
  • Number of DoFs: 6 (Translation, Translation, Translation, Rotation, Rotation, Rotation)
  • DoF Label: U1, U2, U3, UR1, UR2, UR3
  • Integration Membrane: Five-Point Irons Scheme
  • Integration Plate: 3rd Gauss Scheme

docs.title: Background
docs.text:
SGCMS is a four-node flat shell assembled by ShellBase from the simplified generalized conforming membrane SGCMQ and the discrete Kirchhoff plate DKT4.

The membrane part uses a twelve-parameter local stress expansion and a five-point Irons rule, as described on the GCMQ page, and supplies the drilling rotation $\(UR_3\)$.

The plate part imposes the Kirchhoff condition at the four edge midpoints and uses 2-by-2 Gauss points in the plane with three Gauss layers through the thickness.

At a fibre of coordinate $\(z\)$ the strain is $\(\mathbf\varepsilon=\mathbf B_m\mathbf d_m+z\,\mathbf B_p\mathbf d_p\)$, which produces the coupled membrane--bending stiffness blocks described on ShellBase.

Unlike S4, no transverse shear strain is retained, so the plate is a thin-plate model that is free of shear locking.

deviation from theory

The plate part enforces the Kirchhoff condition only at the four midpoints and has no transverse shear energy. The SGCMQ membrane uses the actual edge lengths without the objective-length option of the standalone element, so its drilling interpolation is mesh dependent.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text:
SGCMS
element SGCMS (1) (2...5) (6) [7] [8]
# (1) int, unique element tag
# (2...5) int, node i, j, k, l
# (6) int, material tag
# [7] double, thickness, default: 1.0
# [8] bool string, nonlinear geometry switch, default: false

docs.title: Remarks
docs.text:
1. If the nonlinear geometry is switched on, the transformation between the global and local reference frames will depend on the current displacement. The nonlinear transformation is similar to the corotational transformation, and the local response is still linear. Thus, it follows "large displacement, small deformation" assumption.

  2. Use a plane-stress two-dimensional material such as Elastic2D so that the through-thickness integration yields the correct thin-plate bending stiffness.

implementation limitation

A plane-strain material changes the synthesized bending stiffness, and the uniform drilling mode has no explicit stabilization.

developer note

The five-point Irons membrane rule and the three-layer plate rule are hard-coded.

  • The membrane and plate integrations are fixed by the formulation and are not command-line arguments.
  • The drilling rotation comes from the SGCMQ interpolation and can still lack stiffness in a uniform drilling mode, as noted on Allman.
  • For a moderately thick plate with transverse shear deformation use S4, and for a triangular mesh use DKTS3.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. 10.1002/nme.6066
  2. 10.1002/nme.1620151205
  3. Evaluation of a new quadrilateral thin plate bending element

docs.title: ShellBase
docs.text: The ShellBase class is a base class for all shell elements. It provides basic methods to convert displacement from global to local, or convert resistance and stiffness from local to global.

docs.title: Background
docs.text:
Each shell node has six DoFs: three membrane components and three plate components. ShellBase derives the local direction cosines from the element geometry and assembles the membrane and plate contributions into the full element resistance and stiffness. In a nonlinear geometry analysis the transformation is recomputed from the trial displaced shape.

A flat shell element is obtained by superposing a two-dimensional membrane model and a plate-bending model on the same planar reference surface.

In the local frame the membrane contributes the in-plane translations $\(u,v\)$ and the drilling rotation $\(\theta_z\)$, while the plate contributes the transverse displacement $\(w\)$ and the bending rotations $\(\theta_x,\theta_y\)$.

The global ordering of the six nodal DoFs is $\((U_1,U_2,U_3,UR_1,UR_2,UR_3)\)$, and the implementation uses the index sets $\(m=\{0,1,5\}\)$ for the local membrane block and $\(p=\{2,3,4\}\)$ for the local plate block.

For a node with local membrane vector $\(\mathbf d_m\)$ and plate vector $\(\mathbf d_p\)$, the strain at a fibre of thickness coordinate $\(z\)$ is

\[ \mathbf\varepsilon(z)=\mathbf B_m\mathbf d_m+z\,\mathbf B_p\mathbf d_p , \]

with the in-plane strain vector $\((u_{,x},v_{,y},u_{,y}+v_{,x})\)$ and the plate curvature used for $\(\mathbf B_p\)$.

Integrating this strain through the thickness gives the local stiffness in block form

\[ \mathbf K_{\rm loc}= \begin{bmatrix} \mathbf K_{mm} & \mathbf K_{mp}\\ \mathbf K_{pm} & \mathbf K_{pp} \end{bmatrix}, \qquad \begin{aligned} \mathbf K_{mm}&=\int\mathbf B_m^{\mathsf T}\mathbf D\mathbf B_m\,dV,\\ \mathbf K_{mp}&=\int z\,\mathbf B_m^{\mathsf T}\mathbf D\mathbf B_p\,dV,\\ \mathbf K_{pp}&=\int z^2\,\mathbf B_p^{\mathsf T}\mathbf D\mathbf B_p\,dV, \end{aligned} \]

so the bending stiffness is synthesized from the two-dimensional material matrix $\(\mathbf D\)$ and the $\(z\)$ and $\(z^2\)$ moments.

ShellBase::reshuffle inserts these three-by-three blocks into the six-DoF-per-node layout, and the fibre coordinate is evaluated at Gauss points with $\(z=\xi t/2\)$ and weights proportional to $\(t\)$.

The local triad is built from the first three nodes, with $\(\mathbf e_1\)$ along $\(\mathbf x_2-\mathbf x_1\)$, $\(\mathbf e_3\)$ normal to the plane spanned by $\(\mathbf x_2-\mathbf x_1\)$ and $\(\mathbf x_3-\mathbf x_1\)$, and $\(\mathbf e_2=\mathbf e_3\times\mathbf e_1\)$.

These three unit vectors are stored as the columns of the rotation matrix $\(\mathbf R\)$, so nodal vectors and stiffnesses are transformed with $\(\mathbf d_{\rm loc}=\mathbf R^{\mathsf T}\mathbf d_{\rm glob}\)$ and $\(\mathbf K_{\rm glob}=\mathbf T\mathbf K_{\rm loc}\mathbf T^{\mathsf T}\)$, where $\(\mathbf T={\rm diag}(\mathbf R,\ldots,\mathbf R)\)$.

When the nonlinear-geometry switch is active, the triad is recomputed from the trial displaced nodal positions and the derivative of the triad with respect to displacement contributes an additional geometric stiffness through transform_to_global_geometry, giving a corotational-style large-displacement formulation with a locally linear response.

deviation from theory

This is not a fully nonlinear corotational formulation, because the material response is still evaluated in the local frame with small-strain kinematics. The geometric stiffness comes only from the derivative of the rigid-body triad, not from finite-strain measures. The local triad is taken from the first three nodes, so the local plane is fixed by that choice rather than by a best-fit plane through all nodes.

docs.title: Remarks
docs.text:
ShellBase is not a user-instantiable element and has no element ShellBase command. Use one of its derived elements instead: DKTS3, S4 or SGCMS.

  • Each derived element takes a single two-dimensional material tag, and the same material matrix is used for membrane and bending action through the $\(z\)$ and $\(z^2\)$ integrals.

implementation limitation

There is no separate membrane material, plate material or section definition in these elements. Layered or sandwich shells are only possible through the material's own through-thickness response. Strongly warped geometry is not checked.

developer note

The planarity warning is commented out in the source.

  • The drilling rotation UR3 is supplied only by the membrane part, so an Allman- or GQ12-type membrane can leave a uniform drilling mode without stiffness; see Allman.
