  • The local coordinates are projections of the global nodal coordinates onto the local plane, and the explicit non-planarity warning is commented out in the source, so a strongly warped element should be used with care.
  • With nlgeom enabled the element follows the "large displacement, small deformation" assumption because the local material response remains linear.
  • The separate SectionShell abstraction, for example its Homogeneous implementation, performs a similar eccentricity-based thickness integration for section-aware elements, but the flat shells listed here integrate their layers internally.
  • DKTS3 uses a three-node drilling membrane plus DKT3 plate bending, S4 uses GQ12 plus Mindlin, and SGCMS uses SGCMQ plus DKT4.

docs.title: Contact2D
docs.text:
2D Node(Slave)-Line(Master) Contact Element

  • Number of DoFs: 2
  • DoF Label: U1, U2

docs.title: Background
docs.text:
The Contact2D element enforces frictionless unilateral contact between a slave node and the master line segments formed by consecutive nodes of a master group. It is implemented as a finite element so that both the contact force and its consistent tangent are assembled directly into the global residual and stiffness.

Let $\(\mathbf r_1\)$ and $\(\mathbf r_2\)$ be the current positions of the two master nodes of one segment and $\(\mathbf r_3\)$ that of the slave node, each position being the sum of the original coordinate and the trial displacement. The segment axis is $\(\mathbf l=\mathbf r_2-\mathbf r_1\)$ with length $\(l=\lVert\mathbf l\rVert\)$. The outward unit normal is obtained by rotating the normalised axis by $\(\pi/2\)$,

\[ \mathbf n=\mathbf T\dfrac{\mathbf l}{l},\qquad \mathbf T=\begin{bmatrix}0&-1\\1&0\end{bmatrix}. \]

Define $\(\mathbf s=\mathbf r_3-\mathbf r_1\)$. Contact is active only when the penetration and the parametric coordinate satisfy

\[ u=\mathbf s\cdot\mathbf n\le 0,\qquad t=\dfrac{\mathbf s\cdot\mathbf l}{\mathbf l\cdot\mathbf l}\in[0,1]. \]

The parameter $\(t\)$ is the closest-point projection of the slave node onto the segment, and the condition $\(0\le t\le 1\)$ excludes the extensions beyond the two end nodes.

implementation limitation

A slave node whose closest projection falls outside a segment is ignored even if it penetrates near an end node. Corner and edge contact are not treated.

The penalty method replaces the exact impenetrability constraint $\(u=0\)$ by a contact spring of stiffness $\(\alpha\)$ that resists penetration. The resistance on the slave node is

\[ \mathbf F_3=\alpha\,u\,\mathbf n, \]

and the equal-and-opposite reactions on the master nodes follow from force and moment equilibrium,

\[ \mathbf F_2=-\alpha\,t\,u\,\mathbf n,\qquad \mathbf F_1=\alpha\,(t-1)\,u\,\mathbf n. \]

The distribution $\((1-t):t\)$ is the linear interpolation of the contact force to the segment end nodes, which is the classical 2D node-to-segment weighting. The tangent stiffness is the consistent linearisation $\(\mathbf K_e=-\partial\mathbf F/\partial\mathbf r\)$ of the three nodal resistance vectors. Because $\(\mathbf n\)$ depends on the orientation of the segment, its derivative

\[ \dfrac{\partial\mathbf n}{\partial\mathbf l}=\dfrac{1}{l}\left(\mathbf T-\mathbf n\otimes\dfrac{\mathbf l}{l}\right) \]

is retained, so the tangent remains symmetric and quadratic convergence of the Newton iteration is preserved. A positive $\(\alpha\)$ gives a repulsive force opposite to $\(\mathbf n\)$ for $\(u<0\)$. The gap is not enforced exactly: the residual penetration is of order $\(1/\alpha\)$, so increasing $\(\alpha\)$ reduces penetration at the cost of conditioning. No tangential traction is included, so the contact is frictionless.

implementation limitation

General contact formulations include a tangential traction and a Coulomb friction law. Only the normal penalty force is assembled here, so frictional sliding cannot be represented by this element.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text:
Contact2D
element Contact2D (1) (2) (3) [4]
# (1) int, unique element tag
# (2) int, master group tag
# (3) int, slave group tag
# [4] double, penalty factor

docs.title: Remarks
docs.text:
1. The contact algorithm is implemented via penalty function method as an element. The parameter [4] controls the magnitude of penalty.
  2. No matter whether the nlgeom switch is on or off for connected elements, the contact detection itself is always conducted in a nonlinear manner, similar to the total Lagrangian formulation.
  3. The node-line contact detection is performed for all nodes defined in slave group and lines defined by nodes in master group. There are $\(n-1\)$ line segments for $\(n\)$ nodes in master group.
  4. Master nodes can penetrate lines formed in slave group. To prevent this, define a new Contact2D element by swapping the order of slave and master groups.
  5. Example usage can be seen in the example.
  6. If [4] is omitted, the parser uses a default penalty of $\(1E6\)$.
  7. The penalty acts only on the normal gap; there is no friction or tangential penalty, and a shear transfer must be modelled with a separate element such as Tie.
  8. Contact detection always uses current trial positions, so geometric nonlinearity is active even when the connected elements use a linear formulation.
  9. For the spatial counterpart based on triangular facets, see Contact3D.

docs.title: Contact3D
docs.text:
3D Node(Slave)-Triangular Facet(Master) Contact Element

  • Number of DoFs: 3
  • DoF Label: U1, U2, U3

docs.title: Background
docs.text:
Contact3D is the spatial counterpart of Contact2D. It enforces frictionless node-to-facet contact between slave nodes and the triangular facets formed from the master node group using the same penalty idea. The full derivation of the penalty method, the gap definition and the consistent tangent is given on the Contact2D page, so only the 3D-specific geometry is summarised here.

Three consecutive master nodes $\((\mathbf r_i,\mathbf r_j,\mathbf r_k)\)$ define one planar facet with outward unit normal $\(\mathbf n_f\)$ and area $\(A_f\)$. For a slave node at $\(\mathbf r_s\)$, the signed normal gap is

\[ g=\mathbf n_f\cdot(\mathbf r_s-\mathbf r_i)\le 0. \]

The projection is accepted only when it falls inside the triangle, which the implementation tests with three edge-based quantities $\(h_i\)$, $\(h_j\)$ and $\(h_k\)$ formed from the edge normals. If any $\(h\)$ is positive, the closest point lies outside the facet and the pair is skipped. The nodal weights are the barycentric coordinates $\(n_i=h_i/A_f\)$, $\(n_j=h_j/A_f\)$ and $\(n_k=h_k/A_f\)$. The penalty resistance is assembled as

\[ \mathbf F_s=\alpha\,g\,\mathbf n_f,\qquad \mathbf F_i=\alpha\,n_i\,g\,\mathbf n_f,\qquad \mathbf F_j=\alpha\,n_j\,g\,\mathbf n_f,\qquad \mathbf F_k=\alpha\,n_k\,g\,\mathbf n_f. \]

The consistent tangent contains the derivatives of $\(\mathbf n_f\)$ with respect to all three master nodes as well as the derivatives of the barycentric weights. All facets and slave positions are updated from the current trial configuration before the contact check.

implementation limitation

Contact is checked only when the projection lies inside a master triangle. A slave node outside all facets is ignored even if it is close to an edge. The facet normal is divided by the facet area without a degeneracy guard, so zero-area triangles must be avoided.

deviation from theory

This is a one-pass node-to-facet scheme. Master nodes are not tested against slave facets, so master-side penetration requires a second element with the groups swapped.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text:
Contact3D
element Contact3D (1) (2) (3) [4]
# (1) int, unique element tag
# (2) int, master group tag
# (3) int, slave group tag
# [4] double, penalty factor

docs.title: Remarks
docs.text:
1. The contact algorithm is implemented via penalty function method as an element. The parameter [4] controls the magnitude of penalty.
  2. No matter whether the nlgeom switch is on or off for connected elements, the contact detection itself is always conducted in a nonlinear manner, similar to the total Lagrangian formulation for the precise computation of contact.
  3. The node-facet contact detection is performed for all nodes defined in slave group and facets defined by nodes in master group. There are $\(n/3\)$ facets for $\(n\)$ nodes in master group. So the number of nodes in master group must be a multiple of $\(3\)$.
  4. If [4] is omitted, the parser uses a default penalty of $\(1E6\)$.
  5. Master facets are flat triangles and the contact is frictionless, so only a normal penalty force is transferred.
  6. This is a one-pass scheme, hence master nodes can penetrate slave facets; define a second element with the groups swapped to detect that case, as described on the Contact2D page.

docs.title: Damper01/Damper03
docs.text:
Viscous/Nonviscous Damper

This damper uses displacement and velocity as inputs, not strain and strain rate, which means element length is not used to compute strain or strain rate.

docs.title: Damper01
docs.text:
This Damper01 is a simple 2D viscous/nonviscous damper.

See this example.

  • Number of Nodes: 2
  • Number of DoFs: 2 (Translation, Translation)
  • DoF Label: U1, U2

docs.title: Damper03
docs.text:
This Damper03 is a simple 3D viscous/nonviscous damper.

  • Number of Nodes: 2
  • Number of DoFs: 3 (Translation, Translation, Translation)
  • DoF Label: U1, U2, U3

docs.title: Background
docs.text:
A viscous damper supplies a force proportional to the relative velocity of its two ends, so on its own it dissipates energy without storing it. Let $\(\mathbf c\)$ be the unit vector from node $\(i\)$ to node $\(j\)$, computed once from the initial coordinates, and define $\(\Delta\mathbf u=\mathbf u_j-\mathbf u_i\)$ and $\(\Delta\mathbf v=\mathbf v_j-\mathbf v_i\)$. The element passes the projected displacement and velocity

\[ \epsilon=\mathbf c\cdot\Delta\mathbf u,\qquad \dot\epsilon=\mathbf c\cdot\Delta\mathbf v \]

to the associated one-dimensional material, which returns a force $\(N\)$ and a tangent damping coefficient $\(c_t=\partial N/\partial\dot\epsilon\)$. The element length does not enter these expressions, so $\(\epsilon\)$ is a displacement rather than a strain and the material must use a displacement--force or displacement--velocity law.

deviation from theory

A standard axial bar or dashpot converts the relative velocity into a strain rate by dividing by the member length. This element passes the raw projected velocity, so the material coefficient must be given as force per velocity rather than as a viscosity in stress per strain rate.

The assembled resistance and damping matrix are

\[ \mathbf R_j=\mathbf c\,N,\qquad \mathbf R_i=-\mathbf R_j,\qquad \mathbf C_e=\begin{bmatrix}\mathbf c\\-\mathbf c\end{bmatrix}c_t\begin{bmatrix}\mathbf c&-\mathbf c\end{bmatrix}^{\mathrm T}. \]

If the material also returns a tangent stiffness, the same rank-one projection is applied to form $\(\mathbf K_e\)$. Since the damping matrix is built at element level, the element-level modifiers described on the Modifier page can be used to inspect or replace it.

implementation limitation

Element damping modifiers such as LinearViscosity and ElementalLee skip this element, so its damping must come from the assigned material.

developer note

The constructor sets modify_viscous to false.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text:
Damper01
element Damper01 (1) (2) (3) (4)
element Damper03 (1) (2) (3) (4)
# (1) int, unique tag
# (2) int, node i
# (3) int, node j
# (4) int, material tag of associated (non)viscosity material

docs.title: Remarks
docs.text:
Both viscous and nonviscous materials can be used for this element, see Viscosity.

  1. The material sees the projected relative displacement and velocity, so its stiffness has units of force per length and its damping coefficient has units of force per velocity.
  2. The direction $\(\mathbf c\)$ is fixed at initialisation from the initial node coordinates, so a large rigid rotation of the damper is not followed.
  3. A material that defines only a viscous force, such as a power-law dashpot, is sufficient; a separate spring can be added with Spring01 or with the Maxwell model in Damper02.
  4. Damper05 and Damper06 feed only the relative velocity and contribute a pure viscous force, whereas Damper01 and Damper03 feed both displacement and velocity and may also return a stiffness.

docs.title: Variants
docs.text: Damper05 is the revised 2D damper: element Damper05 (1) (2) (3) (4) takes only the two nodes and one damper material tag, and feeds the material the relative velocity alone instead of both displacement and velocity, so the element length is not used. Damper06 is the 3D counterpart with the same four arguments and three translational DoFs per node.

docs.title: Damper02/Damper04
docs.text:
Maxwell Model

The Damper02 and Damper04 are Maxwell models that use displacement and velocity as inputs, that is, element length is not used to compute strain or strain rate.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
The Maxwell model allows combinations of nonlinear springs and dampers. The algorithm implemented is documented in the following paper.

  1. 10.1016/j.ymssp.2021.108795

docs.title: Damper02
docs.text:
The Damper02 is the 2D version.

  • Number of Nodes: 2
  • Number of DoFs: 2 (Translation, Translation)
  • DoF Label: U1, U2

docs.title: Damper04
docs.text:
The Damper04 is the 3D version.

  • Number of Nodes: 2
  • Number of DoFs: 3 (Translation, Translation, Translation)
  • DoF Label: U1, U2, U3

docs.title: Background
docs.text:
A Maxwell model connects a spring and a dashpot in series. For a prescribed end displacement $\(\epsilon\)$ and velocity $\(\dot\epsilon\)$, the two components carry the same force $\(N\)$ but share the deformation,

\[ \epsilon=\epsilon_s+\epsilon_d,\qquad N=f_s(\epsilon_s)=f_d(\dot\epsilon_d). \]

Eliminating $\(\epsilon_d\)$ gives a scalar evolution equation for the internal spring strain $\(\epsilon_s\)$, which has to be solved locally at every trial state. The implementation uses the Newton--Raphson based state-determination algorithm of Chang and Lee, so the spring may be a rate-independent nonlinear model and the dashpot coefficient may depend on both displacement and velocity.

The element projects the end displacements and velocities onto the initial axis $\(\mathbf c\)$ and passes $\(u=\mathbf c\cdot(\mathbf u_j-\mathbf u_i)\)$ and $\(v=\mathbf c\cdot(\mathbf v_j-\mathbf v_i)\)$ to the Maxwell material, so the element length is again not used. With $\(\beta\)$ the local time-integration parameter and $\(\Delta t\)$ the time increment, the factor $\(\beta\Delta t\)$ controls how the spring strain is interpolated over the increment; $\(\beta=0.5\)$ corresponds to a linear spring strain history. The element assembles the resulting force as $\(\mathbf R_j=\mathbf c\,N\)$, $\(\mathbf R_i=-\mathbf R_j\)$, and forms both a trial tangent stiffness and a trial damping matrix from the Maxwell material.

deviation from theory

As in Damper01, the raw projected displacement and velocity are passed to the material without division by the element length.

developer note

The series spring--dashpot state is found by a local iterative solution rather than by an analytical integration of the governing ODE.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text:
Damper02
element Damper02 (1) (2) (3) (4) (5) [6] [7] [8]
element Damper04 (1) (2) (3) (4) (5) [6] [7] [8]
# (1) int, unique tag
# (2) int, node i
# (3) int, node j
# (4) int, damper tag
# (5) int, spring tag
# [6] bool string, whether to use matrix in iteration, default: true
# [7] int, the maximum delay number, default: 0
# [8] double, beta, default: 0.5

docs.title: Remarks
docs.text:
1. Parameter [7] indicates whether to stack diverged increments into next iteration. If $\(0\)$ is assigned, the material returns a failure flag as long as local iteration fails to converge. If $\(n>0\)$, a maximum $\(n\)$ increments are allowed to be stacked before exit due to divergence.
  2. The [8] parameter controls the local time integration, $\(\beta\in[0,1]\)$ shall be defined. The default value $\(0.5\)$ implies a constant acceleration rule for the spring component in the Maxwell model.
  3. The parameter [6] selects the local solver, with true giving a three-by-three matrix Newton iteration and false a scalar iteration; the matrix form is more robust but costs more per iteration.
  4. When [7]=n>1, a failed local iteration resets the trial state and is counted against the limit, so up to $\(n-1\)$ consecutive failures are tolerated before the state determination is declared divergent.

developer note

The wording that diverged increments are stacked into the next iteration does not reflect the implementation. On a tolerated local failure the code resets the trial state to the converged state and continues the analysis.

  1. Both a tangent stiffness and a damping matrix are returned by the Maxwell material, in contrast to Damper01 where the spring is optional.
  2. This element sets modify_viscous to false, so element damping modifiers such as LinearViscosity skip it.

docs.title: Variants
docs.text: Damper05 is the revised 2D damper: element Damper05 (1) (2) (3) (4) takes two nodes and a damper material tag only, unlike Damper02 it has no spring, delay or beta arguments, and it updates the material from the relative velocity alone. Damper06 is the same revised update in 3D, with three translational DoFs per node; see Damper01.

docs.title: Embedded2D
docs.text:
2D Embedded Element

  • Number of DoFs: 2
  • DoF Label: U1, U2

docs.title: Background
docs.text:
An embedded (or immersed) element ties a slave node to a host continuum element without requiring the node to share a mesh line or nodes with the host. A penalty constraint is enforced between the displacement of the embedded node and the displacement interpolated by the host element shape functions at the node position.

Let $\(\mathbf u_s\)$ be the displacement of the slave node and $\(\mathbf u_a\)$ those of the $\(n_h\)$ host nodes. The host interpolant at the embedded point is $\(\bar{\mathbf u}=\sum_a N_a(\mathbf\xi)\mathbf u_a\)$, where $\(\mathbf\xi\)$ are the natural coordinates of that point in the host element. The penalty energy $\(\Pi=\tfrac12\alpha\lVert\mathbf u_s-\bar{\mathbf u}\rVert^2\)$ gives the constraint vector and force

\[ \mathbf w=\begin{bmatrix}1&-N_1&\cdots&-N_{n_h}\end{bmatrix},\qquad \mathbf R_e=\alpha\,(\mathbf u_s-\bar{\mathbf u})\,\mathbf w, \]

with an associated tangent $\(\alpha\,\mathbf w^{\mathrm T}\mathbf w\)$ assembled once at initialisation.

The natural coordinates $\(\mathbf\xi\)$ are found by an iterative inverse mapping at initialisation. Newton updates $\(\mathbf\xi\leftarrow\mathbf\xi+\mathbf J^{-1}(\mathbf x_s-\mathbf N(\mathbf\xi)\mathbf X_h)\)$ are performed with the shape-function Jacobian $\(\mathbf J=\partial\mathbf N/\partial\mathbf\xi\,\mathbf X_h\)$ until $\(\lVert\Delta\mathbf\xi\rVert_\infty<10^{-14}\)$ or 20 iterations are exhausted. The shape functions are then frozen, so the penalty stiffness remains constant throughout the analysis.

implementation limitation

The natural coordinates are found once from the initial geometry and are not updated as the host element deforms. Initialization fails if the inverse mapping does not converge.

developer note

The inverse mapping is capped at 20 iterations.

deviation from theory

Only translational DoFs are tied. Rotational compatibility between the embedded node and the host rotation field is not enforced.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text:
Embedded2D
element Embedded2D (1) (2) (3) [4]
# (1) int, unique element tag
# (2) int, host element tag
# (3) int, slave node tag
# [4] double, penalty factor, default: 1E4

docs.title: Remarks
docs.text:
1. Currently, the following element types are supported: CP4, CP5, CP7 and CP8.
  2. If [4] is omitted, the parser uses a default penalty of $\(1E4\)$.
  3. Only translational DoFs are tied, and the host element must provide shape functions and their derivatives in natural coordinates.
  4. The slave node should lie inside the host element so that the inverse mapping converges to a meaningful point.
  5. A small penalty permits relative slip, while an excessively large penalty degrades conditioning; see Tie for a purely algebraic penalty constraint and Contact2D for contact without mesh connectivity.

docs.title: Embedded3D
docs.text:
3D Embedded Element

  • Number of DoFs: 3
  • DoF Label: U1, U2, U3

docs.title: Background
docs.text:
Embedded3D is the spatial counterpart of Embedded2D. It ties the three translations of a slave node to the displacement interpolated by a solid host element at that node's position, using the same penalty formulation.

With host shape functions $\(N_a\)$ evaluated at the natural coordinates $\(\mathbf\xi=(\xi,\eta,\zeta)\)$ of the embedded point, the constraint force is

\[ \mathbf R_e=\alpha\left(\mathbf u_s-\sum_a N_a\mathbf u_a\right) \begin{bmatrix}1&-N_1&\cdots&-N_{n_h}\end{bmatrix}. \]

The point $\(\mathbf\xi\)$ is located once at initialisation by Newton iteration on $\(\mathbf J^{-1}(\mathbf x_s-\mathbf N\mathbf X_h)\)$, where $\(\mathbf J=\partial\mathbf N/\partial\mathbf\xi\,\mathbf X_h\)$ is the host Jacobian, and the resulting tangent $\(\alpha\,\mathbf w^{\mathrm T}\mathbf w\)$ is kept constant for the analysis. The full derivation and the choice of penalty factor are discussed on the Embedded2D page.

implementation limitation

The natural coordinates and shape functions are fixed from the initial host geometry and are not updated during the analysis. Initialization fails if the inverse mapping does not converge. No rotational DoFs are tied.

developer note

The inverse mapping uses Newton iteration and is capped at 20 iterations.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text:
Embedded3D
element Embedded3D (1) (2) (3) [4]
# (1) int, unique element tag
# (2) int, host element tag
# (3) int, slave node tag
# [4] double, penalty factor, default: 1E4

docs.title: Remarks
docs.text:
1. Currently, the following element types are supported: C3D8 and C3D20.
  2. If [4] is omitted, the parser uses a default penalty of $\(1E4\)$.
  3. All three translations are tied with the same penalty and no rotational coupling is introduced.
  4. The inverse mapping uses the initial geometry, so large host distortions are not tracked; see Embedded2D for further remarks.

docs.title: Joint
docs.text:
Joint Element

The Joint is a joint element that uses displacement as inputs.

  • Number of Nodes: 2
  • Number of DoFs: varies

docs.title: Background
docs.text:
A joint connects two nodes that may occupy the same coordinates with a set of independent nonlinear springs, one per connected degree of freedom. Because the nodes can coincide, the element is effectively zero length: no axis or element length is used and the relative displacement is passed directly to each material as a scalar deformation.

For the $\(k\)$-th connected DoF, let $\(u_i^{(k)}\)$ and $\(u_j^{(k)}\)$ be the displacement components of the two nodes. The material receives

\[ \Delta^{(k)}=u_i^{(k)}-u_j^{(k)}, \]

and returns a force $\(N^{(k)}\)$ with tangent stiffness $\(k^{(k)}=\mathrm dN^{(k)}/\mathrm d\Delta^{(k)}\)$. The element assembles $\(R_i^{(k)}=N^{(k)}\)$, $\(R_j^{(k)}=-N^{(k)}\)$ and the two-by-two block

\[ \begin{bmatrix}1&-1\\-1&1\end{bmatrix}k^{(k)} \]

for each connected DoF.

The number of material tags equals the number of connected DoFs per node, so $\(m\)$ material tags create $\(2m\)$ element DoFs and the materials act in the order in which the tags are given. No geometric transformation is applied, so the connected DoFs are the global directions encoded on the nodes. This is the multi-DoF generalisation of the single-direction Spring01 element.

deviation from theory

A general joint element projects the relative displacement into a local coordinate system before passing it to the material. This element passes the global displacement components directly, so kinematic coupling between directions is not represented.

implementation limitation

Initialization fails unless the number of material tags equals the number of DoFs per node.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text:
Joint
element Joint (1) (2) (3) (4...)
# (1) int, unique element tag
# (2) int, node i
# (3) int, node j
# (4...) int, material tags

docs.title: Remarks
docs.text:
The Joint element defines a joint connecting two nodes that can coincide with each other regarding their coordinates. The relative displacement is used as strain input. Thus, the corresponding material model shall be defined to use displacement and force. Note in the current implementation the global horizontal and vertical displacements are passed to the material models to compute the response.

The number of connected degrees of freedom can vary based on the number of tags of material models assigned to the element. The material models are used for each DoF sequentially according to the definition. If one wants to define a joint tagged 5 between node 1 and node 2 using material 3 for the first four DoFs, the following command can be used.

Text Only
element Joint 5 1 2 3 3 3 3

The material models must use a displacement--force law, because the input is a relative displacement rather than a strain. For a single connected direction with a defined axis, prefer Spring01, which projects onto the element direction instead of using global components. To impose a constraint instead of a force--deformation relation, use Tie.

docs.title: Mass
docs.text:
Point Mass

  • Number of Nodes: 1
  • Number of DoFs: varies

docs.title: Background
docs.text:
In a dynamic analysis the inertia contribution to equilibrium is $\(\mathbf M\ddot{\mathbf u}\)$, where the element consistent mass matrix is

\[ \mathbf M_e^c=\int_{\Omega_e}\rho\,\mathbf N^{\mathrm T}\mathbf N\,\mathrm d\Omega_e . \]

It is built from the same displacement interpolation $\(\mathbf N\)$ as the stiffness, so it reproduces the kinetic energy of the interpolated field, but it couples neighbouring DoFs. A lumped mass matrix replaces it by a diagonal matrix whose row sums preserve the total mass,

\[ M^{l}_{ii}=\sum_j M^c_{ij},\qquad \sum_i M^{l}_{ii}=\int_{\Omega_e}\rho\,\mathrm d\Omega . \]

A diagonal mass matrix is cheaper and is required by many explicit time integrators, whereas a consistent matrix is generally more accurate for wave propagation. The Mass, Mass2D and Mass3D elements are already lumped: each selected DoF receives the same scalar magnitude $\(m\)$ on the diagonal and there is no off-diagonal coupling.

For a rigid body the kinetic energy is

\[ T=\dfrac12 m\,\dot{\mathbf u}\cdot\dot{\mathbf u}+\dfrac12\mathbf\omega\cdot\mathbf I\,\mathbf\omega , \]

so rotational inertia appears as additional diagonal entries on the rotation DoFs. MassPoint2D and MassPoint3D place the translational mass $\(m\)$ on the translation DoFs and an optional scalar inertia $\(I\)$ on the rotation DoFs, giving $\(\mathrm{diag}(m,m,I)\)$ in 2D and $\(\mathrm{diag}(m,m,m,I,I,I)\)$ in 3D. Because a single scalar $\(I\)$ is used, the inertia tensor is isotropic, which is appropriate for a point-like or spherically symmetric mass lump.

implementation limitation

A full inertia tensor with distinct principal moments is not supported by the point-mass elements. Each assigned DoF receives the same magnitude $\(m\)$, so off-diagonal mass coupling is absent.

A point mass can also be represented as an external D'Alembert inertia load or as an attribute of a node. Defining it as an element makes the mass matrix available during assembly, before loads are applied, and keeps point masses in the same tag pool as the other elements. The element has no stiffness, so it does not contribute to a static analysis.

implementation limitation

The lumped mass modifiers LumpedSimple and LumpedScale skip these elements, so the entered magnitude is used unchanged.

developer note

MassBase sets modify_mass to false.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text:
Mass
Mass (1) (2) (3) (4...)
element Mass (1) (2) (3) (4...)
# (1) int, unique element tag
# (2) int, node tag
# (3) double, magnitude
# (4...) int, dof tag

Point mass is implemented via an element interface that connects only one node. No stiffness is defined within that element. Thus, a Mass object shares the same tag pool with the other elements.

docs.title: Variants
docs.text:
Mass2D creates a planar point mass: Mass2D (1) (2) (3) (4...) accepts at most three DoF tags, which map to U1, U2 and UR3, and no element is created if a tag larger than three is given. Mass3D creates a spatial point mass with at most six DoF tags, which map to U1, U2, U3, UR1, UR2 and UR3; plain Mass is an alias for Mass3D.

  1. The same magnitude is assigned to every listed DoF, so distinct translational and rotational values require MassPoint2D or MassPoint3D.
  2. A DoF tag larger than three in 2D or six in 3D is rejected by the parser.
  3. The mass matrix is constant and the lumped mass modifiers skip these elements, as discussed on the Modifier page.
  4. For a consistent mass matrix use a continuum element with a density-bearing material; Mass only supplies a lumped diagonal contribution.

docs.title: MassPoint
docs.text: The MassPoint element is used to represent a mass point with translational mass and optional rotational inertia.

docs.title: Background
docs.text:
MassPoint2D and MassPoint3D are convenience wrappers around the general Mass element that predefine the DoF set of a point mass. They contribute a constant diagonal mass matrix and no stiffness, so they only enter the inertia term $\(\mathbf M\ddot{\mathbf u}\)$ of a dynamic analysis.

The translational magnitude $\(m\)$ is placed on all translation DoFs and the optional rotational magnitude $\(I\)$ is placed on all rotation DoFs, giving

\[ \mathbf M_e^{2D}=\operatorname{diag}(m,m,I),\qquad \mathbf M_e^{3D}=\operatorname{diag}(m,m,m,I,I,I). \]

This corresponds to the lumped rigid-body inertia $\(T=\tfrac12 m\lVert\dot{\mathbf u}\rVert^2+\tfrac12 I\lVert\mathbf\omega\rVert^2\)$ with an isotropic inertia tensor. See Mass for the distinction between lumped and consistent mass matrices and for a more general DoF assignment.

implementation limitation

A single scalar inertia is assigned to every rotational DoF. An anisotropic inertia tensor with distinct principal moments cannot be specified with these elements.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text:
MassPoint
element MassPoint2D (1) (2) (3) [4]
element MassPoint3D (1) (2) (3) [4]
# (1) int, unique element tag
# (2) int, node tag
# (3) double, translational mass magnitude
# [4] double, optional, rotational inertia magnitude

docs.title: Remarks
docs.text:
1. For 2D elements, DOF::UX and DOF::UY are assigned with the translational mass (equal magnitude), DOF::URZ is assigned with the rotational inertia (optional).
  2. For 3D elements, DOF::UX, DOF::UY, and DOF::UZ are assigned with the translational mass (equal magnitude), DOF::URX, DOF::URY, and DOF::URZ are assigned with the rotational inertia (optional).
  3. MassPoint elements are an alternative to Mass elements, which are more abstract and allow more general assignment of mass.
  4. Omitting [4] creates only the translational DoFs and adds no rotational inertia.
  5. The same scalar $\(I\)$ is used for all rotational DoFs, so distinct per-axis inertia values require several Mass elements with separate magnitudes.
  6. Both magnitudes are constant mass properties, and the lumped mass modifiers skip these elements, as noted on the Mass page.

docs.title: SingleSection
docs.text:
Single Section Analysis

  • 2D:
  • Number of DoFs: 2 (AXIAL, STRONG AXIS ROTATION)
  • DoF Label: AXIAL, RS
  • 3D:
  • Number of DoFs: 3 (AXIAL, STRONG AXIS ROTATION, WEAK AXIS ROTATION)
  • DoF Label: AXIAL, RS, RW

It is often necessary to perform a section analysis to determine the capacity of the target section. The SingleSection element is exactly for this purpose.

To use the element, a proper section shall be defined.

docs.title: Background
docs.text:
A fibre section represents a cross-section by a set of integration points, each carrying a uniaxial material law. For an axial strain $\(\epsilon\)$ and a curvature $\(\kappa\)$ about the bending axis, the strain at a fibre with lever arm $\(y\)$ from the reference axis is

\[ \epsilon_f=\epsilon+y\,\kappa . \]

The section deformation is obtained by integrating the fibre response over the area,

\[ N=\int_A\sigma(\epsilon_f)\,\mathrm dA,\qquad M=\int_A y\,\sigma(\epsilon_f)\,\mathrm dA, \]

and the section tangent is the corresponding integral of the fibre tangents weighted by $\(1\)$ and $\(y\)$. The sign of the lever arm follows the convention of the chosen section model.

The SingleSection element exposes one such section directly at a single node. Its DoFs are passed unchanged to the section as the section deformation, and the section returns the conjugate forces and the consistent tangent. This isolates sectional behaviour from any spatial discretisation, so the element can be used to generate moment--curvature or axial force--strain curves and to validate a section definition before using it in a beam or shell model.

implementation limitation

Later changes to the original section are not reflected in this element. The element has no geometric stiffness of its own.

developer note

The section is copied when the element is initialized.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text:
SingleSection
element SingleSection2D (1) (2) (3)
element SingleSection3D (1) (2) (3)
# (1) int, unique tag
# (2) int, node tag
# (3) int, section tag

docs.title: Remarks
docs.text:
It directly exposes the associated section.

  1. In 3D there are two bending DoFs, RS and RW, so the section deformation has three components and the section must be defined accordingly.
  2. The element has only one node and no geometric stiffness, so it is intended for a section-level analysis rather than for a structural model.
  3. The section is copied when the element is initialised, hence changes to the original section afterwards are not seen by this element.

breaking changes

Before v4, one can use integer indices (1, 2 and 3 in 3D cases) to apply a load or constrain a DoF. Starting from v4, one must use AXIAL, RS and RW to achieve the same purpose.

Text Only
node 1 0 0
material Bilinear1D 1 10 .8 .02
section Rectangle2D 1 12 1 1
element SingleSection2D 1 1 1

// use rs to apply a concentrated load of magnitude 3 to the strong axis bending DoF of node 1
cload 1 0 3 rs 1

docs.title: SphericalParticle2D
docs.text:
Spherical DEM Particle in 2D

A discrete-element particle that attaches a circular disc of given radius to a single node and carries the properties used by pairwise particle interactions: elastic modulus, Poisson ratio and damping, together with its mass. The element defines no stiffness of its own; it contributes a constant diagonal mass matrix and exposes its parameters to the DEM contact constraints.

  • Number of Nodes: 1
  • Number of DoFs: 2 (Translation, Translation), or 3 if inertia is supplied
  • DoF Label: U1, U2, optionally UR3
  • Element Type: DEM
  • Constant Mass Matrix, No Stiffness

docs.title: Background
docs.text:
The discrete element method (DEM) represents a particulate assembly as individual bodies whose motion is integrated in time and whose interactions are evaluated pairwise at contacts. A SphericalParticle2D element attaches a circular disc of radius $\(R\)$ to one node and stores the parameters needed to evaluate a contact, but it defines no stiffness of its own. It contributes only a constant diagonal mass matrix, $\(\mathrm{diag}(m,m)\)$, or $\(\mathrm{diag}(m,m,I)\)$ when rotational inertia is supplied.

For two particles $\(i\)$ and $\(j\)$ with centre distance $\(d\)$, the overlap or compression is

\[ \delta=R_i+R_j-d . \]

A contact exists only for $\(\delta>0\)$. The implementation uses a Hertzian normal law, with pair properties

\[ E^*=\left[\dfrac{1-\nu_i^2}{E_i}+\dfrac{1-\nu_j^2}{E_j}\right]^{-1}, \qquad R^*=\left[\dfrac1{R_i}+\dfrac1{R_j}\right]^{-1}, \qquad \eta^*=\dfrac{\eta_i+\eta_j}{2}. \]

The elastic normal force magnitude is $\(\frac43 E^*\sqrt{R^*\,\delta}\,\delta\)$, and a viscous contribution proportional to the relative normal velocity is superposed, so the contact force is repulsive along the line of centres and the damping opposes the relative approach. The contact force is distributed to the two nodes with equal magnitude and opposite sign, and its linearisation contributes to the global stiffness and damping matrices.

General DEM formulations often add a tangential spring and Coulomb friction, but the current Hertzian interaction is frictionless and acts only along the line of centres. Neighbour search is performed with a cell list whose cell size is twice the largest particle radius.

implementation limitation

The Hertzian interaction implements only the normal force law. Tangential springs and Coulomb friction, which are standard in DEM, are absent.

implementation limitation

The contact law uses only translational positions and velocities. Rotational DoFs do not affect pairwise contact.

developer note

Rotational inertia is stored on the particle. The MolecularDynamics2D constraint is instantiated with rotation disabled.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text:
SphericalParticle2D
element SphericalParticle2D (1) (2) (3) (4) (5) (6) (7) [8]
# (1) int, unique element tag
# (2) int, node tag
# (3) double, particle radius
# (4) double, elastic modulus
# (5) double, Poisson ratio
# (6) double, damping
# (7) double, mass
# [8] double, optional rotational inertia

docs.title: Remarks
docs.text:
1. With five parameters (3)...(7), the element is SphericalParticle2D: it has DoFs U1 and U2 and a mass matrix $\(\mathrm{diag}(m,m)\)$.
  2. If the inertia (8) is given, InertialSphericalParticle2D is created instead: the UR3 DoF is added and the mass matrix becomes $\(\mathrm{diag}(m,m,I)\)$.
  3. The radius, damping, elastic modulus and Poisson ratio are read by DEM interactions to build the effective radius, damping and modulus of a particle pair, so use a unit system consistent with the rest of the model.
  4. Use this element together with an interaction and a MolecularDynamics2D constraint, as in the Other/MD2D example.
  5. The interaction reads radius, elastic modulus, Poisson ratio and damping through the element parameter interface, while the mass only enters the diagonal mass matrix.
  6. The storage scheme must be full, sparse or sparse symmetric so that the constraint can assemble the contact contributions into the global matrices.
  7. The spatial variant with the same contact law is SphericalParticle3D.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. 10.1680/geot.1979.29.1.47
  2. Über die Berührung fester elastischer Körper
  3. ISBN 978-0-521-34796-9

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
Text Only
element SphericalParticle2D 1 1 1. 1e3 .2 1e-4 1.

docs.title: SphericalParticle3D
docs.text:
Spherical DEM Particle in 3D

A discrete-element particle that attaches a sphere of given radius to a single node and carries the properties used by pairwise particle interactions: elastic modulus, Poisson ratio and damping, together with its mass. The element defines no stiffness of its own; it contributes a constant diagonal mass matrix and exposes its parameters to the DEM contact constraints.

  • Number of Nodes: 1
  • Number of DoFs: 3 (Translation, Translation, Translation), or 6 if inertia is supplied
  • DoF Label: U1, U2, U3, optionally UR1, UR2, UR3
  • Element Type: DEM
  • Constant Mass Matrix, No Stiffness

docs.title: Background
docs.text:
SphericalParticle3D is the spatial counterpart of SphericalParticle2D. It attaches a sphere of radius $\(R\)$ to one node and carries the elastic modulus, Poisson ratio, damping and mass used by the pairwise DEM contact law. The element has no stiffness of its own and contributes $\(\mathrm{diag}(m,m,m)\)$ or $\(\mathrm{diag}(m,m,m,I,I,I)\)$ if inertia is supplied.

For a pair with centre distance $\(d\)$, the overlap $\(\delta=R_i+R_j-d\)$ activates a frictionless Hertzian force along the line of centres,

\[ \mathbf F_i=\left[\dfrac43 E^*\sqrt{R^*\,\delta}\,\delta + \eta^*\dot\delta\right]\hat{\mathbf r}_{ij}, \]

where $\(\hat{\mathbf r}_{ij}\)$ points from particle $\(j\)$ to particle $\(i\)$, $\(\dot\delta\)$ is the relative normal approach velocity and the pair properties $\(E^*\)$, $\(R^*\)$ and $\(\eta^*\)$ are defined on the SphericalParticle2D page. The equal and opposite force acts on particle $\(j\)$, and the consistent linearisation supplies tangent stiffness and damping terms for implicit integration. Contact is normal only; no tangential spring or friction law is implemented in the current interaction.

implementation limitation

Only the normal Hertzian law is available. The DEM constraint uses translational velocities only, so the optional rotational inertia does not enter the contact force.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text:
SphericalParticle3D
element SphericalParticle3D (1) (2) (3) (4) (5) (6) (7) [8]
# (1) int, unique element tag
# (2) int, node tag
# (3) double, particle radius
# (4) double, elastic modulus
# (5) double, Poisson ratio
# (6) double, damping
# (7) double, mass
# [8] double, optional rotational inertia

docs.title: Remarks
docs.text:
1. With five parameters (3)...(7), the element is SphericalParticle3D: it has DoFs U1, U2 and U3 and a mass matrix $\(\mathrm{diag}(m,m,m)\)$.
  2. If the inertia (8) is given, InertialSphericalParticle3D is created instead: the rotational DoFs UR1, UR2 and UR3 are added and the mass matrix becomes $\(\mathrm{diag}(m,m,m,I,I,I)\)$.
  3. The radius, damping, elastic modulus and Poisson ratio are read by DEM interactions to build the effective radius, damping and modulus of a particle pair, so use a unit system consistent with the rest of the model.
  4. Use this element together with an interaction and a MolecularDynamics3D constraint, as in the Other/MD3D example.
  5. The cell size used for neighbour search is twice the largest particle radius, so a particle moving more than that distance in one step triggers a speed warning.
  6. Use a full, sparse or sparse symmetric storage scheme so that the contact stiffness and damping can be assembled.
  7. See SphericalParticle2D for the derivation of the Hertzian law and for the reference list.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
Text Only
element SphericalParticle3D 1 1 1. 1e3 .2 1e-4 1.

docs.title: Spring01
docs.text:
Spring Using Displacement

  • Number of DoFs: 2
  • DoF Label: U1, U2

docs.title: Background
docs.text:
A zero-length spring connects the translations of two nodes with a force that depends only on their relative displacement, so it introduces no geometric length scale. Let $\(\mathbf c\)$ be the unit direction from node $\(i\)$ to node $\(j\)$, computed once from the initial coordinates. The material is given the scalar relative displacement

\[ \Delta=\mathbf c\cdot(\mathbf u_j-\mathbf u_i), \]

and returns a force $\(N\)$ together with the tangent stiffness $\(k=\mathrm dN/\mathrm d\Delta\)$. The element assembles the rank-one stiffness and the internal force

\[ \mathbf K_e=k\begin{bmatrix}\mathbf c\\-\mathbf c\end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix}\mathbf c&-\mathbf c\end{bmatrix}^{\mathrm T}, \qquad \mathbf R_i=-N\mathbf c,\qquad \mathbf R_j=N\mathbf c . \]

Unlike Spring02, there is no division by the initial node separation, so the input is a displacement and the material must use a displacement--force law such as a linear or hysteretic spring. The direction $\(\mathbf c\)$ is fixed at initialisation and the formulation is infinitesimal. For finite deformation or rigid-body motion, use the truss elements T2D2 and T2D2S, which update the axis and use a proper strain measure.

deviation from theory

A conventional axial spring converts the relative displacement into strain by dividing by the member length. This element passes the raw projected displacement, so the material stiffness has units of force per length.

implementation limitation

The direction cosine is frozen at initialization and no geometric stiffness is formed. Finite rotations and follower-load effects are not captured.

The same projection is used by Damper01, which passes both projected displacement and projected velocity to a viscosity material. When the two nodes coincide, the direction is undefined, and a multi-DoF connection should use Joint instead.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text:
Spring01
element Spring01 (1) (2) (3) (4)
# (1) int, unique tag
# (2) int, node i
# (3) int, node j
# (4) int, material tag

docs.title: Remarks
docs.text:
The Spring01 uses displacement as the input quantity and computes force. It can be used as a zero-length element to connect two nodes.

Note only infinitesimal strain/deformation formulation is supported. If finite deformation, such as rigid body dynamics, is involved, analysts shall use T2D2 and T2D2S elements.

  1. The material stiffness has units of force per length, since the input is a displacement rather than a strain.
  2. The element axis is taken from the initial coordinates and is not updated during the analysis.
  3. The two nodes must not coincide, otherwise the direction cosine cannot be normalised.
  4. See Spring02 for the strain-based variant and Joint for a coincident-node connection with several DoFs.

docs.title: Spring02
docs.text:
Spring Using Strain

  • Number of DoFs: 2
  • DoF Label: U1, U2

docs.title: Background
docs.text:
Spring02 is the strain-based counterpart of Spring01. The initial node separation $\(L=\lVert\mathbf x_j-\mathbf x_i\rVert\)$ is computed at initialisation, and a separation below $\(10^{-10}\)$ is replaced by $\(L=1\)$ to avoid division by zero. With $\(\mathbf d=\mathbf x_j-\mathbf x_i\)$, the scaled direction $\(\mathbf b=\mathbf d/L^2\)$ gives the scalar input

\[ \epsilon=\mathbf b\cdot(\mathbf u_j-\mathbf u_i) =\dfrac{\mathbf d\cdot(\mathbf u_j-\mathbf u_i)}{L^2}=\dfrac{\Delta}{L}, \]

so the material receives the axial strain $\(\epsilon\)$ and returns a stress $\(\sigma\)$ and tangent stiffness $\(k\)$. The assembled stiffness and internal force are

\[ \mathbf K_e=\dfrac{k}{L^2}\mathbf c\,\mathbf c^{\mathrm T}, \qquad \mathbf R_j=\dfrac{\sigma}{L}\mathbf c,\qquad \mathbf R_i=-\mathbf R_j, \]

where $\(\mathbf c=\mathbf d/L\)$ is the initial unit direction. The derivation of the rank-one projection and the remarks on fixed geometry are given on the Spring01 page.

deviation from theory

For coincident or nearly coincident nodes the resulting strain is not physically meaningful.

developer note

An initial length at or below $\(10^{-10}\)$ is replaced by $\(L=1\)$ before the direction vector is scaled.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text:
Spring02
element Spring02 (1) (2) (3) (4)
# (1) int, unique tag
# (2) int, node i
# (3) int, node j
# (4) int, material tag

docs.title: Remarks
docs.text:
The Spring02 uses strain as the input quantity and computes stress.

  1. The material must use a stress--strain law, since the element divides the relative displacement by the initial length.
  2. The initial length and axis are fixed at initialisation and are not updated.
  3. For a law formulated in displacement and force, use Spring01 instead.

Note only infinitesimal strain/deformation formulation is supported. If finite deformation, such as rigid body dynamics, is involved, analysts shall use T2D2 and T2D2S elements.

docs.title: Tie
docs.text:
Multipoint Constraint Implemented As Element

  • Number of Nodes: varies
  • Number of DoFs: varies

docs.title: Background
docs.text:
A Tie element imposes a linear multipoint constraint by the penalty method, without introducing Lagrange multipliers or additional unknowns. For a weighted sum of selected DoFs the constraint is

\[ \sum_a w_a\,u_a=b , \]

where $\(b\)$ is the right-hand side and $\(w_a\)$ is the weight of the $\(a\)$-th DoF. The penalty energy $\(\Pi=\tfrac12\alpha\big(\sum_a w_a u_a-b\big)^2\)$ gives the rank-one element stiffness and residual

\[ \mathbf K_e=\alpha\,\mathbf w\mathbf w^{\mathrm T},\qquad \mathbf R_e=\alpha\,\mathbf w\big(\mathbf w^{\mathrm T}\mathbf u-b\big). \]

As $\(\alpha\to\infty\)$ the constraint is enforced exactly, but a very large penalty makes the global system ill conditioned.

deviation from theory

The penalty form enforces the constraint only approximately. The residual of the weighted sum is generally nonzero and scales as $\(1/\alpha\)$.

The element is purely algebraic, so it does not use nodal coordinates and the tied DoFs need not have the same type or belong to the same dimension. A geometric constraint that attaches a node to a line is provided by TranslationConnector.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text:
Tie
element Tie (1) (2) (3) [(4) (5) (6)...]
# (1) int, unique element tag
# (2) double, right hand side of the constraint equation, the constraint is homogeneous if this parameter is zero
# (3) double, penalty number, a relatively large number
# (4) int, node tag
# (5) int, dof tag
# (6) double, weight

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
Each Tie element can have multiple DoFs included. For example, to define the following constraint,

\[ 5u_2+6v_4=9, \]

where $\(u_2\)$ and $\(v_4\)$ are horizontal displacement of node 2 and vertical displacement of node 4 in a 2D model, then

Text Only
element Tie 1 9. 1E8 2 1 5. 4 2 6.

In the above command, a large number 1E8 is used as a penalty.

The Tie element does not care about the geometric implication. The tied DoFs can be of different types.

To tie a node to a line, consider the TranslationConnector element.

The penalty should be large relative to the stiffness of the connected structure but not so large that the global matrix loses conditioning. Because the tangent is rank one, a Tie element adds only one constrained mode and does not change the rank of the remaining system. Setting the right-hand side to zero gives a homogeneous constraint, which is the usual choice for connecting coincident nodes.

docs.title: TranslationConnector
docs.text: Translation Connector Implemented via Penalty Method

docs.title: TranslationConnector2D
docs.text:
• Number of Nodes: 3
  • Number of DoFs: 2 (Translation: UX, Translation: UY)
TranslationConnector
element TranslationConnector2D (1) (2) (3) (4) (5)
# (1) int, unique element tag
# (2) int, node i
# (3) int, node j
# (4) int, node k
# (5) double, penalty factor

docs.title: TranslationConnector3D
docs.text:
• Number of Nodes: 3
  • Number of DoFs: 3 (Translation: UX, Translation: UY, Translation: UZ)
Text Only
element TranslationConnector3D (1) (2) (3) (4) (5)
# (1) int, unique element tag
# (2) int, node i
# (3) int, node j
# (4) int, node k
# (5) double, penalty factor

docs.title: Theory
docs.text:
The schematic is shown as follows.

The initial position of node $\(k\)$ is not necessarily on the line defined by nodes $\(i\)$ and $\(j\)$.

The TranslationConnector will pull node $\(k\)$ to the (closest point of) line defined by nodes $\(i\)$ and $\(j\)$.

The ratio $\(c\)$ is computed according to the initial positions and remains constant during the analysis.

With the fixed ratio $\(c\)$, the target point on the line is $\((1-c)\mathbf x_i+c\,\mathbf x_j\)$, and the penalty force on node $\(k\)$ is

\[ \mathbf R_k=\alpha\big[(1-c)\mathbf u_i+c\,\mathbf u_j-\mathbf u_k\big]. \]

The reactions on nodes $\(i\)$ and $\(j\)$ are $\(-(1-c)\mathbf R_k\)$ and $\(-c\,\mathbf R_k\)$, so the three nodal forces are self-equilibrated. Writing $\(\mathbf B=[(1-c)\mathbf I,\ c\mathbf I,\ -\mathbf I]\)$, the initial tangent rows for nodes $\(i\)$, $\(j\)$ and $\(k\)$ are $\(-(1-c)\alpha\mathbf B\)$, $\(-c\alpha\mathbf B\)$ and $\(\alpha\mathbf B\)$, respectively. The tangent is assembled once from the initial geometry and has rank equal to the number of translational DoFs.

implementation limitation

The ratio $\(c\)$ is frozen at initialization. A standard node-to-line constraint re-projects the node at every step, whereas this element keeps the initial parametric position even when the line rotates.

docs.title: Remarks
docs.text:
1. The penalty factor [5] is taken as an absolute value, so a negative input produces the same constraint stiffness.
  2. The ratio $\(c\)$ is frozen at the initial configuration, making this a linear constraint that does not follow large rigid rotations of the host line.
  3. Unlike Tie, the constraint is geometric: node $\(k\)$ is attached to the closest point of the line through nodes $\(i\)$ and $\(j\)$, not to an arbitrary algebraic combination of DoFs.
  4. Choose a penalty large relative to the connected stiffness but small enough to preserve conditioning, as discussed on the Tie page.

docs.title: T2D2
docs.text:
2D Linear Truss

  • Number of Nodes: 2
  • Number of DoFs: 2 (Translation, Translation)
  • DoF Label: U1, U2

docs.title: Theory
docs.text: T2D2 is the canonical page of the truss family; see T3D2 for the three-dimensional element and T2D2S for the section-based variant. A truss element is a two-node bar that transmits only axial force, so its response is derived from a single uniaxial material law.

docs.title: Geometry and strain
docs.text: Let the initial nodal coordinates be $\((x_1,y_1)\)$ and $\((x_2,y_2)\)$, and define $\(L_0=\sqrt{(x_2-x_1)^2+(y_2-y_1)^2}\)$ and the direction cosines $\(c=(x_2-x_1)/L_0\)$, $\(s=(y_2-y_1)/L_0\)$. With the nodal displacement vector $\(\mathbf v=[\Delta x_1,\Delta y_1,\Delta x_2,\Delta y_2]^\mathrm T\)$, the current length is $\(L=\sqrt{(x_2-x_1+\Delta x_2-\Delta x_1)^2+(y_2-y_1+\Delta y_2-\Delta y_1)^2}\)$ and the axial deformation is $\(u=L-L_0\)$. For linear geometry $\(u=\mathbf n^\mathrm T\mathbf v\)$ with $\(\mathbf n=[-c,-s,c,s]^\mathrm T\)$, so the engineering strain is $\(\varepsilon=u/L_0=\mathbf n^\mathrm T\mathbf v/L_0\)$ and the derivatives of $\(u\)$ are constant. With the corotational formulation the direction cosines are updated from the current chord and $$ \frac{\partial u}{\partial\mathbf v}=\mathbf n,\qquad \frac{\partial^2u}{\partial\mathbf v^2}=\frac{1}{L}\begin{bmatrix} s2&-cs&-s2&cs\ -cs&c2&cs&-c2\ -s2&cs&s2&-cs\ cs&-c2&-cs&c2 \end{bmatrix}. $$

docs.title: Resistance and stiffness
docs.text: The strain energy of the bar is $\(U=\int A(u)\sigma(u)\,\mathrm du\)$, where $\(A\)$ is the current area and $\(\sigma\)$ is the uniaxial stress returned by the material. The global resistance and tangent follow by differentiation, $$ \mathbf f=\frac{\mathrm dU}{\mathrm d\mathbf v}=A\sigma\,\frac{\partial u}{\partial\mathbf v},\qquad \mathbf K=\frac{\mathrm d\mathbf f}{\mathrm d\mathbf v} =\left(\frac{\mathrm dA}{\mathrm du}\sigma+A\frac{\mathrm d\sigma}{\mathrm du}\right)\mathbf n\mathbf n^\mathrm T +A\sigma\frac{\partial^2u}{\partial\mathbf v^\mathrm T\partial\mathbf v}. $$ For linear geometry with constant area and engineering strain, $\(\mathrm d\sigma/\mathrm du=E/L_0\)$ and the familiar axial stiffness $\(k=EA/L_0\)$ is recovered. The tangent reduces to $\(\mathbf K=k\,\mathbf n\mathbf n^\mathrm T\)$. When the constant-volume switch is active the area is updated as $\(A=A_0L_0/L\)$, so $\(\mathrm dA/\mathrm du=-A_0L_0/L^2\)$. With the logarithmic strain $\(\varepsilon_l=\ln(L/L_0)=\ln(1+u/L_0)\)$ one has $\(\mathrm d\varepsilon_l/\mathrm du=1/L\)$, and the tangent becomes $$ \mathbf K=\underbrace{\frac{A_0L_0}{L^2}\big(E-\sigma\big)\mathbf n\mathbf n^\mathrm T}{\mathbf K_l} +\underbrace{\frac{A_0L_0}{L}\,\sigma\,\frac{\partial^2u}{\partial\mathbf v^\mathrm T\partial\mathbf v}}{\mathbf K_g}, $$ where $\(\mathbf K_g\)$ is the geometric stiffness and becomes negative in compression. In the implementation the nonlinear geometry switch selects the corotational transformation T2DC, which also assembles $\(\mathbf K_g\)$ from the current axial force.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text:
T2D2
element T2D2 (1) (2) (3) (4) (5) [6] [7] [8] [9]
# (1) int, unique element tag
# (2) int, node i
# (3) int, node j
# (4) int, material tag
# (5) double, cross sectional area
# [6] bool string, nonlinear geometry switch, default: false
# [7] bool string, whether to update sectional area, default: false
# [8] bool string, whether to use log strain, default: false
# [9] double, flexural rigidity, positive to activate Euler buckling limit, default: -1.0

docs.title: Remarks
docs.text:
1. The corotational formulation is implemented, turn on the nonlinear geometry switch to use it.
  2. According to different implementation details, either a constant area or a constant volume assumption is adopted. If the volume is constant, the cross-sectional area would be updated based on $\(A=\dfrac{A_0L_0}{L}\)$.
  3. The computation of strain can be altered from engineering strain (by default) to log strain.
  4. By turning on all three switches, full nonlinearity can be achieved.
  5. The axial force and the material stress are positive in tension and negative in compression, which is the sign convention used by the Euler buckling check below.
  6. The area switch implements a constant-volume assumption corresponding to Poisson's ratio $\(0.5\)$, while the default keeps the area fixed at $\(A_0\)$.
  7. With the log strain option the material strain is $\(\varepsilon_l=\ln(L/L_0)\)$ instead of the engineering strain $\(\varepsilon=u/L_0\)$, which is preferable at large stretches.
  8. The attached material must be a uniaxial Material1D model, and the element initial stiffness is $\(A_0E_0/L_0\)$.
  9. The Euler buckling check of the next section is only available for T2D2; T3D2 has no rigidity argument.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
A nonlinear bar of initial length $\(4\)$ with logarithmic strain, updated area and corotational kinematics is defined by

Text Only
node 1 0 0
node 2 4 0
material MPF 1 100 300 .4
element T2D2 1 1 2 1 100 1 1 1

docs.title: Euler Buckling Limit
docs.text:
[added in version 2.8]

The parameter [9] allows one to define a positive flexural rigidity $\(EI\)$ that will be used to compute the Euler buckling load. When [9] is negative, the check is disabled.

The truss element matches a pinned-pinned condition, for which the Euler buckling load is given by

\[ P_{cr}=\dfrac{\pi^2EI}{L^2} \]

where $\(L\)$ is the length of the truss element.

For a given positive $\(EI\)$, $\(P_{cr}\)$ can be computed using only $\(L\)$, regardless of the used material model. The computed axial resistance will be compared to $\(P_{cr}\)$ and an error will be issued if the axial resistance (in compression) exceeds $\(P_{cr}\)$.

implementation limitation

The critical load is evaluated once at initialisation from the initial element length and is not updated when corotational kinematics change the member length. Exceeding the limit issues an error instead of representing the post-buckling response.

developer note

Exceeding the limit also returns a failure flag.

This is a theoretical upper bound, the design value requires an additional reduction.

docs.title: T2D2S
docs.text:
2D Linear Truss Using Section

  • Number of Nodes: 2
  • Number of DoFs: 2 (Translation, Translation)
  • DoF Label: U1, U2

docs.title: Background
docs.text:
The suffix S stands for Section: the implementation derives from SectionElement1D and takes a section tag, whereas the canonical T2D2 derives from MaterialElement1D and takes a material tag together with a cross-sectional area. The kinematics, the corotational transformation T2DC and the strain measures are identical to those derived on the T2D2 page.

The attached section supplies the axial rigidity, so the initial element stiffness is $\(\mathbf K_0=\mathbf k_{s,0}/L_0\)$. In the corotational case the section is driven by the chosen strain measure, $\(\varepsilon=\ln(L/L_0)\)$ for log strain or $\(\varepsilon=L/L_0-1\)$ for engineering strain, and the tangent is $\(\mathbf K=\mathbf k_s/\varepsilon_\mathrm{den}\)$ with $\(\varepsilon_\mathrm{den}=L\)$ or $\(L_0\)$. The geometric stiffness is assembled from the section resistance as $\(\mathbf K_g=\mathbf T^\mathrm T(N/L)\,\partial^2u/\partial\mathbf v^\mathrm T\partial\mathbf v\,\mathbf T\)$. Because the section owns the area, this element has no area-update switch and no Euler buckling check.

implementation limitation

The parser exposes only the corotational and log-strain switches for this variant, so a constant-volume area update and the Euler buckling check of T2D2 are unavailable.

Suitable one-dimensional sections include Rectangle1D, Circle1D, TrussSection and Fibre1D.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text:
T2D2S
element T2D2S (1) (2) (3) (4) [5] [6]
# (1) int, unique element tag
# (2) int, node i
# (3) int, node j
# (4) int, section tag
# [5] bool string, nonlinear geometry switch, default: false
# [6] bool string, whether to use log strain, default: false

docs.title: Remarks
docs.text:
1. Compared to T2D2, T2D2S uses section instead of material. Hence, sectional area is handled by the corresponding section model.
  2. The nonlinearity cannot propagate into the section level. So it is not possible to update area in T2D2S.
  3. The S suffix denotes the section-based formulation, not a simplified or small-displacement variant.
  4. Use T2D2 when a constant-volume area update or the Euler buckling check is required.
  5. The section must be one-dimensional, and its initial stiffness must represent the axial rigidity $\(EA\)$.

docs.title: T3D2
docs.text:
3D Linear Truss

  • Number of Nodes: 2
  • Number of DoFs: 3 (Translation, Translation, Translation)
  • DoF Label: U1, U2, U3

docs.title: Background
docs.text:
T3D2 is the three-dimensional member of the truss family and follows the derivation given on the canonical T2D2 page. The element connects two nodes in space and carries only the axial force computed from one uniaxial material law.

With initial length $\(L_0\)$ and unit direction vector $\(\mathbf e=[c_x,c_y,c_z]^\mathrm T\)$ along the chord, the axial deformation is $\(u=L-L_0\)$. Under linear geometry the engineering strain is $\(\varepsilon=u/L_0=\mathbf n^\mathrm T\mathbf v/L_0\)$ with $\(\mathbf n=[-c_x,-c_y,-c_z,c_x,c_y,c_z]^\mathrm T\)$. In the corotational formulation $\(\mathbf e\)$ is updated from the current chord and the second derivative of the deformation is $$ \frac{\partial^2u}{\partial\mathbf v^\mathrm T\partial\mathbf v}=\frac{1}{L}\left(\mathbf M-\mathbf n\mathbf n^\mathrm T\right),\qquad \mathbf M=\begin{bmatrix}\mathbf I_3&-\mathbf I_3\-\mathbf I_3&\mathbf I_3\end{bmatrix}. $$ The global resistance and tangent are $\(\mathbf f=A\sigma\,\mathbf n\)$ and $$ \mathbf K=\left(\frac{\mathrm dA}{\mathrm du}\sigma+A\frac{\mathrm d\sigma}{\mathrm du}\right)\mathbf n\mathbf n^\mathrm T+A\sigma\frac{\partial^2u}{\partial\mathbf v^\mathrm T\partial\mathbf v}. $$ The switches [6] to [8] have the same meaning as in T2D2: corotational kinematics, constant-volume area update and logarithmic strain. Unlike T2D2, this element has no flexural rigidity argument and performs no Euler buckling check.

implementation limitation

A compressive member can pass through its Euler critical load without any warning, so buckling must be assessed separately.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text:
T3D2
element T3D2 (1) (2) (3) (4) (5) [6] [7] [8]
# (1) int, unique element tag
# (2) int, node i
# (3) int, node j
# (4) int, material tag
# (5) double, cross sectional area
# [6] bool string, nonlinear geometry switch, default: false
# [7] bool string, whether to update sectional area, default: false
# [8] bool string, whether to use log strain, default: false

docs.title: Remarks
docs.text:
1. The corotational formulation is implemented, turn on the nonlinear geometry switch to use it.
  2. According to different implementation details, either a constant area or a constant volume assumption is adopted. If the volume is constant, the cross-sectional area would be updated based on $\(A=\dfrac{A_0L_0}{L}\)$.
  3. The computation of strain can be altered from engineering strain (by default) to log strain.
  4. By turning on all three switches, full nonlinearity can be achieved.
  5. Tension is positive and compression negative, so the geometric stiffness contributed by the axial force is negative in compression.
  6. The corotational transformation T3DC updates the three direction cosines from the displaced chord, whereas T3DL keeps the initial direction.
  7. The final section-based variant T3D2S delegates the axial stiffness to a section and cannot update the area.

docs.title: T3D2S
docs.text:
3D Linear Truss Using Section

  • Number of Nodes: 2
  • Number of DoFs: 3 (Translation, Translation, Translation)
  • DoF Label: U1, U2, U3

docs.title: Background
docs.text:
The suffix S stands for Section: the implementation derives from SectionElement1D and takes a section tag, while the canonical T3D2 derives from MaterialElement1D and takes a material tag plus a cross-sectional area. The spatial kinematics and the corotational transformation T3DC are the same as those derived on the T2D2 page.

The attached section carries the axial rigidity, so the initial stiffness is $\(\mathbf K_0=\mathbf k_{s,0}/L_0\)$. Under corotational kinematics the section strain is $\(\varepsilon=\ln(L/L_0)\)$ with log strain or $\(\varepsilon=L/L_0-1\)$ with engineering strain, and the tangent is formed by dividing the section stiffness by $\(L\)$ or $\(L_0\)$ respectively. The geometric stiffness is $\(\mathbf K_g=\mathbf T^\mathrm T(N/L)\,\partial^2u/\partial\mathbf v^\mathrm T\partial\mathbf v\,\mathbf T\)$, with $\(N\)$ the section resistance. No area update and no Euler buckling check are available, so T3D2 is the choice when constant-volume area changes matter.

implementation limitation

The parser exposes only the corotational and log-strain switches for this variant, so element-level nonlinearity cannot change the area owned by the section.

Suitable one-dimensional sections include Rectangle1D, Circle1D, TrussSection and Fibre1D.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text:
T3D2S
element T3D2S (1) (2) (3) (4) [5] [6]
# (1) int, unique element tag
# (2) int, node i
# (3) int, node j
# (4) int, section tag
# [5] bool string, nonlinear geometry switch, default: false
# [6] bool string, whether to use log strain, default: false

docs.title: Remarks
docs.text:
1. Compared to T3D2, T3D2S uses section instead of material. Hence, sectional area is handled by the corresponding section model.
  2. The nonlinearity cannot propagate into the section level. So it is not possible to update area in T3D2S.
  3. The S suffix denotes the section-based formulation, not a simplified or small-displacement variant.
  4. Use T3D2 when a constant-volume area update is required.
  5. The section must be one-dimensional, and its initial stiffness must represent the axial rigidity $\(EA\)$.

docs.title: CustomNodeGroup
docs.text: Select and collect nodes into a group based on a custom criterion.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text:
CustomNodeGroup
CustomNodeGroup (1) (2)
# (1) int, unique group tag
# (2) int, expression tag

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
The CustomNodeGroup uses an expression to determine whether a given node shall be included in the group.

It uses the coordinates of the target node (with size adjusted) as the input, and the expression shall return a positive value if the node shall be included in the group. Otherwise, it shall return a negative value.

The following example selects all nodes with x coordinate greater than 0.5.

Text Only
expression SimpleScalar 1 x if(x>0.5)1;else-1;
customnodegroup 1 1

The following example selects all nodes with x coordinate greater than 0.5 and y coordinate less than 0.5.

Text Only
expression SimpleScalar 1 x|y if(x>0.5&y<0.5)1;else-1;
customnodegroup 1 1

Of course, the expression can be more complicated when the expression text is given in a file.

docs.title: ElementGroup
docs.text: An ElementGroup collects element tags under a single group tag so that loads and recorders can target many elements at once. It is analogous to an element "set" in ABAQUS.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text:
ElementGroup
group ElementGroup (1) (2...)
# (1) int, unique group tag
# (2...) int, tags of elements to be included

docs.title: Remarks
docs.text:
1. If no element tags are listed, the group is filled with all elements in the domain when it is initialised.
  2. Element tags can also be generated by generate instead of being enumerated.
  3. An ElementGroup can be referenced by groupbodyforce and GroupElement recorders.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
The following snippet selects all elements and applies a gravity body force, as in the slope analysis example.

Text Only
generate elementgroup 1 1 2880

load groupbodyforce 1 0 -20 2 1

recorder 2 hdf5 GroupElement S 1

docs.title: GroupGroup
docs.text: A GroupGroup combines several existing groups into a single group. It is the nested counterpart of NodeGroup and ElementGroup.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text:
GroupGroup
group GroupGroup (1) (2...)
# (1) int, unique group tag
# (2...) int, tags of groups to be included

docs.title: Remarks
docs.text:
1. Each referenced group is initialised first, so groups that define their members by rules are resolved before they are combined.
  2. The members of all referenced groups are merged into the new pool with duplicates removed.
  3. Groups can be nested, since a GroupGroup may itself reference another GroupGroup.
  4. Referenced group tags that are not present in the domain are simply skipped.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
The following snippet combines two node groups into one group containing nodes 1 through 6.

Text Only
group NodeGroup 1 1 2 3
group NodeGroup 2 4 5 6

group GroupGroup 3 1 2

docs.title: NodeGroup
docs.text: A NodeGroup collects node tags under a single group tag so that loads, constraints and recorders can target many nodes at once. It is analogous to a node "set" in ABAQUS.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text:
NodeGroup
group NodeGroup (1) (2...)
# (1) int, unique group tag
# (2...) int, tags of nodes to be included

docs.title: Remarks
docs.text:
1. The group NodeGroup form stores the listed node tags directly as the group pool.
  2. Nodes can also be selected by rules rather than enumerated by tag via generate, generatebyrule, generatebypoint and generatebyplane.
  3. A NodeGroup can be referenced by group-aware loads such as groupcload, constraints such as grouppenaltybc and GroupNode recorders.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
The following snippet, adapted from Example/Solver/Ramm2.supan, constrains one node and applies a load to the group.

Text Only
node 11 2 8
node 12 3 8

group NodeGroup 1 11 12

fix 1 1 1 11

groupcload 1 0 -20 2 1

recorder 1 hdf5 GroupNode U 1

docs.title: Linear
docs.text:
A Linear integrator basically does nothing and is used as the default integrator in static analysis.

If no integrator is defined in a step, a linear one will automatically be created and used.

docs.title: Background
docs.text: Linear is the plain Integrator base class rather than a separately registered dynamic integrator. It adds no damping or inertia to the equation of motion, so the resistance is simply the stiffness times the displacement. A Static step always uses this integrator.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: The Integrator acts as middleware between Solver and Domain. It is mainly responsible for time integration in which the proper equation of motion can be formulated. The Integrator provides an additional layer and handles the communication between the Solver and the Domain. It can also be deemed as a broker between the two components. A number of different operations, like formulating the global damping model, can be implemented via an Integrator. Several integrators are available in the framework.

docs.title: Implicit Methods
docs.text:
Implicit methods utilize displacement as the primary unknown variable. Consequently, the equation of motion is typically formulated in the following manner:

\[ \bar{\mathbf{K}}\delta\mathbf{u}=\mathbf{R} \]

Within this formulation, $\(\bar{\mathbf{K}}\)$ represents the effective stiffness matrix.

docs.title: Newmark
docs.text:
Choosing the right Integrator depends on your specific application. The Newmark integrator is the most widely used method. It is the de-facto standard in structural dynamics and requires no justification for its selection.

However, the Newmark method is not always the best choice. Second-order accuracy and algorithmic damping cannot coexist in this method. It is sensitive to initial conditions and drops to first-order accuracy if wrong ones are assigned. You may still use it if there are no special needs and the target system is well-behaving.

docs.title: Bathe Two-Step
docs.text: The BatheTwoStep integrator provides a very cost-efficient solution if energy and momentum conservation matter. Its computational performance is highly comparable to the Newmark integrator. It features the same second-order accuracy along with controllable algorithmic damping. It functions as a two-step method that alternates between a trapezoidal step and a backward Euler step.

docs.title: Generalized-$\(\alpha\)$
docs.text: The GeneralizedAlpha integrator can be used to customize algorithmic damping in a single-step method. Several other methods can be recovered by adjusting its two parameters. It requires roughly twice as many vector operations as the Newmark integrator because the equation of motion is satisfied within the time step. This is not considered a severe performance issue since vector operations are inexpensive and implemented in parallel.

docs.title: GSSSS
docs.text:
The most general option available is the GSSSS integrator. Optimal performance regarding overshoot, energy dissipation, and dispersion is achieved using the U0-V0 Optimal scheme.

The GSSSS integrator requires an additional iteration to synchronize the state of the system. Consequently, its computational cost is slightly higher than that of the GeneralizedAlpha integrator.

docs.title: Others
docs.text:
There are other methods implemented as well.

Most of them are Newmark variants that introduce different damping models.

  • UDDNewmark, documented on the UDNewmark page, applies a uniform damping kernel to the restoring and inertial forces through convolution.
  • UDANewmark applies the same universal damping kernel to the inertial force only.
  • LeeNewmark, LeeNewmarkIterative, LeeElementalNewmark and LeeNewmarkFull implement the Lee damping model with different mode sets and stiffness treatments.
  • NonviscousNewmark uses a nonviscous damping model that convolutes the velocity vector.
  • RayleighNewmark applies Rayleigh damping at the global level.
  • WilsonPenzienNewmark incorporates the Wilson-Penzien damping model.
  • OALTS is an optimal A-stable linear two-step method.

docs.title: Explicit Methods
docs.text:
Explicit methods utilize acceleration as the primary unknown variable rather than displacement. Consequently, the equation of motion is typically formulated in the following manner:

\[ \bar{\mathbf{M}}\delta\mathbf{a}=\mathbf{R} \]

Within this formulation, $\(\bar{\mathbf{M}}\)$ represents the effective mass matrix. The explicit nature of these methods stems from the fact that this matrix fundamentally excludes the future stiffness matrix $\(\mathbf{K}_{n+1}\)$.

docs.title: Central Difference (Not Available)
docs.text:
The explicit central difference method is frequently introduced in dynamics textbooks due to its simplicity. The major benefit is that the stiffness matrix does not enter the left-hand side of the equation of motion. This means factorization of the global effective matrix would only be done once under certain conditions. This characteristic leads to very efficient solutions.

However, it is generally difficult to meet those specific conditions. It is not implemented in this framework, and users are discouraged from using central difference in seismic engineering.

docs.title: Tchamwa
docs.text: The Tchamwa integrator is a generalization of the central difference method. It provides a first-order accurate solution featuring controllable numerical dissipation.

docs.title: Explicit Bathe Two-Step
docs.text: The explicit version of the Bathe two-step integrator is available. It is a second-order accurate method that includes controllable numerical dissipation.

docs.title: Explicit Generalized-$\(\alpha\)$
docs.text: The explicit version of the generalized-$\(\alpha\)$ integrator is also available.

docs.title: Others
docs.text:
There are other methods as well.

These are formulated in terms of acceleration and keep the stiffness matrix out of the effective matrix.

  • GSSE is a general explicit integration algorithm.
  • ICL is an improved Chung and Lee method.
  • WAT2 is the second scheme of Wang, Adams and Tamma in a generalized explicit Runge-Kutta-Nyström framework.
  • GeneralizedAlphaExplicit is the explicit counterpart of the generalized-$\(\alpha\)$ method.

docs.title: Does Order of Accuracy Matter?
docs.text:
The answer to this question is complicated.

The order of accuracy is directly reflected in the numerical results for linear problems. Choosing a method with a higher order of accuracy has a direct impact if precision matters. In this specific case, the order of accuracy indeed matters.

It probably does not matter for nonlinear problems where nonlinear material models are involved. The local integration is often done using the implicit Euler method in most implementations of nonlinear material models. The implicit Euler method is only a first-order accurate method. This local integration makes the material model the bottleneck for overall accuracy.

The results would likely not be more accurate than a first-order method even if a higher-order integrator is used. Algorithmic damping and numerical performance are more important as a general rule for nonlinear problems. It is worth considering a higher-order accurate integrator if the material model implementation is known to be second-order accurate. Using a first-order accurate integrator is completely sufficient otherwise.

docs.title: BatheExplicit
docs.text:
Second order explicit time integration method using Noh-Bathe two-step scheme.

The Noh-Bathe scheme has a better energy dispersion behaviour.

References:

  1. 10.1016/j.compstruc.2013.06.007

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text:
BatheExplicit
integrator BatheExplicit (1) [2]
# (1) int, unique integrator tag
# [2] double, spectral radius, \rho_\infty, default: 0.5

docs.title: Remarks
docs.text:
If the model is linear elastic, it is possible to indicate using

Text Only
set linear_system true

to speed up the computation.
