docs.text:
• ISBN 978-1-85617-633-0
  • ISBN 978-1-4398-0247-2
  • Axisymmetric elements

docs.title: Laminated
docs.text:
Parallel Wrapper For 2D Material Models

Combines multiple 2D material models into a single one.

docs.title: Theory
docs.text:
A laminate is an assembly of layers bonded together so that all layers share the same in-plane deformation. For a two-dimensional strain vector $\(\mathbf e=(\varepsilon_{11},\varepsilon_{22},\gamma_{12})\)$, the iso-strain assumption gives $\(\mathbf e^{(k)}=\mathbf e\)$ for every layer $\(k\)$, and the resultant stress and tangent are obtained by summation,

\[ \mathbf s(\mathbf e)=\sum_{k=1}^{n}\mathbf s^{(k)}(\mathbf e), \qquad \mathbf D(\mathbf e)=\sum_{k=1}^{n}\mathbf D^{(k)}(\mathbf e). \]

If the layers have thicknesses $\(t_k\)$, a physical laminate stress resultant is $\(\mathbf N=\sum_k t_k\mathbf s^{(k)}\)$, so the thickness weighting must be absorbed into the parameters or the section assigned to the element, since the wrapper performs an unweighted sum. Classical lamination theory instead builds extensional, coupling and bending matrices from the through-thickness distribution of $\(\mathbf D^{(k)}\)$; this wrapper does not compute those matrices and is intended for membrane-like layers sharing a strain.

deviation from theory

The wrapper adds layer stresses and tangents with unit weight, so the result is a membrane stress per unit thickness rather than the thickness-weighted resultant $\(\mathbf N=\sum_k t_k\mathbf s^{(k)}\)$ of a physical laminate. Any thickness or volume weighting must be absorbed into the layer parameters or the section assigned to the element. No $\(A\)$, $\(B\)$ or $\(D\)$ matrix is formed, so the wrapper cannot represent the bending stiffness of a stacked laminate.

The implementation copies each listed 2D material, evaluates all copies with the identical trial strain, and accumulates their stresses and tangents. Densities are summed during initialization, and recorded histories are concatenated in tag order.

This wrapper is the two-dimensional analogue of Parallel for 1D models and of Stacked for 3D models. Use Rotation2D around a layer whose material axes are not aligned with the global axes, so that differently oriented plies can be combined.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text:
Laminated
material Laminated (1) (2...)
# (1) int, unique material tag
# (2...) int, material tags of 2D models need to be contained

The response of attached 2D material models will be output when recorded. The output has a uniform size and data is arranged in the order as defined.

docs.title: Remarks
docs.text: Every listed tag must refer to a registered 2D material, and the wrapper declares the plane type S, so pair it with plane-stress membrane elements. A host based on PlaneStress already reduces a 3D law to plane stress and can be listed directly. The wrapper has no local iteration or equilibrium solve, because all layers share the same strain by construction; use Sequential for the complementary iso-stress idea in one dimension. Recorded quantities come from the individual layers in tag order, which makes it straightforward to inspect ply-by-ply damage or plasticity.

docs.title: OS146
docs.text:
Open Section Wrapper

Wraps a 3D host material model into a 2D plane model that can be used with open sections.

docs.title: Theory
docs.text:
An open-section material retains only the axial and two transverse shear stress components of a three-dimensional state.

In a thin-walled open section the wall is free on its faces, so the stress components normal to the wall and the shear transmitted across the wall thickness are negligible compared with the axial stress $\(\sigma_{11}\)$ and the two membrane shear stresses $\(\tau_{12}\)$ and $\(\tau_{13}\)$. The wrapper therefore retains the three-component work-conjugate pairs $\((\sigma_{11},\varepsilon_{11})\)$, $\((\tau_{12},\gamma_{12})\)$ and $\((\tau_{13},\gamma_{13})\)$. The indices $\(1\)$, $\(4\)$ and $\(6\)$ in the name refer to the one-based 3D Voigt ordering $\((\sigma_{11},\sigma_{22},\sigma_{33},\tau_{12},\tau_{23},\tau_{13})\)$.

This class derives from the same StressWrapper as PlaneStress and Uniaxial, with active set F1={0,3,5} and constrained set F2={1,2,4}. The constrained stresses $\(\sigma_{22}\)$, $\(\sigma_{33}\)$ and $\(\tau_{23}\)$ are driven to zero by correcting the corresponding strain components with the host tangent block $\(\mathbf D_{OO}\)$. The returned $\(3\times3\)$ stiffness is the static condensation of the host $\(6\times6\)$ tangent, so a consistent host tangent yields a consistent open-section tangent. With the default maximum iteration of one the correction is applied in a single Newton update, while larger values of [3] repeat the evaluation until the constrained stresses are small.

implementation limitation

With the default [3]=1 the constrained stresses $\(\sigma_{22}\)$, $\(\sigma_{33}\)$ and $\(\tau_{23}\)$ are generally not driven exactly to zero.

developer note

The strain correction is computed from the host stress and tangent of the previous step and applied only once. With [3]>1 the loop tests a tolerance relative to the first correction and performs at most [3]-1 host updates, because the counter is increased and tested before each evaluation.

The companion OS146S builds the same three-component response from a 1D axial host and an explicitly prescribed linear shear modulus instead of condensing a 3D host.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text:
OS146
material OS146 (1) (2) [3]
# (1) int, unique tag
# (2) int, 3D material tag
# [3] int, maximum iterations allowed per step, default: 1

The response of attached 3D material model will be output when recorded.

The name OS146 suggests that the first (1) $\(\sigma_{11}\)$, the fourth (4) $\(\tau_{12}\)$ and the sixth (6) $\(\tau_{13}\)$ components are active. All other components are assumed to be zero.

docs.title: Remarks
docs.text: The host must be a registered 3D material, and the wrapper inherits its density. Pair the wrapper with open-section beam elements such as B31OS together with open-section cell or fibre sections and an B3DOSL orientation; the supplied example uses this combination. The wrapper reports a three-component stress and stiffness to the element, where the last two entries are shear resultants rather than in-plane membrane forces. Recorded quantities are forwarded to the host, so the full 3D stress state of the wall is available even though the element only uses three components. An inaccurate host tangent in the constrained block can make the single-update mode leave a residual transverse stress, in which case a smaller step or additional local iterations are needed. For a closed or thick section use a full 3D material instead of this reduction.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
Text Only
node 1 0 0 0
node 2 1 0 0

material Elastic3D 1 100 .2
material OS146 2 1

section Cell3DOS 1 10. 1. 1. 1. 2 10. 10.
section Cell3DOS 2 10. -1. 1. 1. 2 -10. -10.
section Cell3DOS 4 10. -1. 1. 1. 2 -10. 10.
section Fibre3DOS 3 1 2 4

orientation B3DOSL 1 0. 0. 1.

element B31OS 1 1 2 3 1 6

docs.title: OS146S
docs.text:
Open Section Wrapper

Wraps a 1D host material model into a 2D plane model that can be used with open sections.

docs.title: Theory
docs.text:
This reduced open-section wrapper keeps only the axial and two transverse shear stress components of a three-dimensional state. It builds the three-component open-section response without a three-dimensional constitutive law. The axial strain $\(\varepsilon_{11}\)$ is passed unchanged to a one-dimensional host, which returns the axial stress $\(\sigma_{11}\)$ and the axial tangent $\(k=\mathrm d\sigma_{11}/\mathrm d\varepsilon_{11}\)$. The two shear responses are independent and linear elastic,

\[ \tau_{12}=G\,\gamma_{12}, \qquad \tau_{13}=G\,\gamma_{13}, \qquad \mathbf D^{\mathrm{OS}}= \begin{bmatrix} k&0&0\\ 0&G&0\\ 0&0&G \end{bmatrix}, \]

where $\(G\)$ is the shear modulus supplied as the third argument. The diagonal stiffness means that axial yielding or damage in the host does not degrade the shear response, which is a deliberate simplification of the reduced open-section model. Like OS146, the class reports a three-component stress to open-section beam elements while recording the host response.

deviation from three-dimensional theory

A fully three-dimensional constitutive law generally couples the axial and shear responses through the off-diagonal terms of the tangent matrix. The OS146S implementation sets those coupling terms to zero and keeps the shear stiffness constant at $\(G\)$, so axial yielding or damage cannot soften the shear response. Use OS146 with a three-dimensional host when that coupling matters.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text:
OS146S
material OS146S (1) (2) (3)
# (1) int, unique tag
# (2) int, 3D material tag
# (3) double, shear modulus

The response of attached 1D material model will be output when recorded.

The name OS146S suggests that the first (1) $\(\sigma_{11}\)$, the fourth (4) $\(\tau_{12}\)$ and the sixth (6) $\(\tau_{13}\)$ components are active. All other components are assumed to be zero.

The shear response is always linear elastic with the shear modulus specified in the third argument.

The normal strain is sent to the 1D material model as the axial strain.

docs.title: Remarks
docs.text:
argument label in the syntax block

The comment for argument (2) in the syntax block calls it a 3D material tag, but a three-dimensional host is rejected. Supply a one-dimensional material model as the host.

developer note

OS146S::initialize rejects any host whose material type is not D1.

Use a 1D host such as Elastic1D or a 1D hysteretic model, and use OS146 when a full 3D host is available and transverse normal stresses must be condensed. The shear modulus has units of stress and must be positive; it controls only the two shear entries and has no effect on axial yielding. The wrapper inherits the density of the host and provides no strain-rate overload, so rate-dependent axial hosts should be used with care. Use it with open-section beam elements and section definitions as shown in OS146.

docs.title: Parallel
docs.text:
Container of Material Models In Parallel

Combines multiple 1D material models into a single one.

docs.title: Theory
docs.text:
A parallel rheological arrangement connects several constitutive elements between the same pair of nodes, so every element undergoes the same deformation. Compatibility therefore gives $\(\varepsilon^{(k)}=\varepsilon\)$ for every constituent $\(k\)$, while equilibrium of the nodal forces requires the stresses to add,

\[ \sigma(\varepsilon)=\sum_{k=1}^{n}\sigma^{(k)}(\varepsilon), \qquad D(\varepsilon)=\dfrac{\partial\sigma}{\partial\varepsilon}=\sum_{k=1}^{n}D^{(k)}(\varepsilon), \]

where $\(D^{(k)}=\partial\sigma^{(k)}/\partial\varepsilon^{(k)}\)$ is the tangent of constituent $\(k\)$. For a unit-volume representative element with volume fractions $\(f_k\)$ the same relations read $\(\sigma=\sum_k f_k\sigma^{(k)}\)$ and $\(D=\sum_k f_k D^{(k)}\)$, so the parallel arrangement is the iso-strain or Voigt assumption and gives an upper bound on the effective stiffness. For linear springs this reduces to $\(E_{\mathrm{eq}}=\sum_k f_k E_k\)$, and the free energies of the constituents add.

The implementation stores a copy of every listed 1D material and drives all copies with the identical trial strain. It accumulates the trial stress, the trial tangent and, when present, the trial damping from every constituent. The density and the initial tangent are summed in the same way during initialization. Recorded histories are concatenated in the order in which the tags were supplied, so a recorder sees one column block per constituent.

This wrapper is the 1D counterpart of Laminated for 2D materials and Stacked for 3D materials, all of which impose an iso-strain condition. The complementary iso-stress arrangement is Sequential. The wrapper carries no volume or area fraction of its own, so any weighting must be absorbed into the parameters of the constituent materials or into the section assigned to the element.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text:
Parallel
material Parallel (1) (2...)
# (1) int, unique material tag
# (2...) int, material tags of 1D models need to be contained

docs.title: Caveat
docs.text: Please do not include any viscosity-related models into the wrapper. This container is only designed for rate-independent hysteretic models. The response of attached 1D material models will be output when recorded. The output has a uniform size and data is arranged in the order as defined.

docs.title: Remarks
docs.text:
All listed tags must refer to initialized 1D materials; the wrapper reports an error otherwise. Because every constituent sees the full strain, a soft constituent cannot unload simply because a stiff one carries more force; that behaviour belongs to the series arrangement in Sequential. The current source also provides a strain-rate overload that forwards the rate to each host and sums the damping matrices, so rate-dependent hosts are handled consistently when they expose a damping tangent. The Caveat above remains the conservative guidance for rate-independent hysteretic hosts, whose damping matrices are normally empty.

caveat versus implemented behaviour

The original Caveat states that viscosity-related models must not be placed in this wrapper. Rate-dependent hosts are supported when they expose a damping tangent. Treat the caveat as conservative guidance for hysteretic rate-independent models rather than as a hard restriction of the code.

developer note

The current Parallel implementation forwards the strain rate to every host and sums the damping matrices.

The wrapper is natural for truss elements such as T2D2, where the section area supplies the missing force weighting.

docs.title: PlaneStrain
docs.text:
Plane Strain Wrapper

Wraps a 3D host material model into a 2D plane strain model that can be used with 2D membrane elements.

docs.title: Theory
docs.text:
suanPan orders the six 3D Voigt strain entries as $\((\varepsilon_{11},\varepsilon_{22},\varepsilon_{33},\gamma_{12},\gamma_{23},\gamma_{13})\)$, with engineering shears $\(\gamma_{ij}=2\varepsilon_{ij}\)$. A plane strain state describes a body whose dimension in the $\(x_3\)$ direction is large or fully constrained, so that out-of-plane deformation is suppressed. The kinematic conditions are

\[ \varepsilon_{33}=0,\qquad\gamma_{23}=0,\qquad\gamma_{13}=0, \]

while the stress components $\(\sigma_{33}\)$, $\( au_{23}\)$ and $\( au_{13}\)$ are generally nonzero and act as reaction stresses. This is the opposite of PlaneStress, where the out-of-plane stresses vanish and the out-of-plane strains are unknown.

Let $\(\mathbf e^{\mathrm{2D}}=(\varepsilon_{11},\varepsilon_{22},\gamma_{12})\)$ be the strain vector furnished by a membrane element. The wrapper embeds it in the 3D vector by selecting indices $\(F=\{0,1,3\}\)$ and filling all remaining entries with zero,

\[ \mathbf e^{\mathrm{3D}}=(\varepsilon_{11},\varepsilon_{22},0,\gamma_{12},0,0). \]

The host is driven with this full strain, and the wrapper extracts the in-plane stress and the in-plane tangent submatrix,

\[ \mathbf s^{\mathrm{2D}}=\mathbf s^{\mathrm{3D}}_{F}, \qquad \mathbf D^{\mathrm{2D}}=\mathbf D^{\mathrm{3D}}_{F,F}. \]

No local iteration is necessary because the missing strains are specified rather than solved for. For a linear isotropic host with modulus $\(E\)$ and Poisson ratio $\( u\)$ this gives

\[ \mathbf D^{\mathrm{2D}}=\dfrac{E}{(1+ u)(1-2 u)} egin{bmatrix} 1- u& u&0\ u&1- u&0\ 0&0&\dfrac{1-2 u}{2} \end{bmatrix}. \]

The apparent in-plane stiffness grows without bound as $\( u o0.5\)$, reflecting the fact that a fully constrained incompressible body cannot change volume. For this reason a 3D nearly incompressible host requires a formulation that admits $\( u<0.5\)$, and the wrapper simply propagates the host tangent.

The same class also implements the two symmetry variants PlaneSymmetric13 and PlaneSymmetric23. They replace two of the zero out-of-plane entries by copies of in-plane entries before the host is evaluated. The 13 variant sets $\(\varepsilon_{33}=\varepsilon_{11}\)$ and $\(\gamma_{13}=\gamma_{12}\)$, while the 23 variant sets $\(\varepsilon_{33}=\varepsilon_{22}\)$ and $\(\gamma_{23}=\gamma_{12}\)$. Both variants are documented together on PlaneSymmetric.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text:
PlaneStrain
material PlaneStrain (1) (2)
# (1) int, unique tag
# (2) int, 3D material tag

The response of attached 3D material model will be output when recorded.

docs.title: Remarks
docs.text: The host material must be a registered 3D model, and nonlocal 3D hosts are explicitly rejected during initialization. The wrapper copies the host density and uses the in-plane submatrix of the host initial stiffness as its own initial stiffness. Use this wrapper with 2D membrane elements that possess out-of-plane thickness and represent a long or constrained body. For a thin plate or shell use PlaneStress, and for a body of revolution use Axisymmetric, whose hoop strain is computed by the element from the radial displacement. For uniaxial stress states use Uniaxial, which is based on the same condensation idea as plane stress but keeps only the axial component. As with all wrappers, record forwards to the host, so recorded 3D stresses include the reaction components that the element does not see.

docs.title: PlaneStress
docs.text:
Plane Stress Wrapper

Wraps a 3D host material model into a 2D plane stress model that can be used with 2D membrane elements.

docs.title: Theory
docs.text:
suanPan stores a symmetric second-order tensor in Voigt form, using $\(\mathbf e=(\varepsilon_{11},\varepsilon_{22},\varepsilon_{33},\gamma_{12},\gamma_{23},\gamma_{13})\)$ for strain and $\(\mathbf s=(\sigma_{11},\sigma_{22},\sigma_{33}, au_{12}, au_{23}, au_{13})\)$ for stress. The shear entries are engineering shears, $\(\gamma_{ij}=2\varepsilon_{ij}\)$ for $\(i e j\)$, so that the inner product $\(\mathbf s\cdot\mathbf e\)$ equals the tensor contraction $\(\mathbf\sigma:\mathbf\varepsilon\)$. A plane stress state models a thin body loaded in its own plane whose faces are traction free, so that $\(\sigma_{33}= au_{23}= au_{13}=0\)$. The out-of-plane strains $\(\varepsilon_{33}\)$, $\(\gamma_{23}\)$ and $\(\gamma_{13}\)$ are not prescribed by the kinematics, since they arise from Poisson coupling and from the constitutive law.

Partition the tensors into in-plane components $\(I=(11,22,12)\)$ and out-of-plane components $\(O=(33,23,13)\)$. The host material defines $\(\mathbf s=\mathbf s(\mathbf e)\)$ and its consistent tangent $\(\mathbf D=\partial\mathbf s/\partial\mathbf e\)$, which can be partitioned as

\[ egin{bmatrix}\mathbf s_I\\mathbf s_O\end{bmatrix}= egin{bmatrix}\mathbf D_{II}&\mathbf D_{IO}\\mathbf D_{OI}&\mathbf D_{OO}\end{bmatrix} egin{bmatrix}\mathbf e_I\\mathbf e_O\end{bmatrix}. \]

Given the in-plane strain supplied by the element, the wrapper solves the three local equations $\(\mathbf s_O(\mathbf e_I,\mathbf e_O)=\mathbf 0\)$ for the three unknown out-of-plane strains. Linearising these equations at the current trial state gives the correction

\[ \Delta\mathbf e_O=-\mathbf D_{OO}^{-1}\left(\mathbf s_O+\mathbf D_{OI}\Delta\mathbf e_I ight), \]

where $\(\Delta\mathbf e_I\)$ is the in-plane strain increment. The plane stress stress and tangent are then obtained by static condensation,

\[ \mathbf s_I^{\mathrm{2D}}=\mathbf s_I-\mathbf D_{IO}\mathbf D_{OO}^{-1}\mathbf s_O, \qquad \mathbf D^{\mathrm{2D}}=\mathbf D_{II}-\mathbf D_{IO}\mathbf D_{OO}^{-1}\mathbf D_{OI}. \]

For a linear isotropic host the result is the familiar matrix

\[ \mathbf D^{\mathrm{2D}}=\dfrac{E}{1- u^2} egin{bmatrix} 1& u&0\ u&1&0\ 0&0&\dfrac{1- u}{2} \end{bmatrix}, \]

which differs distinctly from the plane strain matrix, especially as $\( u\)$ approaches $\(0.5\)$.

The implementation is shared with Uniaxial and OS146 through the StressWrapper base class. The active set is F1={0,1,3}, namely $\(\sigma_{11}\)$, $\(\sigma_{22}\)$ and $\( au_{12}\)$, and the complementary set F2={2,4,5} is driven to zero by the condensation above. With the default [3]=1 the wrapper performs one Newton update using the host trial tangent and accepts the result without rechecking the residual. Setting [3] greater than one activates local iterations that repeatedly evaluate the host, solve $\(\mathbf D_{OO}\Delta\mathbf e_O=-\mathbf s_O\)$ and stop when the correction drops below the tolerance or the residual is small.

implementation limitation

With the default [3]=1 the constrained stresses $\(\mathbf s_O\)$ are not exactly zero after the update. The reported in-plane stress is condensed with the newly evaluated host tangent, which does not remove that residual.

developer note

The correction is formed from the host stress and tangent of the previous step and applied only once. With [3]>1 the convergence test uses a tolerance relative to the first correction and the counter is tested before each evaluation, so at most [3]-1 corrections are applied.

The returned stiffness is recomputed by condensation from the host trial tangent, so it is the consistent plane stress tangent when the host tangent is consistent. Nonlocal history variables of the host, if any, are appended after the six strain components and carried through unchanged.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text:
PlaneStress
material PlaneStress (1) (2) [3]
# (1) int, unique tag
# (2) int, 3D material tag
# [3] int, maximum iteration, default: 1

The response of attached 3D material model will be output when recorded.

By default, a non-iterative algorithm is implemented. If the strain increment is large, the algorithm may not converge. In this case, the optional argument [3] can be used to activate local iterations. If it is greater than one, the algorithm will perform local iteration up to [3] times.

docs.title: Remarks
docs.text: The host material must be a registered 3D model, and the wrapper inherits its density. The wrapper reports the 2D stress and stiffness to the element, while record forwards to the host so that recorded 3D quantities retain their original layout. See Material2D for the in-plane remapping of recorded stresses. Use this wrapper with membrane, plate or shell elements whose material plane is the $\(x_1\)\(–\)\(x_2\)$ plane. For a thick or constrained body use PlaneStrain instead, and for a body of revolution use Axisymmetric. For an open thin-walled section use OS146, which condenses a different set of stress components. A host with a singular out-of-plane tangent block $\(\mathbf D_{OO}\)$ cannot be used, since the condensation requires its inverse. Large strain increments combined with yielding or softening can leave a noticeable residual in the single-pass mode, so increase [3] or reduce the global step size in that case. Near incompressibility makes $\(\mathbf D_{OO}\)$ poorly conditioned and local iteration particularly valuable.

docs.text:

  • ISBN 978-0-387-97520-7

docs.title: PlaneSymmetric
docs.text:
Plane Symmetric Wrapper

Wraps a 3D host material model into a 2D plane symmetric model that can be used with 2D membrane elements.

docs.title: Theory
docs.text:
This wrapper is a specialisation of PlaneStrain, which readers should consult for the Voigt ordering and the submatrix extraction. Plain plane strain sets $\(\varepsilon_{33}=\gamma_{23}=\gamma_{13}=0\)$, whereas a plane symmetric state imposes that one out-of-plane normal direction behaves like an in-plane direction and that one out-of-plane shear vanishes or mirrors an in-plane shear. The two tokens select which normal direction is identified with the thickness direction.

The implementation starts from the three in-plane strains $\((\varepsilon_{11},\varepsilon_{22},\gamma_{12})\)$ and builds a zero six-vector. For PlaneSymmetric13 it copies $\(\varepsilon_{11}\)$ into $\(\varepsilon_{33}\)$ and $\(\gamma_{12}\)$ into $\(\gamma_{13}\)$. For PlaneSymmetric23 it copies $\(\varepsilon_{22}\)$ into $\(\varepsilon_{33}\)$ and $\(\gamma_{12}\)$ into $\(\gamma_{23}\)$. The host is then evaluated with this reconstructed 3D strain, and the wrapper returns the in-plane stresses and the in-plane tangent submatrix exactly as PlaneStrain does. For an isotropic host these strain constraints produce the corresponding normal-stress symmetry quoted in the Remarks, but for an anisotropic host the result depends on the coupling terms of the host tangent. No local iteration is performed, since all imposed components are prescribed rather than solved for.

imposed strains versus quoted stress symmetry

The Remarks below state the stress equalities $\(\sigma_{11}=\sigma_{33}\)$ with $\(\tau_{12}=\tau_{32}\)$ and $\(\sigma_{22}=\sigma_{33}\)$ with $\(\tau_{12}=\tau_{31}\)$. The wrapper actually imposes strain constraints, namely $\(\varepsilon_{33}=\varepsilon_{11}\)$ and $\(\gamma_{13}=\gamma_{12}\)$ for PlaneSymmetric13, and $\(\varepsilon_{33}=\varepsilon_{22}\)$ and $\(\gamma_{23}=\gamma_{12}\)$ for PlaneSymmetric23. Those stress equalities follow only for an isotropic host with the corresponding elastic symmetry, while an anisotropic host can violate them because of coupling terms in its tangent.

developer note

The strain constraints are implemented in PlaneStrain.cpp.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text:
PlaneSymmetric
material PlaneSymmetric13 (1) (2)
material PlaneSymmetric23 (1) (2)
# (1) int, unique material tag
# (2) int, 3D reference material tag

docs.title: Remarks
docs.text:
1. The token PlaneSymmetric13 indicates $\(\sigma_{11}=\sigma_{33}\)$ and $\(\tau_{12}=\tau_{32}\)$.
  2. The token PlaneSymmetric23 indicates $\(\sigma_{22}=\sigma_{33}\)$ and $\(\tau_{12}=\tau_{31}\)$.

The parser maps PlaneSymmetric13 and PlaneSymmetric23 to the same class as PlaneStrain with an internal symmetry flag, so all three tokens accept exactly two arguments. The underlying host must be a 3D material and must not be nonlocal, matching the restriction of PlaneStrain. The wrapper inherits the host density and extracts the $\(3\times3\)$ in-plane initial stiffness from the host. Use Axisymmetric instead when the hoop strain arises from a radial displacement in a true body of revolution, since that element supplies the hoop strain directly.

docs.title: Prestrain
docs.text:
Prestrain Wrapper

Wraps a uniaxial host material model so that a prestrain can be applied. This may be useful for modelling prestressed reinforced concrete or similar multiphase materials.

docs.title: Background
docs.text:
An imposed or eigenstrain is a strain that develops without a corresponding stress in a free body, such as thermal expansion, shrinkage or the strain imposed by a tensioning operation. The wrapper evaluates the host at a shifted strain,

\[ \varepsilon_{\mathrm{host}}(t)=\varepsilon_{\mathrm{element}}+\alpha(t)\,\varepsilon_0, \qquad \sigma=\sigma_{\mathrm{host}}\!\left(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{host}}\right), \qquad D=D_{\mathrm{host}}\!\left(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{host}}\right), \]

where $\(\varepsilon_0\)$ is the magnitude (4), $\(\alpha(t)\)$ is the value of the amplitude at the current trial time, and $\(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{element}}\)$ is the strain reported by the element. The stress returned to the element is simply the host stress at the shifted strain, so a restrained bar develops stress while a free bar deforms by $\(-\alpha\varepsilon_0\)$ to cancel it. Because the wrapper shifts the strain rather than the stress, any prescribed prestress must first be converted to an equivalent prestrain by a uniaxial calibration. Setting the amplitude tag to zero selects a built-in ramp that grows linearly with time, and an unusable nonzero tag also falls back to a ramp with a warning. The strain rate passed to a rate-dependent host is not shifted, only the strain itself.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text:
Prestrain
material Prestrain (1) (2) (3) (4)
# (1) int, unique material tag
# (2) int, underlying material tag
# (3) int, amplitude tag, set to 0 to use a ramp function
# (4) double, magnitude

docs.title: Remarks
docs.text:
It is necessary to attach an amplitude. The amplitude is in charge of applying the designated prestrain (of the specified magnitude) to the underlying material in a controlled manner.

If only a prestress is available, one can always develop a uniaxial test model to compute the prestrain from the prestress. Thus, we do not provide a Prestress counterpart.

The host must be a registered 1D material, and the wrapper inherits its density, stiffness and damping. The amplitude is evaluated at the trial analysis time and multiplied by the magnitude, so the prestrain can be ramped, stepped or given any user-defined time history. The wrapper adds the prestrain to the element strain before calling the host, so a positive magnitude produces a positive host stress at zero element strain and drives node 2 in the negative direction in the self-equilibrated example above. Recorded quantities are forwarded to the host and therefore refer to the shifted strain state, not to the element strain alone. Use a Parallel container to combine a prestrained constituent with other 1D constituents, or Sequential when the constituents must share a stress instead.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
Text Only
node 1 0 0
node 2 1 0

material Elastic1D 1 100
material Prestrain 2 1 0 1E-2

element T2D2 1 1 2 1 10
element T2D2 2 1 2 2 10

fix2 1 1 1
fix2 2 2 1 2

step static 1
set ini_step_size .1

converger AbsIncreDisp 1 1E-4 10 1

analyze

peek node 2

exit

The above example is a simple demonstration. The prestrain $\(0.01\)$ will be gradually (linearly increasing from zero to the specific magnitude) applied to the second element. The system balances itself without any external load.

The final displacement of node 2 should be $\(0.005\)$ since both elements share the same section properties.

sign of the example displacement

Running this exact input with the suanPan binary gives a final displacement of $\(-0.005\)$ at node 2, not $\(+0.005\)$. The wrapper evaluates the host at $\(\varepsilon+\alpha\varepsilon_0\)$, so a positive amplitude drives the bar in the negative direction when no external load is applied. The magnitude $\(0.005\)$ is correct because the two identical bars share the imposed deformation equally, but the sign in the original statement is reversed.

docs.title: Rotation2D
docs.text:
2D Rotation Wrapper

Alters the inclination of the 2D host material model and is typically used with anisotropic material models.

docs.title: Theory
docs.text:
A two-dimensional anisotropic material stores its constitutive matrix in a local frame whose axes need not coincide with the global element axes. Let $\(\theta\)$ be the counter-clockwise angle from the global axis $\(x_1\)$ to the local material axis $\(x'_1\)$, and write $\(c=\cos 2\theta\)$ and $\(s=\sin 2\theta\)$. In the engineering-shear Voigt convention $\(\mathbf e=(\varepsilon_{11},\varepsilon_{22},\gamma_{12})\)$ with $\(\gamma_{12}=2\varepsilon_{12}\)$, the global-to-local strain transformation used by the implementation is

\[ \mathbf T(\theta)= \begin{bmatrix} \dfrac{1+c}{2}&\dfrac{1-c}{2}&\dfrac{s}{2}\\[2mm] \dfrac{1-c}{2}&\dfrac{1+c}{2}&-\dfrac{s}{2}\\[2mm] -s&s&c \end{bmatrix}, \qquad \mathbf e'=\mathbf T\,\mathbf e. \]

The shear row and column carry factors that differ by two because the same physical shear appears as $\(\gamma=2\varepsilon_{12}\)$ in the vector but as $\(\varepsilon_{12}\)$ in the tensor. Consequently $\(\mathbf T\)$ is not orthogonal, and work conjugacy requires the stress to be mapped back with its transpose rather than its inverse,

\[ \mathbf s=\mathbf T^{\mathrm T}\,\mathbf s', \qquad \mathbf D=\mathbf T^{\mathrm T}\,\mathbf D'\,\mathbf T. \]

The identity $\(\mathbf s\cdot\mathbf e=(\mathbf T^{\mathrm T}\mathbf s')\cdot\mathbf e=\mathbf s'\cdot(\mathbf T\mathbf e)=\mathbf s'\cdot\mathbf e'\)$ confirms that energy is invariant under the change of axes. The initial, current and trial stiffnesses are all rotated with the same expression, so the wrapper preserves the consistency of the host tangent. The transformation is a fixed rotation of material axes for small-strain tensors, not a finite-rotation or corotational formulation. The three-dimensional analogue is Rotation3D, which uses an Euler vector and a $\(6\times6\)$ transformation built from a rotation matrix.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text:
Rotation2D
material Rotation2D (1) (2) (3)
# (1) int, unique material tag
# (2) int, associated material tag
# (3) double, angle rotated (anti-clockwise positive)

The response of attached 2D material model will be output when recorded.

docs.title: Remarks
docs.text: The angle is given in radians, and a positive value rotates the material axes counter-clockwise relative to the global axes. The host must be a registered 2D material, and the wrapper inherits its density. Use this wrapper with orthotropic or other direction-dependent 2D hosts, such as a 2D model wrapped around OrthotropicElastic3D by PlaneStress. An isotropic host yields the same response in every direction, so rotation has no visible effect for such hosts. Recorded quantities are forwarded to the host, so stresses are reported in the material axes rather than in the global axes used by the element. A wrapper can be stacked with Laminated if several differently oriented layers must share the same strain.

docs.title: Rotation3D
docs.text:
3D Rotation Wrapper

Alters the inclination of the 3D host material model and is typically used with anisotropic material models.

docs.title: Theory
docs.text:
An anisotropic material is defined by constitutive tensors whose components are referred to a local material frame $\(\{\mathbf e'_i\}\)$. If the host is evaluated in that local frame, a strain measured in the global frame must be rotated into it and the resulting stress rotated back. Let $\(\mathbf R\)$ be the proper orthogonal matrix generated from the Euler rotation vector described below, so that $\(\mathbf R=\exp([\mathbf\theta]_\times)\)$. The strain tensor transformation applied by the wrapper is

\[ \mathbf\varepsilon'=\mathbf R\,\mathbf\varepsilon\,\mathbf R^{\mathrm T}, \qquad \mathbf\sigma=\mathbf R^{\mathrm T}\,\mathbf\sigma'\,\mathbf R, \]

so that the local material axes are the rows of $\(\mathbf R\)$ and the stress–strain tangent transforms as $\(\mathbf D=\mathbf R^{\mathrm T}\,\mathbf D'\,\mathbf R\)$ when the fourth-order tensor is written with the appropriate index pairing. In the six-component Voigt convention used by suanPan the same operations are represented by a $\(6\times6\)$ matrix $\(\mathbf T\)$ built from products of the entries of $\(\mathbf R\)$. With $\(\mathbf e=(\varepsilon_{11},\varepsilon_{22},\varepsilon_{33},\gamma_{12},\gamma_{23},\gamma_{13})\)$ and $\(\gamma_{ij}=2\varepsilon_{ij}\)$, the first block of $\(\mathbf T\)$ contains $\(R_{ij}^2\)$, the coupling block from normal to shear entries contains $\(R_{ij}R_{ik}\)$, and the shear block contains factors $\(2R_{ij}R_{ik}\)$ and sums $\(R_{ij}R_{lk}+R_{ik}R_{lj}\)$. Because engineering shear is used, $\(\mathbf T\)$ is not an orthogonal matrix, but it is constructed so that the work conjugation $\(\mathbf\sigma:\mathbf\varepsilon=\mathbf\sigma':\mathbf\varepsilon'\)$ holds when the stress is mapped back with $\(\mathbf T^{\mathrm T}\)$.

deviation from theory

The textbook change of basis to axes rotated by $\(\mathbf\theta\)$ uses $\(\mathbf\varepsilon'=\mathbf R^{\mathrm T}\mathbf\varepsilon\mathbf R\)$ with the local axes in the columns of $\(\mathbf R\)$. The suanPan implementation builds $\(\mathbf T\)$ from the entries $\(R_{ij}\)$, so it applies $\(\mathbf\varepsilon'=\mathbf R\mathbf\varepsilon\mathbf R^{\mathrm T}\)$, which is the passive rotation by $\(-\mathbf\theta\)$. For a rotation about the $\(x_3\)$ axis, Rotation3D with rotation vector $\((0,0,\theta)\)$ therefore gives the same material response as Rotation2D with angle $\(-\theta\)$.

The wrapper therefore applies

\[ \mathbf e'=\mathbf T\,\mathbf e, \qquad \mathbf s=\mathbf T^{\mathrm T}\,\mathbf s', \qquad \mathbf D=\mathbf T^{\mathrm T}\,\mathbf D'\,\mathbf T, \]

where $\(\mathbf s\)$ and $\(\mathbf D\)$ are the stress and tangent delivered to the element and primed quantities come from the host. The same expressions are used for the initial and the trial stiffness, so the rotated tangent is consistent whenever the host tangent is consistent.

The three arguments (3) to (5) are the components of a single Euler rotation vector $\(\mathbf\theta\)$. Writing $\(\Theta=\lVert\mathbf\theta\rVert\)$ and $\(\mathbf n=\mathbf\theta/\Theta\)$, the implementation forms the unit quaternion $\(q=(\cos(\Theta/2),\,\sin(\Theta/2)\mathbf n)\)$ and converts it to the rotation matrix

\[ \mathbf R=2q_0\,[\mathbf q]\times+2\,\mathbf q\mathbf q^{\mathrm T}+\left(q_0^2-\mathbf q\cdot\mathbf q\right)\mathbf I, \]

which is equivalent to the matrix exponential $\(\exp([\mathbf\theta]\times)\)$ and rotates by $\(\Theta\)$ about $\(\mathbf n\)$ according to the right-hand rule. The angle is measured in radians, and the three arguments are the Cartesian components of the rotation vector, not three successive Euler angles.

The rotation is a fixed change of material basis applied to small-strain tensor components. It does not rotate the geometry and it is not a corotational or objective-rate formulation for finite rotations. For a planar problem the cheaper Rotation2D wrapper applies the corresponding two-dimensional transformation.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text:
Rotation3D
material Rotation3D (1) (2) (3...5)
# (1) int, unique material tag
# (2) int, associated material tag
# (3...5) double, three components of rotation vector

Rotations in 3D space may have different forms. The Euler vector is used to represent the axis and angle of rotation. Parameters (3) to (5) are three components of the vector $\(\mathbf{\theta}\)$.

The response of attached 3D material model will be output when recorded.

docs.title: Remarks
docs.text:
The host must be a registered 3D material, and the wrapper inherits its density. Use it for orthotropic or otherwise direction-dependent hosts such as OrthotropicElastic3D, whose principal axes are not aligned with the global axes. For an isotropic host the rotated response is identical to the unrotated one, so the wrapper only adds cost. The constructor evaluates $\(\sin(\Theta/2)/\Theta\)$ directly, so a zero rotation vector is not a safe way to request the identity transformation; omit the wrapper in that case.

implementation limitation

A zero rotation vector fills the transformation matrix with NaN values rather than producing the identity. Omit the wrapper entirely when the material axes need no rotation.

developer note

For $\(\Theta=0\)$ the quotient $\(\sin(\Theta/2)/\Theta\)$ is evaluated as $\(0/0\)$.

The wrapper forwards record calls to the host, so recorded stresses are expressed in the material axes and may differ from the global stresses returned to the element. Nested use with dimension-reducing wrappers is possible, for example a rotated host wrapped by PlaneStress, provided the intended material axes are tracked explicitly.

docs.title: Sequential
docs.text:
Container of Material Models In Sequence

Combines multiple 1D material models into a single one.

docs.title: Theory
docs.text:
A series rheological arrangement places several constitutive elements end to end along the same load path. Equilibrium of the force transmitted through the chain means every constituent carries the same stress, $\(\sigma^{(k)}=\sigma\)$, while compatibility makes the total elongation the sum of the individual ones,

\[ \varepsilon=\sum_{k=1}^{n}\varepsilon^{(k)}(\sigma), \qquad S(\sigma)=\dfrac{\partial\varepsilon}{\partial\sigma}=\sum_{k=1}^{n}S^{(k)}(\sigma), \qquad D=\left(\sum_{k=1}^{n}\dfrac{1}{D^{(k)}}\right)^{-1}, \]

where $\(S^{(k)}=1/D^{(k)}\)$ is the tangent compliance of constituent $\(k\)$. With volume fractions the same statement becomes $\(S=\sum_k f_k S^{(k)}\)$, which is the iso-stress or Reuss assumption and gives a lower bound on the effective stiffness. For two linear springs this reproduces the harmonic average $\(E_{\mathrm{eq}}=E_1E_2/(E_1+E_2)\)$ when no fractions are supplied.

deviation from theory

The wrapper adds the constituent compliances with unit weight, so the Reuss average is obtained only when all volume fractions $\(f_k\)$ are equal. No area or volume fraction is read from the input, so any weighting must already be embedded in the constituent parameters.

For a prescribed total strain the local strains of the constituents are not known in advance, so the implementation solves a small nonlinear system at each trial state. The unknowns are the strains $\(\varepsilon^{(k)}\)$ of all $\(n\)$ constituents, the first residual enforces $\(\varepsilon-\sum_k\varepsilon^{(k)}=0\)$, and the remaining $\(n-1\)$ residuals enforce equality of neighbouring stresses $\(\sigma^{(k)}-\sigma^{(k+1)}=0\)$. The Jacobian is assembled from the host tangent stiffnesses with signs consistent with these residuals, and the Newton correction is added to each local strain until the correction or the residual falls below the tolerance. The maximum number of local iterations is fixed at 20 in the class, and failure is reported as an error. The wrapper stiffness is the harmonic sum $\(1/\sum_k 1/D^{(k)}\)$, and the reported stress is that of the first constituent, which equals the common series stress at convergence.

This wrapper is the 1D series counterpart of Parallel, which imposes equal strain instead. It is useful for building Maxwell-type or generalised rheological arrangements from rate-independent 1D laws, although the viscosity-free restriction below still applies. Histories are recorded in tag order, as in Laminated and Stacked. No volume fractions are applied by the wrapper, so any weighting must already be embedded in the constituent parameters.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text:
Sequential
material Sequential (1) (2...)
# (1) int, unique material tag
# (2...) int, material tags of 1D models need to be contained

docs.title: Caveat
docs.text: Please do not include any viscosity-related models into the wrapper. This container is only designed for rate-independent hysteretic models. The response of attached 1D material models will be output when recorded. The output has a uniform size and data is arranged in the order as defined.

docs.title: Remarks
docs.text: At least two constituent tags are required, and the parser rejects a single tag. Every tag must refer to a registered 1D material with a nonzero initial stiffness, since the harmonic average divides by each tangent. The local Newton loop uses the current tangent of every constituent, so strongly nonlinear hosts benefits from smaller global increments. All constituents share a single stress, so a constituent that softens cannot shed load to the others in the way that a parallel arrangement can; this is the characteristic limitation of the series idealisation. Use Parallel for iso-strain combinations and Prestrain when an imposed initial strain rather than a series stress is required.

docs.title: Stacked
docs.text:
Parallel Wrapper For 3D Material Models

Combines multiple 3D material models into a single one.

docs.title: Theory
docs.text:
A stacked material is the three-dimensional form of the iso-strain or Voigt assumption. Every constituent is subjected to the same six-component Voigt strain $\(\mathbf e=(\varepsilon_{11},\varepsilon_{22},\varepsilon_{33},\gamma_{12},\gamma_{23},\gamma_{13})\)$, and the overall stress and tangent are the sums of the constituent quantities,

\[ \mathbf s(\mathbf e)=\sum_{k=1}^{n}\mathbf s^{(k)}(\mathbf e), \qquad \mathbf D(\mathbf e)=\sum_{k=1}^{n}\mathbf D^{(k)}(\mathbf e). \]

For constituents with volume fractions $\(f_k\)$ the physical mixture rule is $\(\mathbf s=\sum_k f_k\mathbf s^{(k)}\)$, so the fractions must be included in the material parameters because the wrapper applies no weighting.

deviation from theory

The wrapper sums stresses and tangents with unit weight, so the Voigt mixture rule is recovered only when all volume fractions $\(f_k\)$ are equal. Any weighting must be built into the constituent parameters or the section assigned to the element, since no fraction is read from the input.

The rule is the upper bound on the effective stiffness of a composite, complementary to the iso-stress lower bound represented in one dimension by Sequential. In terms of energy, the free energies of the constituents add under the common strain, which is consistent with a parallel rheological interpretation.

The implementation makes a copy of each listed 3D material, drives every copy with the same trial strain, and sums the returned stresses and tangents. Densities and initial stiffnesses are summed during initialization, and recorded histories are concatenated in tag order.

This is the three-dimensional counterpart of Laminated for 2D models and of Parallel for 1D models. Use Rotation3D on any constituent whose material frame differs from the global frame.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text:
Stacked
material Stacked (1) (2...)
# (1) int, unique material tag
# (2...) int, material tags of 3D models need to be contained

The response of attached 3D material models will be output when recorded. The output has a uniform size and data is arranged in the order as defined.

docs.title: Remarks
docs.text:
Every listed tag must refer to a registered 3D material, and the wrapper reports a six-component stress and stiffness to solid elements. The wrapper skips the update entirely when the strain increment is below the internal tolerance, which is harmless for rate-independent hosts but worth noting for rate-dependent ones.

implementation limitation

A rate-dependent host cannot evolve in a step whose strain increment falls below the internal tolerance.

developer note

Stacked::update_trial_status returns immediately when the strain-increment norm is below datum::eps, so none of the constituents is re-evaluated.

No local equilibrium solve is performed since compatibility is enforced by giving all constituents the same strain; the model cannot represent load shedding caused by different strains. Use Laminated when a 2D reduction is required, and PlaneStress or PlaneStrain inside the stack for reduced constituents.

docs.title: Substepping
docs.text:
Adaptive substepping wrapper for an associated material model.

Splits a strain increment into smaller subincrements when the host model fails to converge on the full increment.

docs.title: Theory
docs.text:
Rate-independent constitutive integrations based on a return mapping are usually accurate only for sufficiently small strain increments. When a single increment crosses a sharp yield surface or a rapid softening branch, the local Newton iteration may fail or produce a poor state. An automatic substepping strategy applies the total increment $\(\Delta\mathbf e\)$ as a sequence of fractions,

\[ \mathbf e_{k+1}=\mathbf e_k+\delta_k\,\Delta\mathbf e, \qquad \sum_k\delta_k=1, \]

and adjusts the fraction $\(\delta_k\)$ according to whether the host succeeds. The implementation keeps two copies of the host, one representing the committed state and one representing the trial state. At the start of an update the trial copy is recreated from the committed copy, the fraction is initialised to one, and the host is asked to update to $\(\mathbf e_{\mathrm{current}}+(\alpha+\delta)\Delta\mathbf e\)$, where $\(\alpha\)$ is the accumulated fraction. A failed trial resets the success counter and halves the fraction, while a successful trial is committed immediately and advances the accumulated fraction. Every three consecutive successes the fraction is multiplied by $\(1.2\)$, and it is always capped by the remaining fraction $\(1-\alpha\)$. The process ends when the next fraction falls below the internal tolerance, meaning the full increment has been applied. Every attempt, successful or not, counts towards (3), and reaching the limit is reported as an error.

This is a success-driven adaptive scheme rather than the truncation-error-controlled family of algorithms proposed by Sloan, so the fraction changes heuristically instead of being selected from an estimated local error.

deviation from Sloan's substepping

Sloan's method estimates the local truncation error of the stress integration and chooses the substep size to meet a prescribed tolerance. The suanPan Substepping wrapper does not compute an error estimate, so the substep size follows a fixed heuristic rather than a truncation-error target. The reference is included for background only, and the wrapper does not reproduce that algorithm.

developer note

The wrapper halves the fraction after any failed host update and increases it by a factor of 1.2 after every three successes.

The wrapper forwards material type, density and all state getters and setters to the appropriate host copy, so it can wrap a model of any dimensionality. Only the strain-based overload of update_trial_status is implemented, so rate-dependent hosts that require a strain rate are not driven through their rate overload.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text:
Substepping
material Substepping (1) (2) [3]
# (1) int, unique material tag
# (2) int, associated material tag
# [3] int, maximum iteration, default: 20

docs.title: Remarks
docs.text:
Substepping makes a copy of the host material and drives it through a sequence of subincrements. If a trial subincrement fails, the increment factor is halved and the substep is retried. After three consecutive successful substeps, the increment factor is increased by a factor of 1.2. The process ends once the full strain increment has been applied. If the number of attempts reaches (3), the update fails with an error message; the default limit of 20 is set in the input parser.

The wrapper adopts the material type, density, stiffness and history of the host model, so it can wrap any material whose return mapping is reliable only for small increments. Typical applications include sharp yield surfaces and rapid softening, where a single large increment would otherwise fail to converge.

The wrapper only helps if the host signals failure by returning an error code, so a host with a very loose internal tolerance will still accept an inaccurate large increment. Because each successful substep is committed inside the wrapper, a later failure cannot roll back earlier substeps of the same global increment; the global analysis still sees a single trial state. Use smaller global increments when the attempt limit is reached, since that reduces the number of subincrements required for the same accuracy. Combine with PlaneStress or Uniaxial only when the outer reduction itself is accurate, because substepping cannot repair a residual left by a single-pass condensation.

docs.title: Uniaxial
docs.text:
Uniaxial Wrapper

Wraps a 3D host material model into a 1D uniaxial model that can be used with 1D elements.

It is assumed that $\(\sigma_{22}=\sigma_{33}=\tau_{12}=\tau_{23}=\tau_{31}=0\)$.

docs.title: Theory
docs.text:
A uniaxial stress state is the one-dimensional limit of the plane stress condensation implemented by PlaneStress. Only the axial component $\(\sigma_{11}\)$ is active, so the five remaining stress components are prescribed to vanish. Writing the host stress and tangent in the Voigt ordering $\((\sigma_{11},\sigma_{22},\sigma_{33},\tau_{12},\tau_{23},\tau_{13})\)$, the wrapper partitions the strain vector into the axial entry and the five constrained entries. Given the axial strain $\(\varepsilon_{11}\)$ from a truss or beam fibre, it solves

\[ \mathbf s_O(\varepsilon_{11},\mathbf e_O)=\mathbf 0, \qquad \mathbf e_O=(\varepsilon_{22},\varepsilon_{33},\gamma_{12},\gamma_{23},\gamma_{13}), \]

using the host tangent block $\(\mathbf D_{OO}\)$ and the same Newton correction as in plane stress. The reduced stress and tangent are $\(\sigma^{\mathrm{1D}}=\sigma_{11}-\mathbf D_{1O}\mathbf D_{OO}^{-1}\mathbf s_O\)$ and $\(D^{\mathrm{1D}}=D_{11}-\mathbf D_{1O}\mathbf D_{OO}^{-1}\mathbf D_{O1}\)$. For a linear isotropic host this recovers $\(\sigma_{11}=E\varepsilon_{11}\)$ with lateral strains $\(\varepsilon_{22}=\varepsilon_{33}=-\nu\varepsilon_{11}\)$.

The implementation is the StressWrapper base class with F1={0}, so it shares its condensation, local iteration and nonlocal-history handling with PlaneStress and OS146. With the default [3]=1 only one Newton update is made, while larger values trigger local iterations until the constrained stress residual is small.

implementation limitation

With the default [3]=1 the five constrained stresses are not exactly zero after the update.

developer note

The lateral strain correction is computed from the host state of the previous step and applied only once. With [3]>1 the convergence test is relative to the first correction and the counter is tested before each evaluation, so at most [3]-1 corrections are applied.

The host must provide a nonsingular constrained tangent block, and nonlocal history variables are carried after the six strain entries.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text:
Text Only
material Uniaxial (1) (2) [3]
# (1) int, unique material tag
# (2) int, associated 3D material tag
# [3] int, maximum iteration allowed, default: 1

The response of attached 3D material models will be output when recorded.

docs.title: Remarks
docs.text: Use this wrapper with 1D elements such as T2D2 when the constitutive law is available only as a 3D model. To obtain a 1D model from a 1D host instead, use the host directly; Prestrain is the appropriate wrapper when an imposed initial strain is needed. For a two-dimensional in-plane state use PlaneStress, which keeps both normal stresses and the in-plane shear. The wrapper reports a single stress component to the element but forwards recording to the 3D host, so recorded stresses still contain the full 3D state. Increase the optional iteration count or reduce the step size if a large strain increment leaves a residual lateral stress in the single-pass mode.

docs.title: Modal Force Recorder
docs.text:
Extract Modal Elastic Forces from an Eigen Analysis

Minimum version: v4.3.1

The ModalForce recorder post-processes the results of a Frequency step and writes the modal elastic forces. It is the force counterpart of the Modal recorder, which writes frequencies, mode shapes, participation factors and effective modal masses.

The recorder stores an HDF5 file. It does not record a time history; it stores a snapshot of the modal forces computed in the current step when that step is a Frequency step. Consequently, the recorder should be saved immediately after the eigenanalysis. If it is also active in a later non-eigen step, the stored modal data is cleared when that step starts recording.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text:
ModalForceRecorder
recorder (1) hdf5 ModalForce
# (1) int, unique recorder tag

The hdf5 keyword is required in practice because the modal data is written in HDF5 format. The application must be compiled with HDF5 support.

Unlike the Modal recorder, no DoF identifiers are required. The recorder writes the force of every extracted mode for all active nodes and all local elements. The every keyword and object tags are not supported; all remaining tokens are ignored.

The recorder must be defined before the analyze command and it must be saved explicitly.

Text Only
recorder 1 hdf5 ModalForce

step frequency 1 10
analyze

save recorder 1

peek recorder 1 prints a short description of the recorder.

Both modal properties and modal forces are often needed. In that case, define both recorders before the analysis:

Text Only
recorder 1 hdf5 Modal U1
recorder 2 hdf5 ModalForce

step frequency 1 10
analyze

save recorder 1
save recorder 2

Each recorder writes its own file.

docs.title: Computed Quantities
docs.text:
For the generalised eigenproblem

\[ \mathbf{K}\mathbf{\phi}_n=\lambda_n\mathbf{M}\mathbf{\phi}_n, \]

the mode shape is normalised with respect to the mass matrix,

\[ \mathbf{\phi}_n^T\mathbf{M}\mathbf{\phi}_n=1. \]

The modal elastic force of mode $\(n\)$ is

\[ \mathbf{f}_n=\mathbf{K}\mathbf{\phi}_n. \]

The recorder assembles the force element by element,

\[ \mathbf{f}_n=\sum_e\mathbf{K}_e\mathbf{\phi}_{n,e}, \]

rather than using the global stiffness matrix. The global stiffness matrix is modified when boundary conditions and constraints are processed, whilst the element stiffness matrices are not. Consequently, the assembled force vector contains the reaction components at restrained DoFs. On unconstrained DoFs this is the usual elastic restoring force $\(\mathbf{K}\mathbf{\phi}_n=\lambda_n\mathbf{M}\mathbf{\phi}_n\)$. On restrained DoFs it gives the reaction that enforces the mode shape, in the same sign convention as the nodal RF response.

The force vector corresponds to a unit modal displacement. To obtain the peak modal force in a response-spectrum analysis, scale it by the corresponding modal coordinate amplitude, for example $\(\Gamma_{n,j}S_d(T_n)\)$. The participation factor $\(\Gamma_{n,j}\)$ is available from the Modal recorder.

Modes whose modal mass is numerically zero or negative (for example, spurious modes in a model with an inconsistent mass matrix) are not normalised. Their modal elastic force is zero.

global force

The force components are defined in the global coordinate system. They are different from the elemental forces for some element types. For example, with beam elements, the axial force and the transverse shear force are defined in the local frame, thus additional transformations are needed.

docs.title: Output File
docs.text:
The recorder writes

Text Only
R<tag>-ModalForce.h5

to the current output folder. When the application runs with multiple MPI ranks, the file name is prefixed with the rank, for example

Text Only
P0-R1-ModalForce.h5

The output folder can be changed with the output_folder attribute before the save command.

docs.title: Data Layout
docs.text:
Only the forces are stored. Frequencies and mode shapes are available from the Modal recorder. The HDF5 file contains the following objects.

Text Only
R1-ModalForce.h5
├── Mode 1                          one group per mode
│   ├── Nodes
│   │   ├── N1                      (n_dof_node_1, 1)
│   │   ├── N2                      (n_dof_node_2, 1)
│   │   └── ...
│   └── Elements
│       ├── E1                      (n_dof_element_1, 1)
│       ├── E2                      (n_dof_element_2, 1)
│       └── ...
├── Mode 2
│   └── ...
└── ...
  1. Each mode has a group named Mode 1, Mode 2, etc. The group numbering follows the eigenvalue ordering, starting from one.
  2. Each mode group contains two groups, Nodes and Elements.
  3. For every active node, Nodes contains a dataset N<tag>. This is the assembled nodal force vector, that is, the sum of the force contributions of all elements attached to the node. Here <tag> is the node tag, not the node index. For example, node 10 produces Nodes/N10.
  4. For every local element, Elements contains a dataset E<tag>. This is the element force vector

$$ \mathbf{f}_{n,e}=\mathbf{K}e\mathbf{\phi}{n,e}. $$

Here <tag> is the element tag, not the element index. For example, element 10 produces Elements/E10. E denotes an element force; it is not a strain component.

The rows of N<tag> follow the node-local DoF order, that is, the order of the DoFs in the node's internal DoF list. The rows of E<tag> follow the element-local DoF order, which is the node-by-node order used by the element stiffness matrix. Typical examples are:

object type local DoF order two-dimensional solid node U1, U2 two-dimensional beam/shell node U1, U2, UR3 three-dimensional solid node U1, U2, U3 three-dimensional beam/shell node U1, U2, U3, UR1, UR2, UR3

For a two-node Spring01 element in a two-dimensional model, the four rows of E<tag> are [U1 of node i, U2 of node i, U1 of node j, U2 of node j].

The dataset length is the total number of DoFs of the node or element, including constrained DoFs. Constrained components are present in both N<tag> and E<tag>. They are generally nonzero because they contain the reaction that enforces the mode shape.

The nodal force can be recovered from the element forces by summing the element contributions at each shared node. This identity is useful for checking the data layout of a model with a new element type.

docs.title: Reading the Data
docs.text:
The following snippet reads the forces of the first mode.

Python
import h5py
import numpy as np

with h5py.File("R1-ModalForce.h5", "r") as file:
    # node 2 in a two-dimensional model stores [U1, U2]
    nodal_force = file["Mode 1/Nodes/N2"][()].ravel()

    # element 1 stores its nodal DoFs one node after another
    element_force = file["Mode 1/Elements/E1"][()].ravel()

For all modes, loop over file[f'Mode {mode + 1}/Nodes/N{tag}'] and file[f'Mode {mode + 1}/Elements/E{tag}']. Note that Python uses zero-based indexing.

docs.title: Parallel Analysis
docs.text: With multiple MPI ranks, every rank writes its own file. The assembled nodal force vector N<tag> is reduced over all ranks, so each file contains the complete nodal forces for the nodes stored on that rank. The element force datasets E<tag> contain only the local elements of the rank that writes the file.

docs.title: Relation to the Other Modal Recorders
docs.text:
The Eigen recorder writes the raw eigenvalues and eigenvectors to Eigenvalue.h5. The Modal recorder writes frequencies, mode shapes, participation factors and effective modal masses to R<tag>-Modal.h5. The ModalForce recorder writes the modal elastic forces to R<tag>-ModalForce.h5.

The three recorders can be defined in the same analysis if all corresponding quantities are needed.

docs.title: Example
docs.text: A complete worked example, including post-processing, modal combination and validation of the element forces, is given in modal analysis of a shear building.

docs.title: Modal Recorder
docs.text:
Extract Modal Properties from an Eigen Analysis

Minimum version: v4.3.1

The Modal recorder post-processes the results of a Frequency step and writes the modal properties that are commonly used in structural dynamics:

  1. natural frequencies,
  2. mass-normalised mode shapes,
  3. modal participation factors,
  4. effective modal masses.

The recorder stores an HDF5 file. It does not record a time history; it stores a snapshot of the modal properties computed in the current step when that step is a Frequency step. Consequently, the recorder should be saved immediately after the eigenanalysis. If it is also active in a later non-eigen step, the stored modal data is cleared when that step starts recording.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text:
ModalRecorder
recorder (1) hdf5 Modal (2...)
# (1) int, unique recorder tag
# (2...) string, at least one DoF identifier

The hdf5 keyword is required in practice because the modal data is written in HDF5 format. The application must be compiled with HDF5 support.

The DoF identifiers define the directions of the influence vector(s) used for the participation factors and effective masses. The following identifiers are supported.

identifier meaning U1, 1 translation along DoF 1 U2, 2 translation along DoF 2 U3, 3 translation along DoF 3 U4, 4, UR1 rotation about DoF 1 U5, 5, UR2 rotation about DoF 2 U6, 6, UR3 rotation about DoF 3 P, PINNED U1, U2, U3 E, ENCASTRE U1, U2, U3, UR1, UR2, UR3 X, XSYMM U1, UR2, UR3 Y, YSYMM UR1, U2, UR3 Z, ZSYMM UR1, UR2, U3

Duplicated directions are removed and the remaining directions are sorted before the modal properties are computed. At least one valid direction must be given. For example,

Text Only
recorder 1 hdf5 Modal U1
recorder 2 hdf5 Modal U1 U2 UR3
recorder 3 hdf5 Modal E

The recorder must be defined before the analyze command and it must be saved explicitly.

Text Only
step frequency 1 10
analyze

save recorder 1

peek recorder 1 prints a short description of the recorder. Note that every and object tags are not supported for this recorder; all remaining tokens are interpreted as DoF identifiers.

docs.title: Computed Quantities
docs.text:
For the generalised eigenproblem

\[ \mathbf{K}\mathbf{\phi}_n=\lambda_n\mathbf{M}\mathbf{\phi}_n, \]

define the mass-normalised mode shape

\[ \mathbf{\phi}_n^T\mathbf{M}\mathbf{\phi}_n=1. \]

The recorder computes the following quantities for mode $\(n\)$ and direction $\(j\)$.

quantity symbol definition natural frequency $\(f_n\)$ $\(f_n=\dfrac{\sqrt{\lambda_n}}{2\pi}\)$ mode shape $\(\mathbf{\phi}_n\)$ mass-normalised, $\(\mathbf{\phi}_n^T\mathbf{M}\mathbf{\phi}_n=1\)$ participation factor $\(\Gamma_{n,j}\)$ $\(\Gamma_{n,j}=\mathbf{\phi}_n^T\mathbf{M}\mathbf{r}_j\)$ effective modal mass $\(m_{n,j}\)$ $\(m_{n,j}=\Gamma_{n,j}^2\)$

In the above, $\(\mathbf{r}_j\)$ is the unit influence vector in direction $\(j\)$. For example, for U1, every active U1 DoF receives a unit entry and all other entries are zero.

Note

The frequency is stored in hertz. The eigenvalue can be recovered as $\(\lambda_n=(2\pi f_n)^2\)$.

The sign of a mode shape is arbitrary: an eigenvector can be multiplied by $\(-1\)$ without changing any physical result. Consequently, the sign of the corresponding participation factor is also arbitrary. The effective mass is not affected by the sign.

If the full set of modes is computed, the effective masses in a given direction sum to the total mass mobilised by the unit influence vector,

\[ \sum_n m_{n,j}=\mathbf{r}_j^T\mathbf{M}\mathbf{r}_j. \]

This identity is useful for checking that enough modes have been extracted.

Modes whose modal mass is numerically zero or negative (for example, spurious modes in a model with an inconsistent mass matrix) are not normalised.

docs.title: Output File
docs.text:
The recorder writes

Text Only
R<tag>-Modal.h5

to the current output folder. When the application runs with multiple MPI ranks, the file name is prefixed with the rank, for example

Text Only
P0-R1-Modal.h5

The output folder can be changed with the output_folder attribute before the save command.

docs.title: Data Layout
docs.text:
The HDF5 file contains the following objects.

Text Only
R1-Modal.h5
├── Frequency                       (n_mode, 1)
├── U1                              one group per requested direction
│   ├── ParticipationFactor         (n_mode, 1)
│   └── EffectiveMass               (n_mode, 1)
├── U2
│   ├── ParticipationFactor
│   └── EffectiveMass
├── Mode 1                          one group per mode
│   ├── N1                          (n_dof_node_1, 1)
│   ├── N2                          (n_dof_node_2, 1)
│   └── ...
├── Mode 2
│   └── ...
└── ...
  1. Frequency stores one natural frequency per row in hertz.
  2. Each requested direction has a group named after the canonical DoF identifier, for example U1, U2 or UR3. Numeric aliases such as 1 or 6 are accepted in the command, but the group always uses the canonical name. The group contains the participation factors and effective masses for all modes in that direction. Both datasets have one row per mode.
  3. Each mode has a group named Mode 1, Mode 2, etc. The group numbering follows the eigenvalue ordering, starting from one.
  4. For every active node, the mode group contains a dataset N<tag> with the nodal mode shape. Here <tag> is the node tag, not the node index. For example, node 10 produces N10.

The rows of N<tag> follow the node-local DoF order, that is, the order of the DoFs in the node's internal DoF list. Typical examples are:

node type local DoF order two-dimensional solid U1, U2 two-dimensional beam/shell U1, U2, UR3 three-dimensional solid U1, U2, U3 three-dimensional beam/shell U1, U2, U3, UR1, UR2, UR3

The dataset length is the total number of DoFs of that node, including constrained DoFs. Constrained components are present in N<tag> but are zero because the mode shape vanishes at a restrained DoF. For example, in a two-dimensional model every node stores two rows, [U1, U2]; the U1 component is row 0 and the U2 component is row 1. Note that Python uses zero-based indexing.

This layout means that all nodal mode-shape data are available without knowing the global equation numbering. It also means that the row order must be interpreted together with the element types that activate the node DoFs. If only a single translational direction is of interest, it is often convenient to use a model in which that direction is the first local DoF, as in the example below.

docs.title: Reading the Data
docs.text:
The following snippet reads all modal properties from a file written by recorder tag 1 for direction U1.

Python
import h5py
import numpy as np

with h5py.File("R1-Modal.h5", "r") as file:
    frequency = file["Frequency"][()].ravel()
    participation = file["U1/ParticipationFactor"][()].ravel()
    effective_mass = file["U1/EffectiveMass"][()].ravel()

    # node 2 contributes rows [U1, U2] in a two-dimensional model
    mode_shape = np.column_stack(
        [file[f"Mode {mode + 1}/N2"][()].ravel()[0] for mode in range(frequency.size)]
    )

For a two-dimensional model, N2[0] is the U1 mode-shape component of node 2 and N2[1] is the U2 component.

docs.title: Relation to the Other Modal Recorders
docs.text: The Eigen recorder writes the raw eigenvalues and eigenvectors to Eigenvalue.h5. The Modal recorder writes a separate file with the processed modal quantities. The ModalForce recorder writes the modal elastic forces, including the element force vectors. The recorders can be defined in the same analysis if the raw eigenvectors, modal properties and modal forces are all needed.

docs.title: Example
docs.text: A complete worked example, including post-processing, modal combination and validation against a response history analysis, is given in modal analysis of a shear building.

docs.title: Output Folder
docs.text:
By default, all recorders record files and store the data under the initial current working directory. The initial current working directory is the working directory where the main program is executed. Note that here initial is emphasized given the fact that users can use the pwd command to change the current working directory.

Internally, the output folder is managed by an independent path that is initialised to the current working directory when starting the program.

What if we want to manage the output folder separately to better organise the recorded data? It is possible to do so by using the output_folder attribute.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text:
OutputFolder
# check current output folder
peek output_folder

# change output folder
set output_folder (1)
# (1) string, absolute/relative path to the output folder

A few points to note:

  1. The program tries to create the given output folder if it does not exist. The creation itself may fail. In case of any failure, the output folder is not changed.
  2. The output folder can be either absolute or relative (to current output folder).
  3. A special token $pwd is available to set the output folder to the current working directory, which may have been changed manually.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
The following are some examples to demonstrate the usage of the output_folder attribute.

Bash
# on entering, pwd and output_folder are set to the current working directory
suanPan ~<> pwd
/home/theodore/Demo
suanPan ~<> peek output_folder
/home/theodore/Demo
suanPan ~<> pwd ..
# changing pwd does not affect output_folder
suanPan ~<> pwd
/home/theodore
suanPan ~<> peek output_folder
/home/theodore/Demo
# change output_folder, result-u folder will be created
suanPan ~<> set output_folder result-u
/home/theodore/Demo/result-u
# change to another folder, result-f folder will be created
suanPan ~<> set output_folder ../result-f
/home/theodore/Demo/result-f
suanPan ~<> peek output_folder 
/home/theodore/Demo/result-f
# change to pwd, which has been changed previously
suanPan ~<> set output_folder $pwd
/home/theodore
# change pwd and then set output_folder to pwd
suanPan ~<> pwd Demo
suanPan ~<> set output_folder $pwd
/home/theodore/Demo
# the following two folders are created by setting output_folder
suanPan ~<> terminal ls
result-f  result-u
suanPan ~<> exit

docs.title: Control Output Folder For Recorders
docs.text:
The output_folder attribute is a global attribute that will be accessed by recorders when the save command is invoked. This means it is possible to set different folders for different recorders prior to saving the data. The following is a simple example that shows how to store displacement and resistance data in different folders.

The example model is an elastic cantilever beam with a point load at the free end.

Text Only
node 1 0 0
node 2 1 0

material Elastic1D 1 10 1E-4
section Rectangle2D 1 12 1 1
element B21 1 1 2 1 6 1

fix 1 E 1
cload 1 0 10 2 2

plainrecorder 1 Node U 1 2
plainrecorder 2 Node RF 1 2

step static 1 1
set ini_step_size .1
set fixed_step_size true

analyze

# when saving, change the output folder to result-u for displacement recorder
set output_folder result-u
save recorder 1
# change the output folder to result-f for resistance recorder
set output_folder ../result-f
save recorder 2

exit

Now when it is executed, two folders are created under the current working directory. For brevity, the np flag is used to suppress the output to screen.

Text Only
$ tree
.
└── B21.sp

0 directories, 1 file
$ suanpan -np -f ./B21.sp 
$ tree
.
├── B21.sp
├── result-f
│         ├── R2-RF1.txt
│         └── R2-RF2.txt
└── result-u
    ├── R1-U1.txt
    └── R1-U2.txt

2 directories, 5 files

docs.title: Output Type
docs.text:
Currently, the available types of output variables are listed as follows.

Please note, in principle, it is possible to define any types on any recorders, but if the target recorder does not support the type, trivial/empty values will be returned. If a saving recorder does not create any files on the disk, it means that the output type is not available for the target object. For example, recording strain/stress E/S values of any nodes is not possible and will lead to no output.

The complete support list is still under development. In principle, basic types such as displacement/velocity/acceleration are available for nodes. For elemental response, generally stress/strain and their components are available. Certain elements only support some output types. Please feel free to open an issue if you need more information.
